The trip-cost guide works through the fee for a family and for overseas visitors: what a Yosemite trip costs.

GETTING AROUND

### The free shuttle, and the buses beyond the Valley

Once you are on the Valley floor, the Yosemite Valley shuttle is free: no ticket, no pass. Two routes run from 7 a.m. to 10 p.m. The Valleywide route stops at the lodges, food service, campgrounds and trailheads, and the Park Service says a bus arrives every 12 to 22 minutes. The East Valley route covers the campgrounds and trailheads at the east end, every 8 to 12 minutes. That is the bus for Happy Isles, the Mist Trail and the Pines campgrounds. Since YARTS sets down at the lodge, the village and Curry Village, all of them on the shuttle line, you can arrive by bus and never need anything else.

Beyond the Valley the choices narrow. The Mariposa Grove shuttle is free and runs from the Welcome Plaza near the South Entrance about every 15 minutes in season, which this year ends November 30 at the latest. In winter a free shuttle runs between the Valley and Badger Pass whenever the ski area is open, typically mid-December through March. The hikers' bus to Tuolumne Meadows and the Glacier Point tour are fee-based and summer only. For a trip that stays in the Valley, the free shuttle and a bike cover almost everything; the Valley parking guide explains why a driver ends up doing the same thing after parking once.

1 Yosemite Valley Lodge: YARTS stop, bike rental, EV chargers2 Yosemite Village: YARTS stop, bike rental, Bike Share, refillable propane3 Curry Village: YARTS stop, bike rental, refillable propane, EV chargersMap: National Park Service (public domain), cropped.

BY BIKE

### Twelve miles of path, and fifty free bikes

The Valley floor is flat, and the Park Service counts over 12 miles of paved bike paths on it, with a 15 mph speed limit. A bike reaches the meadows, the bridges and the trailheads faster than the shuttle on a busy afternoon, and it parks anywhere.

The Yosemite Bike Share is free. The Yosemite Conservancy and the Park Service launched it in 2018, and the Conservancy has since tripled the fleet. There are 50 bikes, usually available between June and October, with dates that vary each year. Download the LINKA GO app, create an account, and scan the QR code on the bike to unlock it. Rides last up to two hours, and you must start and end at a designated Bike Share hub; look for the blue bikes in the Yosemite Village area.

For a longer ride or a child's bike, the concessioner rents bikes at Yosemite Valley Lodge, Curry Village and Yosemite Village, roughly from early April to late October as conditions allow. A standard bike is $48 for a full day and $36.50 for a half day, and bikes with a child trailer are available.

A Valley bike path in October. Photo: Vulturesong / Wikimedia Commons (CC0)

- Helmets under 18.
Required by law for riders under 18. A rental comes with one.

- E-bikes are allowed.
With fully operable pedals and a motor under 750 watts, wherever a bicycle may go.

- No riding off the pavement.
No off-trail riding and no mountain biking. Bikes stay on paved paths and roads.

- Scooters stay on paths.
Electric scooters are allowed on the bike paths but not on park roads.

In the Mariposa Grove, bikes are allowed only on the grove road between the Welcome Plaza and the Grizzly Giant, when the road is open. Rules from the Park Service's biking page; Bike Share details from the Conservancy.

ZERO WASTE

### What goes in which bin

The first rule is the oldest one: bring less packaging into the park. Carry a refillable water bottle, decant snacks into reusable containers at home, and pack a bag for your own trash. Water bottle refill stations were among the first projects of the park's zero-landfill work, and there is one at The Depot, the Conservancy bookstore at the Mariposa Grove Welcome Plaza.

At Park Service sites (campgrounds, visitor centers, the museum, bus stops and day-use picnic areas) recycling is mixed: everything recyclable goes in one bin unless it is labeled otherwise. Some things never belong there. Styrofoam, bubble wrap, plastic bags and unlabeled plastic are not recyclable in the park's system. At the hotels and restaurants, bins are separated, and food scraps go in the organic waste cans. Organics matter here: a 2015 waste audit found 684.8 tons of organic material going to the landfill every year, 32 percent of the park's landfill waste.

In Yosemite, trash is also a bear problem. The Park Service's rule is to treat trash and recycling like food: keep it in your food locker or put it in a bear-proof bin, never on the picnic table. Improper food storage can bring a fine of up to $5,000, and the bear safety guide explains why a bear that learns a bin is an easy meal rarely unlearns it. Backpackers carry all food, trash and toiletries in a bear-resistant container and pack every bit of it out, the rule the wilderness permits guide covers in full.

The concessioner has done part of the work already. Yosemite Hospitality says it replaced single-use plastic bottles with glass or aluminum across its stores and restaurants in December 2023 and moved its grab-and-go food to compostable packaging. A refillable bottle still beats all of it.

A bear-resistant recycling bin in Upper Pines Campground. Photo: Mx. Granger / Wikimedia Commons (CC0)

The recycling bin

Some plastics, paper, cardboard, glass and metals. At Park Service sites, all in one bin.

The organics can

Food scraps, where the hotels and restaurants provide one.

Never in recycling

Styrofoam, bubble wrap, plastic bags, unlabeled plastic.

Never left out

Trash and recycling go in the food locker or a bear-proof bin.

A propane canister recycling bin in a Valley campground. Photo: Mx. Granger / Wikimedia Commons (CC0)

PROPANE AND FIRE

### Refill the canister, buy the firewood here

The one-pound green propane cylinder is the campground's signature piece of waste. Around 24,000 used cylinders are collected in the park's recycling areas every year, the Conservancy says, and an unknown number go in the trash. If you use one, put the empty in a canister recycling bin, never the trash.

Better, skip the disposable. Refillable canisters from Little Kamper are sold at the Village Store, the Curry Village Gift Shop, the Mountain Shop, the Wawona Store and the El Portal Market, and an empty can be exchanged for a full one at a lower price. It is the single easiest swap in this whole guide for anyone cooking at a campsite.

Firewood has a rule of its own. The park asks you not to bring firewood from more than 50 miles away, because it carries forest pests, and you can buy it at the stores near most campgrounds. Outside the Valley, below 9,600 feet, you may gather dead and down wood under six inches across, but not pine cones, needles or sequoia wood. The camping guide covers the rest of campground life, and the fire restrictions guide covers when fires are allowed at all.

IF YOU DRIVE

### Park once, fill the seats, plug in

A car is still the right tool for some trips: a family of four, where per-person bus fares add up against one vehicle pass; a dawn start before the first bus arrives; a trip that spreads from Glacier Point to Tuolumne. If you drive, drive less inside the park. Park once in the Valley and use the shuttle and the bike paths, fill every seat, and stay inside the park or close to it rather than commuting from a distant town each day.

An electric car has more options than most drivers expect. The Park Service lists chargers in Yosemite Valley, Wawona, El Portal and Tuolumne Meadows, all with J1772 connectors and all level 2. Among the Valley's chargers are 20 at Curry Village, 10 at the Yosemite Falls parking area, 8 at Yosemite Valley Lodge and 6 at The Ahwahnee; the Wawona Store has 24 and the El Portal Market 2. A level 2 charger is slow, so plug in where you plan to spend the day. The Conservancy is working with the Park Service on more chargers in the Valley and Wawona.

Level 2 chargers by location, from the Park Service's EV charging pages. Tuolumne Meadows also has chargers; the park had not published the count.

THE KIT

### Six things that keep a trip out of the bin

- A water bottle.
Fill it at a refill station. The stores sell drinks in glass and aluminum now; a bottle you own beats both.

- Containers and a cutlery set.
Decant snacks at home and carry a fork, so the takeout counter costs nothing but food.

- A bag for your own trash.
On the trail, everything you carry in, you carry out. At camp, it lives in the food locker.

- A refillable propane canister.
Sold at the Village Store, Curry Village, the Mountain Shop, Wawona and El Portal, and an empty trades for a full one at a lower price.

- Your entrance pass, on your phone.
Bought on Recreation.gov before you board, because the gate takes no cash.

- A light pack.
The bus takes any size of backpack, and the park has no luggage storage. Pack for the shuttle, not the trunk.

The packing checklists cover the rest of the gear for each season.

None of this is a sacrifice. The bus from Merced spares you the drive and the hunt for a parking space. On a busy afternoon a bike often beats the car across the Valley. The work behind the scenes, the bins and the compost and the zero-landfill effort that began in 2015 and that the Park Service, the concessioner and the Conservancy now run together, only works if visitors put things in the right place. That part is yours. For a first trip built around the shuttle line, start with the one or two day plan and leave the car at the station.

QUESTIONS

### Car-free and zero-waste Yosemite, answered

Can you get to Yosemite without a car?
Yes. Take Amtrak's Gold Runner to Merced and transfer to the YARTS bus on Highway 140, which runs year-round to Yosemite Valley and connects with the trains at the Merced Amtrak station. In summer YARTS also runs from Fresno, Sonora and Mammoth Lakes. Inside the Valley the shuttle is free, and there are about 12 miles of paved bike paths.
How much is the YARTS bus from Merced to Yosemite Valley?
YARTS lists $22 one way and $44 round trip for an adult between Merced and Yosemite Valley, with reduced fares of $11 and $22. Children 5 and under ride free, and one child aged 6 to 12 rides free with each paid adult. Booking online adds a small fee.
Does the YARTS fare include the Yosemite entrance fee?
The sources disagree. YARTS says gate and non-resident fees are not included in its ticket prices and can be paid to the Park Service on Recreation.gov, while Amtrak's Yosemite page says its tickets include admission. Plan to pay: the per-person pass is $20 for seven days, people 15 and under are free, and the park does not accept cash.
Is there a bike share in Yosemite?
Yes. The Yosemite Conservancy and the Park Service run a free Bike Share in Yosemite Valley with 50 bikes, usually available between June and October. You unlock a bike with the LINKA GO app, rides last up to two hours, and you must start and end at a Bike Share hub. For longer rides, the concessioner rents bikes at Yosemite Valley Lodge, Curry Village and Yosemite Village.
Does Yosemite recycle?
Yes. At Park Service sites recycling is mixed, so everything recyclable goes in one bin unless it is labeled otherwise. Styrofoam, bubble wrap, plastic bags and unlabeled plastic are not recyclable there. Treat trash and recycling like food: keep it in your food locker or use a bear-proof bin.
Can I recycle propane canisters in Yosemite?
Empty canisters go to the park's recycling areas, and around 24,000 are collected each year. A better answer is a refillable canister: the Village Store, Curry Village Gift Shop, Mountain Shop, Wawona Store and El Portal Market sell them, and you can exchange an empty for a full one at a lower price.
Are there EV chargers in Yosemite?
Yes. The park lists chargers in Yosemite Valley, Wawona, El Portal and Tuolumne Meadows, all with J1772 connectors. In the Valley they include Curry Village, Yosemite Falls parking, Yosemite Valley Lodge and The Ahwahnee.

## Yosemite in December: Snow, the Holidays, and the Quiet Weeks Between

URL: https://thetalusfieldjournal.com/articles/yosemite-in-december
Section: Seasonal Guides. Published: 2026-10-01. Last updated: 2026-10-01.
Summary: Yosemite in December: weather, closed roads, chain rules, Badger Pass and the rink, the holiday-week crowd, Curry Village's closure, and camping.

December in Yosemite is three different trips that happen to share a calendar page. The first two weeks are the emptiest stretch of the year that still has lodging open, with the high country shut and most of the ski-season machinery not yet running. The middle of the month is when the winter operations come on: the road to Badger Pass is plowed, the ski shuttle starts, and the Ahwahnee stages the Bracebridge Dinner. And the last week, from about December 23 into the New Year, is one of the busiest weeks of the winter, a holiday crowd arriving in a park that has short days, icy paths, and a fraction of its summer parking. Which December you book decides almost everything else about the trip, so start there.

What follows is the month as the park's own records describe it: the weather normals, the road-closing history, the campground windows, and the dates the concessioner publishes. The general case for the season, including the full chain-control explainer, Badger Pass, and Dewey Point, is in the winter guide. This piece is about what is specific to December.

### The weather, in numbers

The Park Service's normals for Yosemite Valley, at about 4,000 feet, give December an average high of 46°F and an average low of 28°F, with about 5.6 inches of precipitation. That makes December the coldest month of the year by its average high, two degrees below January, and the third wettest, behind January and February. The park says it receives 95 percent of its precipitation between October and May and more than 75 percent between November and March, so a December trip is a trip into the storm season, not the edge of it.

Whether that precipitation arrives as rain or snow on the Valley floor is a storm-by-storm question. The park's own phrasing is that the Valley "can be rainy or snowy in any given winter storm," and that is the honest forecast for any December date booked more than a week out. Up high there is no question: Tuolumne Meadows, at 8,600 feet, averages a December high of 40°F and a low of 12°F, and the park describes most of Yosemite as blanketed in snow from about November through May. Pack for both kinds of Valley day, freezing rain and dry cold, and assume the nights will be below freezing either way.

### What is open, and what the road record says

Yosemite Valley and Wawona are reachable by car all year, the park says, and they are the core of a December trip. Most of the rest is decided before the month starts, and the park's historical dataset of opening and closing dates makes the point plainly.

Tioga Road is closed. In the ten seasons from 2016 through 2025 it closed for the winter between October 21 and November 20 every year. The record holds exactly two exceptions worth knowing about, both dry winters: the park reopened the road from December 23, 1999, to January 1, 2000, and again from December 16, 2011, to January 17, 2012. Neither is a plan. If your December itinerary includes Olmsted Point, Tenaya Lake, or Tuolumne Meadows, take them out.

Glacier Point Road is closed past Badger Pass. In the same ten seasons it closed by late November in every year it opened but one (2021, when it held until December 7). From mid-December through early April, the park plows the first stretch of the road as far as the Badger Pass Ski Area, and no farther; the drive-up view from Glacier Point is not part of any December trip. The rim is still reachable on snowshoes or skis from Badger Pass, which is the winter guide's territory.

The Mariposa Grove is open, but on foot. The grove road closed on November 30 in each of the three seasons from 2023 through 2025, and the free shuttle from the Welcome Plaza near the South Entrance runs no later than November 30 in any year. In December you walk in: the park describes the Washburn Trail as a two-mile route to the grove with 500 feet of gain, and warns that it may be snowy or icy enough for skis or snowshoes. The full walk-in plan is in the Mariposa Grove guide.

### The first half of the month: quiet, with a gap in the rooms

The first two weeks of December are the quiet ones. Thanksgiving traffic has gone home, the holiday crowd has not arrived, and the concessioner's winter rates have started: its current offers at the Ahwahnee and Yosemite Valley Lodge run from November 29 on select dates. This is the stretch where a midweek Valley loop can feel close to empty.

Two things narrow it. The first is Curry Village, the cabin and tent-cabin village under Glacier Point. The concessioner's Curry Village page currently lists it as not open from November 29 through December 10, 2026, and its winter rate there starts December 13. If your plan depends on a Curry tent cabin, check that page for the closure window before you pick dates, because in the first ten days of December the in-park choice may be the Ahwahnee or Yosemite Valley Lodge and nothing in between. The second is that the winter recreation is not running yet. Badger Pass opens when it has snow to open on, and the plowed road and the ski shuttle start with it.

The trails, meanwhile, are often in better shape in early December than later. The park's record of seasonal trail closures shows the Four Mile Trail, the Valley's route up to Glacier Point, closing for the winter as early as November 11 (in 2022) and as late as January 7 (the 2023 season), and in seven of the eight seasons from 2018 through 2025 the closure came in December or later. The Mist Trail's winter closure has ranged across the same span in the seasons the record dates since 2018, from November 11 to January 7. In plain terms, an early-December visitor has a real chance of finding trails open that a late-December visitor will find gated, and no way of knowing in advance. Check the park's conditions page the week you go, and read the winter hiking guide for what stays open once the gates close.

### Mid-month: Badger Pass, the rink, and the Bracebridge Dinner

The park's transportation page says the free shuttle between the Valley and Badger Pass runs whenever the ski area's facilities are open, "typically mid-December through March," and the plowed road to Badger follows the same calendar. For a December visitor that means the ski area, the tubing hill, the snowshoe trails, and the ranger-led snowshoe walks described in the winter guide are mid-month-onward options at best, and only in a year with snow. The concessioner runs a Snow Phone at 209/372-1000 for conditions and ski area information; call it before you build a day around Badger.

The Curry Village ice rink, which the concessioner says has been operating since 1928, is the winter activity that needs no snow and no skill. Its published schedule runs three sessions a day, at noon, 3:30, and 7 p.m., with an extra 8:30 a.m. session on weekends and holidays, and tickets can be bought online in advance or at the Curry Village tour desk. The opening date for each season is set by the concessioner; as of this writing it lists the coming season's as to be determined, so confirm it before you promise a skate to anyone.

Mid-December also belongs to the Bracebridge Dinner, the Ahwahnee's four-hour Tudor dinner pageant, staged on a run of evenings before Christmas. The concessioner's current schedule lists performances on alternating nights from December 8 through December 22, and a ticket covers the dinner and the performance only; the room is a separate booking. What it is, what it costs, and whether it is worth building a trip around are all in the Bracebridge and Vintners' Holidays guide. The practical December note is simpler: on performance nights the Ahwahnee is busy, and its rooms on those dates go first.

Photo: Chris Dunstan / Wikimedia Commons (public domain)

### The holiday week

The Park Service says it directly on its winter page: Yosemite "may be very busy during winter holidays, especially in late December and early January, with traffic congestion and limited parking possible." The concessioner says the same thing in its own language. Every one of its current winter discounts, at the Ahwahnee, Yosemite Valley Lodge, and Curry Village, carries the same blackout window, December 23 through January 2. That is the hotel company telling you when it expects to sell out at full price.

Three things follow. First, holiday-week lodging in the Valley is a book-early problem in a season that otherwise rewards booking late; if the week between Christmas and New Year's is your only window, reserve the room before anything else. Second, the Valley's parking behaves more like a summer weekend than a winter weekday, so arrive early and use the free shuttle once you are parked; the parking guide covers which lots fill first. Third, the evenings have one marquee event: the Ahwahnee's New Year's Eve Dinner Dance, which the concessioner lists for December 31 from 8:30 p.m. to 12:30 a.m. Everything else on the holiday week is the same park as the rest of the month, with more people standing at Tunnel View.

There is no entrance reservation to plan around. The park dropped its timed-entry system for 2026, and entry is first come, first served on the standard pass, which is $35 for a private vehicle. Visitors who are not US residents should read the international visitors page first, because the park's fee page adds a $100 per-person fee for non-residents.

### Driving in: chains are the default

The park's guidance is to expect chain requirements from November through March, which makes December squarely chain season. The rule that catches visitors is not the mounting but the carrying: when a chain control is in effect inside the park, every vehicle must have chains in it, four-wheel drives and rentals included, whether or not the control level requires them on the tires. Under R1, a car under 6,000 pounds with snow tires on at least two drive wheels may go without mounting them; under R2, only a four-wheel or all-wheel drive vehicle with snow tires on all four wheels is exempt from mounting; under R3, everyone chains up. The park lists a citation of up to $5,000 for failing to put chains on when required. The drawn version of that grid is in the winter guide.

The road-conditions line inside the park is 209/372-0200, then 1, then 1, and it is the call to make the morning you drive in. Route choice matters in December: Highway 140 through the Merced River canyon is the lowest approach and the one most likely to take rain while the others take snow, and it is the one route YARTS buses run year-round, from Merced through Mariposa and El Portal. The entrance-by-entrance comparison is in the entrances guide.

### Where to sleep in December

In the park, the Ahwahnee and Yosemite Valley Lodge carry the month. Curry Village rejoins them once its early-December closure ends, and its heated canvas tent cabins are a real option in winter: the concessioner turns the heat on from the Tuesday after Labor Day to the Friday before Memorial Day, though the tents have no plumbing, so the bathroom is a walk on what may be an icy path. Housekeeping Camp is out of season (its current operating season ended October 12), and the Wawona Hotel is closed while the Park Service conducts a condition assessment of the complex, with no reopening date posted. The trade-offs among the remaining options are laid out in the lodging guide.

Camping in December is a small, specific list. Upper Pines is the only campground on reservations all year, and its December dates go on sale on the park's monthly calendar: arrivals from November 15 through December 14 open on July 15, and arrivals from December 15 through January 14 open on August 15, at 7 a.m. Pacific. By the time most people plan a December trip, Upper Pines has been on sale for months, and the honest route in is a cancellation. Camp 4, Wawona, and Hodgdon Meadow are first come, first served in winter. Sleeping in a vehicle anywhere outside a campsite you have registered for is not allowed. Plan on overnight lows below freezing and a tent that can take snow load.

Outside the park, the gateway towns on Highway 140 put you below the snow line most nights and on the year-round bus route, which is the strongest argument for Mariposa or El Portal in December. The town-by-town comparison is on the lodging board.

### A naturalist's December

The waterfalls are low going into the month. The park's description of the winter is that water levels tend to be low, but once some snow and rain have fallen, Yosemite Falls begins flowing again, though not at springtime levels. A wet December brings the falls back from the autumn stains; a dry one leaves them quiet until the new year. Either way the river is low and clear, and the Valley's sound is mostly the absence of crowds.

The trees are worth looking at differently in December. The park notes that California black oaks, the broad trees of the Valley meadows, are winter deciduous but tend to hold their dead leaves, which gives a heavy snowfall a large surface to load, and broadleaf trees do not shed snow the way conifers do. After a wet storm, listen for limbs giving way, and do not linger under an oak with snow on it. The bare crowns also show something the summer canopy hides. A century ago the naturalist Enid Michael wrote in the December 1923 Yosemite Nature Notes that it would be difficult to find any mature oak in Yosemite Valley without its crown of mistletoe, and that bluebirds, Townsend's solitaires, and waxwings eat the berries and plant the seed on the branches where they perch. The clumps are easiest to see now, against the winter sky.

The same bulletin, a year later, recorded a December visitor that confused residents: the varied thrush, a robin-shaped bird with an orange breast and a dark collar that the naturalists described moving singly or in small flocks through the snow-covered Valley, shy enough to vanish while you watch it. Old notes are not a census, and the winter birds of any one December depend on the year, but they are a good reminder of what a quiet month is for.

### How to build a December trip

Pick your third of the month first. If you want the park nearly to yourself and can live without Badger Pass, come in the first two weeks, midweek, and check the Curry Village closure before you choose a room. If skiing, snowshoeing, or the rink is the point, come after mid-month and confirm Badger is open before you drive up. If the holidays are the only time you have, book the room first, accept the crowd, and plan to be parked early.

Then plan the days around light and ice. These are the shortest days of the year, and the Valley's high walls take the sun off the floor earlier still, so plan the long walk for the middle of the day and keep the late afternoon for the rink, a drive to Tunnel View, or a fire. Carry traction cleats for the paved paths, chains for the car, and one unscheduled day for the storm that changes the plan.

Read the conditions page the morning of. Roads, trail closures, chain controls, and the ski area all change by the day in this month. The conditions page collects the park's live feeds and the phone numbers in one place. Come up 140, stay in or near the Valley, and let the weather pick between the snow day and the dry one.

#### December rooms depend on which week

Early December is one of the easiest times of the year to find a room in or near the Valley. The week from December 23 into the New Year is the opposite: the concessioner blacks out its winter rates for it, and the in-park rooms go first. A search on your dates shows quickly which December you are dealing with.

## A Wildfire in Yosemite During Your Trip: What Closes, What Stays Open, and What to Do With the Bookings

URL: https://thetalusfieldjournal.com/articles/wildfire-in-yosemite-during-your-trip
Section: Planning. Published: 2026-09-28. Last updated: 2026-10-03.
Summary: Wildfire in Yosemite during your trip: reading the closure list, smoke by area, closed roads, campsite and permit refunds, and when to keep, move or cancel.

The trip is two weeks out, or four days out, or it started yesterday, and there is a fire in the park. The news has a map with a red shape on it that looks alarmingly close to the word Yosemite. A friend has sent a photograph of an orange sky. The Park Service says the park is open. Those three things are all true at once, and none of them tells you what you actually need to know, which is whether the places you planned to go, the road you planned to drive and the bed you planned to sleep in are on the wrong side of a closure line. This is the article for that question. It is written in the fall of 2026, with the Dome Fire burning above Wawona, but it is about every fire, because fire is, in the park's own words, a natural and essential part of Yosemite, and the way a fire reaches a visitor's trip is much the same each time.

What follows: what "open" means in a Park Service fire notice, three recent fires and the three different shapes they gave a trip, where to read the situation and in what order, why the smoke and the closures are separate problems, what a closed road does to an itinerary, what happens to each kind of reservation, and how to decide between keeping the trip, reshaping it and moving it.

### "Open and operating normally" is a sentence with a list after it

The park's Dome Fire updates carry a version of the same line: Yosemite National Park is open and operating normally, with the following exceptions. Readers tend to hear the first half. The second half is the part that matters, because the exceptions are specific and named. On September 15, 2026, the morning the fire was reported at about 100 acres a quarter mile north of Chilnualna Falls, the exception was one trail: the Chilnualna Falls trail and the trails from the top of the falls toward Buena Vista and Crescent Lakes. By the September 21 update the list had grown to the Ostrander Lake Trail and every area and trail south of it, and the country east of Wawona Road from Chinquapin to Wawona. By the release of September 24 it included Glacier Point Road, closed, in the park's words, "due to reduced visibility from smoke and to safely allow firefighting operations."

So the first thing to do with any fire notice is to skip the reassurance and read the list. A closure is named by a trail, a road, or a pair of place names, and each name can be found on a map and compared with your plan. If nothing on your itinerary is on the list, the fire is, for the moment, a smoke question and a watching brief. If something is, you have a decision, and it is usually a smaller one than the red shape on the news map suggested.

The list also moves, in both directions and without much notice. Nine days separated a single closed trail from a closed road to the park's most visited overlook. The park's own line on when that road comes back is that it "will reopen when conditions allow," which is honest and not a date. Plan as though any closure on the list will still be there on your day, and treat a reopening as good luck rather than a schedule.

Photo: Josh Carter / Unsplash

### Three fires, three shapes

The recent record is the best guide to what a fire does to a visit, and it does not have one shape. It has at least three.

The long closure of one area: the Empire Fire, 2017. Lightning started it, and it was discovered on July 31, 2017, one mile east of the Badger Pass ski area and three quarters of a mile south of Glacier Point Road. The park fought it on three sides to protect Bridalveil Creek Campground, the ski area, the Yosemite West subdivision, Wawona Road and Glacier Point Road, and let the east flank burn toward the Illilouette basin, in the update's words "to continue to enhance forest resiliency in a fire adapted ecosystem." On September 12, six weeks after it was found, it stood at 6,000 acres and 55 percent containment, and Glacier Point Road was still closed "until further notice." For a visitor, that fire was one road and its trailheads, for most of a season, and a smoky morning now and then everywhere else.

The closure of the Valley itself: the Ferguson Fire, 2018. This is the case people remember, and it is the rare one. The Ferguson Fire, the same fire that closed Highway 140 below El Portal, forced the park's hand on July 25, 2018, when it closed Yosemite Valley to visitors. By July 31 the closure covered the Valley, Wawona Road, the Mariposa Grove, the Merced Grove, Hetch Hetchy and other areas, for what the park called "continued unhealthy smoke impacts and ongoing firefighting operations." Even then, Big Oak Flat Road to Crane Flat and the whole of the Tioga Road, with its trails, campgrounds and visitor services, stayed open. The Mariposa Grove reopened on August 13 and the Valley at 9 a.m. on August 14, with Wawona Road still closed between Wawona and the Valley for at least another week and "limited hours and limited visitor services" as the park came back. Twenty days without the Valley, in peak summer, and the high country open throughout.

The fire in the backcountry with a road on its edge: the Dome Fire, 2026. Reported September 15 above Wawona, it spread north and northeast into the footprint of the 2017 Empire Fire, where the park's updates describe crews holding the Bridalveil Creek and Ostrander Lake Trails as the primary contingency line. Cal Fire's incident page, which then listed the cause as under investigation, put it at 5,084 acres and 30 percent contained on the afternoon of September 27, with 781 personnel on it in the park's update of September 25. On September 30 the local press reported that the Forest Service has found the fire human-caused, sparked by an abandoned campfire; the federal incident page still lists the cause as undetermined. Wawona Road stayed open throughout, as did the Valley. What closed was a set of Wawona trails, the backcountry south of Ostrander, and Glacier Point Road.

The pattern across the three is the useful part. A fire in Yosemite usually takes an area, not the park: a road and its trailheads, a drainage and its trails. The whole-Valley closure of 2018 happened, and it could happen again, but it is the exception, and even that one left the Tioga Road open. Plan for the area, and keep the Valley-closure case in mind as the one that would genuinely end a trip.

### Where to read it, in order

There is no shortage of information during a fire in the park. The skill is reading it in the right order, from the source that decides to the ones that describe.

- The park's current conditions page (nps.gov/yose, Plan Your Visit, Current Conditions). This is the list. Road status, trail closures, which campgrounds are open and which are closed, and the fire restrictions in force. If a place is closed, it is on this page.
- The fire's own updates, published in the park's news releases, usually each morning during an active fire. They carry the size, the containment, the day's plan, the full closure list, and a smoke forecast by area. The park's fire news page links them.
- The incident page on InciWeb, the interagency incident site, and the public information map the park links from its updates. The map is where the closure lines are drawn against the roads and trails, which is the comparison you actually need to make.
- fire.airnow.gov for the air, monitor by monitor. This is a separate question from the closures, and the next section is about it.
- The park's phone line, 209/372-0200, for road status and anything the pages have not caught up with.

Social media and news coverage come last, and only as a prompt to check the first two. A news map shows the whole fire in red at a scale where the Valley and Wawona look like neighbors. They are about an hour apart by a winding road, and a fire above one can leave the other untouched. This site's Park Bulletin condenses the current closures on one page, and the conditions board carries the live entrance waits and lot counts, which will tell you on the day how the traffic is shifting around a closed road.

### The smoke is a different problem from the fire

A closure is a line on a map. Smoke has no line. It follows the drainages, settles in the low places overnight, and lifts as the day warms, and it reaches areas the fire itself never will. The Dome Fire's smoke forecasts show both halves of that. The update released September 24 expected periods of air unhealthy for sensitive groups in Wawona and Yosemite Valley in the morning, clearing in the afternoon, and good air in Tuolumne Meadows in the morning with unhealthy-for-sensitive-groups periods later in the day. The next morning's update forecast the same rating for Wawona, the Valley and Tuolumne Meadows, and good air at Hodgdon Meadow and in Mariposa.

Two lessons follow. First, the worst of the smoke in the lower park tends to be in the morning, so a smoky dawn is not a verdict on the day; check again at noon. Second, which part of the park has the clean air changes from day to day and is not always the high country. The rule of thumb that Tuolumne sits above the Valley's smoke is often right, and the smoke-season guide lays out when it is and the AQI thresholds for changing plans, but the Dome Fire's forecasts had Tuolumne under the same rating as the Valley on some days. Read the day's forecast and the monitors, not the rule.

Photo: Sideesh Balasubramani / Pexels

Smoke is also the part of a fire that falls unevenly on visitors. A healthy adult on a Valley walk on a sensitive-groups morning is making a different decision from a family with a small child, anyone with asthma or a heart condition, or anyone planning a long, hard climb, which is when a person breathes the most air. Those are the trips where the smoke forecast, and not the closure list, decides the day.

### What a closed road does to an itinerary

A road closure closes more than the road. Glacier Point Road is the clearest example, because it carries a string of trailheads and a campground as well as the point itself. The Glacier Point guide walks the road mile by mile: Badger Pass, the McGurk Meadow trailhead, the turn for Bridalveil Creek Campground, the shared Sentinel Dome and Taft Point trailhead, Washburn Point, and the point at the end, with the Ostrander Lake and Mono Meadow trailheads along the way. Close the road and every one of those is out of reach by car, along with the Glacier Point Tour, which drives the same pavement. If your plan had a Sentinel Dome sunset or a Taft Point walk in it, the closure takes it.

It does not take the view. During the Dome Fire the park said explicitly that the Four Mile Trail and the Panorama Trail, which reach Glacier Point from the Valley, would remain open to hikers. That is a real hike, not a substitute for a drive, and the Four Mile and Panorama piece has the climb and the day it takes. With the road closed there is no bus at the top to carry you back down, so either trail becomes an out-and-back from the Valley floor. For a fit party it is arguably the better way to see the place anyway. For a party that planned to drive up, the honest substitute is a different viewpoint: Tunnel View, on Wawona Road at the Valley's west end, and Olmsted Point, on the Tioga Road, are both roadside.

Trail closures work the same way at a smaller scale. A closed trail has a closed trailhead, and sometimes a closed parking area. In Wawona during the Dome Fire, the Chilnualna Falls trail was the one that went first. The rest of Wawona did not, and neither did the Mariposa Grove, which does not appear on the closure lists in the park's Dome Fire updates of that week. The comparison to make is always the same: your specific trailhead against the park's specific list.

### What happens to the reservations

This is the part most people are actually asking about, and the answer depends on who holds the booking and whether the park or you are the one who cancels it.

Campgrounds booked on Recreation.gov. The site's policy covers the case where the park closes a facility: "In the event of an emergency closure, the Recreation.gov team or facility manager will refund all fees and will attempt to notify you using the contact information within your Recreation.gov customer profile." Make sure that contact information is current. The harder case is the campground that stays open while you would rather not go. Then the standard cancellation terms apply: a $10 service fee withheld from any refund, and a cancellation the day before or the day of arrival also forfeits the first night's fee. During the Dome Fire the Wawona Campground stayed on the park's open list, and so did every Valley campground. A campground being near a fire does not make it closed, and it does not make its cancellation free.

Wilderness permits. The park's wilderness FAQ is plain that both the application fee and the reservation fee are non-refundable. What it does allow is a change: once a reservation is confirmed, you may adjust the entry date, the group size and the starting trailhead if space is available. If a fire closes your trailhead, a change of trailhead on the other side of the park is the move to try first, and the wilderness center staff can tell you what is open. The permit rules are in the wilderness permits guide; a closed trailhead only changes which one you enter from.

In-park lodging through Yosemite Hospitality. The concessioner's published policy asks for a deposit of the first night at booking and says cancellations or changes "must be received 7 days prior to reservation arrival date to be eligible for a refund." Its published policies page carries no separate clause for fire or park closures. If the park closes the area your room is in, call the reservations line and ask what they are offering; if it has not, the seven-day rule is the one on your confirmation, and it is worth knowing before the fire's next update rather than after.

Gateway-town rooms and rentals. Each has its own terms, and none of them is bound by what the park does. The useful question here is geographic: does the fire, or the smoke, or a closed road, change how you get from this bed to the places you are going? A Groveland room during a fire above Wawona is barely touched. A Wawona or Fish Camp room during the same fire is next to it, and whether that matters depends on the day's smoke and your plans, not the headline.

### Keep, reshape, move, or cancel

Four answers, and most fire weeks call for one of the first two.

Keep the trip as planned when nothing on your itinerary is on the closure list and your party is not sensitive to smoke. Check the conditions page the night before and the smoke forecast that morning, and go.

Reshape the days when one piece of the plan is behind a closure. This is the usual case. Swap the closed road for the open one: if Glacier Point is shut, the Tioga Road day is the obvious trade while that road is open, and the Tuolumne day guide is built for it. Move the long hikes to the afternoons if the smoke is a morning problem, or to the part of the park the day's forecast favors. Keep the Valley walks, which are short enough to take on a hazy morning and drop without regret.

Move the base when the smoke is settling on your bed every night, or a closure has cut your lodging off from the rest of your plan. The same question the Highway 140 closure guide asks applies here: which side of the line is your bed on? A fire in the southern park puts Groveland and the Big Oak Flat side at the far end of the drive from it, and the gateway-town comparison covers the trade-offs of each town. Whether a move is possible depends on your current booking's terms and on what is open on your dates on the other side,.

#### Checking the far side of the park

Groveland is the gateway on Highway 120, at the Big Oak Flat side of the park, on the far side of the Valley from Wawona. Whether a move makes sense depends on the day's smoke forecast and on what is open on your dates. Search before you cancel anything.

Where to stay: every option compared

Availability links are affiliate links. The recommendations do not change for them. Disclosure.

Cancel or postpone in three cases. When the park has closed the area that was the reason for the trip, and a substitute would not be the same trip. When the smoke forecast for your days is at levels your party should not be exercising in, and the smoke-season guide's thresholds give you the numbers. And when the park closes the Valley, as it did in 2018, because at that point every plan built around it has gone. Cancel with the terms in front of you: the Recreation.gov refund for an emergency closure is automatic, and a cancellation of your own is not.

### The fire restrictions come with the season, not the fire

One more thing changes during a fire, though the fire did not cause it. In the dry months the park sets fire restrictions, and in September 2026 they applied below 8,000 feet in addition to the park's normal fire rules. They govern campfires and stoves in campgrounds and the backcountry, they are in force whether or not a fire is burning, and a visitor planning a campfire on a fire week should expect them. The fire restrictions guide explains what the stages allow and how to check the one in force.

### The practical version

When there is a fire in Yosemite during your trip, read the park's closure list before you read anything else, and compare it name by name with your plan. Treat every closure as lasting through your dates and every reopening as a bonus. Check the smoke forecast by area on the morning of each day, remember that the morning is usually the worst of it in the lower park, and move the long hikes accordingly. Trade a closed road for an open one rather than a trip for no trip. Know your bookings' terms before the next update, not after: the park's emergency closures refund campsites in full, wilderness fees do not come back but trailheads can change, and a room's seven days are seven days. And keep the 2018 case in mind for what it is, the one of these three fires that closed the Valley, and a reminder that even then the Tioga Road stayed open.

## Yosemite in October 2026: A Fire, a Closed Road, and the Last Weeks of the High Country

URL: https://thetalusfieldjournal.com/articles/yosemite-in-october-2026
Section: Seasonal Guides. Published: 2026-09-25. Last updated: 2026-10-03.
Summary: Yosemite in October 2026: the Dome Fire and Glacier Point Road closure, Tioga Road's last weeks, Half Dome cable dates, Mist Trail closures, closing dates.

October is usually the easy month to write about: the crowds are gone, Tioga Road is still open, the oaks turn, and the only real question is whether the first storm comes early. October 2026 starts with a different question. A wildfire is burning northeast of Wawona, Glacier Point Road has been closed since the evening of September 23, and the mornings in the Valley have been smoky. The month is still worth the trip, with a different plan than last year's.

What follows is what is specific to this October: the fire and the road it closed, the high country's last weeks, the Half Dome dates, the Mist Trail's repair schedule, and the calendar of things that close. The fall guide covers what every October is like, the color, the animals and the weather, and none of that is repeated here.

### Glacier Point Road is closed, and the fire decides for how long

The Dome Fire was reported on the morning of September 15, about a quarter mile north of Chilnualna Falls, and on September 30 the local press reported that the Forest Service has found it human-caused, sparked by an abandoned campfire. The federal incident page still lists the cause as undetermined. By the evening of September 24 it had burned 4,133 acres at 16 percent containment. Two helicopter pilots were killed fighting it on September 20.

The park closed Glacier Point Road at 6 p.m. on September 23, for smoke that cut visibility along the road and to keep it clear for firefighting. It will reopen when conditions allow, and nobody has put a date on that. Until it does, Glacier Point, Sentinel Dome and Taft Point cannot be reached by car. The rest of the park is open and operating normally, Wawona Road and the Mariposa Grove included.

The trails around the fire are closed until further notice: the Chilnualna Falls trail and the trails above it toward Buena Vista and Crescent Lakes, and the Ostrander Lake Trail and every area and trail south of it, which takes in the country east of Wawona Road from Chinquapin to Wawona.

Glacier Point itself is still reachable on foot. The park has said the Four Mile Trail and the Panorama Trail stay open to hikers, which makes the point a hike from the Valley floor rather than a drive: 9.6 miles round trip and 3,200 feet on the Four Mile Trail, six to eight hours. What the closure takes away is the easy version of that day. The Glacier Point tour bus, which carries hikers up to walk down, runs on the closed road, and its season was always going to end on October 11. Confirm it is running before building a day around it. The Four Mile and Panorama guide covers both trails in full.

Even a quick reopening leaves a short window. Overnight parking on Glacier Point Road ends October 15, the gift shop at the point closes October 25, and the road closes for winter sometime in November. The last two seasons it closed on November 11 and November 12. If Glacier Point is the reason for the trip, keep the plan loose and check the road the week you go. The Glacier Point guide has the rest for when it opens again.

### Smoke settles in the mornings, not the afternoons

The pattern the fire has set runs against the usual advice to start early. Smoke settles overnight in Wawona and the Valley, and the incident's air-quality outlook has had both at unhealthy for sensitive groups in the morning, clearing in the afternoon. Tuolumne Meadows has run the other way, with good air in the morning and worse in the afternoon.

That suggests an order for the day, as long as the pattern holds: the high country early, the Valley later. Check fire.airnow.gov the morning you drive in rather than the night before, because a wind shift changes it overnight. Visiting during smoke season explains how to read the readings and what each band means for a hike.

The Mariposa Grove is open, and its free shuttle runs every 15 minutes from 8 a.m. to 5 p.m. through October 31, with the last bus down at 5:30. For sequoias farther from the fire, the two groves near Crane Flat are the better bet this month: the Tuolumne Grove, 2 miles round trip, and the Merced Grove, 3. Rangers lead a Tuolumne Grove walk on Monday, Wednesday and Thursday at 1 p.m. through November 1.

Photo: Darold Massaro / Wikimedia Commons (CC0)

### Tioga Road: open, on the weather's schedule

Tioga Road is open, and in most years it stays open through October. In the last ten years it closed for the season in November eight times. The two exceptions are worth knowing: October 21 in 2021 and October 31 in 2022. The park does not set the date; the first storm that puts snow on the pass does. When it closes, there is no way through the park to Highway 395.

The high country is at its emptiest now, and it has no services to speak of. The Tuolumne Meadows Visitor Center closes September 27, the store, grill and buses are already done for the year, and the wilderness center closes October 14. There has never been gas at Tuolumne. The Crane Flat store closes October 25, but its pumps stay open year-round, card only. From October 15 there is no overnight parking on Tioga Road. Of the campgrounds along the road, Porcupine Flat closes October 11 and Tamarack Flat and Crane Flat October 12.

Construction adds a few minutes. Monday through Thursday from 8 a.m. to 3:30 p.m., expect delays of about 10 minutes through Tuolumne Meadows and 15 minutes between Olmsted Point and Tioga Pass. The trail between the wilderness center and Lembert Dome is closed for construction, with an alternate signed.

Fill the tank below, carry lunch and warm layers, and call the road line before you set out: 209/372-0200, press 1 then 1. The Tuolumne day covers the drive, and Clouds Rest is the big hike to take off the road while it is still open.

### Half Dome: the last days of the cables

The park's rule is that the last day to use the cables is the day after the second Monday in October. This year that is Tuesday, October 13. The rule has some give in practice: in 2024 the cables came down on October 15, and in 2025 they stayed up until October 22. Plan on the 13th and treat anything after it as luck.

Every day the cables are up needs a permit, and in October a day hiker's only route to one is the daily lottery. Apply two days before the hike, between midnight and 4 p.m. Pacific, on Recreation.gov; results arrive late that night. It costs $10 per person, refunded if you cancel by 11:59 p.m. Pacific the day before or if the cables are not up. The days are short now, so start in the dark with a headlamp. The lottery page has the odds and the strategy, and the Half Dome guide covers the hike.

### The Mist Trail is still closed four days a week

The repair closures that ran through September continue through October, and the park says the schedule is subject to change. The Mist Trail from its junction with the John Muir Trail, above the Vernal Fall footbridge, to the top of Vernal Fall is closed Monday through Thursday, 7 a.m. to 3:30 p.m. It is open Friday through Sunday and on holidays, and normally Monday through Thursday from 3:30 p.m. to 7 a.m. when it is safe.

The signed detour runs up the John Muir Trail past Clark Point. On a weekday, either take that detour or plan Vernal and Nevada for the weekend. The Mist Trail guide has the hike and the detour in detail.

### What closes in October, by date

October is the month the park finishes packing up. The dates, from the current edition of the park's Yosemite Guide:

- October 11: the Glacier Point tour, hiker drop-off and Grand Tour end for the season.
- October 12: the Housekeeping Camp store closes; the laundry stays open. Base Camp Eatery at the Lodge closes at 8 p.m. from today.
- October 14: wilderness permit pickup ends at the Tuolumne Meadows Wilderness Center and at Wawona.
- October 15: no more overnight parking on Tioga or Glacier Point Roads.
- October 16: the Happy Isles Art & Nature Center closes, and its art classes and kids' open studio with it.
- October 18: the Valley Wilderness Center and Big Oak Flat permit pickup close. From October 19, overnight hikers self-register outside the Valley Welcome Center, on the Big Oak Flat porch, or at the Hetch Hetchy entrance kiosk, and rental bear canisters are only at the Valley Welcome Center.
- October 25: bike rentals, the Village Grill, the Mountaineering School, the Glacier Point gift shop, the Crane Flat store and the Wawona golf course close.
- October 26: the Mountain Room Restaurant closes at 9 p.m. and the Pizza Deck runs noon to 9.
- October 31: the Wawona Visitor Center closes, and the Mist Trail's weekday closures are scheduled to end. The free bike share ends in late October, conditions allowing.

The Valley keeps its food, beds and free shuttles through all of it, and the shuttles run 7 a.m. to 10 p.m. daily year-round. Where to eat covers what stays open, and the Park Bulletin carries the full edition, hours included.

### Camping: reservations, then fewer campgrounds

Every campground open in October requires a reservation for at least part of the month. In the Valley, Lower Pines closes October 19 and North Pines October 26; Upper Pines is open all year and reservation-only. Camp 4 takes reservations one week ahead through November 29. Outside the Valley, Hodgdon Meadow and Wawona's loops B and C take reservations through October 26, and Wawona's Loop A through November 29. Sleeping in a vehicle is legal only in a campsite you are registered for.

The camping guide explains how the reservation windows work and what to do when the campground you wanted is full.

### The Valley in October

There is no entrance reservation this year. The park dropped the timed system for 2026, which is covered in Yosemite without reservations. Visitors from outside the United States pay the non-resident fee introduced this year, $100 per person 16 and older on top of the entrance pass, and the international visitor page works out the cheapest way through the gate.

October is the quietest good month of the year. The crowd forecast puts October weekday pressure at 46 on a scale where a July weekend is 100, and October weekends at 68. Midweek needs no entrance strategy at all. On a weekend, be in before mid-morning, when the Valley lots can still fill.

Two things in the Valley are different this year. The El Capitan Bridge is under repair through December, with 15-minute delays Monday through Friday from 7 a.m. to 7 p.m.; shuttle stop 9 at El Capitan Meadow is closed, and the footpath over the bridge is shut on weekdays, which splits the Valley Loop Trail into two out-and-backs on a weekday. And the waterfalls are what they always are in October: Yosemite Fall is dry, Mirror Lake is a meadow, and Bridalveil runs low. Come for the walls and the oaks, not the water.

Photo: Sideesh Balasubramani / Pexels

### Weather: warm days, cold nights, and the first storms

The park's averages for October put the Valley at a high of 71 and a low of 41, with 1.6 inches of precipitation for the month. Tuolumne Meadows averages 57 and 26, with 1.8 inches. That is a 30-degree swing in the Valley and a hard frost at Tuolumne most nights. Pack for both ends of the day.

Storms are possible from late October. Chain restrictions are most common from November to March, but when one is in effect every vehicle must carry chains, four-wheel drive and rentals included, so carry them for any trip in the last part of the month. The days are shortening fast. A headlamp belongs in every pack, and a hike that would finish at dusk in September finishes in the dark now.

Fire restrictions are still in force: fires only in portable stoves, grills and established rings, never unattended, and out cold before you walk away. The Forest Service, as reported on September 30, has traced the Dome Fire to an abandoned campfire. The fire restrictions piece explains the rules and how to check the current stage.

### What is on, with dates

The dated events this month are small, and most are free.

- Peace of Place, photographs by Alan Ross, John Sexton, Anne Larsen, Roman Loranc, Bob Kolbrener and Jeffrey Conley at The Ansel Adams Gallery, runs through November 7, free to walk through. The artist reception is October 10, 1 to 3 p.m. The gallery opens at 10 a.m. from October 1.
- Stewardship Series: Little Fires Everywhere, a Yosemite Conservancy program on fire ecology, October 23, 2 to 4 p.m. Registration is required at Yosemite.org. The timing needs no comment.
- Yosemite Shorts and Stories, 45 minutes of short films, talks and performances by park staff, at 4:30 p.m. in the auditorium behind the Exploration Center on October 5, 6, 7, 12, 13, 16, 17, 23, 26, 27, 28 and 30.
- Hodgdon Meadow evening program, 6:30 p.m. on October 16, 17, 23 and 24. The Crane Flat campground program ends October 9.
- Ask-a-Climber, spotting scopes on El Capitan at El Capitan Meadow, daily from 12:30 to 4:30 p.m. through October 30. Watching climbers on El Capitan explains what you are looking at.

Ranger walks from the Welcome Center and the Valley Lodge run through October 30, and the ranger programs guide explains how to find the rest. The schedule changes, and the park posts additions to its online calendar.

### How to plan October 2026

Build the trip around the parts the fire does not touch: the Valley midweek, Tioga Road while it lasts, and the Crane Flat sequoias. Hold Glacier Point as a maybe. If the road reopens, it is a bonus; if it does not, walk up the Four Mile Trail and see the same view with more earned. Check the air each morning and the road status before any drive to the high country.

The first half of the month holds the most: Half Dome through the 13th, the Glacier Point bus through the 11th if it runs, overnight parking on the high roads through the 14th, and the last staffed permit desks through the 18th. The second half is quieter and colder, with Tioga Road open until the first storm says otherwise. The Planning Guide has the rest of the trip, and the conditions board has the live gate waits the week you go.

## The Yosemite Falls Trail: Columbia Rock, the Top, and the Loop at the Bottom

URL: https://thetalusfieldjournal.com/articles/yosemite-falls-trail
Section: Trails and Hikes. Published: 2026-09-24. Last updated: 2026-09-24.
Summary: The Yosemite Falls Trail and the Lower Yosemite Fall loop: Park Service distances, Columbia Rock, the top, water, parking, shuttle stops, and each season.

Two different walks go by the name Yosemite Falls, and people pick the wrong one in both directions. One is a paved mile at the bottom of the waterfall that takes half an hour and asks nothing of you. The other is a trail built in the 1870s that climbs 2,700 feet up the north wall of the Valley, in the sun, on loose granite, with no water anywhere on it. It is easy to start up the second in sandals because the sign said Yosemite Falls, and easy for a strong hiker to skip the first because it looks like a sidewalk. This is both of them, in the order most people meet them, with the numbers the Park Service publishes and the sensible turnaround point on the big one.

### One waterfall in three pieces

Yosemite Falls drops 2,425 feet from the rim to the Valley floor, one of the tallest waterfalls in the world, but it does not do it in one leap. The Park Service breaks it into three: Upper Yosemite Fall at 1,430 feet, the middle cascades at 675 feet, and Lower Yosemite Fall at 320 feet. From Yosemite Village and the lodge you see the whole stack at once, which is why it reads as a single fall in every photograph. On foot it separates again. The paved loop takes you to the bottom of the last 320 feet. The trail climbs beside the first 1,430 and puts you on the rim above it.

Watch the film: Yosemite FallsYosemite Nature Notes · Episode 2Yosemite FallsThe Park Service's own short film on the fall: three tiers, one creek, and a flow that runs on snowmelt and runs out.Film: National Park Service. Nothing loads from YouTube until you press play.

The other thing to know before choosing is that the water is seasonal, and more seasonal than most visitors expect. The Park Service gives the fall's flow as approximately November through July, with the peak in May, and it says plainly that Yosemite Falls is often a trickle or completely dry by August. The lower fall is often dry from late July or August through October. The storms of late fall bring it back. The waterfall guide covers the calendar for every fall in the Valley; for this one, the short version is that a spring hike and an August hike are two different trips, and only one of them ends at a waterfall.

Photo: Micah Bochart / Wikimedia Commons (public domain)

### The Lower Yosemite Fall loop: the one everyone should walk

The Park Service's figures for the Lower Yosemite Fall Trail are a one-mile loop, about 50 feet of elevation gain, easy, 30 minutes. It is paved throughout and open all year, and it is the short walk that shows you the whole of Yosemite Falls, upper and lower, before ending at a wooden footbridge across Yosemite Creek at the base of the lower fall. In spring and early summer, when the fall peaks, the Park Service's own description is that you can expect to get sprayed standing on that bridge. Exhibits along the loop cover the natural and cultural history of the area.

Three details make it a better walk. First, walk it clockwise, which is the Park Service's recommendation for the best views; starting on the western side puts the full height of the fall in front of you from the first steps. Second, the accessible half is the eastern one: the Park Service describes the eastern portion, from the shuttle stop to the base of the fall, as wheelchair accessible when it is not covered in ice or snow, so a visitor using a chair goes out and back on that side rather than around the loop. Third, the restrooms and the one drinking fountain are on the western side, near the start; there is nothing else along the way.

There is no parking at the trailhead. The Park Service sends drivers to the Yosemite Village or Yosemite Falls parking areas, and it sends everyone else to the free Valleywide shuttle, which runs from 7 am to 10 pm, to stop #6; from there the bike path leads to either side of the loop. You can also walk the bike path from the Valley Visitor Center, which adds about half a mile. The shuttle guide has the routes and the frequencies, and the practical advice is the same as for most of the Valley: park once in the morning and ride.

One rule matters here. Stay on the paved trail. Above the footbridge the creek bed is a jumble of boulders that look like an invitation to scramble closer, and the Park Service is direct about them: the rocks are slippery even when dry, and scrambling off-trail there has led to serious injuries. In winter, expect ice in places, especially on the short climb to the footbridge on the western side.

Photo: James St. John / Wikimedia Commons (CC BY 2.0)

### The Yosemite Falls Trail: what the numbers mean

The big trail is one of Yosemite's oldest, built between 1873 and 1877, and it starts somewhere most people would not guess: near Camp 4, on the Valley Loop Trail. It climbs immediately, switchback after switchback, first through oak woodland and then onto open, exposed benches with the Valley falling away below. The Park Service publishes two sets of numbers for it, because it is really two hikes:

- Columbia Rock: 2 miles round trip, 1,000 feet of elevation gain, moderate, 2 to 3 hours.
- Top of Yosemite Falls: 7.2 miles round trip, 2,700 feet of elevation gain, strenuous, 6 to 8 hours.

Read the second line carefully. Seven miles sounds like an easy day to anyone who hikes at home, and it is the gain that decides it: 2,700 feet in 3.6 miles averages 750 feet of climbing per mile, and it comes with no shade on the upper half and nothing to drink. The time estimate is for a fit hiker moving steadily. A family that turns a 2,000-foot day into an afternoon at home should plan on the long end of the range, or on Columbia Rock.

The climb, from the Park Service figures quoted in this article: straight lines between the published points, not a surveyed profile. Most of the effort that decides the day comes after Columbia Rock.

The trail is not the only hard climb out of the Valley. The Mist Trail to Vernal and Nevada Falls carries its own crowd and its own wet granite staircase; the Mist Trail guide covers that one. The Yosemite Falls Trail has fewer people above Columbia Rock, a much bigger climb, and more sun. Which of the two to pick on a given day usually comes down to the heat.

### Columbia Rock: the honest turnaround

The first mile is the one to plan around. The Park Service describes it as a one-mile, 1,000-foot climb via dozens of switchbacks to Columbia Rock, an overlook with the Valley floor below and Half Dome and Sentinel Rock across it. It is a real climb, short enough for most healthy visitors who take it slowly, and the Park Service calls it a worthwhile trip at any time of year.

Past Columbia Rock, the Park Service suggests going on another half mile, some of it downhill, to a view of Upper Yosemite Fall itself. This is the best value on the trail: the Park Service calls it a stunning view of the upper fall, and in spring, depending on the flow, you may feel its mist. For most visitors, that viewpoint is the right place to turn around: about three miles round trip, the Valley view and the upper fall both, and none of the upper half. Remember that the downhill stretch out is uphill on the way back.

Above that point the trail changes. The Park Service calls the upper half steep and rocky, and it is the harder half. If the first mile was hard work, the next two are harder, and there is no shame in taking the viewpoint as the destination.

### Above Columbia Rock: the upper half

Three things make the upper switchbacks hard. The first is exposure to the sun: the Park Service notes that the upper portion receives no shade until late afternoon or early evening, which on a summer morning or midday means the whole climb is in direct sun. The second is the footing. There are long stretches of loose sand over rock, and the Park Service lists sprained ankles and knee injuries as common here. The third is the length of the climb, which keeps going well after it feels like it should have stopped.

The heat is the part to respect most. The Park Service's own advice is to start as early as possible, to drink plenty and often, to rest in the shade where there is any, and to eat salty snacks, and it tells hikers going to the top to carry 4 quarts or liters of water per person, because there is none on the trail. The heat safety guide treats this trail as one of the park's two big summer heat traps, for exactly this reason. In July and August, the sensible start is at first light, and the sensible plan has a turnaround time.

The Park Service also asks hikers to know their limits, and it is specific that pre-existing medical conditions can be easily exacerbated on the steep ascent. That matters if anyone in your group has a heart or breathing condition, because the trail offers no easy way out once you are high on the wall.

### The top, and the two ways to keep going

The top of the trail is a surprise. After the size of the waterfall from below, Yosemite Creek above the lip is small, the Park Service notes, a mountain stream running over granite toward an edge you cannot quite see. That is why it is dangerous. The Park Service asks hikers to use extreme caution near the creek, to remember they are directly above a waterfall, and not to swim or wade in the creek above the fall. The water that looks gentle here goes over a 1,430-foot drop a short distance downstream.

From the top, two extensions are signed. East to Yosemite Point, following signs for North Dome, adds 1.6 miles round trip; the Park Service describes its views of Half Dome as rivaling those from the North Dome trail, with Lost Arrow Spire up close. West to Eagle Peak, following signs for El Capitan, adds 5.8 miles round trip, to the highest point on the north rim of Yosemite Valley. Yosemite Point is the one worth planning for if you have the legs and the water; Eagle Peak turns a hard day into a very long one.

Sleeping on the rim is a different trip. A wilderness permit is required for any overnight stay in the Yosemite Wilderness, and the Park Service is explicit that no permit is needed for a day hike on this trail (the one day-hike exception in the park is Half Dome). If you want the rim at dusk, you are either walking down in the dark with a headlamp or applying for a permit.

### The trail by season

The Park Service lists the Yosemite Falls Trail as open all year, with conditions that change completely from one season to the next.

Spring is the trail at its best. The fall is at its peak, and on one section of the climb you may get wet from its spray. It is also the season with the most people on it. Start early for parking and for the cooler air.

Summer is hot and dry. The Park Service warns that the loose decomposed granite gets slippery, and by August the fall may be only a trickle. The Valley and Columbia Rock views are still there, so a summer hike is for the view and the climb. Start at first light or not at all.

Fall is the dry season for the waterfall and a cooler season for the climb, which makes it the kinder time to try the top if the summer heat is what put you off. Check the Yosemite Falls webcam first if the water matters to you: a dark stain on the cliff is what most fall visitors will find, until the late-fall storms.

Winter splits the trail in two. The lower portion faces south and takes direct sun, so it is often snow-free while other trails are icy; the Park Service calls Columbia Rock worthwhile at any time of year, and the winter hikes guide ranks this trail as the season's most reliable ascent for that reason. The upper portion is the opposite. It receives little or no sun in winter and can be very icy, or buried under feet of snow, and the Park Service warns that early mornings and late afternoons, when the ice is hardest, are the most dangerous times to be on it. Columbia Rock is a winter hike. The top usually is not.

### The ice cone, from the archive

Winter gives the upper fall one thing no other season does. The Park Service tells visitors to look for the ice cone at the base of the upper fall, a mound of ice built at the foot of the 1,430-foot drop. The park's own naturalists measured it in the 1930s. In the May 1935 Yosemite Nature Notes, Park Naturalist C. A. Harwell described a March expedition with a clinometer, compass, and tape, drenched by wind-blown spray, that put that year's cone at an estimated 220 feet high and 500 feet across, some six million cubic feet of ice by his arithmetic. He explained how it forms: frozen spray builds a white fan up the cliff on cold nights, the morning sun breaks it loose, and it crashes into the basin at the foot of the fall, where some of the falling water freezes on top of it. You can read Harwell's account in the Nature Notes archive, and an earlier trip to the cone, with the mountaineer Norman Clyde, in the May 1932 issue. They reached it with an ice axe and a rope; Beatty's 1932 account notes that the cone can be plainly seen from the south side of the Valley, which is where most people have watched it since.

### The practical details

- Trailhead: on the Valley Loop Trail near Camp 4. Ride the Valleywide shuttle to stop #7 and walk directly across the street to Camp 4, then follow the trailhead signs.
- Parking: the Camp 4 lot is for campers only. Day hikers use the Yosemite Falls parking area across the street, just beyond the Camp 4 entrance.
- Water: a drinking fountain near the trailhead in Camp 4, and nothing on the trail. Carry 4 quarts or liters per person for the top.
- Restrooms: in Camp 4, near the trailhead. None on the trail.
- Not allowed: pets, bicycles, and strollers, anywhere on the Yosemite Falls Trail. Do not cut the switchbacks; it erodes the trail and causes injuries.
- Food: keep it within arm's reach at all times, pack out every peel and shell, and do not feed the wildlife.
- Camping nearby: Camp 4 itself is the nearest campground. From mid-April into late fall its sites go by reservation on Recreation.gov a week before arrival, at $10 per person per night, and from late fall to spring it is first-come, first-served and can fill early on fine mornings.

### Which one is yours

If you have one morning in the Valley, walk the lower loop clockwise and stand on the footbridge. If you have a morning and some energy, climb to Columbia Rock and go on the extra half mile to the upper fall view, then come back down for lunch; it is the best short climb in the Valley and the one most visitors should do. If you have a full day, 4 liters of water, a first-light start, and legs that have climbed 2,700 feet before, go to the top and add Yosemite Point. And if it is August, the water will not be there and the sun will, so start early or take the view from Columbia Rock and save the top for the cool months.

Check conditions before you go, especially for ice in winter and for heat in summer. Then start early.
