## Cell Service in Yosemite: What Works Where, Carrier by Carrier, and How to Plan for None

URL: https://thetalusfieldjournal.com/articles/cell-service-in-yosemite
Section: Planning. Published: 2026-09-21. Last updated: 2026-09-21.
Summary: Yosemite cell service by carrier and place, per the Park Service: the Valley's east end works, Tioga Road does not. Where the Wi-Fi is, and the offline kit.

The map goes grey somewhere past the last gateway town, the blue dot stops moving, and the group text about where to meet for lunch never sends. Later, at a trailhead on Tioga Road, somebody wants to check the smoke forecast, or the Half Dome lottery result that was supposed to arrive last night, and the phone in their hand is a camera with a flashlight. It surprises almost everyone the first time, because the question "is there cell service in Yosemite" gets a shrug on most websites and a marketing line from the rest. The Park Service publishes a carrier-by-carrier coverage table, and it is more specific than the shrug. This is that table in plain language, with the places you can find Wi-Fi, the handful of things on a trip that need a signal, and how to set up a phone so that it is useful with no bars at all.

### The short answer

There is usable service on the three national carriers in the east end of Yosemite Valley, and very little anywhere else. That east end is the developed part of the Valley: Yosemite Village and the visitor center, the Ahwahnee, Curry Village, the Pines campgrounds. Outside it, coverage is a list of specific spots that depends on which carrier you pay, and the list is short. The park's own summary, on its Frequently Asked Questions page, is the sentence to plan around: "Cell service is available with some carriers in some areas, but is limited. Do not expect to have reliable service around the park."

Two consequences follow. First, anything that has to happen on a phone (a lottery result, a reservation confirmation, a route, a forecast) should be done or downloaded before the signal drops, which on every road in is well before the entrance station. Second, the plan for an emergency cannot be "we will call": the park says call or text 911, and the honest reading of the coverage table is that on most trails and all of the high country, neither will connect.

### The Park Service's coverage table, carrier by carrier

The National Park Service keeps an Internet Access and Cell Service page for Yosemite that lists coverage by carrier and location. Its last stated update was April 16, 2024, so treat it as the park's best description rather than a live map, and expect the real signal to be a little worse than the list on a crowded weekend. What it says, condensed:

- AT&T: voice and 4G LTE data in Yosemite Valley and at Glacier Point, "primarily in eastern Yosemite Valley," with FirstNet. At Tuolumne Meadows, "no cell service."
- T-Mobile: 4G LTE and voice in Yosemite Valley, "primarily in eastern Yosemite Valley." That is the whole entry.
- Verizon: the longest list. 4G LTE and voice in Yosemite Valley (again, primarily the east end), Foresta and Wawona; 4G and voice at Crane Flat; 4G LTE data and voice in El Portal, marked "limited and unreliable coverage"; and at Tuolumne Meadows, "cell service is not reliable. 4G LTE may be available."

Read the gaps as carefully as the entries. Tioga Road between Crane Flat and Tuolumne Meadows does not appear for any carrier. Neither does Hetch Hetchy, the Mariposa Grove, Glacier Point Road below the point itself, or any trail. Absence from the table is not proof of silence, but it is the park telling you not to count on anything there, and it matches what the high road is like in practice: essentially dead from Crane Flat to Lee Vining, which the park's own Tuolumne note confirms by naming Lee Vining, outside the park, as "the nearest reliable cell and traditional phone service." The same note adds that pay phones at Tuolumne "may not be available," so the old fallback is not one to plan on either.

One discrepancy is worth knowing about, because you will meet it. The park concessioner's travel-tips page says signals are "typically strongest in Yosemite Valley near the Visitor Center, Tuolumne Meadows, Crane Flat, and El Portal." On the Valley, Crane Flat and El Portal, that agrees with the Park Service, carrier permitting. On Tuolumne Meadows, it does not: the Park Service lists no service there for AT&T and unreliable service for Verizon. When the two disagree, plan on the Park Service's version, which is the pessimistic one, and be pleased if a bar appears at the store.

Photo: Pacific Southwest Region USFWS / Wikimedia Commons (public domain)

### Where the signal drops on the way in

Every approach loses service before the gate. The entrances guide puts it as a rule rather than a warning: cell service dies well before the park boundary on every road in. On Highway 140, Mariposa is the last town, and El Portal's "limited and unreliable" Verizon coverage is the last flicker before Arch Rock. On Highway 41, Oakhurst is the last town, then nothing through the South Entrance until the Wawona pocket, which the table lists for Verizon only. On Highway 120 from the west, Groveland is the last town, and after the Big Oak Flat entrance there is Crane Flat for Verizon and nothing else until the Valley. From the east over Tioga Pass, Lee Vining is the last signal for the entire length of the road.

The practical translation is a rule about the last town: whatever needs a network, do it in the last town. Send the meeting plan, screenshot the reservation, load the route, refresh the forecast. A room in one of the gateway towns is the last reliable Wi-Fi you will see; inside the park you will be back on a network only in the few places listed next.

### Wi-Fi: who gets it, and where

The Park Service lists three kinds of internet access inside the park, and none of them is a hotspot you can lean on for real work.

- Hotel guests. Internet access is available to registered overnight guests at the Ahwahnee, Yosemite Valley Lodge and Curry Village. The concessioner adds the caveat that matters: bandwidth "is limited to light use, such as checking email." Do not plan to join a video call from a Curry Village tent cabin. The park's page also lists the Wawona Hotel, which has been closed since December 2024 for a structural assessment; the in-park lodging guide has the current state of every property.
- The two county libraries. Mariposa County runs small branches in Yosemite Valley and in Wawona, with public computers and Wi-Fi. The catch is the hours. The county's own listing has the Yosemite branch, on Village Drive in Yosemite Village, open Tuesday and Wednesday from 11 am to 6 pm, and the Wawona branch open three days a week outside summer and Monday through Saturday between Memorial Day and Labor Day. Small-branch hours change; check the county page before you drive to one.
- Degnan's Kitchen in Yosemite Village and El Portal Market, outside the Arch Rock entrance, where the park says free Wi-Fi is available. Degnan's is the one public network in the Valley that depends on neither a room key nor a library schedule, and it sits inside the east-end pocket where the carriers work anyway.

Nothing on that list is in the high country, at Glacier Point, in the Mariposa Grove, or at Hetch Hetchy, and the Tuolumne Meadows Lodge and White Wolf are not on the park's internet list at all. If a trip depends on being reachable, it is a Valley trip in a hotel, and even then the honest expectation is email.

Photo: Rennett Stowe / Wikimedia Commons (CC BY 2.0)

### The five things on a Yosemite trip that actually need a signal

Most of a visit needs no network. The visitors who are miserable about coverage are usually the ones who did not sort out these five before the last town.

1. The Half Dome daily lottery. The permit is required seven days a week whenever the cables are up, and the daily lottery runs on a two-day clock: you apply two days before your hiking date, between midnight and 4 pm Pacific, and the park says results go out "late that night." To hike Saturday you apply Thursday and learn Thursday night. If Thursday night finds you at a campsite in Tuolumne Meadows or on the west end of the Valley, the email that tells you whether you are hiking will not arrive until you are somewhere with service. Apply from the last town or from the east end of the Valley, and be in the same kind of place when the result is due. The Half Dome piece covers the permit system in full, including why Clouds Rest needs none of this.

2. The entrance pass and every confirmation. The park does not take cash at the gate; it takes cards and mobile payment, and a digital America the Beautiful pass bought on recreation.gov "can be saved to a mobile device and used immediately." Saved is the word. A pass that lives in an email you have to open at the kiosk is a pass you cannot show at Arch Rock. The same goes for the campground reservation, the lodging confirmation, the wilderness-permit reservation and the YARTS ticket: screenshot each one, or save it to the phone's wallet or files, in the last town. The wilderness centers, where a reserved permit is actually issued, keep 8 am to 5 pm hours, and the ranger at the desk wants to see the reservation, not watch you try to load it.

3. Driving directions. The park's FAQ warns that "GPS units often provide incorrect driving directions in and around Yosemite" and tells you to use its own written directions instead. The failure has two halves: a routing app that loses the network can keep navigating only if the map is already on the phone, and even then it may route you onto a road that is closed for the season. Download the offline map area for the whole park and the gateway corridor before you leave home, and decide which entrance to use before you leave rather than letting the phone pick.

4. Conditions, smoke and traffic. The things you would like to check from inside the park are exactly the things that need a network: the road status, the air-quality forecast on fire.airnow.gov that the park points to during a fire, the day's weather, the parking situation. Check them in the last town and once more from the Village if you pass through. The park also runs a text-alert line for Valley traffic, text ynptraffic to 333111, and a text needs a signal like anything else; sign up before the canyon, and expect the alerts to arrive in bursts when you next find coverage. The Park Bulletin and the conditions board on this site are built for that last-town check, and the smoke-season piece has the decision tree for a trip that meets a fire.

5. Meeting up. A group that splits at the trailhead cannot text its way back together. Agree on a place and a time before anyone walks off, and make the place a shuttle stop or a building, not "the meadow."

### Emergencies without a bar

The park's instruction is plain: "If you have an emergency, call or text 911. Ambulance service is available 24 hours per day." The Yosemite Medical Clinic, at 209/372-4637, sits in the Valley between Yosemite Village and the Ahwahnee, and the park's general line is 209/372-0200. All of that assumes a connection, and on the coverage table above a connection exists in the east end of the Valley, in a handful of pockets, and nowhere on a trail that the park will vouch for. So the emergency plan has to be made for the case where the phone does nothing.

Satellite from the phone. Apple's Emergency SOS via satellite works on iPhone 14 or later in the United States, requires being outside with "a clear view of the sky and horizon," and is free for two years after the phone's activation, with terms after that set by Apple. Some recent Android phones offer a comparable satellite SOS; check the maker's support page for your model rather than assuming. On a Yosemite trail, "a clear view of the sky" is a real constraint: it is available on a dome, a meadow or a river bar, and not under a forest canopy or at the bottom of a slot like Tenaya Canyon. If your phone has the feature, test the demo mode at home, and know that it is a way to summon help, not a way to text the group.

A satellite messenger. Backpackers and anyone doing a long day out of the Valley should consider a dedicated two-way satellite communicator, sold by several makers with a subscription. It lets you send "running late, all fine" as well as "send help," which is most of what a family at home actually wants. The first-backpacking-trip piece covers the rest of the wilderness kit.

The old system. Tell someone your route and your turnaround time, and tell them when to worry. A search starts when someone who knows the plan reports that you are overdue, not when a phone goes silent, so that someone should be outside the park with a working phone and a written plan. On the trail, the fastest call for help is often another hiker walking out to a road, and the rangers at the wilderness centers, the visitor center and the entrance stations are the people to reach.

### The offline kit: what to load before the last town

A phone with no signal is still the best map, guidebook and camera you are carrying, provided the things it needs were put on it while it had a network.

- An offline map area in whichever maps app you use, drawn large enough to cover the gateway corridor and the whole park, Tioga Road included. This is the single item that prevents the most trouble, and it takes two minutes on the hotel Wi-Fi the night before.
- The National Park Service app, with Yosemite downloaded. The park's own description is the reason to bother: you "can download content from entire parks for offline use," which gets you the park map, the shuttle stops, the trail descriptions and the program calendar without a bar.
- The current Yosemite Guide, the park's free newspaper, as a PDF from the park website; the paper copy handed out at the entrance station never needs a signal, so keep it on the dashboard.
- Screenshots of every reservation, permit and pass, and a photograph of the campsite number and the parking spot when you leave the car.
- The Field Guide's offline download, if you carry it: the guide was built offline-first because the park mostly is, and the one tap that downloads the map, the hikes and the entries is meant to be pressed on a network, before Oakhurst or Mariposa or Groveland falls behind you.

Then turn on airplane mode with location left on: a phone hunting for a network it cannot find runs its battery down, the offline map works without the radio, and the cold nights at elevation are hard enough on a battery already. Carry the battery pack you would carry anyway, and treat the paper map from the gate as the copy that cannot run out.

### Region by region, what to expect

Yosemite Valley, east end. The best coverage in the park, on all three carriers, and the only place the park lists T-Mobile at all. The Village, the visitor center, Curry Village, the Pines campgrounds and the Ahwahnee are inside it, and so is Degnan's Kitchen with its public Wi-Fi. It is still a deep canyon with a summer crowd sharing the towers, so a bar in the Village is not a promise of one at Happy Isles.

Yosemite Valley, west end. Tunnel View, Bridalveil Fall, El Capitan Meadow and Valley View are past the developed pocket, which is what the park's "primarily in eastern Yosemite Valley" qualifier describes: expect the signal to fade as you drive west, and to be unreliable at the viewpoints where everyone is trying to post the same photograph.

Glacier Point. Listed for AT&T only, at the point itself; nothing on the road, at Washburn Point, or on the Sentinel Dome and Taft Point trails is listed for anyone. Plan the sunset rendezvous before you leave the Valley.

Wawona and the Mariposa Grove. Wawona is a Verizon pocket, with the county library for Wi-Fi on its posted days. The Mariposa Grove, its shuttle and its trails are not listed. When a fire is burning near Wawona, as one was in September 2026, the park points visitors to fire.airnow.gov for smoke forecasts, and that is a page to load in Oakhurst.

Crane Flat, Foresta and El Portal. Verizon spots only. Crane Flat matters because it is the junction where the drive turns onto Tioga Road: for a Verizon phone it is the last signal until Lee Vining, and for the other carriers the Valley was.

Tioga Road and Tuolumne Meadows. Nothing reliable for anyone, by the park's own account. Tenaya Lake, Olmsted Point, the Cathedral Lakes and Lembert Dome trailheads, the Tuolumne campground and the wilderness center are all off the network for practical purposes. This is where a group splits up on a whim and cannot regroup, where a hiker on Clouds Rest expects to text a summit photograph and cannot, and where the Half Dome lottery email sits unread. Any Tuolumne day plan has to assume all of this.

Hetch Hetchy. Not listed for any carrier, and the road is open only from sunrise to sunset. For the phone, treat it as trail country.

The trails, all of them. No trail appears in the table. A summit or a ridge may catch a bar from a distant tower on a good day; the bottom of a canyon will not. Treat any signal above the Valley floor as a bonus and never as part of the plan.

### The practical version

Do the phone work in the last town: send the plan, screenshot the reservations and the pass, download the offline map, the park app and the guide, apply for the lottery and know where you will be when the result comes. Assume nothing works on Tioga Road, on Glacier Point Road, at Hetch Hetchy or on any trail, and assume the west end of the Valley is worse than the east. If someone needs to reach you, you are staying at a Valley hotel and checking email, not taking calls. Carry the paper Guide from the gate, a battery pack, and a written plan left with someone outside the park, and for a long day or any night out, a satellite messenger or a phone that can reach one. Then put the phone in airplane mode and look up. The park is not withholding a signal out of spite. It is a granite trough three thousand feet deep with mountains on every side, and the towers were never going to win.

---

## Glacier Point: How to Visit and When the Road Is Open

URL: https://thetalusfieldjournal.com/articles/glacier-point-how-to-visit
Section: Planning. Published: 2026-09-17. Last updated: 2026-09-26.
Summary: Glacier Point: the drive, the road's open dates since 2000, the summer Badger Pass shuttle rule, sunrise vs sunset, every hike off the road, the bus, winter.

As of September 26, 2026, Glacier Point Road is temporarily closed for the Dome Fire, and the park says it will reopen when conditions allow. Hikers can still reach the point: the park says the Four Mile and Panorama Trails remain open. The concessioner's Glacier Point Tour and its one-way hiker ticket run on the road, and its listing still shows them through October 12 with no fire notice, so confirm they are running before you buy. Checkthe Park Bulletin for the road's status on the day you are going.Glacier Point is on every first visitor's list, and more of those visits go wrong here than anywhere else in the park. The view is as advertised; the problem is the plan. The road is closed for roughly half the year. In summer the parking lot at the end of it fills by mid-morning, and the Park Service now turns the overflow around and sends it to a shuttle eleven miles back down the road. And the drive is about an hour each way from Yosemite Valley, a number most people learn in the car. This is the standing guide: what is at the top, how the road works and when it is open, the shuttle rule that governs a summer visit, the walks that start from the road, the bus up, and the ski route that is the only way in from December to spring.

### What is at the top

The Park Service puts the overlook at 3,214 feet above Curry Village, and that height is what you came for. The Valley shows Half Dome from below and Tunnel View from the side; here you are level with it, close enough to read the joints in its face, with the Merced canyon dropping away underneath you and Vernal and Nevada Falls stacked in it like two steps of a staircase. Yosemite Falls is across the Valley. East, past Half Dome, the Clark Range and the high peaks hold snow into early summer.

From the parking area a paved, wheelchair-accessible trail of about 300 yards leads to the point, a ten- or fifteen-minute walk on a gentle grade. There are restrooms, a stone amphitheater, a snack bar and gift shop in season, and on the terrace below the shop a bronze relief model of the country you are looking at, worth two minutes so the peaks have names. Drinking water is a bottle-filling station that the park describes as available from late spring to early fall, which means it may not be running in the first weeks of the season or the last; carry your own. This is the highest-return view per step in Yosemite, and the non-hiker's guide treats it as the anchor of a day for exactly that reason.

A naturalist's note on what you are seeing. The Valley below is U-shaped, flat-floored and straight-walled, and the waterfalls fall from side valleys that hang in the air far above the floor. Both are the signature of ice: a trunk glacier deepened the main canyon far faster than the side streams could cut down, and when it melted, the side valleys were left stranded on the rim with their creeks pouring out of them. The stepped Merced canyon under your feet, the giant staircase of the geologists, is the same story told in the canyon's own granite.

Photo: Pavel Špindler / Wikimedia Commons (CC BY 3.0)

### The road, mile by mile

Glacier Point is about 30 miles and an hour from Yosemite Valley, and the same hour from Wawona. From the Valley you take the Wawona Road, which is Highway 41 inside the park, south for about 13 miles to the Chinquapin junction, then turn onto Glacier Point Road and follow it about 16 miles to the end. There is no regular shuttle between the Valley and the point: you drive, you ride the paid tour bus, or you walk up.

The road has its own stops. Badger Pass, the ski area, is five miles in. The McGurk Meadow trailhead follows, then the turn for Bridalveil Creek Campground, then the shared Sentinel Dome and Taft Point trailhead a couple of miles short of the end, then Washburn Point, whose lot sits just south of Glacier Point and whose view of Vernal and Nevada Falls is more direct than the point's own. Most people who drive straight through and complain about the parking never stopped at Washburn, which is the answer to the parking.

Two rules of the road. Vehicles longer than 30 feet and anything towing a trailer are not allowed past the Sentinel Dome parking lot, so a large RV ends its drive there. And there is no usable phone signal for most of the road, which means the conditions you check at breakfast are the ones you are carrying; the Park Bulletin is the place to check.

### The season, in the park's own dates

The Park Service's standing language is that the road is open to cars "from approximately late May through October or November," but the window swings wider than that. The park publishes the dates, and over the twenty-six seasons from 2000 through 2025 Glacier Point Road opened as early as March 28 (2015) and as late as July 15 (2023, a construction year), with most openings falling in May. It did not open at all in 2022, when it was closed for a rehabilitation project. The closing is a weather call, made after the first significant snowfall: most closings land in November, the earliest on record in that span was October 31 (2003) and the latest was December 12 (2008), and in 2021 the road stayed open into the first week of December.

Plowing begins around April 15, and the park says plainly that it cannot predict the opening date even in late spring. So a trip booked for the first half of May is a coin toss on this road, and one booked for the second half of November is a coin toss the other way. In every season since 2000 in which the road opened at all, it was open by mid-July and stayed open through October. Two dates inside the season are fixed rather than forecast: overnight parking anywhere on the road is prohibited from October 15, which matters if you were planning to leave a car at the Four Mile trailhead, and the road closes to cars the moment the snow makes it, with no reopening promised. The early-season piece describes the first weeks after the gate comes up, when the water is off and the snack bar may be shut; the fall guide covers the other end, when the road is among the last of the high roads to close.

### The summer rule: when the lot fills, you ride from Badger Pass

This is the part of a summer visit that the older guides, and until now this site, did not carry. The Park Service's Glacier Point page, updated in June 2026, sets it out: from mid-May to September, between 10 am and 4:30 pm, when the Glacier Point parking lot fills, rangers stop cars at the Badger Pass turnoff and have you park there and ride a free shuttle to Glacier Point and the trailheads along the road. If you reach the Badger Pass turnoff before 10 am or after 4:30 pm, you drive through to Glacier Point and every trailhead. Parking at Badger Pass takes RVs and trailers but not full-sized commercial buses.

The shuttle leaves Badger Pass every 20 minutes and stops at the Sentinel Dome and Taft Point trailhead, Washburn Point, and Glacier Point; on request or a flag-down it also stops at the McGurk Meadow, Ostrander Lake, and Mono Meadow trailheads. The first shuttle leaves Badger Pass at 10 am, the last leaves Badger Pass at 4:30 pm, and the last shuttle leaves Glacier Point at 5:30 pm, after which there is no shuttle of any kind. Three groups can drive to their destination at any hour regardless: vehicles displaying an accessibility placard, people holding a wilderness permit for a Glacier Point Road trailhead, and people with a campsite at Bridalveil Creek. The park adds that the details may change during the summer, so read its page in the week you are going, not this one.

In practice, a summer visit to Glacier Point has two good hours, early and late, and a shuttle in between. Arrive before ten and the day is yours, including the hikes. Arrive at noon on a July Saturday and plan on Badger Pass, a twenty-minute wait and a ride, and a last bus down at half past five that ends any idea of staying for the light. Arrive after 4:30 and you drive again, into the evening the lot was built for. The park frames the rule as mid-May to September. In October the same lot can fill for sunset with nobody managing it, and that is the case the next section is about.

### The hour decides the rest

Sunrise is the clean answer in any month. The lot is empty, the light reaches the high peaks east of the Valley first and works down the walls in order, Half Dome before the Clark Range before the floor, and you are driving back down as the first shuttle of the day is loading at Badger Pass. The cost is an alarm set for the small hours and a rim that can run twenty degrees colder than the Valley.

Sunset is the answer people want, and it has a catch the summer rule does not solve. After 4:30 pm you can drive up, but the lot at the end of the road is finite and a sunset crowd can fill it in any month the road is open, with no shuttle to fall back on after 5:30 pm. So arrive with an hour to spare, and if the Glacier Point lot is full, take the Washburn Point lot a short way back and walk: the sunset on Half Dome is the same, the falls are more in view, and the crowd at the railing is a fraction. Then remember the drive down is an hour in the dark, on a road with deer on it.

Midday is for the hikes, which start from lots the shuttle serves; if you are riding it anyway, the Sentinel Dome and Taft Point lot is a stop.

### The walks, from the point and from the road

These are the Park Service's numbers. From the shared trailhead a couple of miles short of the end of the road, Sentinel Dome is 2 miles round trip with 400 feet of gain, one to two hours, and finishes on a bare granite cap with a 360-degree view that includes El Capitan, Half Dome, and Yosemite Falls; the park's one instruction is to stay off the dome in a thunderstorm. From the same lot, Taft Point is 2.2 miles round trip, with about 200 feet of climbing on the way back, through forest and meadow to a rim overlook that faces El Capitan and Yosemite Falls across the Valley. The Fissures beside Taft Point are joints in the granite, narrow cracks with drops the park puts at up to 2,000 feet, and a short railing guards the point itself and nothing else. The two trails join through the Pohono Trail into a loop of roughly five miles, which is the walk most first visitors should do on a day the Mist Trail is a queue. Pit toilets are at the trailhead lot. Pets and bicycles are not allowed on any of these trails.

Lower on the road, McGurk Meadow is 1.6 miles round trip and nearly flat, a wildflower walk in early summer to a historic cabin, and the same trailhead continues to Dewey Point at 7.6 miles round trip with 750 feet of gain, four to five hours, for a rim view from the west end of the Valley. Mono Meadow is 3 miles round trip and wet most of the summer, with a steep 900 feet to climb on the way back. Ostrander Lake is 12 miles round trip and 1,500 feet, a full day.

From the point itself, three trails go down. The Four Mile Trail is 4.8 miles one way to the Valley floor and a very steep descent, three to four hours down, about 3,200 feet, and there is no water anywhere on it; the loop that climbs it and comes down the Panorama Trail is the day hike this site rates highest in the park. The Panorama Trail is 8.2 miles one way past Illilouette Fall to the top of Nevada Fall and down the John Muir or Mist Trail, six to eight hours, with an 800-foot climb out of the Illilouette drainage that surprises people who expected a descent. The Pohono Trail runs 12.5 miles along the south rim to Tunnel View. All three are one-way problems: the tour bus sells one-way tickets up and does not pick up at the point, so the standard shape is bus up and walk down.

### The bus, if you would rather not drive

The park concessioner runs the Glacier Point Tour whenever the road is open, and for the 2026 season it listed May 9 through October 12, departing the lobby entrance of Yosemite Valley Lodge at 8:30 am and 1:30 pm for a trip of about four hours that takes in Tunnel View on the way. Round trip was $72.50 for adults and $50.50 for children two to twelve, and the one-way ticket, the hiker's fare, was $28.50 for adults and $18.25 for children. The full-day Grand Tour, eight hours from the Lodge at 8 am, added the Mariposa Grove for $141 and $71. The prices are the concessioner's for one season and will move, so treat them as the scale rather than the quote. For a group with someone who cannot or would rather not drive a mountain road twice in a day, the bus is the right answer.

Photo: Jackhen1992 / Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 4.0)

### After dark

The Park Service lists Glacier Point and Washburn Point among its stargazing spots for the plain reason that they sit at 7,000 feet with an open sky to the south and the Valley's lights well below the rim. Summer brings astronomy programs at the point, run variously by the park, the Yosemite Conservancy, and the concessioner, some ticketed; the park's calendar and the current Yosemite Guide are the schedule, and the stargazing guide explains what the site's darkness is worth. The logistics are the same as sunset with the lights off: no shuttle after 5:30 pm, an hour down in the dark, and a coat you did not think you needed in July.

### Winter: the road ends at Badger Pass

From roughly mid-December through March the first five miles of Glacier Point Road are plowed to Badger Pass, the ski area that has run there since 1935, and everything beyond it is closed to cars and groomed for skiing and snowshoeing. It is not possible to drive to Glacier Point in winter. What is possible is to ski the road, 10.5 miles one way, as a 21-mile day for strong cross-country skiers or as an overnight. The concessioner's Glacier Point Ski Hut, twenty bunks at the point that hosted guided overnight trips from December to March, did not open for the 2025-26 winter, which the concessioner attributes to a lack of power; check whether it has reopened before you plan around it. The alternative is camping, with a wilderness permit available at the Badger Pass Ranger Station without a reservation. Tire chains may be required on the plowed section from late fall into early spring, and a free Badger Pass shuttle runs from the Valley on the days the ski area operates. The winter guide puts this in the context of a season when the Valley is open and the rim is not.

### Sleeping on the road

Bridalveil Creek Campground is the one place to spend the night on Glacier Point Road with a car. Sites have a fire ring, a picnic table, and a food locker, and sit near a bathroom with drinking water and flush toilets; reservations are through recreation.gov, and the park asks you to read a site's details there before booking because length limits vary. The reason to sleep here rather than in the Valley is the summer rule above: a Bridalveil Creek camper drives the road at any hour, sunrise and sunset included, without a shuttle in the way. The site's campground guide ranks it against the park's other twelve.

### What used to be here

The stone amphitheater stands where two hotels did. In 1871 James McCauley won permission to build a toll trail from the base of Sentinel Rock to Glacier Point, the route that became the Four Mile Trail, and in 1873 the innkeeper Charles Peregoy put up the Mountain House at the overlook for the people who climbed it. The Glacier Point Hotel followed in 1917, with rooms for some two hundred guests, and the Park Service's own history allows that "there may have never been a better balcony view." Campfires built for the Mountain House's guests were pushed over the edge, and from Camp Curry the falling embers looked like a waterfall of fire. That became the Firefall, and the June 1934 issue of Yosemite Nature Notes, in the site's archive, has the assistant park naturalist's own account: a quarter cord of red fir bark burned down to coals near the overhanging rock, a call of "Let the fire fall" exchanged with Camp Curry at nine o'clock, and a stream of embers dropping some 1,400 feet to a ledge. The hotel was damaged by the snowpack of the winter of 1968 to 1969 and did not open that summer, the Firefall was cancelled for good, and on July 10, 1969 an electrical fire in the empty building, fed by the pile of fir bark left beside it, took the hotel, the Mountain House, and a stand of trees.

### Three shapes of a Glacier Point day

The morning drive. Leave the Valley before first light, drive through the Badger Pass turnoff while it is unstaffed, park at the end of the road, walk the 300 yards, and take your time at the railing. Washburn Point on the way down, McGurk Meadow if it is June, and back in the Valley by lunch.

The hike day. Drive early or ride the shuttle to the Sentinel Dome and Taft Point lot, walk the loop, eat on the rim, and cover the last stretch to the point in the afternoon with your legs already loose. Or buy the one-way bus ticket and come down the Four Mile or the Panorama Trail on foot, which makes the descent the main event.

The sunset. Arrive after 4:30 pm with an hour in hand, take Washburn Point if the end of the road is full, and stay until the color has gone off Half Dome. Drive down slowly. If you want to do it without the parking anxiety at all, book a night at Bridalveil Creek and drive the road at any hour. The trip-planner map will place the point, the trailhead, and the campground on the road for you.

## Clouds Rest Hike: The Summit Above Half Dome, and When to Go

URL: https://thetalusfieldjournal.com/articles/clouds-rest-hike
Section: Trails and Hikes. Published: 2026-09-14. Last updated: 2026-09-14.
Summary: Clouds Rest: 14 miles, 2,300 feet, no permit, from Tenaya Lake on Tioga Road. The route, the ridge, the overnight, and the October window after the cables drop.

Most people arrive at Clouds Rest by way of a refusal. The Half Dome lottery said no in March, or it said no again two days before the hike, or the trip landed in the weeks after the cables came down, and somebody at a trailhead or on a forum said the same sentence: do Clouds Rest instead, it is higher and there is no permit. That sentence is true, and it undersells the hike. Clouds Rest is a 9,926-foot summit reached by a maintained trail from Tioga Road, no lottery and no cables, ending on a granite spine with the whole park arranged around it and Half Dome sitting below you. It is the best big summit day in Yosemite that needs no permit. This is how it goes, and when.

The site has recommended this hike before, in passing, inside the Half Dome piece and in the monthly notes. It has never had a full guide. What follows is the trail from the trailhead the Park Service measures from, the season it lives in, the overnight version, and the few weeks each autumn when it becomes the only summit of its kind still open.

### The numbers, from the Sunrise Lakes trailhead

The standard day starts at the Sunrise Lakes trailhead at the west end of Tenaya Lake on Tioga Road, a little over 8,000 feet up and about a mile and a half east of Olmsted Point. The Park Service's figures for the round trip to the summit are 14 miles, 2,300 feet of elevation gain, and eight to ten hours. Both of those last numbers deserve a note. The gain is not one climb: the trail goes up, comes back down, and goes up again, so the day carries more climbing than the net suggests, and the time estimate is honest for a fit party moving steadily with a real stop on top.

For comparison, the Half Dome day from Happy Isles is 14 to 16 miles with 4,800 feet of gain, starting on the Valley floor at about 4,000 feet, and it needs a permit whenever the cables are up. Clouds Rest starts twice as high, climbs half as much, and needs nothing but a parking space. Its summit is more than a thousand feet higher than Half Dome's.

The same trailhead serves the shorter Sunrise Lakes walk, 10.4 miles round trip and 1,300 feet of gain, which shares the first climb with Clouds Rest and then turns off toward the lakes and the High Sierra Camp. It is the fallback if the day turns, and a fine hike in its own right.

Photo: Michael Hogarth / Wikimedia Commons (public domain)

### The route, in the order it comes at you

The creek. Tenaya Creek crosses the trail within the first few hundred feet. In a heavy snow year it is a cold, knee-deep ford in June; by midsummer it is a rock-hop, and by the end of a dry summer it can be nearly dry. If you are here in early season, carry something to cross in.

The first climb. After a gentle mile and a half through lodgepole forest and over granite slabs, the trail turns uphill and gains roughly a thousand feet in a run of switchbacks to the ridge above Tenaya Canyon. This is the hardest sustained stretch of the day and it comes early, at altitude, on cold legs. Old stone steps and retaining walls mark the way. Take it at a pace you can hold.

The junction and the meadow. At the top of the climb the Sunrise Lakes trail branches off toward the lakes; Clouds Rest continues on the other fork. The trail then loses a few hundred feet into a quiet forested basin with a small pond and a meadow that can be marshy in early season. It is the emptiest part of the day and the last place you will see reliable water.

The second climb. The trail turns toward the summit ridge and begins the second ascent, steady rather than steep, with the trees thinning as it goes. The first views down into Tenaya Canyon arrive here, and they make the case for the rest of the hike.

The ridge. Then the forest ends. The last stretch to the summit follows a narrow granite ridgeline, the spine of the mountain, with Tenaya Canyon dropping away on one side and the Merced drainage on the other. The Park Service describes it in one line and adds one caution: stay off the summit and the ridgeline during thunderstorms or when the rock is wet. It is walking, not climbing. No ropes, no scrambling on the main line, and the granite grips well when dry. But the exposure is real, it is worse in wind, and anyone who dislikes heights will feel it. An older, less maintained path skirts below the crest; the site's Half Dome piece describes it, and it is easy to lose. Most people walk the spine.

The summit. The top is a long, narrow platform, big enough to sit on and eat lunch. The Park Service's description is a 360-degree view of Tenaya Canyon, Yosemite Valley, and countless high Sierra peaks, and for once the official prose is not overselling. Half Dome is south of you and below you, the Valley is laid out to the west, the Cathedral Range and the high country to the east, the Clark Range to the south. You have been looking up at Half Dome all week. This is the place where you look down at it.

### Water, altitude, and the summit before noon

Water. Reliable water is in the first miles only: the creek at the trailhead and the seasonal streams and pond in the basin, which can be dry by late summer. From the second climb to the summit and back there is nothing. Carry three liters as a floor and four on a hot day. A filter is worth its weight early in the season and dead weight by September.

Altitude. The entire day is spent between 8,000 and 10,000 feet. A party arriving from sea level and starting this hike the morning after driving up will feel it as a headache, a shortness of breath on the first climb, and a general slowness that the mileage does not explain. Sleep a night at Tuolumne or in the high country first if you can, drink before you are thirsty, eat before you are hungry, and treat a headache with nausea as a reason to descend, not to push.

Lightning. This is the hazard the ridge was built for. The Park Service's guidance for Yosemite is that thunderstorms are most common June through September, that hikers above the treeline or along a rim should plan to be there in the morning and to summit before noon, and that after a storm you should stay in a safe place until 30 minutes after the last thunder. On Clouds Rest, that means a trailhead start at or before first light in summer and a firm turnaround rule: if cloud is building over the crest by late morning, the summit waits for another day. There is no shelter on the spine and no fast way off it.

Wet rock. The same caution covers rain that has already fallen. Granite that grips like sandpaper when dry is a different surface when wet, and the ridge is not a place to learn that.

What to wear and carry. Footwear with real traction, layers for a summit that is often 15 to 20 degrees cooler than the Valley and windy on a day that felt still below, sun protection for the exposed upper half, and the day-pack basics. Bears use these trails; secure your food at every stop, and read the bear piece if you are new to the park's rules.

### Getting to the trailhead: you are driving

The trailhead is reachable by vehicle only while Tioga Road is open, which the Park Service puts at typically late May or early June until sometime in October or November; the road closes for the season after the first significant snowfall. In 2026 the road opened May 15. From Yosemite Valley the drive up to Tenaya Lake is well over an hour, and the Tuolumne piece covers what else is up there for the non-hikers in the car.

Parking at the trailhead is limited, a small lot with vault toilets and food lockers, and it fills early on summer weekends. Arrive early or expect to walk in from the shoulder where parking is permitted; check the signs, because not every stretch of shoulder is. The early start you want for the lightning rule solves the parking problem at the same time.

Do not plan on a bus. The free Tuolumne Meadows shuttle and the hikers bus from the Valley are summer services that end in mid-September; in 2026 both stopped on September 13. The YARTS Highway 395/120 East route runs from July 1 through September 30 in 2026 and stops at the Tuolumne Meadows store and visitor center, White Wolf, Crane Flat and Yosemite Village, but not at Tenaya Lake. For most of the season, and for all of the autumn window below, the Sunrise Lakes trailhead is a place you drive to.

Olmsted Point, about a mile and a half back toward the Valley at roughly 8,400 feet, is where you look at the mountain before you climb it: Clouds Rest fills the view up Tenaya Canyon with Half Dome over its shoulder, and a quarter-mile trail out onto the point walks you through the glacial erratics the ice left there. Ten minutes at the rail on the way in, and you will recognize every stage of the trail from above.

### The autumn window: between the cables and the snow

Here is the part of the calendar that makes this hike more than a Half Dome consolation prize. Half Dome's cables come down, in the Park Service's standing rule, the day after the second Monday in October, conditions permitting; in 2026 that is October 13, and once they are down the summit is a mountaineering objective, not a hike. Tioga Road, meanwhile, stays open until the first significant snowfall, which in most years is weeks later. Clouds Rest lives in the gap.

The park's own historical dates say how wide the gap has been. The cables have come down between October 10 and October 16 in nine of the last ten seasons the park's table records, and as late as October 22 in 2025. Tioga Road closed for the season on November 1 in 2015, November 16 in 2016, November 14 in 2017, November 20 in 2018, November 19 in 2019, November 5 in 2020, October 21 in 2021, October 31 in 2022, November 15 in 2023, November 11 in 2024, and November 12 in 2025. In every one of those years but one the road outlasted the cables by at least 19 days, and in seven of the ten seasons the park lists both dates the gap was three weeks or more. The exception was 2021, when the road shut nine days after the cables came down. The window is real and it is not guaranteed, which is exactly the kind of plan this site exists to make honestly.

Photo: Cory Goehring

What an October day up here feels like comes from the Park Service's climate table for Tuolumne Meadows, at 8,600 feet: an average high of 57 and an average low of 26 in October, against 65 and 32 in September, with October's precipitation more than three times September's. By November the averages are 47 and 20. So the trailhead is frosted at dawn, the creek crossing is trivial, the summit is cold and can be windy, the thunderstorm season is largely behind you, and the first real storm of the winter is a possibility on any given week. Layers, a warm hat, and a hard look at the forecast the night before replace the lightning rule as the day's discipline. The days are shorter too; the eight-to-ten-hour estimate does not shrink because the light did.

Three dates govern the autumn version and they arrive within a day of each other. Overnight parking on Tioga Road, including the Sunrise Lakes trailhead, ends October 15, which closes the overnight option below for the rest of the season. The Tuolumne Meadows Wilderness Center closes around October 14, after which wilderness permits are by self-registration at the station. And the cables, as above, come down in the middle of that same week. From mid-October to the road closure, then, Clouds Rest is a day hike, from a car you drive up that morning, in conditions you check the night before on the conditions page and the bulletin. Put another way: it is the highest walk-up summit in the park, with no permit, no bus, and almost nobody on it. The fall piece lays out the rest of what the season closes and opens, and the dates page keeps the cables rule and the road on one calendar.

### Staying out: the overnight version

Clouds Rest as a backpack is an easier day and a better summit, because you can be on the ridge at dawn or in the last light without a 14-mile day around it. Two rules from the permit system shape it.

A wilderness permit is required for any night out, and the Park Service is explicit that none is needed for a day hike, with one exception, Half Dome. The Sunrise Lakes trailhead carries a daily quota of nine lottery permits and six first-come, first-served, and it is one of the trailheads marked Half Dome eligible, meaning a backpacker starting here can apply for the Half Dome add-on, which is required even for permit holders whenever the cables are up. Sixty percent of the quota goes through the weekly lottery 24 weeks ahead and the remaining forty percent is released seven days ahead; reservations carry a $10 fee per permit and $5 per person. The wilderness permit guide walks the whole system, and the first-backpack piece covers what the permit does not tell you.

Once you are out, the wilderness regulations apply as written: an approved bear-resistant canister is required for food storage in all areas of the Yosemite Wilderness, camps go at least 100 feet from any water and any trail and at least a mile from any road, campfires are prohibited above 9,600 feet (which rules out the summit ridge and the upper mountain), and groups are capped at 15. The forested basin between the two climbs is where most parties sleep on the way up, high enough to make the summit morning short and below the treeline for the night; pick a site that meets the distance rules rather than the first flat spot by the pond.

And the seasonal limit again, because it is the one that catches people: no overnight parking on Tioga Road from October 15. The backpack is a summer and early-autumn plan. After the middle of October, the only Clouds Rest is the day hike.

### From the Valley, and the through-hike

There is a longer Clouds Rest, and it is the one the strong parties post about. The mountain can be approached from below, up the Half Dome corridor from Happy Isles through Little Yosemite Valley and then on to the summit, and the Park Service's own guided version, run with the Yosemite Conservancy, is a three-day, 17-mile through-hike from Tenaya Lake to Yosemite Valley over the top. Do the arithmetic against the seven-mile approach from Tenaya and the Valley side comes out at roughly ten miles one way, which puts a Valley round trip at about twenty miles with all of Half Dome's climbing and then some. A fit party with a very early start does it as a day; a few add the Half Dome summit on the way back, with a permit, and turn it into an all-day epic. Neither is the Clouds Rest this article recommends to someone deciding what to do with a Tuesday.

The through-hike is the better plan for the ambitious. Two cars, or the YARTS run while it operates, and a wilderness permit from the Sunrise Lakes quota; the climb is done from the high side, the summit comes on day one or day two, and the descent drops through Little Yosemite Valley to the Valley floor. Little Yosemite Valley has no potable water and a campground with communal food lockers; the Merced is the water source and it must be treated. Note that from the Happy Isles side the rules run the other way, with no camping between the Valley and Little Yosemite Valley and a first night required at the campground there.

### Half Dome or Clouds Rest, when you can have either

If you hold a Half Dome permit and the day is dry, hike Half Dome. The cables are singular and there is nothing else like them in any national park; the lottery guide covers the two lotteries, including the daily one that runs two days ahead of the hike, from midnight to 4 pm Pacific, for a share of the 300 places a day. The Park Service caps that trail at about 225 day hikers and 75 backpackers.

If you do not hold one, or the date is outside the cable season, or the idea of the Mist Trail in August makes the decision for you, Clouds Rest is not the second choice. It is a higher summit, a bigger view, a cooler start, a trail with a fraction of the company, and a ridge walk that asks something of you without asking for a harness. The people who have done both split more evenly than you would expect. Go stand on the spine and decide for yourself.

The practical close, then: check conditions the night before, drive to the Sunrise Lakes trailhead before first light, carry three liters and a warm layer, be on top before noon, stay off the ridge if it is wet or the sky is building, and turn around without argument if either happens. Fourteen miles, 2,300 feet, no permit, and Half Dome under your boots.

## Las Vegas to Yosemite: The Drive, and the Pass That Decides

URL: https://thetalusfieldjournal.com/articles/yosemite-from-las-vegas
Section: Planning. Published: 2026-09-10. Last updated: 2026-09-10.
Summary: Las Vegas to Yosemite: drive time both seasons, the Tioga Pass question, the Tonopah and Death Valley roads, where to sleep, the winter route via Bakersfield.

A great many first trips to Yosemite begin at an airport in Nevada. Las Vegas is where the cheap flights land, where the Southwest road trip starts, and where a visitor who has already seen the Grand Canyon and Zion looks at the map and notices Yosemite. The map leaves out that there are two entirely different drives between the two places, that the calendar chooses which one you get, and that the shorter, more beautiful one does not exist for about half the year. Nobody planning from a routing app in February finds that out until the road sign at Lee Vining tells them.

So here is the trip in the order the decisions come: the number to plan around, the pass, the summer road and the winter road, where to sleep on the way, and the version of the trip that works.

### The number that decides everything

The Park Service's own directions page gives two figures for Las Vegas, and this article is about the difference between them. In season, by US 95 and Highway 120 over Tioga Pass, it is 400 miles and about eight hours to Yosemite Valley, and the page dates that road June through October. In winter, by I-15 and Highway 41 through Bakersfield and Fresno, it is 495 miles and eight to ten hours. Both figures are to the Valley floor in clear conditions, with no stops that matter. Both are longer than the routing app will admit, because the app does not know that the last stretch of either road, seventy-odd miles from Lee Vining or ninety-odd from Fresno, is slow mountain highway with a fee station and a line at the end of it.

Treat eight hours as the floor, not the estimate. Yosemite Valley is about seven miles long, and a time quoted to the Valley means its west end; Curry Village, the trailheads, and the east-end lots are another fifteen or twenty minutes on, plus parking. The honest planning number, either season, is a full day behind the wheel, and it does not leave room for a day trip. Yosemite from Los Angeles is a two-night trip at six hours each way. From Las Vegas it is a two-night trip at the very least, and the version worth the fuel is three.

Eight hours in season, ten in winter, and the road itself changes with the month. Whatever else you plan, plan the pass first.

### The question to ask before any other: is Tioga Pass open?

Everything about this trip hangs on one road. Highway 120 crosses the Sierra at Tioga Pass, 9,945 feet, the highest highway pass in California, and it is the only way into Yosemite from the east. The Park Service's standing description is that Tioga Road is typically open to vehicles from late May or June until sometime in November. In 2026 it opened on May 15, unusually early. The closing end has no date at all: it is a judgment made on a forecast when the first serious snow arrives, and in the last five seasons it fell between October 21 and November 15. An itinerary that crosses the pass in the last week of October is a bet. One that crosses it in December is not an itinerary.

While the pass is open, Las Vegas to Yosemite is a desert-and-mountain drive that arrives in the high country and drops into the Valley from above. While it is closed, the trip is a drive around the southern end of the Sierra Nevada that arrives through the South Entrance, and it shares its last two hundred miles with the Los Angeles route. They are not variations on one drive, and the rest of this piece takes them one at a time.

Check the road before you book anything, and again the night before you leave. The park's road line is 209/372-0200, then 1, then 1; the park's current conditions page and the Park Bulletin carry the same status, and the conditions page collects the webcams and forecasts around it. The Park Service's own warning about navigation applies here with more force than anywhere else in California: the park has no single address, phone apps have routed winter visitors toward the closed pass for years, and if a road sign and a screen disagree, the sign is correct.

### The summer road: two ways to reach US 395

The season road has a fixed final act, the crossing from Lee Vining over the pass, and two ways to reach it from Las Vegas. They are very different drives, and the difference is Death Valley.

The Park Service's road, through Tonopah. This is the 400-mile version the directions page quotes. US 95 runs north out of Las Vegas through the empty middle of Nevada to Tonopah; from Tonopah, US 6 heads west to Benton, just inside California, and Highway 120 continues west to US 395 a few miles south of Lee Vining. It is a fast, nearly featureless road through sagebrush basin and range country, and it has the great virtue of being the shortest. It also has almost nothing on it. Towns are far apart and the services in them are small, so the fuel discipline is simple: fill the tank whenever a pump appears and you are below half, and carry water and food.

Through Death Valley. The other road leaves US 95 at Beatty and enters Death Valley National Park on Nevada 374, or leaves Las Vegas by Pahrump and enters on California 190 from Death Valley Junction. Either way it crosses the park on Highway 190, past Stovepipe Wells and Panamint Springs, and comes out at Olancha on US 395, from where the road north runs through Lone Pine, Bishop, and past Mammoth Lakes to Lee Vining. It is somewhat longer than the Tonopah road and slower per mile, and in the right month it is one of the great drives in the country: a second national park on the way to the first, at the lowest and hottest end of the state on the way to one of the highest.

The right month is the problem. Death Valley's summer is not a warm spell; it is the hottest weather on the continent. The park reports average July highs of 116°F at Furnace Creek, temperatures that often top 120°F in the shade, and overnight lows in the 90s. Its own summer guidance is that it does not recommend hiking in the lower elevations in the summer at all, that visitors should stay on paved roads and close to an air-conditioned car, drink at least a gallon of water a day, and stay with the vehicle if it breaks down. Read that as a description of the drive, not a warning to hikers: in July the Death Valley road is a transit through a place you cannot get out of the car in, and the Tonopah road is the better choice. Death Valley's own pleasant seasons are winter and spring, when its January highs average in the high 60s, and those are precisely the months when Tioga Pass is shut. The two parks' seasons are nearly opposite, which is the single most useful fact in planning this trip.

Two windows make both parks work in one drive: late May and June, once the pass has opened and before the desert has fully committed to summer, and October into early November, after the desert has cooled and before the pass closes. Both are gambles at the edges, and the October one depends on a closing date nobody knows in advance. Inside those windows, the Death Valley road is the trip. Outside them, it is either an oven or a dead end.

Practicalities for the Death Valley road, from the park's own pages. Gas is sold at three places inside the park, Furnace Creek, Stovepipe Wells, and Panamint Springs, and the Park Service's warning about relying on a vehicle's navigation system there is in capital letters, because GPS routings have sent drivers onto dead-end and closed roads for years. The park has no staffed entrance stations: the fee is $30 per vehicle for seven days, paid online in advance, at automated machines that take physical cards only, or at the Furnace Creek visitor center and the Stovepipe Wells ranger station in business hours, and the park does not accept cash. An America the Beautiful pass covers it, and covers Yosemite's vehicle fee at the other end, which takes the $80 pass most of the way to paying for itself on a two-park trip before you count anything else.

Photo: Cory Goehring

### The pass itself: the last seventy-four miles

From Lee Vining, the Park Service quotes 74 miles and two hours to Yosemite Valley, and the two hours are honest only if you refuse to stop, which nobody does. The road climbs more than 3,000 feet in about twelve miles to the pass, where the Tioga Pass entrance station collects the park fee: $35 per private vehicle, good for seven consecutive days, cards or mobile payment only, no cash. In 2026 every non-US resident aged sixteen and older also pays a $100 non-resident fee on top of the vehicle fee unless the party holds an annual pass; the international visitors page works the arithmetic, including the case where a single $250 non-resident pass covers the car.

Two things about the road east of the pass. There is no gas between Lee Vining and Crane Flat, roughly sixty miles of mountain highway with serious climbing in it, and the old Tuolumne Meadows station that some travel sites still list has been out of operation for years; fill up at Lee Vining, the last pump on the east side. And in the shoulder months the pass is a different place from the Valley: mornings in the 20s and 30s when the Valley is mild, black ice at dawn and dusk near Olmsted Point and on the climb, and chain controls that the park says can be posted as early as September. Carry chains from mid-September on, whatever the forecast says, because the rule inside the park is that every vehicle must have them in possession when controls are in effect, four-wheel drives and rental cars included.

Then the reward. The Tioga Road is not a transit corridor but the high country of the park, and an eastern arrival sees it at its best: Tuolumne Meadows at 8,600 feet, Tenaya Lake against its domes, and Olmsted Point, where Half Dome appears from behind for the first time. A day in Tuolumne Meadows makes the case for giving it the whole day rather than the windshield, and on this trip you have already paid for the drive. Descend to the Valley in the late afternoon, when the day-use cars are leaving.

### Where to break the drive in season

The shape that works is to sleep on the east side of the mountains and cross the pass in the morning. Eight hours from Las Vegas puts you at the Valley floor at dusk with nothing seen; six or seven puts you in the Eastern Sierra with the evening to spare and the best road in the park still ahead, in daylight, the next day.

Lee Vining is the natural place to stop, and the gateway towns comparison is candid about what it is: a tiny outpost between Mono Lake and the pass, the only east-side gateway, and no substitute for the western towns as a Valley base. For one night on the way through it is exactly right. Its services are thin and seasonal on top of thin, the Tioga Gas Mart with the Whoa Nellie Deli runs roughly late April to late October, the market is small, and the nearest full supermarket is in Mammoth Lakes, about thirty miles south. Mammoth Lakes and June Lake are the deeper bench of rooms and the sensible fallback when Lee Vining is full, at the cost of thirty to forty minutes added to the morning.

In the two shoulder windows, the other honest overnight is inside Death Valley or at its edge, at Furnace Creek, Stovepipe Wells, or Panamint Springs, which turns the drive into two comfortable days, the desert one afternoon and evening and the whole of the Eastern Sierra and the pass the next. In summer, do not: the park's own guidance is to be in an air-conditioned car and moving.

#### The east-side night, on the way

A Lee Vining bed means crossing Tioga Pass in the morning with the high country ahead of you in daylight instead of behind you in the dark. Rooms are few and seasonal; when the town is full, Mammoth Lakes and June Lake are the next bench, half an hour south.

### The winter road: around the bottom of the mountains

When the pass is closed, the Park Service's published detour from Las Vegas is I-15 south to Barstow, Highway 58 west to Bakersfield, Highway 99 north to Fresno, and Highway 41 north into the park: 495 miles and eight to ten hours. There is no shortcut. The other high passes north of Tioga close for the winter as well, and the alternative the Park Service publishes for the Eastern Sierra towns, north through Minden and over US 50, is the wrong direction from Nevada's south end. From Bakersfield on, this is the Los Angeles drive, and everything in that piece from Highway 99 north applies: the tule fog on the Valley floor in the wet months, the climb through Oakhurst and Fish Camp, and the arrival at Tunnel View that the southern approach alone delivers.

Three things change in winter beyond the mileage. Chains. The park says chains are most often required from November through March, sometimes as early as September or as late as May, and most often on the higher roads, the Wawona Road from the South Entrance among them. All vehicles must carry them when controls are posted, four-wheel drive and rentals included, and the fine for not having them runs to several thousand dollars. The winter guide explains the R1, R2, and R3 levels and why Highway 140 from Merced is the lowest and most reliable road when a storm is on; from Bakersfield that means staying on 99 past Fresno to Merced and coming in through Mariposa, a longer drive but the road least likely to be turned around. Daylight. Ten hours of driving in December is most of the daylight there is, which is the strongest argument for the Bakersfield or Oakhurst night. The Grapevine does not apply: the Barstow road joins 99 at Bakersfield without crossing Tejon Pass, though Highway 58 does cross the Tehachapi Mountains, so check it with everything else.

There is a better winter shape than the straight run, and the Park Service's own detour table contains it. Its Death Valley detour, Highway 190 west to US 395, south to Highway 14, Highway 58 to Bakersfield, then 99 and 41: 450 miles and about nine hours, is the route from the middle of Death Valley, not from Las Vegas, and that is the point. Winter is Death Valley's season. Drive from Las Vegas into the desert the first day, sleep there, and take the detour road to Oakhurst or Fish Camp the second, and the winter trip stops being a penalty and becomes a two-park drive in the months when the desert is at its best. The pass you cannot cross is the price; the desert in January is what it buys.

Photo: Aniket Deole / Unsplash

### The loop, and the question of which way round

Most people driving from Las Vegas are not driving back to Las Vegas the same way, and in season the trip is best planned as a loop: in over Tioga Pass, out through the South Entrance and down to Bakersfield and Barstow, which is the winter road driven in the other direction. Do it that way round rather than the reverse. Arriving from the east puts the high country first, when you are fresh and the light is on the domes, and saves the Valley for the middle of the trip; leaving by the south puts the Mariposa Grove on the way out, a quarter mile inside the gate, and the Tunnel View stop on the last morning. The reverse loop spends the fresh day on the flat and crosses the pass tired, in the afternoon, with the Eastern Sierra descent in the dark. If the return is to San Francisco instead, the same logic holds, in from the east and out by the west, and the entrances guide lays out the western roads.

### Without a car

Mostly this trip does not work without one, and it is better to say so plainly. There is no scheduled public bus from Las Vegas to the park that I know of. What does exist is the last leg: in summer, YARTS runs a Highway 395 bus from Mammoth Lakes through June Lake and Lee Vining, over the pass to Tuolumne Meadows, White Wolf, Crane Flat, and Yosemite Valley. The 2026 season is July 1 through September 30 for the main runs, with a published adult fare of $30 one way from Mammoth Lakes to the Valley, $16 to Tuolumne Meadows, and $6 from Lee Vining to Tuolumne; reservations are sold online in limited numbers and walk-ons ride as space permits. It solves the mountain crossing for anyone who can reach Mammoth Lakes by other means, and the shuttle and YARTS guide covers the rest of the system. Commercial tour operators sell multi-day Yosemite bus trips out of Las Vegas; I have not taken one, but they exist, and they are the honest answer for a visitor with no licence.

### The shape of the trip that works

In season, three nights. Leave Las Vegas after breakfast on the Tonopah road, or on the Death Valley road in the two shoulder windows, and sleep in Lee Vining or Mammoth Lakes. Cross Tioga Pass early, spend the day between Tuolumne Meadows, Tenaya Lake, and Olmsted Point, and drop into the Valley for the evening. Give the Valley the whole of the next day. On the fourth morning leave by the South Entrance, walk the Mariposa Grove while it is still cool, stop at Tunnel View on the way past, and drive the long southern road home or on to the coast.

In winter, the same three nights with the geography reversed. Las Vegas to Death Valley the first day, and a night in the desert while it is mild. Death Valley to Oakhurst or Fish Camp the second, by 395, 14, 58, 99, and 41, chains in the trunk. Into the park early on the third morning, Tunnel View and the Valley, and a second Valley night for the winter light. The high country is not on this version, because it is under snow, and the Valley in winter is a better consolation than most first-time visitors expect.

Either way, three checks before you leave the hotel: the pass, on the park's road line; the desert forecast, because 116°F changes what a breakdown means; and the chain rule, if the month is anywhere between September and May. The planning guide will build the read list for your dates, and it knows which months close which roads.
