## Highway 140 Closed? How to Get Into Yosemite Anyway

URL: https://thetalusfieldjournal.com/articles/highway-140-closed-yosemite
Section: Planning. Published: 2026-09-07. Last updated: 2026-09-07.
Summary: Highway 140 to Yosemite closed? The detours from Mariposa by 41 and 120, what it means for a Mariposa or El Portal booking, the YARTS bus, and how to check.

The message arrives the day before the trip, or the morning of it, and it is always the same road. Highway 140 is closed. A rockslide in the Merced River canyon, a fire that started on the shoulder, a storm that brought the wall down onto the pavement at the park boundary. The room in Mariposa is paid for. The bus ticket from Merced is booked. The routing app has quietly rewritten the drive from an hour and a quarter to something over two, by way of towns you have never heard of, and the park itself is open, which somehow makes it worse. This is the article for that morning. It is also the article for the week before, because the road that closes most often in Yosemite is the one most people are told to take, and knowing what a closure does to a trip is the difference between a rerouted day and a wrecked one.

What follows is the geography of why it is always this road, the closure ledger of the last twenty years, the one question that decides everything (which side of the barricade is your bed on), the two detours from Mariposa and what they cost, what to do about the booking, the bus, how to check in the right order, and the construction project that will make delays in the canyon a fact of life through the end of the decade.

### Why it is always this road

Highway 140 is the road from Merced and Mariposa, and it reaches the park by following the Merced River up its canyon to the Arch Rock Entrance. It is the lowest of the five approaches, which is why the entrance guide calls it the all-weather route and why Mariposa County's own visitor office calls it the easiest road to drive into Yosemite in winter: it sees the least snow and the least chain control, and it delivers you onto the Valley floor faster than any other gate. The Park Service quotes 44 miles and an hour and a quarter from Mariposa to Yosemite Valley, and 81 miles and two hours from Merced.

The same geography is the problem. For its last stretch the road runs along the floor of a steep river canyon, with the Merced on one side and rock on the other, and a canyon like that closes for reasons no other approach shares. Rock comes down onto it: the Ferguson slide of 2006 buried the original roadbed near El Portal and has never been cleared, and a debris slide in March 2025 shut the road for nine days. Fires start on it: a motorhome that caught fire on the shoulder in August 2011, sparks from a vehicle's metal fragments in October 2014, and, in September 2026, a fire that Cal Fire's incident page places at Highway 140 and Colorado Road and lists as under investigation, which closed the road from Briceburg to the Bug hostel for three days before one lane reopened under traffic control. And when the big fires come through Mariposa County, they come through the 140 corridor: the Ferguson Fire of 2018, the Briceburg Fire of 2019, the Oak Fire of 2022, which started at Highway 140 and Carstens Road near Midpines, burned 19,244 acres, and closed the highway in two segments between Triangle Road and Briceburg.

None of that makes 140 a bad road. It is still the right one for most Valley trips and for nearly every winter trip. It makes it a road whose closure you should have a plan for, in the way that a Tioga Road trip needs a plan for Tioga being shut. The difference is that Tioga closes on a schedule, and 140 closes on a Tuesday afternoon.

Photo: Cory Goehring

### The closure ledger

A short list, because the pattern is the point. Each of these is in a Park Service, Caltrans, or Cal Fire record.

- 2006. The Ferguson slide, a series of major rockslides, takes out the highway near El Portal. Traffic has run on a temporary bypass, over one-lane bridges, ever since.
- August 2011. The Motor Fire: a motorhome catches fire on 140 about ten miles west of Arch Rock, and the road closes to incoming traffic about ten miles east of Mariposa.
- October 2014. The Dog Rock Fire, started by sparks from hot metal fragments off a vehicle, closes the El Portal Road entrance from October 7 to the morning of October 12.
- January 2017. Rockfalls after heavy rain and snow close 140 at the park entrance and 120 at Big Oak Flat on the same morning. Highway 41 is the only way into the Valley; the park runs ranger-led convoys through the closed roads that afternoon.
- February 2017. The reverse case. Storm damage shuts Big Oak Flat Road between Crane Flat and Foresta and blocks Highway 41 at Fish Camp, and 140 is the only vehicle access to Yosemite Valley and Wawona.
- July 2018. The Ferguson Fire closes 140 from the Bug hostel to just west of Cedar Lodge in El Portal.
- October 2019. The Briceburg Fire, 5,563 acres, starts at 140 and Briceburg Bridge Road and closes the highway for about a week.
- July 2022. The Oak Fire, 19,244 acres, closes 140 between Triangle Road and Briceburg and two stretches of Highway 49 south of Mariposa.
- March 2025. A debris slide across both lanes at about ten at night on March 17 closes the road from Savage Trading Post at Briceburg to Cedar Lodge in El Portal. One-way traffic control resumes March 26.
- September 2026. The Colorado Fire closes 140 from Briceburg to the Bug hostel on September 1. One lane reopens under traffic control on September 4 and both lanes on September 5.

Ten closures in twenty years is the long-run rate, and it undercounts, because it leaves out the shorter shuts for rock work and the planned construction closures that are about to start. Plan on the road being closed at some point in any given year. Plan on it closing during your trip about as seriously as you plan on rain.

### The only question that matters: which side of the barricade is your bed on

Every closure has limits, and the limits decide the trip. Highway 140 from Mariposa runs up through Midpines, past the Bug hostel, drops to the river at Briceburg, follows the canyon east through Cedar Lodge and El Portal, and enters the park at Arch Rock. A closure is named by its two barricades, and the first thing to do with any closure notice is find those two names on a map.

Look at the recent ones. The March 2025 closure ran from Briceburg to Cedar Lodge. The 2018 closure ran from the Bug to just west of Cedar Lodge. The September 2026 closure ran from Briceburg to the Bug. In all three, El Portal sat on the park side of the barricade. A room at Cedar Lodge or Yosemite View Lodge was still reachable, and reachable from the Valley: the guest drives in through the South Entrance or Big Oak Flat, crosses the park, and comes down the El Portal Road from the east to a lodge that has lost its western approach and nothing else. The Mariposa side of the same closure is the opposite case. A room in Mariposa is fully reachable from Merced and cut off from the park, and every day of the trip becomes a detour.

Then there is the 2014 shape, when the fire was at the boundary and it was the El Portal Road entrance itself that shut. That closure put El Portal on the wrong side and Mariposa on the same side, and it made no difference to either: neither could reach the Valley on 140, and both drove around.

So before the routing app, before the phone calls, read the two place names in the closure. If your lodging is east of the eastern barricade, the trip is nearly intact and the only change is which entrance you use on the drive in. If it is west of the western one, you are in the detour business for as long as the closure lasts, and the rest of this article is for you.

### The two detours from Mariposa

Caltrans's standing instruction when 140 is shut is the one it gave in March 2025: seek alternate routes along Highway 41 and Highway 120 into the park, and watch the changeable message signs on 41, 49, 99 and 120 for the current status. From Mariposa that means one of two drives.

South, by Highway 49 to Oakhurst and Highway 41. This is the detour nearly everyone takes. Highway 49 leaves Mariposa southbound as a winding two-lane foothill road with few places to pass and reaches Oakhurst in something like forty minutes; from Oakhurst it is twenty to twenty-five minutes up 41 to the South Entrance, and from the South Entrance another hour of mountain road to the Valley floor. Call it two to two and a half hours from Mariposa to the Valley in clear conditions, against the hour and a quarter the Park Service quotes for 140. It has consolations. You pass the Mariposa Grove welcome plaza immediately inside the gate, Oakhurst is the last full-size supermarket on any approach, and the road enters the Valley through the Wawona Tunnel at Tunnel View, which the 140 approach never sees.

North, by Highway 49 to Coulterville and across to Highway 120. The alternate-route notices in recent closures have pointed Highway 49 travelers this way as a second option, and on the map it looks shorter for anyone bound for Hetch Hetchy or the Tioga Road. Treat it with respect. It is a long way of mountain road with little on it, and it delivers you to the Big Oak Flat Entrance, which is the north end of the park: fine for Crane Flat and the high country, and another forty-five minutes of park road from the Valley. In September 2026 it also delivers you into the Big Oak Flat Road fire-safety work between Foresta and Crane Flat, which the park lists at fifteen-minute weekday delays with no end date. If the Valley is the destination, the southern detour is usually the faster one even when it is not the shorter one.

For anyone driving from the Bay Area or the Central Valley, the answer is simpler, and worse. The park's own figures for the 140 approach are four hours from San Francisco, two and three-quarters from Manteca, and two and a half from Modesto, all to the Valley floor. With 140 shut, the routing app will send you up Highway 120 through Groveland or down 99 to Fresno and up 41, and both add real time to a drive that already did not fit in a day. Add the entrance queue at whichever gate now carries the 140 traffic as well as its own.

### What a closure does to the booking

Three cases, and only one of them needs a decision.

A room in El Portal, on the park side of the barricade. Keep it. You lose the direct drive from Merced once, on the way in, and get it back the moment the road reopens. Confirm with the lodge that guests are being routed in through the park, drive in by 41 or 120, and use the Valley as normal. This is the trip that a closure barely touches, and it is one more argument for El Portal that the gateway-town comparison already made on other grounds.

A room in Mariposa, for one night on the way in. Keep it, and change the morning. The detour costs an hour or so each way, and one extra hour on one drive is not worth a cancellation fee. Leave earlier than you had planned, because the southern gate will be taking the 140 traffic and the Valley's parking does not know the road is closed.

A room in Mariposa as the base for several days in the Valley. This is the decision. Two hours and more each way, every day, turns a Valley base into a long commute, and the honest arithmetic is that a three-night Mariposa stay behind a closure costs you the better part of a day in the car that a room in Oakhurst or Groveland would give back. Whether a move is possible depends on three things this article cannot know: what your Mariposa booking's cancellation terms are, how long Caltrans is saying the closure will hold, and what is available on your dates on the other side. The first is on your confirmation. The second is on Caltrans's QuickMap and in its advisories, and the March 2025 slide is the pattern to plan around: the initial notice gave no reopening timeframe at all, and the road came back under one-way control nine days later. The third is the part worth checking before you decide anything, because in high season the answer is often that there is nothing to move to.

If you do move, move toward the gate you will use. Oakhurst for a Valley trip, because the 41 approach is the one that arrives at Tunnel View and the Grove; Groveland only if the high country was the point. Fish Camp, at the park line on 41, is the closest bed to the South Entrance. The in-park options are the ones a closure cannot touch at all, and they are booked months out; the in-park guide has the calendar.

#### Checking the other side of the closure

Oakhurst is the base for the southern detour, and whether a move makes sense depends entirely on what is open on your dates. Search it before you cancel anything. Groveland is the equivalent for the northern gate.

Search Oakhurst lodging →
Where to stay: every option compared

Availability links are affiliate links. The recommendations do not change for them. Disclosure.

And do not cancel a Mariposa room for a one-day closure. Rock work, a short fire, a downed line: plenty of 140 closures are measured in hours or a day, and the town is a fine place to wait one of those out. It is the multi-day closures, the slides and the big fires, that change the shape of a trip, and Caltrans's advisories say which kind this is as soon as its engineers have looked at the road.

### Winter is the serious case

Every closure above was a nuisance in summer and would have been something else in January. Highway 140 is the winter road because it is the low road: when it is shut in winter, the detours are the two approaches that climb higher and ice sooner, and the winter guide is blunt about what that means. From roughly November through March, chain control can go up on any road into the park, the law requires you to carry chains when it does, even in a four-wheel drive with snow tires, and rangers turn cars around at the checkpoints. A winter 140 closure therefore has a second question behind the first: not only can you get around, but is the car you are driving allowed up the road you are being sent to. Carry chains on any winter trip whatever the forecast says, so that a closure notice sends you to Oakhurst and not home.

January 2017 is the case to remember. Rockfalls and snow closed 140 and 120 on the same morning and left Highway 41 as the only vehicle route into the Valley, with ranger convoys through the closed roads at set hours. A month later the storm damage had flipped it, and 140 was the only road in. Winter closures come in sets, and the road that is open at breakfast may not be the one that is open at dinner.

### The bus does not outrun the barricade

YARTS runs the Highway 140 route from Merced through Catheys Valley, Mariposa, Midpines and El Portal to Yosemite Valley in every season, and it is the only one of its four routes that runs in winter. It is the answer to the entrance line, the parking, and the chains; the transit guide makes the case in full. It is not an answer to a closed road. The bus drives the same pavement the cars do, and when Caltrans closes the canyon the 140 route runs as far as the last open stop and turns around: in March 2025 YARTS said its riders could get only as far as the Bug hostel at Midpines, and during the Colorado Fire YARTS posted a service change on the route and reported full service restored on the afternoon of September 4. A rider in the Valley with a ticket down to Merced on a closure day has the same two choices as a driver: wait for the road, or go out the other way.

The other way exists, in season. The Highway 41 route from Fresno runs May 22 to September 25 in 2026, and the Highway 120 route from Sonora runs May 22 to September 30, so a summer rider stranded in the Valley can reach Fresno's airport and Amtrak station on the 41 bus and connect from there. In winter there is no second bus, which is one more reason the winter case is the serious one. Fares on the 140 route are 22 dollars from Merced, 12 from Mariposa, and 8 from El Portal, one way, with the park entrance fee not included, and YARTS answers its phone at 877-989-2787. Call before you walk to the stop.

### How to check, in the right order

The confusion on a closure morning is that two agencies cover two different sets of miles and neither one's page tells you about the other's. Highway 140 outside the park boundary is Caltrans's road. From Arch Rock to the Valley it is the El Portal Road, and it belongs to the Park Service. A closure at Briceburg will not appear on the park's road-status table, which will say, truthfully, that the El Portal Road is open. Check both, in this order.

- Caltrans, for the road outside the park. QuickMap, at quickmap.dot.ca.gov, is the live map of every state highway with closures, chain controls and incidents drawn on it, and roads.dot.ca.gov gives the same information as a text list by highway number, which is faster on a poor connection: enter 140. Mariposa County's visitor office also lists the Caltrans highway information line, 1-800-427-7623. The initial closure advisory will name the two barricades, which is the fact you need from it.
- The park, for the road inside it. The current-conditions page at nps.gov/yose lists every park road's status and the current roadwork, and the recorded line at 209-372-0200, press 1 then 1, carries the same. This is also where the entrance you are being detoured to will show its own restrictions, like the Big Oak Flat Road delays.
- Cal Fire, if it is a fire. The incident page at fire.ca.gov is where the acreage, the containment, the evacuation zones and the road closures are posted and dated, and it is the record every news story is quoting. It is updated in rounds, so a closure lifted at four in the afternoon may not be on it until the next update.
- YARTS, if you are riding. The phone number above, and the service notices on its site.
- The lodge. They know which side of the barricade they are on and how their guests got in today.

The conditions page here keeps the webcams and the entrance-wait links on one screen, and the Park Bulletin carries the standing roadwork and alerts from the current park newspaper, which is the right place for the delays that last for weeks and the wrong place for the closure that happened at lunch. For that, go to Caltrans first.

### The rock shed, and the next five years

The 2006 Ferguson slide is the reason the canyon has a signal-controlled one-lane section at all, and the permanent fix is finally under way. Caltrans's Ferguson Rock Shed Project builds a protective structure of eleven pre-cast concrete segments, about 675 feet long and 40 feet wide inside, on the highway's original alignment, and removes the temporary one-lane bridges that traffic has used for twenty years. The first phase removed 320,000 tons of slide material. The construction of the shed itself is a 285-million-dollar job that Caltrans schedules to begin in summer 2026 and to take five years, which puts completion at the start of the next decade.

For a visitor that means two things. The one-lane signal near El Portal stays until the shed is finished, so the 140 approach carries a few minutes of waiting at the signal on every trip. And a construction site inside an active slide zone will generate planned closures and one-way controls of its own, on top of the unplanned ones this article has been about. Caltrans announces those in advance with the hours stated, and they show on QuickMap like anything else. The road that closes without a schedule is about to also close on one. Look at the map the week before, and again the morning of, and go in by whichever gate is open with the car already carrying chains, a full tank from Mariposa or Oakhurst, and a plan for the day that does not depend on the hour you arrive.

The fires that close the 140 corridor are also the fires that fill the park with smoke, so a road closure and a bad air day are often the same week; the smoke-season guide covers the second half of that problem. If you would rather sit out a closure in the northern gateway instead, Groveland lodging is the Highway 120 equivalent of the Oakhurst search above.

## Los Angeles to Yosemite: The Drive and Where to Break It

URL: https://thetalusfieldjournal.com/articles/yosemite-from-los-angeles
Section: Planning. Published: 2026-09-03. Last updated: 2026-09-03.
Summary: Los Angeles to Yosemite: the real drive time, the I-5/99/41 route, when to leave, where to stay on the way, winter chains, the 395 alternative, and the train.

Los Angeles is the largest city within a day's drive of this park, and it is the one whose visitors arrive with the least accurate picture of the drive. The map shows a straight run up the middle of the state. The routing app quotes something under five hours. And every summer a great many people leave the San Fernando Valley at nine in the morning, expecting lunch in Yosemite Valley, and reach the South Entrance in the middle of the afternoon with the Valley's parking already full and the best of the light already gone. The distance is not the problem. The shape of the drive is.

So here is the drive as it actually is, in the order it comes at you: the number to plan around, the four pieces of road, when to leave, where to break the trip, what winter does to it, the eastern alternative that is worth knowing about and usually not worth taking, and the version without a car.

### The number that decides everything

The Park Service's own directions page puts Yosemite Valley at 313 miles and six hours from the Los Angeles area, by I-5 north to Highway 99 north to Highway 41 north through Fresno. That figure is to the Valley floor, not to the park boundary, and the distinction is the whole article. The South Entrance is where the fee gets paid; the Valley is where nearly everyone is going, and the last leg between them is slow mountain road. From Fresno alone the Park Service quotes 94 miles and two hours fifteen minutes to the Valley, which is a good deal longer per mile than anything south of it.

Treat six hours as the clear-conditions floor, not the estimate. It assumes you clear the Los Angeles basin before the freeways fill, stop once, and meet no line at the gate. Add a proper breakfast, a fuel stop, an entrance queue on a summer weekend, and the twenty minutes at Tunnel View that nobody skips, and a realistic door-to-trailhead figure is seven hours. Yosemite Valley is also about seven miles long, and a time quoted to the Valley means its west end: Curry Village, the Happy Isles trailhead, and the east-end lots are another fifteen or twenty minutes on, plus parking.

Six hours is the number the park quotes. Seven is the number to plan a day around. Neither one leaves room for a day trip.

That last clause is the point. The Bay Area day trip is a marginal proposition at four to five hours each way. At six or seven, it is not a proposition at all. Yosemite from Los Angeles is a two-night trip at minimum, and the whole question is how to spend the first day so that the driving buys something.

### The road, in four pieces

The Grapevine. I-5 leaves the basin over Tejon Pass, a little above four thousand feet, and this is the one part of the drive that behaves like mountain road in the wrong season. In a winter storm the pass closes outright rather than going to chain control, sometimes for hours, and the closure holds every northbound car in Los Angeles County until the ice is gone. From roughly November into March, check the pass before you leave, not at the bottom of it. The rest of the year it is some forty miles of grade and truck traffic and nothing more.

Highway 99. Where I-5 and 99 split at the foot of the Grapevine, take 99. It runs through Bakersfield and Fresno on the flat floor of the San Joaquin Valley: two lanes each way, heavy with trucks, and featureless enough that the temptation is to make time. Two things worth knowing. The first is that the Fresno interchange with Highway 41 is well signed and easy, which is more than can be said for the Bakersfield stretch, where 99 threads through the city and the lane discipline is poor. The second is tule fog, the ground fog that settles over the Valley floor after rain in the wet months, roughly November through February. It can take visibility from a quarter mile to a few car lengths in seconds, it is worst overnight and in the early morning, and the Highway 99 corridor south of Fresno is where the multi-car pileups happen. If you are leaving Los Angeles at four in the morning in January, you are driving into it at exactly the wrong hour. Leave later, or accept a slow and cautious run through Tulare County.

Highway 41. Off 99 at Fresno, this is the road that does the climbing. It leaves the flat of the Valley floor, crosses the foothills through Coarsegold, reaches Oakhurst at about 2,300 feet, and then climbs in earnest through Fish Camp to the South Entrance. Oakhurst is the last full town: the last full-size supermarket, the last real choice of fuel. Fish Camp, twelve miles on at the park line, is a resort and a handful of inns. Inside the park, gas is available at Wawona, Crane Flat, and El Portal 24 hours a day by credit card, and nowhere in Yosemite Valley, so fill the tank in Oakhurst regardless of what the gauge says.

The Wawona Road. The Park Service's name for Highway 41 inside the boundary. The Mariposa Grove welcome plaza is the first right after the entrance station, less than a quarter mile in; Wawona itself, with its store, its gas pump, and its closed hotel, is six miles on; and then the road runs another hour of curves north through forest with almost nothing to see, until it enters the Wawona Tunnel, built in 1933 and close to a mile long. The tunnel's east portal is Tunnel View. El Capitan on the left, Bridalveil Fall on the right, Half Dome at the back of the frame, and parking on both sides of the road. It is the best orientation to the Valley's geography that exists, it is free, and it belongs to the southern approach alone: the 140 and 120 routes reach the Valley floor without it. Whatever else the six hours cost, they buy you this arrival.

Photo: Aniket Deole / Unsplash

### When to leave

The constraint at the far end is parking, not daylight. In 2026 there is no day-use reservation to hold, and the park manages the season with staffed intersections and monitoring rather than a gate count. What that has produced on the busiest summer weekends is Valley day-use lots full somewhere between seven and eight in the morning, which is an hour that no car leaving Los Angeles the same day can reach. The parking guide covers what to do once you are in; the point here is that the arrival hour is decided before you leave home.

Three honest shapes for the first day:

- Drive up and sleep in Oakhurst or Fish Camp. Leave Los Angeles at any civilized hour, arrive in the late afternoon, eat, and be at the South Entrance the next morning before the gate has a line. This is the version that works on a summer weekend, and it is the one I recommend to nearly everyone.
- Drive straight through, midweek, and make the Grove the first stop. Leave before five, arrive at the welcome plaza by late morning, take the free shuttle up to the sequoias, and reach the Valley in the mid-afternoon when the morning's cars are starting to leave. This works on a Tuesday in June. It does not work on a Saturday in July.
- Drive straight through with a Valley bed booked. If you hold a room or a campsite inside the park, arrival hour matters much less, because your parking comes with the reservation. Arrive when you arrive, and use the evening. The catch is that in-park lodging books out months ahead; see where to stay in Yosemite for how far ahead, and by which website.

On this drive, midweek decides whether the straight-through plan works at all.

### Where to break the drive

The southern approach has a natural overnight, which is one of its real advantages over the Bay Area routes. Oakhurst is the largest gateway town by population and amenities, with more chain lodging and chain dining than the other four combined, a full supermarket for the cooler, and the South Entrance twenty to twenty-five minutes up the road. It is not charming. It is convenient, predictable, and on the way, and for a party arriving tired from Los Angeles those are the qualities that matter. The Valley is seventy-five to ninety minutes beyond it, which is the number that makes Oakhurst a good first night and a poor base for a Valley-centered trip: three hours of driving a day is what booking there for a week costs.

Fish Camp, at the park line, is the closer option on this corridor: Tenaya Lodge at Yosemite, a full resort two miles from the gate, plus a few small inns. It trades Oakhurst's services for setting and puts you four minutes from the entrance station. Wawona, six miles inside the park, would be the obvious third choice, and its historic hotel is closed. It shut on December 2, 2024, for a comprehensive condition assessment after a roof project turned up problems, and as of this writing the concessioner lists no reopening date. The Wawona store and gas pump are open; the hotel is not, and any listing that suggests otherwise is stale.

Fresno is the fallback, and the airport city. It puts the South Entrance about an hour and a quarter away and the Valley about two hours fifteen minutes, and it is the right overnight only if you are flying in late or the mountain towns are full. Everything on the flat is cheaper and less interesting than everything on the hill.

Photo: Nieves / Pexels

#### The first night, on the way

An Oakhurst or Fish Camp bed turns a seven-hour push into an afternoon drive and a morning at the gate before the line forms. The chain hotels along Highway 41 in Oakhurst are the deepest bench of rooms on any approach to the park, which is why they are usually the last to fill.

Search Oakhurst lodging →
Where to stay: every option compared

Availability links are affiliate links. The recommendations do not change for them. Disclosure.

### What winter does to this drive

Highway 41 stays open all year, and it is the road the Park Service names first when it lists where chains are required most often. Its standing language is that chains are required more often on the Wawona Road, the Big Oak Flat Road from the west, and the Badger Pass Road than on the Highway 140 approach or the roads inside the Valley, that chain requirements are expected from November through March, and that they can arrive as early as September or as late as May. The rules themselves are covered in the winter guide; the two that catch drivers from Los Angeles are that every vehicle must carry chains when controls are in effect, four-wheel drives and rentals included, and that rangers turn cars around at the checkpoint. A rental picked up at LAX comes with all-season tires and no chains, and a rental company's all-wheel-drive badge does not satisfy the requirement. Buy a set that fits before you leave the flat, and practice fitting them in a dry parking lot rather than on the shoulder in the dark.

The winter alternative is to stay on Highway 99 past Fresno to Merced and take Highway 140 up the Merced River canyon to the Arch Rock Entrance. It is the lowest and most reliable approach to the park, it sees chain control least often, and the Park Service quotes it at 81 miles and two hours from Merced to the Valley. It costs you the Grove, Wawona, and the Tunnel View arrival, and it adds distance on the flat while subtracting it on the mountain. On a stormy week in January that is a trade worth making; the entrances guide has the full comparison. The rest of the year, 41 is the road.

Check three things on a winter morning, in this order: the Grapevine, the tule fog forecast for the San Joaquin Valley, and the park's own road line, 209-372-0200, then 1 and 1. Caltrans's statewide line is 800-427-7623. The conditions page keeps the webcams and the forecast links in one place.

### The eastern road, and when it is worth it

There is a second way to Yosemite from Los Angeles, and every summer someone recommends it as the scenic route without mentioning what it asks. Highway 14 north through Mojave to US 395, then up the east side of the Sierra past Lone Pine, Bishop, and Mammoth Lakes to Lee Vining, and finally Highway 120 west over Tioga Pass, at 9,945 feet the highest highway pass in California. It is a superb drive. It is also longer than Highway 41 on the odometer, slower per mile, and it delivers you to the wrong end of the park: from Lee Vining the Valley is about 75 miles and ninety minutes at a minimum over the Tioga Road, with no gas between Lee Vining and Crane Flat, and the stops that make the road famous, Tuolumne Meadows, Tenaya Lake, Olmsted Point, each add half an hour you will not resist.

Then there is the season. The Park Service's standing description is that Tioga Road is typically open to vehicles from late May or June until sometime in November; in 2026 it opened on May 15, unusually early. Outside that window the road does not exist as far as your itinerary is concerned, and the Park Service's own detour from Lee Vining to the Valley with the pass closed runs to 390 or 410 miles and eight hours, north to Minden, Nevada, then over the Carson Range and back down the west slope. Nobody should discover that at Lee Vining in April.

When the eastern road earns its place: when the high country is the point of the trip rather than the Valley, when you are making a loop, in over Tioga and out through the South Entrance or the reverse, or when you can spare a night in the Eastern Sierra on the way. A day in Tuolumne Meadows makes the case for the first of those. For a straight Valley trip in the summer window, 41 remains faster, simpler, and cheaper in fuel, and it is the road to take.

### Without a car

Two versions, and both are better than they sound.

The train. Amtrak's San Joaquins do not reach Los Angeles by rail; the Los Angeles leg is an Amtrak Thruway bus from Union Station to Bakersfield, where the train takes over north through the Valley to Merced, and at Merced the YARTS bus up Highway 140 completes the trip to the Valley floor, year-round. It is a long day of connections, and it delivers you to the shuttle line in the Valley with no car to park, which on a summer weekend is worth more than it costs. Whether the YARTS fare covers the park entrance fee is a question the park's pages and YARTS's own currently answer differently; the shuttle and YARTS guide lays out both positions, and the conservative advice is to budget for the fee and treat a wave-through as a bonus.

The plane. Fresno Yosemite International is the closest commercial airport to the park, a short hop from LAX, and in summer YARTS runs a Highway 41 bus straight from it. The 2026 season runs from May 22 through September 25, with two morning departures from Fresno, calling at the Fresno Amtrak station, the airport, north Fresno, Coarsegold, Oakhurst, Tenaya Lodge, the Mariposa Grove, and the Wawona store before reaching the Valley, with two returns in the late afternoon and evening. The published fare to Yosemite Valley is $20 one way and $40 round trip for an adult, reduced fares for seniors, children, and veterans, children five and under free, and one child aged six to twelve free with each paying adult. Reservations are taken online and walk-ons ride as space permits. Outside that window the Fresno leg needs a rental car, and the rental car needs chains.

Photo: YARTS

### What the trip costs at the gate

The park entrance fee is $35 per private vehicle, good for seven consecutive days, and $20 per person for anyone arriving on foot, by bicycle, or on a non-commercial bus. An America the Beautiful annual pass covers the vehicle fee. There is no reservation fee in 2026 because there is no reservation. Fuel, food, and the night in Oakhurst are the real costs, and the trip budget works through them for a range of party sizes.

### The shape of the trip that works

Put it together and the Los Angeles trip has a natural order that the other approaches do not. Drive up the first afternoon and sleep in Oakhurst or Fish Camp. Be through the South Entrance early the next morning, park at the Mariposa Grove welcome plaza, and take the shuttle up to the sequoias while the grove is still cool and quiet. Drive the Wawona Road north in the late morning, stop at Tunnel View, and arrive on the Valley floor for the afternoon and evening, when the day-trippers are leaving and the light on the north wall is doing its best work. Give the Valley the whole of the next day. Leave on the third morning, early, down the same road, with the Grapevine and the 405 still ahead of you but nothing you have not already done once.

Two nights is the minimum that makes the drive pay. Three is the trip. The three-to-five-day plan adds Glacier Point and the high country in the seasons that have them; the planning guide will build the read list for your dates. And whichever version you choose, check the Park Bulletin the night before you leave, because a road that was open last week is the one thing on this list that can change.

## Yosemite Facelift: How to Volunteer for the Park Cleanup

URL: https://thetalusfieldjournal.com/articles/yosemite-facelift-volunteer-guide
Section: Planning. Published: 2026-08-31. Last updated: 2026-09-09.
Summary: How to volunteer for the Yosemite Facelift: 2026 dates, registration, camping, what volunteers do, and how to fit it into a normal trip.

The current Park Bulletin edition ends with a line easy to skim past: looking just past this edition, the Yosemite Facelift, the park's biggest volunteer cleanup, runs the last week of September, free with registration. It reads like a footnote, but the event has grown into the largest volunteer stewardship event held in any national park. No experience is required, no gear is required, and you do not need to be a climber, despite the event's roots. This guide covers the schedule, registration, camping, and what a first-timer should expect.

### What the Facelift actually is

The Yosemite Facelift started in 2004 as a one-day cleanup organized by climber Ken Yager and the Yosemite Climbing Association, a response to the trash accumulating in the meadows, along the roads, and at the base of the big walls after a summer of heavy use. It has run every September since, grown from a single day to five, and grown from a climbers' project into a parkwide event that draws families, retirees, college groups, and first-time visitors alongside the climbing community that founded it. The Yosemite Climbing Association still organizes it, in partnership with the National Park Service, and the event is now widely described, by the Park Service among others, as the largest volunteer stewardship event held in any national park. Since 2004, volunteers have removed more than a million pounds of trash and debris from the park and surrounding public land, along with hundreds of specialized high-angle cleanup projects on the granite walls.

The timing is deliberate. Late September sits right after the park's heaviest visitation and right before the roads start closing down for the season, which makes it the one week that catches a full summer's accumulated litter before the snow buries it and before another year of foot traffic grinds it further into the trail tread. It is also one of the best weeks of the year to actually be in Yosemite: the crowds that peaked in July and August have thinned since Labor Day, the light is lower and better for photographs, and the high country is usually still fully open. The Facelift did not choose this week for the hiking, but volunteers benefit.

Photo: Cory Goehring

### This year's dates, and how the week is organized

The 2026 Facelift runs September 23 through 27, five days that land squarely in the park's best shoulder-season week: after Labor Day thins the crowds, before the High Sierra Camps and the Tuolumne store finish closing out the season. Each day follows roughly the same shape. Registration and cleanup projects run from 8 am to 4 pm, based out of a check-in area on the Mall near the Yosemite Valley Visitor Center, with additional check-in points at Crane Flat and in Tuolumne Meadows later in the week. A raffle with donated gear runs from 5 to 6 pm. Evening programs, films, guest speakers, and sponsor booths, run from 7 to 10 pm, usually in the auditorium near the Visitor Center; past programs have featured well-known climbers including Alex Honnold and Tommy Caldwell, though the specific evening lineup is not finalized until close to the event. You do not need to attend every day, or stay for the evenings, to take part.

### How to register

Registration is free and has to be on file before you're assigned to a project: YCA's own sign-up form, plus the National Park Service's Volunteer Agreement, the standard form for anyone doing volunteer work inside the park. That does not mean you had to plan ahead. Online registration closes shortly before the event, and once it does, walk-up volunteers are still welcome: you register in person at the Yosemite Village Mall, where the tables open at 8 a.m. Wednesday through Saturday and 8 a.m. to noon on Sunday, and pick a project from there. Beyond that, there is no minimum commitment. Volunteers can show up for an hour, a single day, or the full week, and the organizers are explicit that every contribution counts, whether that's one afternoon on the Valley Loop Trail or all five days on a high-angle wall crew. A smaller group of core volunteers commits to being available most of each day to staff the registration tables, weigh and sort collected trash, hand out litter-pickers and bags, or lead a project; that role is by request, not a requirement to participate at all.

### What volunteers actually do

Most projects are straightforward: litter pickup and roadside cleanup along the park's trails, campgrounds, meadows, and waterways, using pickers, bags, and safety vests supplied by the National Park Service's volunteer office at check-in. You show up, get assigned an area, and spend the day walking it. Registration staff sort volunteers into projects each morning, and the areas rotate through the week so the same stretch of road or trail isn't worked twice while another goes untouched. For everyone with no rope training or climbing background, and that is most people who show up, the trailside and roadside projects are the bulk of the week, and they need no prior experience: a pair of gloves, closed-toe shoes, and a willingness to bend over repeatedly for a few hours.

### Inside the specialized cleanup: what comes off the walls

Alongside the roadside work, a smaller number of specialized high-angle cleanup projects put experienced climbers to work with the park's Climbing Management team, rappelling into the base and lower faces of walls like El Capitan to remove gear left behind by climbers over the season. Those projects are self-selecting: you need the rope skills and your own systems to be on one, and nobody is assigned to a wall crew who hasn't done that kind of work before. What comes down is a specific kind of trash that a roadside picker never sees. Reporting on past Facelifts has documented abandoned portaledges, static ropes, and full camping setups stashed under boulders near the base of the wall, along with more ordinary litter, water bottles and food wrappers, that migrated up into terrain nobody walks. It is the part of the event that gets the most attention from climbing media, and it is the smallest slice of the week's actual volunteer hours; the roadside and trail crews move the real tonnage.

### What to bring, and what's provided

The National Park Service's volunteer office supplies the core gear at check-in: litter pickers, trash bags, and safety vests. What you bring yourself is the same list as any day outside in the Sierra in late September: closed-toe shoes you don't mind getting dirty, work gloves if you have them, sun protection, a layer for the cooler mornings, and water. The park's own guidance for anyone working outdoors here holds during Facelift week the same as any other: carry roughly a quart of water per person for every two hours on your feet, more in direct sun. If your group is camping through the week rather than day-tripping in, everything from the site's camping guide applies, food storage rules included; a Facelift campsite is still a Yosemite campsite, bears and all.

### Where you camp

Facelift volunteers camp alongside everyone else in the park's standard campgrounds, with several set aside specifically for the event: Camp 4, Upper Pines, and Crane Flat in the Valley area, plus overflow at Tamarack and in Tuolumne Meadows for anyone working the high-country projects later in the week. Camp 4, the walk-in campground long associated with Yosemite's climbing community, hosts a block of Facelift campers each year, with event hosts on site to help newcomers find a spot. Yellow Pines, a campground the National Park Service normally does not open to the general public, is reserved as the event's dedicated volunteer campground and includes group sites for larger crews. Facelift sites are deliberately shared rather than assigned to one party, which the organizers present as a way to meet other volunteers, and at Upper Pines and Crane Flat there is a two-car limit per site. Standard per-night campground fees apply throughout, the same as any other Yosemite reservation, and requests for the event's dedicated camping blocks typically open each spring, historically the first of May. Yosemite Climbing Association members get priority access to those blocks, which is worth knowing if you're planning to come every year rather than just this one.

If you would rather sleep in a bed than a shared Camp 4 site, one lodge has built an offer around the event. Rush Creek Lodge, on Highway 120 just outside the Big Oak Flat entrance, runs a Facelift lodging package with its sister property, Evergreen Lodge: a guest at either lodge who volunteers is offered a complimentary spa day use at Rush Creek, magnesium foot soak included, on top of the room. There is no promo code; the lodge's standing rule applies, the earlier you book the lower the nightly rate. The same page lists a separate Groveland Facelift on September 12, a one-day cleanup of the gateway side of 120 that the lodge started with the Yosemite Climbing Association in 2022 and now runs with the US Forest Service, with coffee and pastries in the morning and live music and prize drawings at the end of the day. For anyone coming in on 120 it is a warm-up for the main event, and the lodge asks that volunteers for either register through the Yosemite Climbing Association ahead of time, though day-of sign-up is accepted. Rush Creek has no arrangement with this site; it is here because it is the only lodging offer tied to the Facelift. How that stretch of 120 compares with the Mariposa and Oakhurst sides is in the gateway towns comparison.

Photo: US National Park Service / Wikimedia Commons (public domain)

### Families and first-timers

The event is explicitly family-oriented: parents bring kids, and the only formal requirement is a signed waiver for each participant under 18. There's no minimum age stated by the organizers, and the roadside and meadow cleanup projects are exactly the kind of task a kid can meaningfully help with, unlike a lot of the park's other volunteer opportunities. If you've never done anything like this before, the Facelift is built for that: check-in staff hand you gear, assign you a project, and the work itself, picking up trash along a trail you'd otherwise just be walking, requires no orientation beyond showing up. The park's other free programs are a good comparison point: like a ranger walk, the Facelift asks nothing of you going in except a few hours.

A ranger walk shows a visitor the park. A Facelift shift makes you a temporary member of the crew that keeps it running: sorting trash at the registration table, walking a mile of shoulder along Southside Drive, or hauling a bag out of a pullout that a hundred cars a day drive past without seeing. For a visitor who has already seen the main sights and wants a different reason to come back, it is a good one.

### What the week adds up to

The scale is bigger than the "cleanup" framing suggests. In 2023, 1,501 volunteers logged 12,151 hours and removed 10,432 pounds of trash and debris. In 2024, 1,337 volunteers put in more than 7,000 hours and removed 13,112 pounds. Those numbers move around year to year with weather and turnout, but the pattern holds: more than a thousand volunteers and five figures of trash in a single week. Since the event's founding in 2004, the cumulative total across all those Septembers passes a million pounds, which is the figure the Yosemite Climbing Association itself uses.

### Fitting it around the rest of your trip

The Facelift lands in the same week the site's September guide already covers, and the same conditions apply: the Tuolumne shuttle and hikers bus stop mid-month, the High Sierra Camps are closing out, and the Valley itself is at its quietest post-Labor Day version of the year. Fire restrictions are typically still in force this time of year, which matters if your group is planning a campfire after a day of trail work. If you're combining a Facelift day with hiking, note that the Mist Trail is closed between the Vernal Fall footbridge and the top of Vernal Fall on weekdays, Monday through Thursday from 7 a.m. to 3:30 p.m., through late October for repairs; the Mist Trail guide covers the detour. Check the current Park Bulletin the week you go for anything that's changed since this was written, road work, program schedules, and event details all shift closer to the date.

None of it requires you to plan a separate trip. A Facelift day slots into an ordinary Yosemite visit the way a ranger program does: pick a morning, show up at check-in, and spend a few hours on a project whose results you can see on the drive out.

## Bracebridge Dinner and Vintners' Holidays: An Honest Guide

URL: https://thetalusfieldjournal.com/articles/bracebridge-dinner-and-vintners-holidays
Section: Seasonal Guides. Published: 2026-08-27. Last updated: 2026-10-03.
Summary: Bracebridge Dinner and Vintners' Holidays, explained: what they cost, what's included, when tickets sell out, and whether they're worth it.

Two names turn up every year in the same searches: the Bracebridge Dinner and Vintners' Holidays. Both happen at the Ahwahnee. Both get described online as "iconic," "legendary," "bucket list." None of that tells you what the evening actually is, what it costs, or whether the tickets you want are still there to be had. They are two different events, on two different calendars, sold two different ways, and conflating them is how people book the wrong one or miss the window on both. What follows covers each event's format, cost, sale window, and whether it is worth the trip.

### Two events, not one

Vintners' Holidays runs in November: four multi-day sessions built around California winemakers, each ending in a five-course paired dinner. A session includes a "Meet the Vintners" opening reception, four tasting seminars led by the visiting winemakers, and the closing gala dinner, sold as a package with a room at the Ahwahnee, Yosemite Valley Lodge, or Curry Village. The session package and the room are booked separately, and the seminars are held in public space and open to the public.

The Bracebridge Dinner runs in December: a single, several-hours-long dinner theater pageant, staged repeatedly through the month in the Ahwahnee's Great Lounge and dining hall. It is Tudor-costumed, live-sung, built around a seven-course feast, and involves a cast and crew that runs past a hundred people. Unlike Vintners' Holidays, a Bracebridge ticket buys the performance and the meal only. A room at the Ahwahnee is a separate booking, and plenty of guests drive in for the evening and drive home after. The rest of the month, the roads, the chain rules and the holiday-week crowd, is in the December guide.

The overlap that confuses people: both are staged in the same building by the same concessioner, both are the kind of thing a magazine calls "a Yosemite Christmas tradition," and both get lumped into vague web copy that never says which one has a wine list and which one has a knight in it. They don't compete for the same night. They compete for the same kind of trip: one built around a single expensive evening instead of a week of trails.

What the Bracebridge Dinner actually contains, if the name means nothing to you: a cast of characters (a pious parson, a French chef, a wild Scottish cousin, a lusty widow of several husbands, and a Lord of Misrule who runs the room) leads guests through a procession of courses, including a boar's head and a baron of beef carried in by costumed servants, some of the props original to the 1920s production. A professional chorale sings carols between courses, there's a wassail bowl, and the whole thing runs about four hours. It is closer to theater than to dinner: a play that serves you seven courses.

### Where both of these came from

The Bracebridge Dinner is nearly a century old. The Ahwahnee opened in 1927, and the hotel's then-president, Donald Tresidder, wanted an opening-season holiday spectacle to match it. He hired pageant director Garnet Holme to build one around Washington Irving's Old Christmas at Bracebridge Hall, and the first dinner ran that December. Holme died in 1929; the hotel handed the rewrite to a young photographer who had been playing the production's "Lord of Misrule," and Ansel Adams's version of the script is substantially the one still performed. For decades the dinner was one of the hardest tickets in California: through 2002, roughly 2,000 seats a year were allotted by lottery against as many as 60,000 applications. The concessioner has since added performances and moved to first-come, first-served sales, which makes tickets easier to get but not cheaper.

Vintners' Holidays is younger and started smaller: a 1982 idea from the Ahwahnee's then-beverage manager and chief concierge to fill the hotel's slow weeks between the fall shoulder season and the December rush, built around a handful of visiting winemakers. It grew into a recurring, sponsor-driven program that now runs four sessions every November.

One historical wrinkle worth knowing if you read anything written between roughly 2016 and 2019: during that window, a trademark dispute with the park's former concessioner forced Yosemite Hospitality to rename the Ahwahnee "The Majestic Yosemite Hotel" and rebrand several of its programs. The dispute was resolved and the original names, including the Ahwahnee and the Bracebridge Dinner itself, came back into official use afterward. If you find an older review or brochure using the "Majestic" branding, it is describing the same place and the same dinner.

Photo: Chris Dunstan / Wikimedia Commons (public domain)

### What each one costs, and what the money buys

Vintners' Holidays packages, room included, have started somewhere north of $450 per person based on double occupancy in recent years; the exact number moves with which room category and which session you pick, and rises from there for the Ahwahnee's better rooms. That price covers the reception, all four seminars, the closing gala dinner, and the room itself for the length of the session. Measured against a standalone hotel stay plus a nice dinner out, it is not an outlandish add, since you are paying for a room you would have booked anyway plus an unusual set of wine programming.

The Bracebridge Dinner is the pricier evening on a per-hour basis, because you are buying only the performance and the meal. Tickets have run into the several hundreds of dollars per adult for years, and after the dinner's return in December 2024 following a five-year pause, reporting on that season put prices over $500 a person, with lower-priced passes for children. That buys a few hours. It does not include a room, and there is no discount for guests already staying at the hotel.

Both events run through the same channel, travelyosemite.com or 888-413-8869, which is also the number the Field Guide's own Park Bulletin lists for park lodging generally. Neither ticket type shows up on the general lodging-availability tools that cover the gateway towns; they are inventory the concessioner controls directly.

### What books out first

The two events sell out on different schedules. Bracebridge Dinner tickets typically go on sale eight to nine months before the December performances, which for a given year lands around March or April, and they have sold out every year since the dinner's return. If you are reading this in late summer hoping to walk into a December seat, expect the good dates, and often all of them, to be gone by the time the leaves turn. The dinner also runs on a fixed schedule of specific performance nights across the month, roughly every other day from early to late December, so there is no such thing as "just show up on a slow Tuesday": every night is its own sold ticket allotment.

The 2026 dinners run on eight nights: December 8, 10, 12, 14, 16, 18, 20 and 22, all at the Ahwahnee, according to the concessioner's ticket page. The Madera County visitors bureau bills this season's as the 99th Bracebridge Dinner. As of October 3, the page marked December 12 sold out and four more nights almost sold out or going fast. Tickets, and the Bracebridge lodging packages that pair a room with a performance night, are on travelyosemite.com or at 888-413-8869.

Vintners' Holidays lodging books on the same 366-day window as any other Ahwahnee, Lodge, or Curry Village reservation, one year and a day ahead, rolling. That means the November session dates open to booking roughly a year before each one runs, and the same logic the Field Guide has laid out for in-park lodging generally applies here without modification: set a reminder for the morning that window opens if your dates are fixed, and if you miss it, check back regularly. Cancellations happen continuously, with a real wave in the final weeks before any date, and a Vintners' Holidays package that shows sold out in July can have space again in September.

If you want this December's Bracebridge Dinner and you haven't already booked it, you are likely working the cancellation list, not the original sale. If you want next December's, the move is to watch for tickets to go on sale in the spring and buy immediately. Vintners' Holidays gives you more runway either way, since it rides the same rolling booking window as a normal room, and cancellations reward the same persistence.

Photo: Ahmed Radwan / Wikimedia Commons (CC0)

### What the park is actually like that week

Neither event happens in isolation from the season around it. Tioga Road and the upper stretch of Glacier Point Road are typically closed by November, chain requirements on the Valley approach roads are a real possibility on any given night, and the days are short: the sun is down well before five in December, and the drive out after a late Bracebridge performance is a dark, possibly icy, mountain drive. The winter guide covers what's open, what's closed, and how the chain rules actually work, and it is worth reading before you commit to a same-day drive-in-drive-out Bracebridge trip rather than staying the night. If dinner is the whole point of the visit, book a room: the biggest risk in the plan is the road afterward.

### Is it worth it

For the right trip, yes, with conditions attached. Neither event is manufactured hotel programming: Vintners' Holidays is real access to working winemakers in small-group seminars, and the Bracebridge Dinner is a nearly century-old theatrical production that exists nowhere else, with a cast size no $500 restaurant tasting menu matches. If the occasion justifies the spend (an anniversary, a milestone birthday, a new family tradition), both deliver something a normal trip here does not.

They are not the way to introduce a family to Yosemite for the first time, and they are not a budget trip by any definition; a standard visit here costs a fraction of either package. The Bracebridge Dinner in particular is not built for young children: the performance runs about four hours, the dress code is formal (a dark suit or cocktail dress at a minimum, tuxedos and gowns are common, and costumes on guests are discouraged since the cast is already wearing them), and most guidance around the event treats it as unsuited to kids under ten. Vintners' Holidays, being a room package built around wine seminars, is even less of a kids' event by design. They also are not primarily hiking trips: both happen in the shortest, darkest weeks of the year, with most of the high country locked behind winter road closures, so the days around the event are for the Valley floor, not the granite above it. If what you actually want is a normal winter visit to this park, at a normal winter price, the season itself is the better article to read, and a standard room at any of the Valley's lodges gets you the empty trails and the clearing-storm photographs without the four-figure evening.

If the Ahwahnee itself is sold out for the dates you want, whether for a Vintners' Holidays package or a room to pair with a Bracebridge ticket, the gateway towns are the fallback, though none of them replicate the point of either event, which is being inside the building where it happens. A live availability search around the park is the fastest way to see what's actually left on your dates before you decide the trip doesn't work this year. For a bite that doesn't require a costume or a wine glass, the Ahwahnee's dining room also runs its regular seasonal menu on nights neither event is happening, covered along with the rest of the Valley's kitchens in the Field Guide's restaurant guide.

#### Before you write off this season

The Ahwahnee itself books through the concessioner, not here. But if it's full for your dates and a gateway-town stay would still make the trip work, this is a two-minute way to see what's actually open nearby.

## Yosemite fire restrictions: what's banned, what still works

URL: https://thetalusfieldjournal.com/articles/yosemite-fire-restrictions-explained
Section: Planning. Published: 2026-08-24. Last updated: 2026-10-03.
Summary: Yosemite's Stage 1 fire restrictions, explained: what's banned below 8,000 feet, what still works, and how to check before your trip.

You bought a bundle of firewood at the gas station in Mariposa, because that is what you do before a Yosemite camping trip. You get to the site, unload the cooler, and find a ranger notice zip-tied to the fire ring: no wood fires until further notice. The bundle rides home unopened. Yosemite is under Stage 1 fire restrictions right now, and every summer a fresh set of visitors arrives not knowing that the rules changed since the last time they camped here, or that they ever change at all.

The restrictions are not complicated once someone lays them out, but nobody hands you the list at the entrance station. Here is what is banned, what still works, why the line sits where it does, and how to check whether any of this has changed by the time your trip starts.

### What is in effect right now

Yosemite implemented Stage 1 fire restrictions at 12:01 a.m. on Friday, August 7, 2026, parkwide below 8,000 feet in elevation. The park cited hot, dry weather, low fuel moisture, and windy conditions raising the potential for fast wildfire growth, on the recommendation of the Yosemite Fire Program. The restrictions apply until further notice, which in practice means until conditions improve enough for the park to lift them, not on a fixed calendar date.

This is separate from, and layered on top of, the small lightning-caused fires that made news partway through August. An early-morning storm on August 12 started eight fires in the park, including ones near Aspen Valley, Dewey Point, and Wawona Road; the largest reported was a couple of acres. None triggered evacuations or site closures. They did not cause the ban. They came from the same dry conditions that triggered the restrictions a few days earlier, and they help explain why the park is in no hurry to lift it.

The rule has a cost when it is ignored. The Dome Fire was reported on the morning of September 15, about a quarter mile north of Chilnualna Falls above Wawona, while the restrictions were in force. On September 30 the local press reported that the Forest Service has found it human-caused, sparked by an abandoned campfire; the federal incident page still lists the cause as undetermined. The fire has closed Glacier Point Road and the Ostrander Lake Trail and everything south of it, and two helicopter pilots were killed fighting it on September 20. The Park Bulletin carries the closures as they stand, and Yosemite in October 2026 covers what the fire means for a trip this month.

### What is actually banned

Below 8,000 feet, parkwide: no building, maintaining, attending, or using a wood or charcoal fire, including twig stoves, the small backpacking stoves that burn sticks instead of fuel. That covers a campfire at your site, a charcoal grill, a hibachi, anything that burns solid fuel.

Smoking is restricted too. Below 8,000 feet, smoking is prohibited except inside an enclosed vehicle, inside a campground or picnic area where wood and charcoal fires are otherwise permitted, or in a posted designated smoking area. That is a real change from ordinary conditions, and it catches people who assume the fire rules and the smoking rules are the same thing. They are related, but the smoking rule is broader.

### What still works

You can still cook, and you can still have light and heat at your site. Portable stoves that burn pressurized gas, liquid fuel, or propane are permitted, and so are alcohol stoves, including the small tablet or cube stoves backpackers carry. If your plan for the trip was a camp stove for dinner and a headlamp for light, none of that changes.

Established fire rings in developed areas keep working, with one exception. Designated frontcountry campgrounds and picnic areas below 8,000 feet are exempt from the wood and charcoal ban, so a ring at Upper Pines or Wawona Campground can still hold a fire. Residential areas in the park's developed communities are exempt too, with one carve-out: in El Portal and Foresta, only charcoal fires are allowed, not wood, because those two communities carry the highest structure-fire exposure in the park. Everywhere else the exemption for residential and developed areas covers both.

Above 8,000 feet, in the wilderness, campfires are allowed in existing fire rings, up to 9,600 feet. That upper bound is a standing, year-round wilderness regulation rather than a fire-danger rule: above 9,600 feet, wood is scarce and slow to regenerate at that elevation, so fires are prohibited there regardless of fire restrictions. The 8,000-to-9,600-foot band is the one place in the park right now where a wood campfire, built in a ring that already exists, is legal. That is most of the high country above Tuolumne Meadows and along the Sierra crest, and almost none of the Valley, Wawona, or the areas most visitors camp in.

The Stage 1 restrictions in effect since August 7, 2026, by elevation, drawn from this article. The 8,000-foot line is set each season and can move; the park's fire restrictions page has the current text.

Photo: Cory Goehring

### Two rules, not one, and they are not the same rule

Even outside fire restrictions, Yosemite Valley and Hodgdon Meadow run a standing seasonal rule: from May through September, wood fires there are allowed only in the evening, roughly 5 to 10 p.m. That rule exists for air quality, not fire danger. The Valley is a granite trough that traps cold air and smoke overnight, and a hundred and fifty morning campfires produce a haze the whole floor has to breathe. The campground guide covers that rule for a normal summer.

Stage 1 restrictions cancel that evening window. Right now, in the Valley and at Hodgdon Meadow, there is no evening exception, because the wood-fire ban is total below 8,000 feet regardless of the hour. When the restrictions lift, the standing evening-only rule comes back into force for whatever remains of the summer season.

### Why the line sits at 8,000 feet, and why it moves

Fuel moisture, the amount of water held in dead grass, brush, and duff, drops fastest at lower, hotter, drier elevations. The Valley floor and the foothill approaches dry out first and stay driest longest. The high country holds moisture later into the season, sees fewer visitors overall, and has a shorter, cooler fire season by nature. Drawing the restriction line by elevation targets the most dangerous terrain instead of banning fires park-wide when only part of the park is at risk.

The number itself is not fixed. It reflects that year's conditions and gets set, and can be reset, by the park's fire managers as the season develops. In some past seasons the working elevation line has sat lower, closer to 6,000 feet, when conditions were more severe or a fire was actively burning nearby. In 2026 it is 8,000 feet. The mechanism is what stays constant: check the current line before you assume last year's trip rules still apply.

### How to check before you drive up

Three places, and check them close to your trip rather than when you booked it, because restrictions can tighten, loosen, or shift elevation with a week's notice.

The park's own fire restrictions page (nps.gov/yose/planyourvisit/firerestrictions.htm) states whatever is currently in effect, in the same terms used here. The current conditions page (nps.gov/yose/planyourvisit/conditions.htm) rolls fire restrictions in with road and trail status, so it is worth a look regardless. And the Park Bulletin on this site tracks what the current NPS Yosemite Guide edition says is happening, updated roughly every five weeks, alongside the day-to-day alerts that move faster than that. None of these substitute for the others; the fire restrictions page is the one with the actual rule text.

### What this means for your specific trip

Car camping in a Valley or Wawona campground. Bring a camp stove. Firewood bought at the gate is of no use right now. Marshmallows can be toasted over a canister stove, and a lot of campers do this anyway once they realize a stove is faster and does not leave you smelling like smoke in the tent.

Backpacking above 8,000 feet. You can build a fire in an existing ring, below 9,600 feet, if your route takes you that high. Most first and second nights out of trailheads at Tuolumne, Glacier Point Road, or the Valley rim start below that line, so plan on your stove for at least the early part of most routes. The backpacking guide covers permits, bear canisters, and the rest of what the paperwork does not tell you.

A day trip with a picnic. Grills in designated picnic areas are exempt, so a charcoal grill at a developed picnic site still works. A campfire ring you find along a trail or a beach that is not in a designated campground or picnic area does not count as an exemption, restrictions or not.

Smoking anywhere in the park below 8,000 feet. Car, permitted campground, or posted smoking area. Nowhere else, restrictions or not, and the fine-print addition during restrictions is that "permitted campground" now specifically means one where fires are still allowed under the current rules, which narrows the list.

### This is a different question from whether your trip will be smoky

The two get confused often, but different pages answer them. Fire restrictions are about ignition: whether you personally can start a flame. Smoke is about air quality: whether a fire burning somewhere else, in the park or upwind of it, is putting particulate into the air you are breathing. You can have a trip under full fire restrictions with perfectly clear skies, and you can have a trip with no restrictions at all where the Valley is gray from a fire three counties away. Neither condition predicts the other.

The smoke season guide covers the second question in full: how to read an AQI number, where in the park the air tends to be cleanest on a bad day, and when to flex your itinerary uphill. This piece only answers the first one. If you are checking one page before a late-summer trip, check both; a clean-air day can still be a no-campfire day, and a smoky day does not excuse a fire that restrictions do not allow.

### Violating the ban is not a technicality

Fire restriction violations are enforceable federal citations, and if an unattended or illegal fire escapes and requires a suppression response, the person responsible can be held liable for the cost of putting it out, which can far exceed any fine. Every fall, Yosemite's fire crews run planned burns specifically because prescribed fire keeps the forest from becoming the kind of fuel load that turns an escaped campfire into the summer's news story. A ranger who finds an unattended fire during Stage 1 restrictions is not treating it as a judgment call.

### When restrictions usually lift

Restrictions like this one typically go into effect in July, after a stretch of hot, dry weather has pushed fuel moisture down, and they come off when temperatures drop and real rain falls, not on a schedule. Historically, Yosemite has close to a 90 percent chance of a season-ending precipitation event, defined as two or more inches of rain, by October 31. Recent examples: fire restrictions were rescinded in September 2022 after a cooling, wetter pattern moved in, and again in late October 2021 after a combination of rain, snow, and cooler temperatures reduced the danger enough for the park to lift them. Most years land somewhere in that window: sometime after Labor Day, before Halloween, tied to whichever storm actually delivers.

That overlaps almost exactly with the shoulder season this site already covers in detail. The fall guide walks through the sequence of closures that follows Labor Day, and the smoke season guide covers the separate, related question of air quality when a fire is actually burning nearby. Fire restrictions, smoke, and the shoulder-season closures are separate but move on roughly the same schedule, and a September or early-October trip can run into any combination of the three.

### The practical version

Check the fire restrictions page in the days before you leave, not when you booked. Pack a camp stove regardless of what the restrictions say on the day you check, because conditions can tighten between booking and arrival. If a wood fire at 9 p.m. under the stars was the whole point of the trip for you, that experience is currently available only above 8,000 feet, in an existing ring, and it comes back everywhere else the week the park says the conditions allow it. Until then, cook on a stove.

- Fire Restrictions, NPS Yosemite
- Current Conditions, NPS Yosemite
- Yosemite Fire Information and Updates, NPS Yosemite
