## Yosemite itinerary for 3, 4 or 5 days: one park per day

URL: https://thetalusfieldjournal.com/articles/yosemite-in-three-to-five-days
Section: Planning. Published: 2026-08-23. Last updated: 2026-09-26.
Summary: A Yosemite itinerary for 3, 4, or 5 days: the Valley, Glacier Point, the Tioga high country, and Hetch Hetchy, one park per day, plus the winter version.

The third day changes a Yosemite trip. A one-day visit is triage, and we have argued at length that triage done early and done well is a great trip. A two-day visit is triage plus one earned view from above the Valley floor. On the third day, nothing is the only chance you will get. You can wait out a morning of weather, take the wrong turn, stay an extra hour at the place that turned out to be the point, and the trip absorbs it. Most of the bad advice about Yosemite itineraries comes from people planning day three the way you have to plan day one, as a checklist against a clock.

The organizing idea comes from the shape of the park: Yosemite is four parks under one name. The Valley is a canyon: you stand at the bottom of it and look up. The rim, the Glacier Point country, is the same canyon from the top edge, looking down. The high country along Tioga Road is a third landscape entirely, open granite and meadow at 8,600 feet. And the far corners, Wawona with its sequoias in the south and Hetch Hetchy in the northwest, are each most of a day by themselves because of where the roads go. These four are separated by an hour or two of mountain driving in directions that point away from each other. A trip of three to five days works when you give each one its own day and stop trying to splice them. One park per day.

### The roads decide the menu

First, the constraint. Two of the four parks hang off seasonal roads. Glacier Point Road typically opens in mid-to-late May; in 2026 it opened on May 9, and it closes for the winter with the first serious snow, typically in November. Tioga Road opened May 15 in 2026, unusually early, and closes with the first serious snow, typically in November. From roughly November into May, in a normal year, the menu is shorter: the Valley, Wawona, and Hetch Hetchy, which are exactly the plowed roads. The winter version of this itinerary is at the bottom of the piece, and it is a full trip.

So the first step in planning a three-to-five-day visit is checking which of the four parks your dates can reach. The trip selector does this arithmetic for you month by month, the Park Bulletin carries the current road status, and the Park Service's road line is the last word in the shoulder weeks. Every plan below assumes you have done that check.

### Day one: the Valley, exactly as if it were your only day

Day one does not change because you have more days behind it. Arrive before 8 a.m., park once, and work the floor: Tunnel View at first light, Bridalveil, the Lower Yosemite Fall loop, Cook's Meadow, then a slow hour on a rock by the Merced. That sequence, the reasoning behind it, and the things to refuse are the whole subject of the one-and-two-day guide, so it is not repeated here. Do that day as written.

The Valley goes first because it is the best orientation. The Valley teaches you the park's scale, its shuttle, its parking, and its light in one pass, at the bottom of the elevation ladder, on the day your legs are freshest and your alarm discipline is still intact. It is also the day most protected from weather: the floor is walkable in rain that would waste the rim. If your parking goes wrong or the day runs long, nothing downstream breaks, which is not true in the other direction.

One addition earns its place on a multi-day trip: end the day at Valley View or back at Tunnel View for last light. On a one-day visit that is a luxury against the drive home. On day one of four it is fifteen minutes, and it is the first time you will have seen the same stone in two different lights.

Photo: Joshua Earle / Unsplash

### Day two: the rim

Day two climbs to the top of the wall you spent yesterday underneath. Glacier Point Road leaves Wawona Road at Chinquapin and runs about seventeen miles to a paved overlook at 7,200 feet that puts you at eye level with Half Dome, with yesterday's entire itinerary laid out three thousand feet below you. The order of operations matters less than the two rules: bring water, because there is no drinking water at Glacier Point this season, and get up the road in the morning, because the point and its parking are a zoo by midday in summer.

The shape of the day: stop at Washburn Point first, the overlook a bend before Glacier Point that most cars skip, which trades the Valley view for the best roadside look at Vernal and Nevada Falls stacked in their granite staircase. Then Glacier Point itself, a 0.3-mile paved walk from the lot. Then back down the road a mile and a half to the shared trailhead for Sentinel Dome and Taft Point: about 2.2 miles round trip each, around five miles if you do both, one an open granite cap with a 360-degree horizon and the other a fissured ledge hanging straight over the Valley. Do both if the legs agree. Eat lunch on the rim. The long version of this day, including the sunrise variant, is in the Glacier Point Road guide.

Strong hikers have a second way to spend this day, and it is the best hard day in the park: up the Four Mile Trail from the Valley floor to Glacier Point and down the Panorama Trail past Illilouette and Nevada Falls, about thirteen miles and 3,200 feet of climbing, no car shuffle required. That is its own article, and on a five-day trip it arguably belongs on day four instead, with the driving version of the rim on day two. Either order works. Doing both versions is the kind of thing this trip finally has room for.

### Day three: the high country

Day three goes up, properly up. Tuolumne Meadows sits on Tioga Road roughly 55 to 60 miles from the Valley, call it an hour and a half each way without traffic and closer to two in July, and the drive is half the day: out of the forest, past Olmsted Point's straight look down Tenaya Canyon at the back of Half Dome, along the shore of Tenaya Lake, and out into a meadow system at 8,600 feet ringed by granite domes.

The high country rewards modesty. The marquee walks are short and flat because at this elevation you are already standing in the view: Pothole Dome at the meadow's west end, a mile round trip; Olmsted Point's half-mile nature trail; Soda Springs and Parsons Memorial Lodge, a flat mile and a half to naturally carbonated springs that children refuse to believe. Lembert Dome, 2.8 miles and 850 feet, is the earned view if you want one. The altitude is real and it is the thing that ruins high-country days: drink water, expect to move slower than the mileage suggests, and be off the open granite when the afternoon thunderheads build. The full day, including what is actually open up there this year, is in the Tuolumne guide, with Cathedral Lakes as the serious-hike upgrade.

When Tioga Road is closed, day three points south instead: the Mariposa Grove, an hour-plus from the Valley, where the parking sits two miles below the trees at the Welcome Plaza and a free shuttle covers the gap in season. The Grizzly Giant Loop, about two miles among trees that predate the Roman Empire, plus the Wawona Meadow Loop's flat 3.5 miles and a look at the covered bridge, is a full and unhurried day. In winter you walk the closed grove road itself, two quiet miles up, and usually have the Grizzly Giant to yourself.

Photo: Michael Hogarth / Wikimedia Commons (public domain)

### Day four: one far corner, or one serious hike

By day four the famous list is done. Spend the day on one thing; there are two candidates.

The far corner: Hetch Hetchy. The park's second glacial valley, an hour and three quarters from Yosemite Valley in the northwest corner, dammed in 1923 and still one of the best days in the park: across O'Shaughnessy Dam, through the tunnel, and along the north wall to the base of Wapama Falls, about five miles round trip of rolling trail with almost nobody on it. In spring the waterfalls are the equal of anything in the Valley; in July the draw is the lack of crowds. Two logistics rule the day: the access road runs on posted gate hours, roughly sunrise to sunset, and there is no food or fuel out there, so the day travels on what is in the car. The Hetch Hetchy piece carries the history and the trail detail.

The serious hike. If day two stayed on pavement, day four is the day to spend your legs: the Four Mile and Panorama loop above, or the Mist Trail corridor to the top of Vernal or Nevada Fall, three to seven miles of granite stairs and spray. Half Dome belongs to this day too, but only on its own terms: it is permit-only whenever the cables are up, the permits run through a preseason lottery in March and a daily lottery two days out, and a multi-day trip in cable season should play the daily lottery for its middle days rather than promise anyone the summit. Plan day four so that winning the lottery upgrades it and losing it costs nothing. In winter, the serious-hike slot has its own answer, and it is a shorter list worth reading before you commit.

### Day five: the day you stop collecting

Day five has no new territory in it, on purpose. Four parks, four days; the fifth is the first day you are in Yosemite with nothing left to get. Spend it at the pace the place actually runs at. Rent bikes and ride the Valley's twelve miles of paved path, the best transportation in the park, with rentals running roughly April through October. Walk into a ranger program, which is the cheapest expertise you will ever stand next to. Go back to whichever hour of the trip was the best one and have it again: the same rock on the Merced, the same meadow at last light. Fish, sketch, read in a camp chair, watch the climbers on El Capitan from a meadow with your coffee.

This may sound like a wasted vacation day. What I can report, from twenty seasons of watching visitors from the inside, is that the people who come back every year are not the ones who saw the most things. They are the ones who, at some point, stopped. Day five is where that happens on schedule. If you cannot sit still, the alternative is to make day five the second far corner, Hetch Hetchy if day four was a hike, and demote the slack to the afternoons. But try the empty day once.

Photo: KatieRound / Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 4.0)

### Three days, four days, five: what each length buys

The frame above is five days. Compressing it is subtraction, not redesign.

- Three days is the Valley, the rim, and the high country, the three road-connected parks, one per day. This is the shortest trip that sees Yosemite's actual range, canyon floor to alpine meadow, and it is the length I recommend to first-time visitors who ask what enough means. When a seasonal road is closed, its slot goes to Wawona and the grove, or to Hetch Hetchy.
- Four days adds the choice you were forced to skip: the far corner or the serious hike.
- Five days adds the empty day, which gives the other four some margin. Five is also the first length where basing in two places can beat one, on which more below.

Past five days you are into a different kind of trip: a night in the wilderness, a second lap of the high country, the repeat-visit rhythm where you stop needing articles like this one. A three-day version of this plan is also wired into the itineraries page, where you can open it on the map, reorder it, and carry it with you.

### The winter version

From roughly November into May the rim and the high country are under snow and their roads are closed, and the four-parks frame compresses to this: day one is the Valley as above, colder, emptier, and better-looking under fresh snow. Day two goes up to Badger Pass, where the closed stretch of Glacier Point Road becomes a groomed track and the winter rim is reached on snowshoes, most famously at Dewey Point, about seven miles round trip to the Valley's edge. Day three is the Mariposa Grove on foot up the closed road, or Hetch Hetchy, which sits below four thousand feet and is the corner of the park most likely to be snow-free all winter, gate hours and storm closures permitting. Days four and five, if you have them, are the ice rink, the clearing storms, and the quiet. Chains ride in the car all winter, no exceptions worth planning around. The winter guide is the season's logistics; the winter hiking guide is the trail inventory that survives the snow.

### Where to sleep, and whether to move

The base question changes with length. For three or four nights, pick one bed and keep it: the hour you save on a clever mid-trip move is paid back double in packing, checkout, and the parking you gave up. Base as close to the Valley as the budget allows, because every day but one starts there: in-park if you can land it, which means booking when the 366-day window opens or camping via the five-month release, otherwise El Portal for proximity or Mariposa for a real town, with the full comparison in the gateway towns piece.

Five days in summer is the one case where splitting the base earns its friction: three nights Valley-side for days one, two, and the far corner, then two nights east at Lee Vining, at the eastern foot of Tioga Pass, so the high-country day ends near the high country instead of two hours from it. That order also points your departure east toward Mono Lake and 395 if that is the way home. If it is not, keep the single base and eat the Tioga drive twice; the drive is worth it.

### Common questions

Is three days enough for Yosemite? Yes, and it is the shortest visit that is. Three days covers the Valley, the Glacier Point rim, and the Tioga high country, one per day, without hurry. One or two days is a good trip too, but it is a different kind of trip, covered in its own guide.

How many days is ideal? Four or five. Four adds Hetch Hetchy or one serious hike to the three-day core. Five adds a day with nothing scheduled, which is often the best day of the trip.

Can you do Glacier Point and Tioga Road on the same day? You can drive it; you should not. They point in opposite directions from the Valley, each is two to four hours of driving round trip, and combining them turns both into windshield scenery. One park per day.

What order should the days go in? Valley first, rim second, high country third, the far corner or the big hike fourth. The Valley teaches you the park; the rim reuses that knowledge from above; the high country needs the earliest start and the most settled weather, so it benefits from a day of acclimation before it.

Does this work in winter? The compressed version does: the Valley, Badger Pass and the snowshoe rim, the grove on foot or Hetch Hetchy. Tioga Road and Glacier Point Road are closed in winter, typically November into May, so the summer version of days two and three does not exist then.

Do I need a reservation to enter Yosemite in 2026? No. There is no day-use or peak-hours reservation in 2026. You need the $35 seven-day vehicle pass, and international visitors age 16 and up pay the $100 per-person surcharge in effect since January 1.

Should I plan Half Dome into a three-to-five-day trip? Only as an upgrade, never as the spine. Permits are a lottery, preseason in March or daily two days ahead, so build day four to be good without the summit and let a winning application improve it.

### The honest pitch

Three to five days is the first Yosemite trip where the constraint is not the clock, and the discipline is to keep the four parks separate. The Valley, the rim, the high country and the far corners each take a full day. Give each one its day and hold the fifth one empty.

#### One bed, four days of alarms

Every day of this plan but one starts near the Valley, which makes the base the biggest single decision in it. A search on your dates shows what is still holding rooms, in the park and in the gateways, before you commit the itinerary to a bed that is an hour further from day one than it needs to be.

## Yosemite winter hikes: the trails that stay open

URL: https://thetalusfieldjournal.com/articles/yosemite-winter-hikes
Section: Trails and Hikes. Published: 2026-08-23. Last updated: 2026-08-23.
Summary: What you can actually hike in Yosemite in winter: Valley floor trails, Columbia Rock, the Vernal Fall winter route, Hetch Hetchy, Wawona, and what is closed.

The email arrives every year around the first week of December, from somebody with a booked room and a creeping suspicion: asking whether there is anything to hike in Yosemite in winter. The answer is yes, with limits. The park's trail inventory shrinks by something like two thirds when the snow settles in, the famous names on the closed list are exactly the ones people came for, and nothing at the entrance gate explains which is which. But what stays open is real hiking through an empty park, and most of it needs nothing more exotic than boots, traction cleats, and a respect for the clock. This is the inventory: what closes, what stays open, and the season's one real climb. The winter guide covers the rest of the season, chains, Badger Pass, the rink, and the December guide takes that month on its own; this piece is only about the trails.

The season this article describes runs from the first lasting snow, usually late November, into April: the Valley floor melts out first after each storm, the shaded corners hold their ice longest, and the Four Mile Trail stays gated into May. Where you fall inside that window matters less than the day's conditions.

### How winter hiking works here: elevation, aspect, ice

Three facts organize everything below. First, elevation. The Valley floor sits at about 4,000 feet, low enough that snow falls, sticks for a while, and usually melts back off the flat ground within days; the rim above it sits at 7,000-plus and holds a snowpack all season. That two-thousand-foot difference is the entire difference between a trail on this list and a trail on the closed list.

Second, aspect. The Valley runs east to west, so its north side, the Yosemite Falls side, faces south and takes sun all day, while the south side and every shaded recess hold their snow and ice for weeks after a storm. A south-facing trail can be bare and dry three days after a foot of snow while a shaded stretch of the same valley stays icy. This is why the season's one reliable climb is on the sunny wall, and why the Mist Trail's shaded stair is closed.

Third, ice. The thing that ends winter hikes in Yosemite is almost never an avalanche or a storm. It is a paved path that glazed overnight, or a shaded switchback polished by a hundred boots. Traction cleats, the strap-on spikes sold under a dozen names, cost little, weigh nothing, and convert most of the Valley's winter hazards back into walking; carry them and trekking poles on anything that climbs, and put the cleats on before the ice gets interesting rather than after. Add the short days, with the sun down before five in December and off the shaded floor well before that, and the rules follow: start mid-morning after the night's ice softens, set a turnaround time, and be off the trail by the time the light leaves it. Check the Park Bulletin and the Park Service conditions page the morning you walk; every entry below is subject to the current storm.

### Closed, so you can stop wondering

The famous closures first.

- The Four Mile Trail closes for the winter, typically from the first lasting snow into May. In lean stretches the Park Service sometimes opens the lower three miles to a gate below Union Point, and that lower section still carries ice in the shade; the switchbacks above stay shut. The loop it anchors is a May-through-fall project.
- The Mist Trail's granite stair beside Vernal Fall closes in winter, along with the John Muir Trail between Clark Point and the top of Nevada Fall. The reason is falling ice: large icicles form on the overhanging rock above both stretches and fall onto the trail, and the spray that makes the stair famous in June makes it a sheet of ice in January. A winter route survives, covered below.
- Half Dome is out of season: the cables typically come down the day after Columbus Day and do not go back up until the Friday before Memorial Day, and in between the summit is a mountaineering objective, not a hike. The Half Dome piece explains the system.
- Everything on Tioga Road and upper Glacier Point Road, Cathedral Lakes, Tuolumne, Sentinel Dome, Taft Point, is behind closed gates and under feet of snow. The rim can be reached in winter, but on snowshoes or skis from Badger Pass, which is a different sport and a different article.

Photo: Ahmed Radwan / Wikimedia Commons (CC0)

### The Valley floor, which stays yours

The floor is the winter park's main stage, and its flat trails stay open all season, snow or not. The difference from summer is that you will be nearly alone on them.

The Lower Yosemite Fall loop, about a mile, paved and flat, changes character completely in winter. The fall itself is modest until the late-winter melt begins, but the amphitheater compensates with winter features: on cold mornings the spray builds a frost apron over the talus, and after storms the whole recess hangs with ice that booms when it cuts loose. The paved loop is exactly where the black-ice warning applies; this is a cleats-in-pocket walk, not a sneakers walk.

Cook's Meadow and Sentinel Meadow, a mile of boardwalk, are the winter photograph you already know: Half Dome and Yosemite Falls over frosted grass, at their best in the hour after a clearing storm and in the fog that forms over the Merced on cold mornings. The boardwalk glazes overnight; short steps, and cleats if it shines.

Mirror Lake, about two miles round trip on pavement to the lake and roughly five as the Tenaya Creek loop when conditions allow, is a better winter walk than a summer one, for a simple hydrological reason: winter is when the lake starts being a lake again. The seasonal pool that shrinks to a meadow by August refills with the first storms, and the reflections that named the place come back while the crowds are elsewhere. Tenaya Canyon keeps the sun late and loses it early; expect ice in both directions and give the loop away on icy days rather than forcing it.

The Valley Loop Trail is the sleeper of the season. The full circuit runs about 13 miles and the half loop about 6.5, but nobody owes it a lap: it is a chain of flat segments along the base of the walls, and in winter the western reaches toward Bridalveil and El Capitan are as close to having Yosemite Valley to yourself as daylight gets. Pick a stretch, walk it out and back, and add Bridalveil Fall, a half-mile round trip that in winter trades its spring violence for rime and quiet.

### The one real climb: Columbia Rock, and sometimes the top

The season's one serious hike is on the sunny wall. The Yosemite Falls Trail from Camp 4 climbs south-facing switchbacks that melt out fast between storms, which makes it the most reliably hikeable ascent in the winter park. Columbia Rock, about two miles round trip and 1,000 feet up several dozen switchbacks, is the destination that fits most winter days: a railed perch with the Valley laid out below, Half Dome and Sentinel Rock across the way, earned before lunch. Another half mile, some of it downhill, reaches the full frontal view of Upper Yosemite Fall, which in cold snaps runs past a growing cone of frozen spray at its base, the season's most underrated sight.

The continuation to the top of the fall, about 7.2 miles round trip with 2,700 feet of gain, is a conditions call, not a default. The upper third holds snow and ice long after Columbia Rock is dry, the final traverses are shaded and exposed, and the overlook's granite is no place for glazed boot soles. In a lean January it goes with cleats, poles, and an early turnaround honestly held; in a deep one it does not go at all. If you make the top, you will likely share one of the park's great summit views with single digits of people. Decide at Columbia Rock, not at the trailhead, and let the mountain overrule the plan.

Photo: KatieRound / Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 4.0)

### The Merced corridor, by its winter route

The trail most first-time winter visitors ask about is the Mist Trail, and the winter version is shorter and gentler but still worth doing. The Vernal Fall footbridge stays open all season: about 1.6 miles round trip from Happy Isles with 400 feet of gain on a paved grade whose shaded stretches ice hard, cleats again. The footbridge view of Vernal Fall over a low, clear, green winter Merced is quieter than the spring spectacle and better composed.

Above the bridge, the winter route follows the John Muir Trail toward Clark Point: at the fork, the gate on the upper John Muir Trail is closed, and the left fork drops to rejoin the Mist Trail just upstream of Vernal Fall, so the top of Vernal remains reachable when conditions cooperate. Nevada Fall does not: with the stair and the upper John Muir Trail both closed, there is no winter walking route to its brink, and the corridor's winter ambitions should end at Vernal. Go for the moving water and the empty canyon, and read the Mist Trail guide for the rest of the year's version.

### Hetch Hetchy, the winter secret

The best pure winter hiking in Yosemite is in its lowest corner. Hetch Hetchy sits below four thousand feet in the park's northwest, low enough that most winter weeks its trails are dry, or briefly white and then dry again. Lookout Point, about 2 miles round trip with 680 feet of gain from near the entrance station, buys a panorama of the reservoir and Wapama Falls for an hour and a half of walking. The main event, the Wapama Falls trail from O'Shaughnessy Dam, about five miles round trip of rolling granite ledge along the north shore, is a legitimate all-winter day hike: the falls begin returning with the first big rains, the south-facing trail takes what sun exists, and the valley that holds a hundred quiet visitors in July holds a dozen in January.

Two winter caveats. The access road is gated on posted hours, roughly sunrise to sunset, so the day has a hard frame; and snow can close the road entirely for days after a storm, so check conditions before making the drive. It is an hour and three quarters from Yosemite Valley, which is why it is empty.

### Wawona and the sequoias on foot

The south end of the park keeps two winter walks. The Wawona Meadow Loop, a flat 3.5 miles around the old meadow and golf course, stays walkable nearly all winter at Wawona's 4,000 feet, collecting snow just often enough to be worth timing. And the Mariposa Grove becomes, in my view, a better trip in winter than in July: the grove road closes to vehicles at the end of November, the shuttle stops, and the grove goes quiet. You walk up the closed road or the Washburn Trail, about two miles and a few hundred feet either way, then the Grizzly Giant Loop's two miles among snow-loaded sequoias, and you will meet more coyote tracks than people. Firm snow is boots-and-cleats; fresh snow is snowshoes; the grove guide has the winter section. Sequoias under snow are the best thing this park does in the cold months, and almost nobody sees it.

### When the boots stop working

Above the Valley rim the season belongs to snowshoes and skis, and the line between that world and this article is the snow line itself. The marked winter routes out of Badger Pass, most famously the roughly seven-mile round trip to Dewey Point on the Valley's edge, are the way to stand on the winter rim, and the ranger-led snowshoe walks are the gentlest possible introduction. All of it, along with the chain rules that govern every drive in this piece, lives in the winter guide. The one crossover worth repeating here: snowshoes are for deep fresh snow, and on the packed, icy trails of the Valley floor they are worse than boots with cleats. Match the tool to the surface.

### Common questions

Can you actually hike in Yosemite in winter? Yes. The Valley floor's trails stay open all season, Columbia Rock is a real 1,000-foot climb that melts out between storms, the Vernal Fall footbridge stays reachable by its winter route, and Hetch Hetchy and Wawona hike nearly all winter at their lower elevations.

Is the Mist Trail open in winter? The granite stair beside Vernal Fall closes, along with the John Muir Trail between Clark Point and the top of Nevada Fall, because of falling ice. The winter route runs to the Vernal Fall footbridge and, conditions allowing, to the top of Vernal via Clark Point. Nevada Fall has no winter walking route.

Is the Four Mile Trail open in winter? No. It closes with the first lasting snow, typically into May, occasionally reopening its lowest miles to a gate below Union Point in lean spells.

Do you need snowshoes or just boots? On the Valley floor, Hetch Hetchy, and Wawona: boots, with traction cleats in your pocket for ice. Snowshoes earn their weight above the rim, out of Badger Pass, and in the Mariposa Grove after fresh snow.

What is the best winter hike in Yosemite? For effort against reward: Columbia Rock. For solitude and open trail: Wapama Falls at Hetch Hetchy. For the sight nobody expects: the walk up the closed road to the sequoias of the Mariposa Grove.

When does winter hiking season end? Gradually, from below. The floor is spring by April while the Mist Trail stair and the high trails shed their closures with the ice, and the Four Mile Trail waits for May. In between, this list and the March guide overlap on purpose.

### The honest pitch

Winter removes most of the trail map and most of the crowds. Walk the floor with cleats in your pocket, climb to Columbia Rock on the sunny wall, take the winter route to Vernal's footbridge, spend one day at Hetch Hetchy and one among snowbound sequoias, and you will have done five hikes that July cannot offer at any price. Watch the conditions page like a local, turn around when the ice says so, and be out of the shade by four.

#### The trailheads are short; the daylight is shorter

Every walk on this list is governed by a winter sun that quits before five, which makes sleeping close the difference between hiking and commuting. Winter is also the season the rooms actually exist: a search on your dates will show in-park and gateway beds at prices July does not believe in.

## Yosemite in March: Weather, Snow, and a Tale of Two Seasons

URL: https://thetalusfieldjournal.com/articles/yosemite-in-march
Section: Seasonal Guides. Published: 2026-08-20. Last updated: 2026-08-20.
Summary: Yosemite in March: weather, what is open and closed, chain rules, waterfalls and frazil ice, the foothill bloom, spring break crowds, and planning for both.

March is the month I have stopped trying to predict. I live in El Portal, down the Merced River canyon from Yosemite Valley, and in the span of four recent Marches I have watched this park buried and closed for weeks under record snow, watched a blizzard shut every road into it on the first weekend of the month, watched five feet of new snow land on Tuolumne Meadows in two weeks, and watched a March so hot and dry it erased roughly half the winter's snowpack in thirty days. Nobody planning a trip gets to know in advance which of those Marches they have booked.

This month is two seasons on the same calendar page. One March is spring. The afternoon touches 70 degrees in the Valley, the waterfalls are audibly coming back to life, the redbud is blooming along the highway, and you have the place at a fraction of its summer crowds. The other March is the biggest winter month of the year, the one the Sierra has an actual name for. You cannot choose between them. What you can do is plan a trip that works in either, and that is a solvable problem. Here is how.

### The month that cannot pick a season

Start with the record, because the ranking guides will tell you March is a mild shoulder month and the last few years say otherwise. In 2023, back-to-back winter storms buried the park under as much as fifteen feet of snow at the upper elevations; the Valley floor took 40 inches in a single day, breaking a daily record that had stood since 1969, and Yosemite closed at the end of February and did not reopen until March 18, its longest weather closure in decades. That snowpack held Tioga Road shut until July 22, the latest opening on record. In 2024, a blizzard closed the park again on March 1; it reopened in stages over the following days. In 2025, the winter rangers measured 61 inches of new snow at the Tuolumne Meadows weather plot in the first half of March alone. And in 2026, the opposite: an unusually hot, dry March cut the park's snowpack roughly in half, from about 65 percent of average at the start of the month to 37 percent by April 1, and pulled the whole waterfall season weeks ahead of schedule.

The swing is not new. Sierra forecasters have called a big late save "Miracle March" since 1991, when the Tahoe-area snowpack went from about 15 percent of normal on the first of the month to nearly 75 percent by its last week, and the name has been earned again several times since. In March 2018 the Tuolumne rangers logged 51 inches in the month's opening storm and 123 inches for the month. What is new, in my time here, is how hard the pattern has leaned on this month lately: the storms that defined each of the last several winters landed in March or within a day of it, while the quiet Marches have been quieter and warmer than they used to be. The month is not averaging out. It is splitting into its two extremes.

March is not a compromise between winter and spring. It is a coin flip between them, and you plan for the coin, not the season you are hoping for.

### The weather, in numbers

The long-term normals for Yosemite Valley, which sits near 4,000 feet, put March at an average high of 57 and an average low of 34, with about five and a half inches of precipitation, which keeps it among the wettest months of the year. Both halves of the coin live inside those averages. A dry, sunny stretch will run Valley afternoons into the 60s and sometimes to 70, with nights still dropping to freezing; a storm cycle will drop snow to the Valley floor one day and turn it to rain the next, because March storms play games with the snow line that January storms do not. The high country is a different world entirely: Tuolumne Meadows at 8,600 feet is under a deep snowpack all month, every year, no matter what the Valley is doing.

The practical translation: pack for both seasons, whatever the ten-day forecast says when you leave. Sun protection and a t-shirt layer for the warm afternoon, real insulation and waterproofs for the storm, and a car packed for winter even if you never open the trunk kit. The forecast at ten days is a mood, not a plan.

### What's open, what's closed

Yosemite Valley is open, along with Wawona and the Hetch Hetchy road, on the same year-round basis as the rest of the winter season. The closures that shape a March trip are the same ones that shape a January trip, and it is worth being blunt about them, because several of the guides ranking for this month get them wrong.

Tioga Road is closed. All of March, every year. Plowing does not usually even begin until mid-April, and in the last several years the road has opened as early as May 15 in a dry year and as late as July 22 in a big one. If a March guide tells you to take a scenic drive through Tuolumne Meadows, close the tab; the writer has not been here. Glacier Point Road is plowed only as far as the Badger Pass ski area, and only while the ski area is operating; when Badger closes for the season, the road closes entirely at Chinquapin until its spring opening most often in May, and in six of the last fifteen years in April. The drive-up view from Glacier Point does not exist in March. Mariposa Grove Road is closed for the season too, but the grove itself stays open the same way it does all winter: you park at the South Entrance and walk the closed road, about two miles each way, to sequoias that may still be holding snow.

The two winter amenities are the fine print of a March trip, because both of them end as the month begins. The Curry Village ice rink skates its final sessions in the first days of March; in 2026 the season ended on March 2. Badger Pass traditionally runs into late March or early April, but that tradition is wobbling: in 2026 it closed for the season on March 18, and the winter before that it never opened at all. If skiing or the Dewey Point snowshoe is the point of your trip, come early in the month and check the operating status before you drive up, because when Badger is done, so is your trailhead.

### Driving in: assume chains until the forecast proves otherwise

Chain control is a normal part of March. The park's own guidance is to expect chain requirements on any road from November through March, and the rule that catches visitors is not the mounting, it is the carrying: when controls are posted, every vehicle must carry chains, including four-wheel drives and rentals, whether or not they end up on the tires. The full R1/R2/R3 system is explained in the winter guide, and the road-conditions line, 209/372-0200, is the thing to call the morning you drive in.

Route choice matters more in March than almost any other planning decision. Highway 140 through the Merced River canyon is the lowest approach to the park, low enough that it usually takes rain while the higher entrances take snow, which is why it carries the old name "All-Weather Highway." Highway 41 from Oakhurst and Highway 120 from Groveland both climb well over 5,000 feet and see chain control far more often. The full comparison is in the entrances guide; the March summary is the same as the January one. Take 140 if you can.

### The waterfalls are waking up

Here is the spring half of the month, and it is real. The falls that spent the autumn as stains on granite are waterfalls again by March: winter rain and the first warm-spell melt have rebuilt Yosemite Falls to the point that you can hear it across the Valley, and every storm that lands as rain sends it up another notch. It is not peak flow. The main melt pulse arrives with sustained warm weather, usually in May or June, though a dry winter like 2026 can pull the peak weeks earlier. What March offers instead is the sound of the system turning back on, with almost nobody standing at the viewpoints. The month-by-month schedule is in the waterfalls guide.

March also sits inside the season of the park's strangest small phenomenon. On cold mornings after clear nights, the mist from the waterfalls freezes into frazil ice, a slush of crystals that flows down Yosemite Creek like slow wet concrete and piles into white banks along the channel. The Park Service says it happens in spring, especially April but sometimes March and May, on mornings before about 9 a.m. when overnight lows freeze and the falls are running hard; the footbridge area below Lower Yosemite Fall is the classic place to look. There is a whole Yosemite Nature Notes film about it, and a cold March morning after a storm is one of your better chances all year of seeing it yourself.

One expectation to manage: the firefall is a February event. The alignment that lights Horsetail Fall runs roughly mid-to-late February, and while a faint version can still fire in the first evenings of March when the fall has water and the western sky is clean, that is a consolation prize for people already here, not a reason to book the first week of March. If the firefall is the trip, come in February.

### The bloom is in the canyon, not the Valley

The other thing March has that no other month quite matches is on the drive in, not in the park. The Merced River canyon along Highway 140 sits low enough that its spring arrives while the Valley is still flipping its coin, and by the middle of the month the canyon is usually in full color: redbud flaring magenta along the river, and the Hite Cove Trail, whose trailhead is on 140 at Savage's Trading Post, about eight miles west of El Portal, carrying one of the best poppy blooms in the Sierra foothills. The bloom there typically peaks around mid-March. Two cautions that the wildflower photos never carry: the trail is narrow across steep slopes with a poison oak understory, and parking is a handful of shoulder pullouts, so arrive early and check the trail's current status before you count on it. The Valley's own famous bloom, the dogwoods, holds until late April. The full elevation-by-elevation calendar is in the wildflowers guide.

### Crowds, spring break, and the reservation question

Averaged across 2010 to 2024, March brings roughly 160,000 visits to Yosemite against about 625,000 in July, which makes the crowd math simple: on a typical March weekday you are visiting a park running at about a quarter of its summer load. Parking exists. Viewpoints are quiet. Lodging can be booked weeks out instead of a year out. The exception is spring break: the weekends of mid and late March, and Easter week when it lands in the month, concentrate most of the month's traffic into a handful of days, and a warm, sunny spring-break Saturday can produce entrance lines that feel like June. If you have any flexibility, midweek March is one of the emptiest good-weather windows of the whole year.

As of the 2026 season there is no entry reservation to think about: the park dropped its timed-entry system, so entry is first come, first served with the standard entrance fee, in March and every other month. Day-of conditions, closures, and webcams are collected on the conditions page.

### The March homework for a summer trip

Two calendar items live in March even if your trip does not. The Half Dome preseason lottery takes applications during March, which means the month you are reading about is also the month to apply for a cables permit for the summer. And the park's bears begin emerging from their dens in March and April, males first, sows with cubs last, each of them down as much as a third of its body weight and single-minded about food. Spring bears are their own subject, but the March translation is simple: food storage rules are already in full effect, and the animals moving at dusk are one more reason to drive the park roads slowly. Daylight helps you here. The clocks change on the second Sunday of March and Valley sunsets jump from about six to about seven in a single night, with the days stretching noticeably longer by the week.

### How I would build a March trip

Base in or below the Valley, and keep a flexible day. The Ahwahnee and Yosemite Valley Lodge run year-round, Curry Village on a limited early-season schedule, and the gateway towns down 140 put you under the snow line most nights. Give the trip three nights if you can, and treat one day as the swing day you rearrange around the forecast.

If you get the winter March, you have won something, whatever it does to your plans. A clearing storm is the best photographic condition this park offers, and March delivers the last reliable ones of the season: fog tearing off the walls, fresh snow outlining every ledge on El Capitan, and viewpoints that in summer hold a hundred people holding six. Be at Tunnel View when the storm breaks, then walk the Valley loop while the snow is still on the oaks; it rarely survives the next warm afternoon. The photography guide covers where to stand.

If you get the spring March, work the water and the low country. Lower Yosemite Fall and the Valley loop in the morning, with a detour to the creek below the fall if the night was cold and clear, on the chance the frazil is running. The canyon bloom on the drive in or out. A walk up the closed Mariposa Grove road to the sequoias. And an afternoon doing the thing March is quietly best at, which is standing at famous viewpoints without waiting for them.

Camping in March is real but specific: Upper Pines takes reservations year-round, and Camp 4, Wawona, and Hodgdon Meadow run on winter first-come procedures, with nights at or below freezing as the working assumption. Check the current campground status before you commit a March night to canvas.

### The takeaway

March is the last month of winter and the first month of spring, and it refuses to tell you in advance which one you are getting. Come with chains in the trunk and sunscreen in the same bag. Book a base that works in both seasons, keep one day loose, and let the forecast, not the itinerary, decide whether your best day is spent photographing a clearing storm or standing in a canyon full of poppies. Either version is the quiet park, running at a quarter of its summer volume, a few weeks before the crowds return for the year. Both are worth the drive. That's the trip.

#### March rooms exist, except when school lets out

This is still the season when lodging can be booked weeks ahead instead of a year, with one exception: the spring-break weekends of mid and late March fill first, and Easter week behaves like summer. A search on your dates shows quickly which March you are dealing with.

## Camping in Yosemite for the First Time

URL: https://thetalusfieldjournal.com/articles/camping-in-yosemite-first-time
Section: Planning. Published: 2026-08-07. Last updated: 2026-08-07.
Summary: First time camping in Yosemite? What the campground is really like: the bear box, the cold you did not pack for, quiet hours, and what goes wrong.

The reservation is the part everyone warns you about, and it is the part everyone plans for. Five months out, seven in the morning, a browser tab and a fast finger. What nobody prepares you for is the four o'clock on a Thursday afternoon when you actually arrive: the site is smaller than the photo, the metal box by the picnic table is a different shape than you pictured, your cooler does not fit inside it, the family twenty feet away is having a conversation you can follow word for word, and you have about three hours of usable daylight to turn a car full of gear into a place to sleep.

This is not the guide to which campground to book. That one already exists, and it covers all thirteen of them, the three booking windows, and the cancellation game. This is the other thing: what a night in a Yosemite campground is actually like, and which of its assumptions will catch you out the first time. I have been camping in this park for close to twenty years, and I have watched a great many first nights go sideways. Almost none of them went sideways for a reason anyone would call their fault. They went sideways because a campground is a set of unwritten conventions, and nobody hands you the list.

### Start by correcting the picture in your head

The word "camping" is doing two jobs, and Yosemite only does one of them.

If the picture in your head is a tent alone in trees, quiet, the nearest human a mile off, that is backpacking, and it is a real thing you can do here with a wilderness permit. It is not what a Yosemite campground is. The three Valley campgrounds hold roughly 380 sites between them, packed into a floor that is a mile wide, and Upper Pines alone holds well over half of those. You will see your neighbors. You will hear your neighbors. On a July Saturday the Pines complex has the population of a small town and the density of a parking lot with trees in it.

This is not a complaint, and it is not a reason to skip it. Sleeping on the Valley floor is still the best way to experience this park, for the plain reason that you are inside it at the hours when it is worth being inside it: the ninety minutes after the day visitors leave, and the ninety before they come back. But if you arrive expecting solitude and find a village, you will spend the first evening disappointed by something that was never on offer.

Arrive expecting solitude and you will spend the first evening disappointed by something that was never on offer.

Photo: Andrei Serikov / Pexels

### What is in the site, and what is emphatically not

A standard Yosemite campsite gives you a numbered dirt or gravel pad, a picnic table, a steel fire ring with a grate, and a metal food locker. That is the inventory. Everything else you brought or you do without.

What is not there, in rough order of how much it surprises people:

No showers. Not at any campground in the park. Not the Valley ones, not Wawona, not Tuolumne. The nearest public showers are at Curry Village, they cost about five dollars, and in peak season the line reaches the point where you have to decide how much you actually mind. Baby wipes and a gallon jug do most of the work. Plan for three days of not being clean and it stops being a problem; plan for a shower and it ruins an evening.

No hookups. Anywhere. No electricity, no water spigot at the site, no sewer. There are dump stations, and there are shared water taps along the loops, but nothing runs to your pad. If you are in an RV you are on batteries and generator hours; if you are in a tent you are on whatever you charged in the car.

No reliable cell signal. There is some, in some parts of the Valley, some of the time. Treat it as a pleasant accident rather than infrastructure. Download your maps, screenshot your reservation, and tell whoever is expecting to hear from you that they will not.

Toilets vary, and the variation matters. The Valley campgrounds have flush toilets and drinking water. The primitive ones up Tioga Road can mean vault toilets and, in some seasons, no potable water at all, which turns your water jug from a convenience into the trip. Check the specific campground's current listing rather than assuming; the small ones change season to season.

### The bear box is a ritual, not a container

Every site has one. It is a steel locker, roughly 35 inches deep by 43 inches wide by 28 inches high in the newer generation, and noticeably shorter, about 18 inches of interior height, in the older ones you will find at some of the higher campgrounds and at trailhead lots. Read that second measurement again, because it is the one that ambushes people: an 18-inch box will not swallow a tall wheeled cooler standing up, and a first-timer who arrives at Bridalveil Creek with a 62-quart upright discovers this at dusk.

What goes in it is anything with a smell. Food, obviously, and drinks, and the cooler itself even when empty. Also toothpaste. Sunscreen. Lip balm. Bug spray. Soap and shampoo. Dish rags. Trash, until you carry it to the dumpster. The half-eaten granola bar in the door pocket of your car, which is the single most common violation in this park and the reason the parking lots are full of vehicles with peeled door frames. Nothing scented stays in the car overnight, and nothing scented stays out on the table while you walk to the bathroom.

The failure mode is almost never ignorance. Nobody arrives here unaware that Yosemite has bears. The failure is the latch. You unload dinner, you cook, you carry the plates back, your hands are full, and you swing the door shut without dropping the latch pin. A closed unlatched box is an open box to a bear that has opened four hundred of them. A recurring share of the park's incidents trace to exactly that gesture, and they cluster in the busiest lodging areas in early summer, when the greatest number of people are doing it for the first time.

The rule is enforced, with fines running as high as five thousand dollars. The stronger argument is that a bear that gets human food once comes back, gets bolder, and eventually gets killed for it, and that the chain of events starts with somebody's hands being full. The bear guide covers the rest of it. For your first night, one habit carries most of the weight: latch it every single time, including the times you are coming right back.

Bears do not need hours. They need the ninety seconds you spent walking to the restroom.

### You are going to be colder than you planned for

This is the second-most-common first-timer mistake and the one that ruins the most sleep.

Yosemite Valley sits at about 4,000 feet. Tuolumne Meadows sits at about 8,600. That is a different climate, and the park sells both under one name. A July night on the Valley floor is mild. A July night in Tuolumne can drop into the high thirties, and it will do that under a clear sky on the same date that the Valley is pleasant. People pack one sleeping bag for "summer in Yosemite," and half of them are packing for the wrong half of the park.

The working rule: look up the elevation of your specific campground, not the park, and then treat the forecast low as optimistic by several degrees, because the published forecast is usually for a valley station and cold air pools in the low ground overnight. A 20-degree bag is never wrong here in any season. A 40-degree bag is fine on the Valley floor in midsummer and a long, thin night anywhere above 7,000 feet.

The other half of that equation is under you, not over you. Most people who are cold at night are cold because the ground is taking their heat, not because the bag is thin. A cheap closed-cell foam pad under a decent air pad fixes more cold nights than a warmer bag does, and costs a fraction as much. Bring a warm hat to sleep in. It looks ridiculous and it works.

### The campground runs on a clock nobody posts at the entrance

Four times govern the day. Learn them before you arrive.

Check-in and check-out are both around noon. Which means the site you booked may still have somebody in it when you arrive at eleven, and it means your last morning is not a leisurely one. Plan the drive out accordingly.

Generator hours are 7 to 9 in the morning, noon to 2, and 5 to 7 in the evening. Outside those windows, generators are off, and this is enforced socially more than officially. If you are tent camping next to an RV, those three windows will define your mornings. If you are in the RV, running it at 6:45 is how you meet the campground host.

Quiet hours are 10 PM to 6 AM. Enforcement varies with the host and with the loop. Your realistic options against a noisy neighbor are a polite request, earplugs, or the host, and the third one works. Bring the earplugs anyway.

Wood fires in Yosemite Valley are restricted to the evening in the summer months. The reason is air quality: the Valley is a granite box with cold air sinking into it, smoke settles and stays, and a hundred and fifty morning campfires make a haze that the whole floor has to breathe. In the cooler months the restriction lifts. Check the current hours when you check in, because the window and the season it applies to both get adjusted.

And a fifth thing that is not a time but belongs with them: do not bring firewood from home. Moving firewood is how insect pests get moved into new forests, and the standing advice statewide is to buy it where you burn it. Gathering downed wood is prohibited in the Valley and in the sequoia groves outright. Buy a bundle at the store on your way in.

### Set up in daylight. All of it.

The single biggest decision on a first Yosemite camping trip is what time you arrive, and the answer is earlier than you think.

Pitching a tent you have never pitched, in the dark, by headlamp, after four hours of driving and an entrance line, with a partner who is also tired, is how a lot of first nights go bad. So is learning your camp stove for the first time at nine at night when everyone is hungry. So is discovering that your air pad has a slow leak.

Two fixes, both free. Pitch the tent once in the yard or the living room before you leave, and run the stove once. The point is for your hands to learn the sequence. And aim to be in the site by mid-afternoon. In the summer that leaves hours of light; in October it is the difference between a camp and a scramble.

The order that works once you are there: tent up first, then bedding inside it, then the bear box loaded, then everything else. Bedding goes in before dinner because a sleeping bag that has been lofting for four hours is warmer than one pulled out of a stuff sack at ten. The bear box gets loaded before you start cooking, not after, because after is when you are tired, your hands are full, and the latch pin is the thing that gets forgotten.

### The neighbors, the raccoons, and the jays

Campground etiquette in Yosemite is mostly one rule with several faces: do not walk through other people's sites. The loop road is the hallway. A site is somebody's room, even when it looks like an empty patch of dirt, and cutting the corner between two of them to reach the bathroom is the thing that gets you looked at.

The rest is small. Headlamps have a red setting; use it after dark and you will not be sweeping a white beam through three tents on your way back from the restroom. Six people to a site and two vehicles to a site are hard limits, not guidelines, and campgrounds do check. Dishes get washed at the utility sink, not at the drinking-water tap. Gray water goes in the drain, not on the ground, because the ground is where the raccoons investigate.

On which: raccoons are the animal you will actually meet. Bears are the famous problem and the well-managed one. Raccoons are relentless, dexterous, and entirely unafraid, and they will work a tent zipper for a tube of toothpaste. Every bear rule doubles as a raccoon rule. Anything scented in the box means anything, including the thing in the tent pocket you forgot about.

And the jays. Steller's jays work the campgrounds from first light, hopping table to bear box in that strutting way they have, and they are watching your lunch with more attention than you are. Leave a sandwich unattended and it is gone. Once you stop taking it personally, the jays are one of the pleasures of the place.

### The oaks drop branches on hot afternoons

Almost nobody knows this one, and a first-timer has no way to learn it except by being told.

California black oaks, the big spreading ones that shade the best sites on the Valley floor, shed limbs in still, hot weather. The phenomenon has a name, summer branch drop, and the unnerving part is that it happens on calm days rather than windy ones, and the break tends to occur some feet out along the limb rather than at the trunk, which is exactly where the visual cues you would look for are absent. The tree looks fine. The limb looks fine. It comes down anyway.

The precaution is simple: on a hot, windless afternoon, do not pitch your tent directly under the spread of a big oak if you have another option in the site, and do not set an infant carrier, or a folding chair holding someone who cannot move quickly, directly beneath one. If you hear cracking overhead, move first and look second. The Park Service raises this every summer. It reads as alarmist until you have seen the size of what comes down.

Photo: Jackhen1992 / Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 4.0)

### The things that actually go wrong

Compressed, from watching them happen:

Assuming the camping reservation gets you into the park. It does not. The entrance fee is separate, it is $35 per vehicle for seven days, and the gate is cashless. Getting in is a separate problem from the reservation.

Booking a riverside loop for late spring in a big snow year. The low-lying Valley sites nearest the Merced are lovely in August and can flood or close in a high-runoff May. It happens regularly.

Booking by campground name and not by site. Campground-wide vehicle length maxima are not site limits. Individual sites carry their own, often much shorter, and yours is the one that governs. If you are towing anything, read the specific site's listing.

New boots. Not a camping mistake exactly, but the one that ends the most first trips early. Whatever is going on your feet should have a hundred miles on it before it comes here.

One headlamp for the group. Everybody needs their own, and it needs to be a headlamp rather than a flashlight, because loading a bear box in the dark takes two hands.

Planning the drive in and the first hike on the same day. The drive is the day. Arrive, set up, walk to the meadow, eat, sleep. The park will still be there in the morning.

### The second night

The first night in a campground is administration. You are solving problems, and the place is a list of things you do not know yet.

The second night is different, and it is the whole reason to do this. By then the tent goes up in nine minutes, the bear box has an order that makes sense, you know which way the bathroom is without thinking, and the campground has stopped being a logistics problem and become a place. The fire is down to coals. The generator people are asleep. The river is the loudest thing for a mile. Somewhere in the trees an owl is working, and the granite walls above you hold the last gray light for a long time after the sky behind them has gone dark and filled up.

By then you are living in the park, on the ground, on the same floor that Ahwahneechee families tended with fire for centuries and that the ice left when it pulled back. The reservation was hard. The box is awkward. The showers do not exist. None of that is what you remember.

#### For the night the campground plan does not survive

A closure, a flooded loop, a reservation that never came through, or a first night that did not work. Every camper eventually has one of these, and solving it with a live availability search of the nearest gateway beats driving Highway 140 after dark looking for vacancy signs. Mariposa here; the other towns are one page over.
