## First Yosemite Backpacking Trip: What the Permit Doesn't Say

URL: https://thetalusfieldjournal.com/articles/first-yosemite-backpacking-trip
Section: Trails and Hikes. Published: 2026-08-07. Last updated: 2026-08-07.
Summary: Planning a first Yosemite backpacking trip: lingering snow, creek crossings, mosquito timing, altitude, bear canister rules, and four beginner routes that work.

The permit is the part everyone plans for. It has a date, a deadline, a fee, and a screen that tells you whether you got it, and because it is the only part of the trip with a scoreboard, it absorbs most of the anxiety. Then the permit prints, and it tells you a trailhead, a start date, a party size, and a set of regulations, and nothing about the three things most likely to shape your trip: how much snow is still up there, how high the creek is running, and whether the meadow you were planning to camp in is currently a mosquito event.

Those are the conditions, and they change on their own schedule. The permit guide covers the system: the lottery, the release dates, the fees. This piece is about what you walk into once the paperwork is behind you, written for the trip that is your first one.

### What the permit reserves, and what it does not

This distinction is commonly misunderstood, and it produces bad planning.

A Yosemite wilderness permit reserves a trailhead and a start date. It does not reserve a campsite, because with a few exceptions there are none to reserve. It does not certify that your route is passable, that a bridge is standing, that a ford is safe, or that the pass on day two is clear of snow. The park meters the first day and leaves the rest to your judgment, which makes conditions research your job rather than the agency's.

Two riders come with it, both covered in the permit guide: a night in a backpackers' campground before your start and after your exit, and the option to add Half Dome to a wilderness permit instead of playing the day-hiker lottery.

### The road opens before the country does

The mistake that turns around the most first trips: Tioga Road opening is a headline, and people read it as the high country being open. They are different things.

Tioga Road tops out at 9,945 feet and gets plowed. The passes on your itinerary do not. Over the long historical record the road has opened in late May on average, with a spread that runs from the first week of May in a bare year to late July after a monster winter. In 2026 it opened on May 15. What clears weeks to a month later is everything the plows never touch: north-facing switchbacks, benches above 9,500 feet, the shaded side of any pass, and the snowfields that sit in exactly the bowls that trails like to traverse.

Aspect matters as much as elevation, and it catches people who have only read the map. Two slopes at the same altitude a mile apart can be bare granite and waist-deep rotten snow, depending on which way they face and how much afternoon sun they take. A trip that reads as an easy 3,000 feet of gain on the topo becomes a route-finding exercise across a snowfield with a runout, which is a different trip requiring different equipment and a different set of skills.

The honest early-season rule: in a normal year, if your route holds you above about 9,500 feet for any length of time, June is a gamble and early July is when it stops being one. In a heavy year, add weeks. In a lean year, subtract them. Snowpack in California swings wildly, from single digits as a percentage of average in the driest years to well over 200 percent in the wettest, so nothing about last year predicts this one. Read the current conditions report for your specific trailhead before you finalize, and be willing to move down a drainage.

The road opening tells you the plows finished. It tells you nothing about the pass on day two.

Photo: Stephen Leonardi / Pexels

### The creek is the most dangerous thing on your itinerary

Water-related accidents are one of the leading causes of death in this park, and they are not concentrated in the dramatic places. They happen at crossings, on the days the crossing looked fine. In 2017, after one of the biggest winters on record, a thru-hiker drowned fording Rancheria Creek in Kerrick Canyon in the park's northern backcountry, in July, weeks after anyone would have called it spring. The hazard is a route that is trivial in September and lethal in June, at the same place, with no sign to mark the difference.

Peak runoff generally arrives from late May into June, but that window shifts earlier in a low-snow year and later in a big one, and it moves through the day as well as through the season. Snowmelt-fed creeks run lowest in the early morning, before the day's sun has worked on the snowfields upstream, and highest in the late afternoon and evening. A crossing you would not attempt at four in the afternoon is often unremarkable at seven the next morning. Building your day around that single fact is the cheapest safety measure in backpacking.

The rest of it is standard and worth committing to memory before you need it. Unbuckle your hip belt and sternum strap before you step in, so the pack can be shed if you go down; a pack full of air will hold you face-down. Face upstream, use trekking poles as a third and fourth point, and move sideways rather than forward. Never cross immediately above a log jam or a strainer, because that is where current pins a swimmer. Knee-deep and pushy is already serious; thigh-deep and pushy is a no. A crossing you cannot do changes the trip, and the alternative campsite on this side of the water is a perfectly good place to sleep.

### The mosquitoes follow the snowline uphill

First-timers are rarely warned about this, and it will govern their evenings.

The mechanism is simple and it makes the timing predictable. Mosquitoes emerge from the standing water that snowmelt leaves behind, roughly a couple of weeks after a given elevation band melts out. So the peak is not a fixed date. It climbs the mountain through the summer, arriving in the mid-elevation meadows first and reaching the high basins last. By rough consensus the worst of it in Yosemite runs from about mid-June into early July across most elevations you can drive to, eases through late July, and is largely finished by September. In a low-snow year the whole sequence shifts earlier.

This is why the meadow campsite is a trap in the wrong week. Meadows are where the standing water is. Move a few hundred feet onto a dry granite bench with a breeze, and it is a different night.

For gear: a head net weighs almost nothing and is the single highest-return item in the pack during the peak weeks. Permethrin at 0.5 percent goes on clothing and gear only, never skin, and survives several washes. On skin, DEET in the 20 to 30 percent range or picaridin at 20 percent or higher does the work; higher DEET concentrations mostly buy duration rather than better protection. Treated clothing plus a repellent on the exposed skin is the combination that actually holds up, and long sleeves in July are not the sacrifice they sound like at 9,000 feet.

### You are about to sleep higher than you ever have

Tioga Road allows something unusual in American mountains, and slightly dangerous. You can leave sea level in the morning, park at a trailhead near 8,500 feet in the afternoon, and be asleep at 9,300 by dark. That is a very fast ascent profile, and it is close to the exact pattern altitude guidance tells people to avoid.

The numbers to hold: acute mountain sickness becomes possible for some people somewhere around 8,000 feet, symptoms typically show up six to ten hours after arriving at altitude rather than immediately, and they usually resolve within a day or two provided you do not keep climbing. Standard guidance suggests spending a night or two around 8,000 to 9,000 feet before going higher, and above roughly 9,800 feet, not raising your sleeping elevation more than about 1,600 feet per night.

A first Yosemite trip is a good place to respect that cheaply, because the geography cooperates. Camp the night before at Tuolumne Meadows, about 8,600 feet, rather than driving up and starting the same afternoon. It costs you an evening and buys you a headache-free first day. If somebody in the party is feeling it, the treatment is not aspirin and pushing on; it is stopping the ascent, and if it is not improving, going down. Descending reliably treats it.

Here are the elevations of the usual first destinations, for the arithmetic: Little Yosemite Valley around 6,100 feet, the Cathedral Lakes around 9,300 to 9,600, Sunrise Lakes in the 9,200 to 9,400 range, Vogelsang above 10,000. That last one is a beautiful place and a poor choice for a first night out of a car from the coast.

### The afternoon builds a storm

Sierra summer weather has a daily rhythm, and it holds. Mornings are clear. Clouds build over the crest through the middle of the day. By early afternoon, in the months when monsoon moisture reaches this far, you can have a real thunderstorm, gone again within the hour.

The whole safety protocol follows from the timing. Be over your pass and off exposed high ground by around midday. Not because a storm is guaranteed, but because a storm at one in the afternoon is a normal event in July and August, and the place you do not want to be when it arrives is the highest object on a granite ridge. There is no safe shelter above treeline. A tent is not shelter, a lone tree is worse than nothing, and the useful moves are getting lower, getting off ridgelines and out of shallow caves, and spreading the party out so a single strike cannot take everyone.

Alpine starts in the Sierra are standard practice.

### The cold nobody packs for

High-country Yosemite in midsummer is not warm at night. At 8,600 feet in Tuolumne, overnight lows in July and August commonly sit somewhere in the thirties to low forties, on the same nights the Valley floor is comfortable in a t-shirt. Clear skies at altitude radiate heat away fast, and the coldest hour is the one before dawn.

Practically: a 20-degree bag is the honest choice for a Yosemite high-country summer trip, a 30-degree bag works if you sleep warm and layer, and a 40-degree bag is a bad night waiting to happen. Insulation under you matters as much as over you, and it is the thing beginners skimp on; a pad with a decent R-value fixes more cold nights than a heavier bag does. Sleep in a hat. Eat something before you get in the bag, because your body needs fuel to make heat all night.

And an early-season or late-season trip should assume snow is possible. The first dusting in the high country can arrive in September, and it usually melts within a day, and it is still a miserable night if your kit assumed August.

### The canister, and Yosemite's stricter list

A bear canister is required for overnight wilderness travel in Yosemite. Parkwide, not zone by zone, not a suggestion, not satisfied by hanging your food from a branch. Counterbalance hanging has not been an accepted method here for many years, because the bears in this park learned to defeat it.

The detail that trips up experienced backpackers arriving from elsewhere: Yosemite maintains its own approved-container list, and it is narrower than the general certifications other agencies accept. Soft-sided bag-style containers of the Ursack type are not on it. If you have been using one happily in another range, it does not carry over. Confirm your specific model against the park's current list before you drive out, because the check at the permit desk is real and being turned around at the trailhead over a food container is a bleak way to start.

Renting solves it. Canisters rent from the staffed wilderness centers for a few dollars a week plus a refundable deposit, and returns are easy. Everything scented goes inside: food, obviously, but also toothpaste, sunscreen, lip balm, soap, the wrappers you have been carrying, and the trash. Pack the canister at home once before the trip. Watching somebody discover on the trailhead pavement that six days of food does not fit into a BV450 is common and avoidable.

### The water, and a panic you can partly put down

The standard advice is to treat everything, and that remains the right default for a first trip: a filter, chemical tablets, or UV, chosen for what you will actually use rather than what looks best.

But the received wisdom about Giardia in the Sierra is worth a more accurate framing, because it has been studied. A long series of surveys of high Sierra water led by researchers at UC Davis, sampling roughly a hundred sites across Yosemite and the parks to the south, found that a majority of them had no detectable water-quality problem at all, and that contamination correlated overwhelmingly with cattle and pack-stock use rather than with backpackers. Coliform bacteria showed up in nearly every grazed site sampled and were rare in the backpacker-only ones. Measured Giardia cyst concentrations in the alpine sites were extremely low, low enough that the authors described the risk to humans as minimal. A separate study of backcountry travelers in the Tahoe-area wilderness found actual cyst acquisition in a small single-digit percentage.

What to do with that. Not to stop treating water, and the point is contested among people who study it. Do use it to aim your caution correctly: the real signal in the Sierra is what is upstream of you, and the meaningful risk is downstream of grazing, stock camps, and heavily used trail corridors, not a spring-fed alpine outlet. Fill high, fill above the pack station and above the meadow with horse traffic, and treat it anyway. It costs little.

### The regulations that ride along

Short list, all of them easy to comply with and all of them things people get cited for out of ignorance rather than intent.

Camp at least 100 feet from water and from the trail. Call it forty paces. This is the most-violated rule in the wilderness and the one with the most visible consequences, since lakeshore camping is what turns a shoreline into a network of bare social trails.

No campfires above 9,600 feet, ever. The trees up there grow slowly enough that a season of campfires undoes a century. Between 6,000 and 9,600 feet, existing rings only. And below that, seasonal fire restrictions come and go with conditions, so check the current status for your dates rather than assuming, particularly late in a dry summer.

Group size caps at 15 on trail, and 8 for cross-country travel.

Human waste: a cathole six inches deep, 100 feet from water, trail, and camp, and toilet paper comes out with you. Not buried. Out.

Little Yosemite Valley has its own rules because of its volume: parties starting at Happy Isles or Glacier Point on an LYV itinerary camp there the first night, in a designated area with lockers and a composting toilet.

Photo: Cory Goehring

### Four first trips that work

All four are short, well-signed, reliably watered, and free of any crossing that becomes a decision in a normal year past early July.

Cathedral Lakes, from Tioga Road at Tuolumne Meadows. Roughly four and a half miles in, and nine or so round trip, with somewhere between a thousand and 1,400 feet of cumulative gain depending on which lakes you visit, to a pair of them sitting under one of the most photographed spires in the range. It is the standard first Yosemite overnight for good reason, and consequently one of the harder permits to draw. The day-hike version is the same trail if the permit does not come through, and it has the full breakdown of the walk.

Sunrise Lakes, from Tenaya Lake. About ten and a half miles round trip with roughly 1,300 feet of gain, most of it in one steep block of switchbacks after a flat opening, and three lakes at the top so you have options on where to put the tent.

Glen Aulin, down the Tuolumne from the meadows. Longer on paper at about eleven miles round trip, but only around 800 feet of elevation change, which makes it gentler than its mileage suggests and an unusually good pick for somebody who is fit but new to a loaded pack. Check bridge status before you go, since this route crosses the river.

Little Yosemite Valley, from Happy Isles. Under ten miles round trip with about 2,000 feet of gain, up past Vernal and Nevada Falls on the Mist Trail, which means your approach is one of the best day hikes in the park. Skip the Half Dome add-on the first time. With the cables it becomes a fundamentally harder trip.

### What actually goes wrong

Yosemite runs on the order of a couple of hundred search-and-rescue operations a year, and the number has been climbing, partly because satellite messengers now let people call for help from places where previously they would have walked out. The distribution is instructive: the modal patient is not a lost mountaineer, it is somebody with a lower-body injury on a maintained trail. Extremity injuries dominate the backcountry medical calls. Falls are the mechanism most likely to be fatal.

The failure modes on a first trip are ordinary, which means they are preventable. In rough order of how often I have watched them happen:

Feet. Untested boots, no blister kit, no attention paid until it is a wound. Tape the hot spot when you feel it, not at camp.

Too much pack. A first-timer's pack is routinely ten to fifteen pounds heavier than it needs to be, and the weight goes onto knees and ankles descending, which is where the injuries are.

Too much mileage. Day one with a full pack at altitude is not a day hike. Half the distance you would walk unloaded is a reasonable planning figure for a first trip.

Arriving at the trailhead in the afternoon. Late start, storm, and a headlamp descent into camp.

No plan for the crossing. Not because the party was reckless, but because nobody had decided in advance what "too high" looks like, so the decision got made while standing in it.

### The part that makes it worth the paperwork

Ninety-five percent of Yosemite is designated wilderness, and on any given day almost none of it has anyone standing in it. The first mile past a trailhead clears out the crowd. By the second, the country is yours.

The first night out is mostly logistics, the same as a first night in a campground. You are cold, or the pad is odd, or you are listening to noises. Then the light comes up on granite you cannot see from any road, and there is nobody in it, and the permits, quotas and canister volumes start to look like a fair price.

Go somewhere small the first time. Then go back.

## Yosemite Day Trip From San Francisco: The Honest Math

URL: https://thetalusfieldjournal.com/articles/yosemite-day-trip-from-bay-area
Section: Planning. Published: 2026-08-07. Last updated: 2026-08-07.
Summary: Yosemite as a day trip from San Francisco or San Jose: real drive times, daylight math, parking, the one-day Valley plan that works, and the train alternative.

It is a bit under two hundred miles from San Francisco to Yosemite Valley. On a map that looks like an easy out-and-back for a Saturday. Every summer a great many people look at that map and reach the obvious conclusion, and a large fraction of them arrive in the Valley at half past eleven, spend four hours in a place that deserves four days, and drive home in the dark wondering why the trip felt like a day in a parking lot.

The day trip is not impossible. I have done it, and I have watched thousands of people do it, and some of them have a good day. But it works on a narrow set of conditions, and most of what is written about it omits the arithmetic. So here is the arithmetic first, and then, if you are going anyway, how to spend the hours you actually get.

### The number that decides everything

Ignore the routing app. It will tell you something in the region of three and a half hours from San Francisco, and that number assumes an empty I-580 through the Altamont, no stop for gas or coffee or a bathroom, no line at the entrance station, and a driver who does not slow down for the hundred-odd curves on the New Priest Grade.

The honest planning figure, door to Valley floor, is four to five hours each way from San Francisco or Oakland, and about the same from San Jose. The entrances guide puts Highway 140 from the Bay at roughly three hours forty-five minutes to the Arch Rock gate in clear conditions, and Highway 120 through Groveland at about four hours to the Big Oak Flat entrance with another forty-five minutes of park road after it. Both of those are optimistic once real life is added. Call it nine hours of driving for the round trip and you will not be disappointed.

Set that against daylight, which is the real budget.

Around the summer solstice, Yosemite Valley gets close to fifteen hours of it, with sunrise near half past five and sunset around twenty past eight. Leave the Bay at five in the morning and you are on the Valley floor by nine or nine thirty; leave the Valley at five in the afternoon and you are home around ten at night. That is a seventeen-hour day for seven or eight hours in the park, and it is a workable, tiring day.

Around the winter solstice the same park gets about nine and a half hours of daylight, and the sun is behind the south rim well before it sets. The earliest sunsets of the year fall in the first week of December, around twenty to five. Leave the Bay at five in the morning in December and you arrive at nine thirty to a Valley that goes dark at four thirty, and to hold any margin against ice on the drive home you want to be moving by three. That is five usable hours, half of them in flat winter light, and the last two hours of the drive home in the dark on a mountain road in winter.

June buys you seven hours in the park for seventeen hours of your day. December buys you five, and asks you to drive Highway 140 in the dark to get them.

### Which road, and when

Two routes matter from the Bay, and the choice is seasonal rather than a matter of taste.

Highway 120, through Groveland to the Big Oak Flat entrance, is the shorter line from San Francisco and San Jose and the natural pick from roughly May into October, especially if any part of your day involves the high country. The climb out of the Central Valley is the Priest Grade, and it comes in two versions: the old one, which is short, steep, narrow, and closed to trailers and heavy vehicles, and the new one, which is longer, gentler, and full of curves. Take the new one. The old one saves about eleven minutes.

Highway 140, through Mariposa and up the Merced River canyon to Arch Rock, is the all-weather road and the winter answer. It stays lower than any other approach, it sees chain control least often, and it puts you on the Valley floor faster once you are through the gate. It has one permanent quirk: the 2006 Ferguson rockslide buried the original roadbed near El Portal, and traffic has run on a signal-controlled one-lane bypass ever since. Caltrans is building the permanent fix, a rock shed, and it is a project measured in years rather than months, so plan on the signal being there. It costs you a few minutes and occasionally more on a busy afternoon. The canyon is also slide-prone in a wet spring, and emergency closures for rock scaling happen; check road status before you commit to it in storm season.

From roughly November into March, chain control can go up on any approach to this park. Carrying a set that fits your car is required inside a control area regardless of what you drive; whether you have to actually fit them depends on the level, and under the lighter levels an all-wheel-drive vehicle on snow tires is usually waved through. Under the strictest level everybody chains up. Either way the set has to be in the car: cars do get turned around at the checkpoints. Buy chains before you leave the Bay, where they are cheaper than anywhere within a hundred miles of the park, and put them on once in your driveway so the first time is not in a storm on a shoulder.

### The gate is not the bottleneck. The parking lot is.

In 2026 there is no day-use reservation to show. The systems that ran from 2020 through 2025 are gone, and you drive up. The entrance fee is $35 per vehicle, good for seven days, and the gate takes cards only. An $80 America the Beautiful pass covers it if you have one, and the $100 per-person surcharge introduced in January 2026 applies to non-US visitors.

Removing the reservation moved the queue. On peak summer weekends the entrance lines run an hour or more from mid-morning through late afternoon, and the Valley day-use lots fill early. The reported pattern over the 2026 season has been lots full somewhere between seven and eight in the morning on the busiest weekends, which is before a driver who left San Francisco at five in the morning can physically arrive.

That reshapes the trip. A day-tripper who leaves at five on a July Saturday is arriving into a full Valley. There is nowhere to put the car, and the answer at that point is to keep circling, which is how people end up spending ninety minutes of a seven-hour visit looking for a space. The parking guide is worth reading before you go, and the operating principle is the one the Park Service repeats every year: park once, and then do not move the car. The free Valley shuttle runs from early morning until late evening and reaches nearly everything you would drive to.

The most useful point in this article: a Bay Area day trip on a summer Saturday is a fundamentally different and worse trip than the same day trip on a Tuesday. Midweek often decides whether the trip works at all.

Photo: Stephen Leonardi / Pexels

### The one day that works

Assume you arrive around nine thirty and need to be driving out by four thirty. Seven hours. This is the version that produces a good day, and its rule is that you pick one part of the park and let the rest go.

Stop at Tunnel View on the way in if you came up Highway 41 or over from 120 via Wawona Road. It is twenty minutes including the photograph, it is the single best orientation to the Valley's geography that exists, and it costs nothing. If you came in on 140 it is a detour and worth taking on the way out instead, in better light.

Park once, in the Valley, and get on the shuttle. Yosemite Village or the Yosemite Falls area. Do not plan to move the car again until you leave.

Lower Yosemite Fall, a short paved loop to the base of the lower fall. Under an hour. In May it is thunderous and you will get wet; by August it can be dry, and this is worth knowing before you build a day around waterfalls. The waterfall guide has the seasonal timing.

Cook's Meadow Loop, a mile on boardwalk and flat path, with Yosemite Falls behind you and Half Dome ahead. Half an hour, entirely level, and the best half hour in the Valley for the effort. This is the one I send people to when they have an hour and no other information.

Bridalveil Fall, at the west end, reopened in 2023 after a long rehabilitation with a rebuilt trail, new viewing platforms, and proper parking. Short, paved, and it runs year-round rather than drying up in late summer.

Lunch on the ground somewhere, which you brought, because the food options in the Valley are limited, expensive, and busy at exactly the hour you want them. A cooler in the car is worth more on a day trip than on any other kind of Yosemite trip, because your time is the scarce resource and a queue for a sandwich costs forty minutes of it.

If there is time left, El Capitan Meadow, and a pair of binoculars. In spring and autumn there are reliably people on the wall, less so in the midsummer heat, and finding them is the most memorable twenty minutes many visitors have here.

That is a full, unhurried day, and every item on it is flat, paved or nearly so, and inside a two-mile radius.

### The plans that do not work

Three reasonable-sounding additions eat day trips.

Adding Glacier Point. It is about thirty miles from the Valley and roughly an hour each way, so it is a two-hour round trip out of your seven before you have stood anywhere. The view is one of the great ones on the continent, and there is a version of the day trip built entirely around it, arriving late afternoon for the light. What does not work is treating it as a bonus stop on a Valley day. Pick one.

Adding Mariposa Grove. About an hour to Wawona, then a mandatory seasonal shuttle to the grove itself, then the walk, then all of it in reverse. Three hours minimum, realistically more with a shuttle wait. On a day trip it takes the whole day, which is a fine day. The grove guide covers doing it properly.

Adding a real hike. The Mist Trail to the top of Vernal Fall is not a long hike, but it is a serious one, and on a day-trip schedule you will be climbing it in the middle of a hot afternoon with a four-hour drive waiting for you. People do this and then drive home exhausted, which is the actual safety issue with Yosemite day trips: the dangerous part is Highway 120 at ten at night with a driver who has been awake since four.

### The train, which is better than it sounds

There is a car-free version, and for some people it is better.

Amtrak's San Joaquins run from the Bay Area to Merced, with bus connections from San Francisco to Emeryville and a direct BART interchange at Richmond, and the first departures land in Merced in the morning. YARTS, the regional transit system, runs buses from the Merced station up Highway 140 into Yosemite Valley year-round, timed to meet the trains, and the two can be booked as a single ticket.

The advantages are real: you skip the entrance line entirely, you have no parking problem to solve, the free Valley shuttle takes it from there, and somebody else drives home while you sleep. The disadvantage is equally real: the combined transit time runs roughly four to four and a half hours each way, which is no faster than driving and less flexible, and the schedule rather than your judgment decides when you leave the Valley. A same-day round trip is possible but tight, and it typically leaves fewer hours in the park than the car does.

Confirm before you book whether your fare includes the park entrance fee, because the published answer varies depending on where you read it, and budget for the $35 either way. The shuttle and YARTS guide has the current routes and the cases where driving still wins, and the timetables move seasonally, so check them rather than trusting any article, this one included.

### What it costs

A round trip from San Francisco is close to four hundred miles. At the sort of gas prices California has been carrying through 2026, and they have been at or near record highs, the fuel alone runs roughly seventy to a hundred dollars depending on the vehicle, and buying it in El Portal or Mariposa rather than before you leave the Central Valley costs meaningfully more. Add the $35 entrance fee, which you pay in full for one day's use of a seven-day pass.

The entrance fee is not per day. A day-tripper pays $35 for one day; a family that stays two nights in a gateway town pays the same $35 for three. Set the marginal cost of the second day against a night in Mariposa, Groveland, or El Portal, and the overnight is often the cheaper way to buy time in the park. The trip-cost guide works the whole calculation.

### When the day trip is genuinely the right call

There are four cases, and in all four I would tell you to go.

Midweek, from October into April. This is the real answer, and almost nobody does it. The Valley in November on a Wednesday is close to empty, the parking problem does not exist, the entrance line does not exist, the waterfalls are running again after the autumn rains, and the light is low all day. You get fewer hours, and better ones. Winter here is the most underrated season in the park.

A specific errand. You want to see Horsetail Fall in the third week of February, or the dogwood in May, or El Capitan on a clear October afternoon. A day trip with one objective and no itinerary is a completely different experience from a day trip trying to see Yosemite.

The reconnaissance. You have never been, you are not sure it is for you, and you would rather spend a Tuesday finding out than book three nights on faith. Go, do the Valley loop above, and come back properly.

You are already halfway. If you are coming from the eastern edge of the Bay or from the Central Valley, the arithmetic changes materially and most of this article's pessimism relaxes.

### And when it is not

If what you want is a day in mountains, in trees, on a trail, away from a city, and Yosemite is only the name you know for that, then the day trip is the wrong tool and there are better ones within an hour of your house.

Point Reyes is roughly an hour and a half from San Francisco and gives you an entire day of coastline, elk, and empty trail. Mount Diablo is under an hour from either side of the Bay and on a clear winter morning has one of the longest sightlines in North America. Henry Coe is forty minutes from San Jose and is genuinely rugged country that almost nobody visits. Pinnacles is a national park roughly two hours out with condors in it. Castle Rock and the Skyline ridge are twenty minutes from the Santa Cruz Mountains side. Big Basin has reopened for day use as it rebuilds from the 2020 fire, and watching a redwood forest come back is its own kind of thing to see.

Every one of those gives you six to ten hours on the ground for two to three hours of driving. Yosemite gives you five to seven hours on the ground for eight or nine hours of driving. If the goal is a day outside, the local parks win. If the goal is Yosemite specifically, the recommendation is a night in a gateway town, an entrance at seven in the morning, before the crowds arrive.

### If you are going anyway

Most people will. The short version:

Go on a weekday. Leave before five. Fill the tank in the Central Valley, not at the park. Pack a cooler and eat out of it. Check road status and chain control the night before and again that morning. Pick one part of the park and let the other parts go. Park once. Take the shuttle. Start driving home before you feel ready, because the last two hours of that drive are the part that goes wrong. Swap drivers if you can, and if you cannot, stop in Mariposa or Groveland for coffee whether or not you want it.

And know what you are buying. You are not seeing Yosemite in a day, You are seeing a mile of the Valley floor in the middle of the day, which is the least interesting mile at the least interesting hour, and it is still going to be one of the more startling things you have looked at.

#### The version of this trip that actually works

One night in a gateway town converts a nine-hour drive with seven park-hours into two mornings at the gate before it opens up, for less than most people assume. Mariposa is the Highway 140 town and the shortest run to the Valley floor; Groveland is the 120 answer if you came through Groveland.

## Swimming in Yosemite: Where to Get in the Merced River

URL: https://thetalusfieldjournal.com/articles/swimming-in-the-merced
Section: Seasonal Guides. Published: 2026-08-07. Last updated: 2026-08-07.
Summary: When it is safe to swim in the Merced River in Yosemite, the best beaches, the places swimming is prohibited, cold water shock, and how to check the flow.

On a hot August afternoon the Merced River is the best thing in Yosemite Valley: green water over pale granite, shade from the black oaks, El Capitan overhead, and a temperature drop of twenty degrees the moment you get in. It is also the setting for a steady run of rescues and drownings, year after year, and the Park Service pulls fifteen to twenty people out of the water in a normal season. The difference is mostly the calendar, and secondarily knowing the rules.

### The season is the safety rule

The Merced is a snowmelt river. It does not warm up gradually and evenly the way a lowland river does; it runs high, fast and near freezing through the spring melt, then drops over a few weeks into something entirely different. The same stretch of water that will drown a strong adult in May is a place where six-year-olds stand around in ankle-deep water in August.

The practical version, and this is the one the site has taken as its position for years: do not swim in the Merced in spring. Through the melt the current is stronger than it looks, the water is cold enough to disable you in under a minute, and spring is when people get carried off the bank. By high summer, once the flow has dropped and the water has had weeks of sun on shallow granite, it becomes the family swimming river everybody pictures. By September it is low, warm and slow.

As a rough guide: the swimming season runs from about mid-July into September, and in June the answer is almost always not yet. But the transition does not happen on a date: it moves several weeks in either direction with the snowpack. In a heavy year the river can still be running spring volumes well into July. What matters is the flow on the day you are standing there.

### How to check before you get in

There is a gauge on the Merced at Pohono Bridge, at the west end of Yosemite Valley, and it is the number the park itself regulates against. The park's own boating rule keys off it: when the Pohono Bridge gauge reads above four feet at eight in the morning, flotation is mandatory for everyone on the water. That threshold is a useful signal even if you have no intention of getting into a boat. If the river is high enough that the Park Service has made life jackets compulsory for rafters, it is not a swimming day, and no amount of the water looking calm at your particular beach changes that.

Check current river conditions and any posted closures on the park's conditions page before you go, and look at the river itself when you arrive. Water moving fast enough to push a stick along faster than you would walk is water that will move you too.

### Cold water is what actually gets people

The mental model most visitors carry is hypothermia: cold water is dangerous because you slowly get too cold. That model kills strong swimmers, because the dangerous part happens in the first minute.

Going into cold water triggers an involuntary gasp, followed by breathing you cannot control. If your head is under at the moment of the gasp, you inhale water. If it is not, you spend the next half minute or so hyperventilating and unable to hold a breath, which is exactly when a current is deciding where you go. Then, over the following minutes, your hands and forearms stop doing what you ask of them, well before you feel dangerously cold. Strong swimmers drown in snowmelt because the cold temporarily takes away their ability to swim.

Get in gradually rather than jumping, so the gasp happens while you are standing up in shallow water. Do not enter cold water alone. Do not enter it upstream of anything you would not want to be swept into. And treat the first thirty seconds as the hazard, rather than the swim.

Photo: Robert Schrader / Pexels

### Where people swim

Swimming is permitted in the Merced through Yosemite Valley, and there are no lifeguards anywhere on it. There is no designated swimming area and no supervised beach. There are a handful of places where the river has laid down sand and slowed enough to be sensible.

Sentinel Beach is the default: a sandy bank on the south side with a picnic area attached, calm by late summer, and Half Dome visible from the water. It is the one to take small children to.

Cathedral Beach, downstream, is wider and deeper, with El Capitan filling the view upstream. Better for adults who want to swim, and worth more caution earlier in the season because the current through it is stronger than Sentinel's.

Devil's Elbow is a bend on Northside Drive that turns into a good swimming reach once the river drops. The Swinging Bridge area, on Southside Drive with Upper Yosemite Fall in the view, is shallow and sandy and the best wading spot in the Valley for toddlers. Jumping or diving from the bridge itself is not permitted. Note also that there are two Swinging Bridges in this park: this one, and a different one down in Wawona.

Wawona, on the South Fork of the Merced at 4,000 feet with a much smaller drainage above it, has the warmest swimming in the park and is worth the drive on a heat-wave afternoon. Tenaya Lake, at 8,150 feet on Tioga Road, is the opposite proposition: a real sand beach and cold water, covered in the Tuolumne day guide.

### Where you must not, which is not a matter of judgment

Swimming is prohibited, not discouraged, in a specific list of places. Above Vernal Fall, that means Emerald Pool and the Silver Apron. It also means Hetch Hetchy Reservoir and the first mile up its tributaries, the Dana Fork of the Tuolumne, Lake Eleanor where posted, and the Wawona domestic water intake and the hundred yards above it.

The Emerald Pool closure is the one people argue with, because it is a beautiful green pool at the top of a hard climb on a hot day, and the water above it looks flat. The Park Service has documented what happens there. In one afternoon, five teenagers were injured sliding down the closed Silver Apron. On another, two eighteen-year-olds swimming in the Emerald Pool were caught by a current they had not seen in water cold enough to take their breath, and one of them was pulled out by a passing stranger. In both incidents everyone lived.

In July 2011 three visitors in their twenties, Hormiz David, Ninos Yacoub and Ramina Badal, climbed over the metal guardrail about twenty-five feet above the brink of Vernal Fall, after other hikers had called out to them not to. All three went over. The recoveries took months. The Mist Trail guide makes the same point from the trail's side, and it is the single rule on that trail that has cost the most lives: the water above a waterfall is moving faster than it appears, the granite under it is polished and frictionless, and there is no version of losing your footing there that you recover from.

Never swim above a waterfall. Not at the top of Vernal Fall, not at the top of Nevada Fall, not in any pool that drains toward an edge you cannot see over.

### Rafting, and the flotation rule

The Valley's classic float runs from Stoneman Bridge down to Sentinel Beach, a slow three miles through the middle of the Valley, and it is a good way to spend a ninety-degree afternoon. Rafts are rented in season at Curry Village, with a shuttle back. Season, price and age or weight minimums move year to year, so check current-season details rather than trusting a number you read somewhere, including here.

If you bring your own inflatable, the rules that matter are these. Boating is restricted above Little Yosemite Valley and below El Capitan Bridge. Children under thirteen must wear a life jacket on the water at all times. And when the Pohono Bridge gauge is above four feet at eight in the morning, everybody wears one, regardless of age or competence. The Merced has tipped plenty of people off pool inflatables and into the water.

### The hazards that are not the cold

Strainers. A submerged log or a fallen branch lets water through and does not let you through. This is the classic river killer and it is invisible from upstream. Never swim toward or under downed timber in moving water.

Foot entrapment. Standing up in moving water deeper than your knees is how a foot gets wedged between rocks and the current puts you face down. If you are being carried, float on your back with your feet up and pointing downstream, and do not try to stand until you are out of the current.

Slick rock. Granite at the waterline grows a film of algae that is far more slippery than it looks, and most Merced injuries are not drownings at all. They are people going down hard on rock. Water shoes are not overkill here; the riverbed is cobble and the banks are polished stone.

Water that looks slower than it is. A smooth surface means depth, not calm. The fastest water in a river is usually the water making the least noise.

### Getting in without wrecking the bank

The Park Service asks visitors to enter and leave the river only at sandy beaches, for erosion control. The Merced through the Valley is a protected Wild and Scenic river, and the few miles of riverbank through the developed part of the Valley take an enormous amount of foot traffic. Banks that get scrambled up and down collapse, the vegetation that holds them goes, and the beach itself eventually goes with it. Sections are fenced and revegetating for exactly this reason.

So: walk to the sand, get in from the sand, get out at the sand. It is also the safest way in: the places where the bank is intact and steep are the places where the current is doing the work.

### With children

Pick Sentinel Beach or the Swinging Bridge shallows and stay there. Put small children in life jackets even when they are only standing in ankle-deep water, because the transition from ankle-deep to over-their-head can be one step on a shelving sandbar. Water shoes for everyone. Assign one adult to watch the water and nothing else, and rotate that job, because drowning is famously quiet and a group of adults who are all half-watching is a group where nobody is watching. The guide to Yosemite with kids has more on structuring a Valley day around a river afternoon rather than fitting it in if there is time left.

### The short version

- Do not swim during the spring melt. High summer into September is the season, and the changeover moves with the snowpack rather than the calendar.
- If the Pohono Bridge gauge is above four feet, the park requires life jackets on the water. Treat that as the river telling you it is not a swimming day.
- Cold water disables you in the first minute, before hypothermia is anywhere in the picture. Get in slowly, never alone.
- Swim at the sandy beaches: Sentinel, Cathedral, Devil's Elbow, Swinging Bridge. There are no lifeguards on the river.
- Swimming is prohibited above Vernal Fall, at Emerald Pool and the Silver Apron, and in the several other places the park lists. That is a rule, not advice.
- Never swim above any waterfall, anywhere, at any flow.
- Enter and exit only at sandy beaches, for the bank's sake and for yours.
- Wawona is warmer, Tenaya Lake is colder, and both are worth the drive.

None of this argues against getting in the water. It argues against doing it with no plan, in flip-flops, on the hottest afternoon of the year. An hour on a sandbar in cold water is one of the cheapest pleasures in the park, and the precautions above cost almost nothing.

### Sources

- Water Activities, NPS Yosemite
- Boating and Rafting, NPS Yosemite

- Vernal Fall search and rescue, July 2011, NPS Yosemite
- Turning Blue in the Emerald Pool, NPS Yosemite
- Merced Wild and Scenic River Plan, NPS Yosemite

## Tuolumne Meadows in a day: a Yosemite high-country plan

URL: https://thetalusfieldjournal.com/articles/tuolumne-meadows-in-a-day
Section: Planning. Published: 2026-08-07. Last updated: 2026-08-07.
Summary: How to spend a day in Tuolumne Meadows: the Tioga Road drive, what is open in 2026, easy walks for families and non-hikers, altitude, and thunderstorms.

Most people meet Tuolumne Meadows through a windshield at forty miles an hour on their way to Mono Lake, and come away thinking it was scenery, not a destination. That is a failure of itinerary design. Yosemite Valley is a canyon: you stand at the bottom and look up. Tuolumne is the opposite country, a broad open meadow at around 8,600 feet with the river running through it and granite domes standing loose around the edges, and you are on top of it rather than under it. It is worth a day. This is how to spend one, no climbing required.

### The drive, and the two hours nobody budgets

Tuolumne Meadows sits on Tioga Road, Highway 120 through the park, roughly 55 to 60 miles from Yosemite Valley. Call it an hour and a half each way in no traffic, and closer to two in July. That is three to four hours of driving bracketing your day, and that is what ruins Tuolumne itineraries: people leave the Valley at ten, arrive at noon, eat, walk for an hour, and drive home having seen a meadow through a window.

Leave early. The drive is part of the day, climbing from 4,000 feet in the Valley to 8,600 at the meadows and to 9,945 at Tioga Pass, the highest highway pass in California. From the east side it is a much shorter approach: Lee Vining to Tioga Pass is about twelve miles, and the meadows are a few miles further in.

Tioga Road opened on May 15 this year, unusually early, and it is open now. The opening-weekend piece covers the early-season version of this day, which is a different trip, and the Tioga Road opening page tracks when the road comes back each spring. For the drive in, turnout by turnout, see Tioga Road, stop by stop. One current caution: there is water distribution system construction near the visitor center, with one-way traffic control and short holds. Budget a few extra minutes and do not treat a queue as a closure. There is no vehicle reservation required to enter Yosemite in 2026.

### What is actually open, which changes every year

This is the section to read before you go, because the high country's services are seasonal, thin, and have been seriously disrupted for several years running. The point is to avoid driving two hours to a building that is not open.

There is no gas at Tuolumne Meadows. Start here, because it is the one that strands people. The old station has been out of operation for years and travel sites still list it. Inside the park on the west side, Crane Flat is the only fuel, pay-at-pump around the clock, and the point where Tioga Road begins. On the east side your next fuel is Lee Vining, about forty-five minutes past the meadows. Fill up at Crane Flat on the way in whether or not you think you need to.

The store, grill, and post office run a short summer season out of a temporary structure, and have for several years. Tuolumne Meadows Lodge runs roughly early June to mid-September in tent cabins. The campground came back in 2025 from a three-year, twenty-six-million-dollar rehabilitation as a 336-site campground, reservable through recreation.gov. White Wolf Lodge, down the road toward Crane Flat, has been closed by sewer line damage, with its campground running at reduced capacity and no potable water. The visitor center and wilderness center operate in season.

Every one of those is a moving target. Call the park's information line before you commit a day to a meal or a bed up there, and in the meantime pack as though nothing is open: your own lunch, your own water, and more of both than you think. That is also the better way to do this day.

Photo: basiciggy / Pexels

### The walks that are not hikes

The high country's reputation is for big days: Clouds Rest, Mount Dana, Cathedral Lakes. That reputation keeps families and non-hikers away, and it is misleading. Tuolumne has an unusually good supply of very short walks that deliver the whole landscape, because at 8,600 feet you are already standing in the view. Distances below are round trip.

Olmsted Point nature trail. Half a mile, a hundred feet of climb, half an hour. A short walk off the pullout onto open granite, looking down Tenaya Canyon at the back of Half Dome and up at Clouds Rest. This is the single highest ratio of view to effort on Tioga Road, and it is doable in sandals on a driving day.

Pothole Dome. One mile, two hundred feet, an hour. At the west end of the meadow. You walk the meadow edge and then up glacier-polished granite that is gentle enough to stroll. Ten minutes of climbing buys the entire sweep of Tuolumne Meadows. If you do one thing in this article, do this one.

Soda Springs and Parsons Memorial Lodge. A mile and a half, a hundred feet, an hour and a quarter. Flat, on an old road, from the Lembert Dome lot across the meadow. At the end there are springs bubbling up naturally carbonated out of the ground, which children tend not to believe, and a stone Sierra Club lodge from 1915 where a good deal of the argument about what national parks are for was thrashed out.

Tenaya Lake loop. Two and a half miles, flat. A big subalpine lake at 8,150 feet with a real sandy beach at the east end, ringed by a level trail. This is the family stop: the beach works for people who want to do nothing at all, and the loop works for people who want to move.

Lukens Lake. A mile and six tenths, two hundred feet. Off Tioga Road well west of the meadows, through forest to a shallow lake in a wildflower meadow. Good for small children and fine in mosquito season if you come prepared for them.

May Lake. Two and four tenths of a mile, five hundred feet. Steeper than the others but short, ending at a lake directly under Mount Hoffmann in the geographic center of the park.

### If you want one real hike

Lembert Dome is the classic: two and eight tenths of a mile with 850 feet of climb, up the back of the dome that stands over the east end of the meadow, finishing on bare granite with the whole basin underneath you. Allow two and a half hours. It is a walk-up rather than a scramble, but the last stretch is open rock with real exposure at the edges, so it is a poor choice with a child who runs.

Dog Lake shares its trailhead: also two and eight tenths of a mile, 650 feet, one steady climb and then a shallow, unusually warm lake with Mount Dana and Mount Gibbs on the skyline. It is the most swimmable water in the high country.

Gaylor Lakes, right at the Tioga Pass entrance, is two and six tenths of a mile and 500 feet, and starts at almost 10,000 feet, so it feels harder than it reads. Elizabeth Lake is four and eight tenths of a mile and 1,000 feet from the campground. And Cathedral Lakes, the high country's most famous day hike, is a genuine 11 miles: a full day on its own, not something to bolt onto this one.

The common mistake is choosing a hike when what the day needed was a meadow, a lunch, and three hours of not driving.

### The altitude is real, and it is the reason your day went badly

Tuolumne Meadows is more than 4,500 feet above the Valley floor. If you slept in the Valley, or flew into California two days ago, you are arriving at an elevation your body has no preparation for. It does not usually present as dramatic mountain sickness. It presents as a headache after lunch, a shorter temper than usual, a child who is suddenly done, and a walk that felt much harder than a mile ought to feel.

The mitigations are simple: drink considerably more water than you want to, eat more than you planned, go slower than feels natural on the first walk of the day, and treat the first hour up there as an adjustment rather than an achievement. If a headache does not respond to water, food, and rest, the treatment is elevation loss, and you have a car and a road that descends 4,000 feet. Use it rather than pushing on.

### The afternoon storm, which ends the day earlier than you want

In July and August the Sierra high country builds thunderstorms out of a clear morning with startling speed. The pattern is reliable enough to plan around: clear at dawn, cumulus stacking by late morning, and the possibility of lightning from early afternoon on.

The practical rule is to do the exposed thing first. Domes, summits, and open granite in the morning; meadow, forest, lakeshore, and lunch in the afternoon. Being the highest object on a bare granite dome with a storm building is the specific way this landscape hurts people, and it is entirely avoidable by reordering your day. Carry a rain shell in a daypack even when the morning makes it look ridiculous. The heat and weather guide goes further into lightning.

### Water, and the swimming question

Tenaya Lake and the Tuolumne River are both swimmable, in the sense that people swim in them and are pleased with themselves afterward. At 8,000 feet and above, water that has recently been snow is cold in a way that a Valley swimmer is not braced for, so the same rules apply as everywhere else in this park: get in where there is a beach, do not swim alone, and take the first thirty seconds seriously. The swimming guide covers the physiology, which matters more in cold water than anyone expects.

Bring all your drinking water. There is very little to buy up there and the seasonal facilities cannot be assumed. Two liters a person is a floor, not a target, at that elevation and that sun.

### A day, laid out

- Leave the Valley by seven. Fill the tank at Crane Flat as you turn onto Tioga Road.
- Tuolumne Grove on the way, if you have the appetite. Two and a half miles and 500 feet down among two dozen giant sequoias, with the entire climb on the return. Skip it if the day is already full; it is a real hike despite the roadside trailhead.
- Olmsted Point, mid-morning. Half a mile, and the moment the scale of the place lands.
- Pothole Dome, late morning. Exposed granite, done before the weather thinks about it.
- Lunch in the meadow or at Tenaya Lake. Yours, from the car, because the alternative may not be open.
- Soda Springs and Parsons Lodge, early afternoon. Flat, shaded in stretches, and under trees if a storm arrives.
- Tenaya Lake beach until you are ready to leave. This is the part everyone remembers and the part every itinerary cuts.
- Drive out over Tioga Pass to Mono Lake if you are staying east, or back down to the Valley with two hours in hand before dark.

### The short version

- Budget three to four hours of driving around the day. Leave the Valley by seven.
- There is no gas at Tuolumne Meadows. Fill up at Crane Flat.
- Pack all food and water. Seasonal services up there cannot be assumed and several are still disrupted.
- The best short walks are Olmsted Point (half a mile), Pothole Dome (one mile), and Soda Springs (a mile and a half). None require being a hiker.
- Tenaya Lake is the family stop: sandy beach, flat loop, cold water.
- Do exposed granite in the morning. Afternoon thunderstorms are the season's normal behavior.
- The altitude is 8,600 feet. Drink more, eat more, go slower, and descend if a headache will not shift.
- Cathedral Lakes is a separate day. Do not staple it onto this one.

The reason to give Tuolumne a whole day rather than a scenic hour is that it is the only part of Yosemite where the landscape lets you stand still in the middle of it. In the Valley you look up at the landscape. In the meadows you are standing in it, and that takes longer than driving through.

### Sources

- Current Conditions, NPS Yosemite
- Tuolumne Meadows, NPS Yosemite

- Water Safety, NPS Yosemite

## Mariposa Grove: how to visit Yosemite's giant sequoias

URL: https://thetalusfieldjournal.com/articles/mariposa-grove-how-to-visit
Section: Planning. Published: 2026-08-07. Last updated: 2026-08-07.
Summary: How to visit Yosemite's Mariposa Grove: the free shuttle, where to park, the four trails, accessible access, winter on foot, and the rules that surprise people.

Most visitors arrive at the Mariposa Grove with the same wrong plan: they intend to drive to the trees. You cannot, not in summer, and not since 2018. The parking is two miles down the hill by the South Entrance and a free shuttle covers the gap. Nearly everything else that goes wrong on a grove day follows from not knowing that one fact, so this piece starts there and works outward.

### The geography, which is the whole problem

The grove sits in the park's southern corner, immediately inside the South Entrance on Highway 41. It is not near Yosemite Valley. From the Valley floor it is about an hour of driving each way, which is the single most underestimated number in this article.

Once you are through the entrance station you reach a roundabout almost at once, and the Mariposa Grove Welcome Plaza is the first right, less than a quarter mile in. That is where you park. The grove itself, what the Park Service calls the Arrival Area, is another two miles up Mariposa Grove Road, and in season that road is closed to private vehicles. A free shuttle covers the two miles. It is not relaxed on quiet days. It is the permanent arrangement the 2018 restoration created, for reasons covered below.

1 South Entrance, Highway 41. The Welcome Plaza parking is the first right at the roundabout, under a quarter mile in, too small to show at this scale.2 The grove, two miles up Mariposa Grove Road. Free shuttle about every 15 min, about 10 min up, no reservation; closed to private cars in season, and a disability placard may drive it. The Washburn Trail walks the same two miles.Map: National Park Service (public domain), cropped.

The four walks, drawn from the distances in this article. Upper-grove distances vary between sources; read the map at the Arrival Area before the long walks.

### The shuttle

It is free, there is no ticket, and individual riders need no reservation. Buses run roughly every fifteen minutes and take about ten minutes to cover the two miles. They are wheelchair accessible, with lifts and tie-downs, and chair users board first.

The Park Service does not publish a hard date for the season. Its standing language is that the shuttle begins no earlier than April 15 and ends on or before November 30. That is a commitment to a window, not a promise about a day, and it exists because the opening depends on when the road is clear of snow.

There is one firm 2026 date, though it applies to other vehicles. Buses and vehicles over about twenty-one feet must reserve grove parking through recreation.gov, and that reservation window this year runs May 3 through November 30. It is a reasonable proxy for the operating season, because the reservations exist to manage a road the shuttle is running on. Treat it as an inference, not a timetable. Secondary sites publish hour-by-hour tables that disagree with each other, and none of them is a Park Service figure. Check the posted hours at the plaza when you arrive, and note the last downhill departure before you walk away from the stop. People miss it, and the walk down is two miles.

Photo: Nieves / Pexels

### If you hold a disability placard

The road closure has an exception. A vehicle displaying a disability placard or plate may drive Mariposa Grove Road to the Arrival Area, and there is accessible parking at the top. The spaces are described by the Park Service as very limited, which in practice means a handful, so this is a privilege that works best early in the day. The Big Trees Loop at the top is paved and flat, which makes the grove one of the more rewarding accessible destinations in the park. The accessibility guide covers what the placard does and does not get you elsewhere in Yosemite.

### Walking up instead

You can also walk from the plaza to the grove on the Washburn Trail, which climbs roughly two miles and a few hundred feet through mixed conifer forest before the first sequoias appear. There are two reasons to do it. First, the shuttle queue on an August afternoon can be long enough that walking is competitive. Second, on foot you watch the forest change as the sequoias appear.

### The four walks, in order of ambition

The Big Trees Loop. Three tenths of a mile, paved and boardwalked, flat, wheelchair accessible, starting from the Arrival Area. It passes the Fallen Monarch, the toppled sequoia whose upturned root mass appears in one of the most reproduced photographs in the park's history, a US Cavalry troop and their horses drawn up along the trunk. If someone in your group cannot walk far, this is the loop that still gives them the grove.

The Grizzly Giant Loop. About two miles with a few hundred feet of climbing, and the one to do if you are only doing one. It takes in the Bachelor and Three Graces, the Grizzly Giant itself, and the California Tunnel Tree. Two hours is a comfortable allowance, including time spent stopping at the trees.

The Guardians Loop. Six and a half miles or so into the upper grove, with something over a thousand feet of gain. This is where the crowds thin to almost nothing, and where the Faithful Couple, the Clothespin Tree, and the Telescope Tree are. Give it however long you would normally give a six-mile hike, then add an hour.

The Mariposa Grove Trail to Wawona Point. Roughly seven miles round trip from the Arrival Area with a similar amount of climbing, ending at an overlook above the Wawona basin. It is the full day, and the only one of the four that ends with a view instead of a tree.

Distances and gains published for the upper-grove trails vary between sources by enough to matter on a hot afternoon, and some trail-aggregator sites use loop names that do not appear on Park Service signage. Read the map at the Arrival Area before you commit to the long options.

### The trees worth knowing by name

The Grizzly Giant is the one people come for. The Park Service calls it the largest sequoia in Yosemite and puts its age at roughly 2,900 years. Other published estimates run a little higher, which is the normal state of affairs for a tree nobody is going to cut down and count. Look at the first big limb rather than the trunk: it is thicker than the whole of most mature trees you have ever stood under, and it shows the scale better than the trunk does.

The California Tunnel Tree stands a short way past it, cut through in 1895 so that stagecoaches could be photographed driving through it. It is the only living tree in Yosemite you can still walk through. The more famous one, the Wawona Tunnel Tree, was cut in 1881 and fell in 1969 under a heavy snow load, and its stump is up in this same grove. The tunnel trees piece is the longer version of that story, which is less about vandalism than about what nineteenth-century Americans thought a national park was for.

The Bachelor and Three Graces are four trees growing so close that their root systems are effectively one, which is the practical argument for staying on the trail. Sequoia roots are shallow and wide, running out in a plate rather than down in a taproot, and the thing that kills a mature sequoia is almost never fire or disease. It is losing its footing.

Watch the film: Big TreesYosemite Nature Notes · Episode 11Big TreesThe Park Service on how deep snow and a long growing season build a tree the size of the Grizzly Giant.Film: National Park Service. Nothing loads from YouTube until you press play.

### Winter, when the road closes

Mariposa Grove Road closes to vehicles for the winter at the end of November and reopens when the snow allows, which has meant anywhere from early April onward in recent years. The reopening date moves with the snowpack and is not worth planning around more than a week out.

The grove itself does not close. The road and the trails stay open to foot travel, and walking, snowshoeing, or skiing the two miles up from the South Entrance makes a quiet February day. You will likely have the Grizzly Giant to yourself. Note that this is not a sanctioned snow-play area; the park's designated sledding hill is at Crane Flat, on the other side of the park. The winter guide has the rest of the cold-season picture.

### What the 2018 restoration changed, and why

For three years the grove was closed entirely. It reopened on June 15, 2018. What came out: the lower-grove parking lot, the gift shop, the pit toilets, and the commercial tram tours that had run through the trees for decades. Roughly four acres of habitat were restored, boardwalks went in over the wet ground, and the wetland hydrology the roads had interrupted was reconnected. The bill came to about forty million dollars, split evenly between the Park Service and the Yosemite Conservancy.

The reason is a single finding from the park's own survey work. The overwhelming majority of young sequoias in this grove, juveniles and saplings both, were growing within about a hundred feet of wetlands. The seeds need bare, wet mineral soil to take. Paving the wet ground and routing traffic across it did not kill the big trees, which is why the damage went unnoticed for a century. It quietly removed the next generation. The piece on sequoias and fire is the natural history behind that, and the two failures are related: a grove can look healthy and produce no new trees.

The trams are not coming back. That is not a scheduling problem or a budget problem. It is the point of the project.

### The rules that catch people out

Dogs are not allowed on any trail in the Mariposa Grove, including the paved ones. This is the rule that surprises people most, because Yosemite's general policy does allow leashed dogs on paved trails, and the Tuolumne Grove up on Highway 120 permits them on its paved section. The Mariposa Grove is an explicit exception. Dogs are fine in the parking lot and are not allowed on the shuttle, which means one adult stays with the car. The pets guide lays out where a dog can and cannot go in this park, and the answer is narrower than most owners expect.

Food stays within arm's reach. The picnic area at the plaza is a well-known bear spot. A daypack left on a table for three minutes is a daypack a bear has learned to check. The bear guide explains why a food-conditioned bear is usually a dead bear, which is the part that should change behavior.

Stay on the trail and off the root plates. See the Bachelor and Three Graces, above. Compacted soil over a sequoia's roots is a slow injury that nobody watches happen.

Bikes are allowed on Mariposa Grove Road but never on the trails, and only while the road is open to vehicles.

Buses and vehicles over about twenty-one feet need their own reservation. They book Mariposa Grove parking separately through recreation.gov; private cars do not. There is no separate fee for the grove beyond park entrance, and there is no park-wide vehicle reservation in effect for 2026.

### Timing, and the parking lot

The Welcome Plaza lot holds a few hundred vehicles and fills on busy days. It is a smaller number than it sounds, because grove visits are long and the turnover is slow: a lot that holds three hundred cars and empties every three hours serves far fewer people than one that turns over every forty minutes. Various sites will tell you it fills by eight, or by nine, or that you must be there by seven thirty. None of those are Park Service figures. Early morning and late afternoon work. Midday on a summer weekend does not.

For the day itself, allow two hours as an absolute floor, and that only buys the shuttle both ways and the Big Trees Loop. Half a day is right for the Grizzly Giant Loop with time to stand around. A full day is the upper grove. Add the hour each way from the Valley if that is where you are staying, and consider whether the grove wants to be paired with Wawona rather than squeezed onto a Valley day. The one or two day guide takes a position on that trade.

### The short version

- You cannot drive to the trees in season. Park at the Welcome Plaza by the South Entrance and take the free shuttle two miles up.
- The shuttle needs no reservation, runs about every fifteen minutes, and is wheelchair accessible. Its season runs roughly mid-April to the end of November, with no fixed dates published.
- A disability placard lets you drive the road. Accessible parking at the top is very limited.
- Big Trees Loop, three tenths of a mile and wheelchair accessible, is the everyone-can-do-it option. The Grizzly Giant Loop, about two miles, is the one to do if you do one.
- No dogs on any grove trail, paved included. This is an exception to the park's usual rule.
- In winter the road closes to cars and the grove stays open on foot. Snowshoe it.
- Allow two hours minimum, half a day to do it properly, plus an hour each way from the Valley.

The shuttle is part of the restoration. The old parking lot sat on the wet ground where young sequoias take root, and the two-mile ride costs visitors about fifteen minutes.

### Sources

- Mariposa Grove Welcome Plaza, NPS Yosemite

- Bears and Food Storage, NPS Yosemite
- Restoring the Mariposa Grove of Giant Sequoias, Yosemite Conservancy
