## Yosemite Bear Safety: What to Do When You See a Bear

URL: https://thetalusfieldjournal.com/articles/yosemite-bears-safety-guide
Section: Wildlife and Nature. Published: 2026-06-16. Last updated: 2026-10-01.
Summary: Bear spray is banned in Yosemite. So is most of what you think you know about bears. A naturalist's guide to six myths and what actually keeps you safe.

You packed bear spray. You saw it on every packing list for every national park trip you've ever planned. It's sitting in the side pocket of your pack right now, and when you get to the Yosemite entrance station, a ranger is going to confiscate it. Bear spray is illegal in Yosemite, not merely discouraged. Possession and use are both prohibited. It is classified as a weapon under National Park Service regulations, alongside pellet guns and crossbows. This surprises roughly half the visitors I talk to on any given day.

I've worked in this park for close to two decades. I see bears regularly. What I see even more regularly is visitors who have absorbed a set of bear facts from the internet that are confidently wrong, internally contradictory, and occasionally dangerous. People show up with a canister of capsaicin on their hip and a head full of grizzly bear survival tips for a park that has not had a grizzly bear in it since 1895. They've read the wrong guide for the wrong park and prepared for the wrong animal.

### Myth 1: Bear spray works in Yosemite

Bear spray is remarkably effective against grizzly bears. A landmark 2008 study by Tom Smith and Stephen Herrero, published in the Journal of Wildlife Management, analyzed 83 bear spray incidents in Alaska involving 175 people and found it stopped aggressive behavior 92% of the time. That's a better track record than firearms. It's also completely irrelevant here, because there are no grizzly bears in Yosemite. There have not been since around 1895, when the last one was shot near Crescent Lake. The California grizzly has been extinct for over a century.

Is bear spray legal in Yosemite? No. Not in any form, not under any circumstances. Why bear spray is illegal in Yosemite, including the California-wide question, is its own piece.

Yosemite has only American black bears, Ursus americanus, somewhere between 300 and 500 of them. They are a fundamentally different animal in temperament, size, and behavior. An adult male black bear in Yosemite weighs between 250 and 350 pounds. An adult male grizzly can top 700. More importantly, the behavioral profile is different. Grizzlies are territorial and defensive. Black bears are opportunistic and, overwhelmingly, avoidant. The tools you need for each species are not the same.

The NPS ban on bear spray in Yosemite is laid out in the Superintendent's Compendium, which classifies it alongside "pellet guns, BB guns, bows and arrows, crossbows, blowguns, spearguns, spear-fishing equipment, and nets." Possession is prohibited. Use is prohibited. It is a weapon, and weapons are not permitted. The reasons are practical, not bureaucratic. Bear spray is not needed for black bears. The encounters that would theoretically justify it do not happen here. A USGS study found that capsaicin residue left on surfaces actually attracts bears.

In a park that sees over 3.5 million visitors a year, the risk of bear spray being deployed against humans, intentionally or accidentally, is not theoretical. And the Bear Team will tell you the biggest problem: visitors mis-deploy spray in situations that are not remotely threatening, causing unnecessary harm and stress to bears that were doing nothing wrong.

What works instead is your voice. The Bear Team says it plainly: "Your voice is your most effective tool." The specifics are below.

If you're heading to Yellowstone, Glacier, Grand Teton, or Denali, absolutely bring bear spray. Those parks have grizzlies, and in grizzly country, bear spray is the single most effective deterrent available to a hiker. That fact gets repeated so often and so universally that it has bled into advice for parks where it does not apply. Yosemite is one of those parks. This one does not have grizzlies, does not need bear spray, and does not allow it.

### Myth 2: Playing dead works with black bears

This is grizzly advice applied to the wrong species, and it is the most dangerous myth for Yosemite visitors because people confuse species-specific guidance all the time. With a grizzly, playing dead can work because the majority of grizzly attacks are defensive. The bear perceives a threat, charges, makes contact, and once the threat is neutralized (you, lying still and not fighting), the bear often disengages. The attack is about eliminating a threat, not acquiring food.

With a black bear, playing dead makes you easier to investigate. A black bear that is pushing past avoidance behavior and making contact is almost never being defensive. It is being curious or, in extremely rare cases, predatory. Lying motionless on the ground does not signal "I am not a threat." It signals "I am available."

The correct response to a black bear that will not leave is the opposite of playing dead. Make yourself as large as possible. Yell aggressively. If the bear makes contact, fight back. The NPS official guidance could not be more direct: "If you are attacked by a black bear, DO NOT PLAY DEAD. Try to escape to a secure place. If escape is not possible, try to fight back using any object available. Concentrate your kicks and blows on the bear's face and muzzle."

This distinction matters because people Google "what to do if you see a bear" and get advice written for grizzly country, then apply it in black bear country. There are no qualifiers in the search results. There's just "play dead," floating around the internet without species context, waiting to become a very bad decision.

### Myth 3: Hanging food from a tree works

Yosemite's bears defeated every hanging method decades ago, and the story of how they did it is one of the more entertaining arms races in wildlife management history.

The park first tried the classic rope-over-a-branch technique. Bears chewed through the ropes. Then came the counterbalance system, where you'd hang two equal-weight bags over a high branch so neither could be pulled down from the ground. Bears climbed to the branch and dropped onto the bags from above, tearing them free on the way down. Then the park installed metal food-storage poles in backcountry campsites. An avalanche knocked them down. Rachel Mazur, Yosemite's wildlife branch chief, documented this entire arms race in her book Speaking of Bears, and the progression has a certain comic inevitability to it. Every solution the park tried, the bears solved within a season or two.

The breakthrough came from an unexpected place. Behavioral ecologist Barrie Gilbert was watching a nature documentary one evening and saw a lion pawing uselessly at an ostrich egg on smooth ground. The egg just rolled away. The shape defeated the claws. Gilbert realized a smooth, hard-shelled container could do the same thing for bear-proofing food, and the portable bear canister was born. Bears cannot open them. They try. They roll them around, they chew them, they throw them off cliffs. The canisters hold.

The current regulation is absolute: bear bagging is prohibited in Yosemite. Bear canisters are required for all overnight wilderness trips. You can rent one at any wilderness center in the park for $5 per week. In frontcountry campgrounds, every site has a metal bear box. Use it. These are not suggestions. They are enforceable regulations, and they work.

### Myth 4: Black bears are dangerous to humans

Zero fatal bear attacks in Yosemite's recorded history, going back to the park's establishment in 1890. None.

Across all of North America, the continent's approximately 750,000 black bears kill fewer than one person per year. Dr. Lynn Rogers, who has spent over 50 years conducting field research on black bears, puts the risk in perspective: your chances of being murdered by another human are 60,000 times greater than being killed by a black bear. Since 1900, black bears have killed roughly 60 people across the entire continent. No mother black bear has ever killed anyone defending her cubs. That last point directly contradicts one of the most deeply held pieces of bear mythology, but it is true. Mother black bears bluff-charge, huff, jaw-pop, and retreat. They do not attack.

California did not record its first-ever fatal black bear attack until 2023, and it happened in Downieville, roughly 200 miles from Yosemite, involving a food-conditioned bear that had been drawn to cat food left on a porch. The circumstances were specific and tragic, but they were not analogous to a bear encounter on a trail or in a campground.

What I tell visitors, and I tell them this constantly, is that the river is more dangerous than the bears. The granite is more dangerous than the bears. Your own car, driving tired on Highway 140 at 10 PM after a long day of hiking, is more dangerous than the bears. Yosemite's bears are not trying to hurt you. They are trying to eat acorns and berries and occasionally whatever you left in your cooler. The fear is disproportionate to the risk by orders of magnitude. If you want to worry about something in this park, worry about the heat.

Watch the film: Black BearsYosemite Nature Notes · Episode 26Black BearsThe Park Service on the animal behind the myths: several hundred black bears, and what visitors get wrong about them.Film: National Park Service. Nothing loads from YouTube until you press play.

### Myth 5: That brown bear is a grizzly

Are there grizzly bears in Yosemite? No. There have not been for over a century. I hear this question every week during the summer season. A visitor comes up to me, excited and a little scared, and says they saw a brown bear. What they mean is they saw a grizzly. What they actually saw is a black bear that happens to be brown.

American black bears come in black, brown, cinnamon, blonde, and even blue-gray. The name refers to the species, not the color. In the western United States, over half of all black bears are some shade of brown. The variation is genetic, driven by a recessive gene that affects melanin production, and it varies geographically. In the eastern states, most black bears are black. In the West, anything goes.

There are no grizzlies in Yosemite. The last one in the park was shot near Crescent Lake around 1895. The last grizzly in the entire state of California was killed in 1922. The California grizzly has been extinct for over a century. It survives only on the state flag, which is a peculiar kind of memorial.

That cinnamon-colored bear you saw grazing near the meadow at dusk is a black bear. If you want to confirm this, look at the profile. Black bears have a straight facial profile, tall ears relative to their head, and no shoulder hump. Grizzlies have a dished face, smaller ears, and a prominent muscular hump above the shoulders. But you do not need to memorize those field marks for Yosemite. There is only one species here.

A California bill, SB 1305, would fund a roadmap for grizzly reintroduction by 2028. Even if it moves forward, actual reintroduction would be years or decades away.

### Myth 6: Bears hibernate all winter

At Yosemite's elevation, this is not quite right. Black bears enter torpor, which is physiologically distinct from true hibernation. A true hibernator, like a ground squirrel, drops its body temperature to near freezing and cannot be easily roused. A black bear in torpor drops from a normal body temperature of about 100 degrees Fahrenheit to roughly 88 degrees. Its metabolism decreases by about 75%. Its heart rate slows. But it can wake up. It does wake up, sometimes for days at a time.

At Yosemite's mid-elevations, where the Valley floor sits at about 4,000 feet and most campgrounds cluster between 4,000 and 8,000 feet, bears are sometimes active during warm winter periods. Food availability is the primary driver, not temperature alone. A stretch of warm days in January can bring bears out of their dens to forage. They have been documented digging under snow for cached acorns.

This matters practically because it means food storage rules apply year-round, not just during the summer season. If you're camping in Yosemite in November or March, the bear boxes are not decorative. Use them. I have spoken with visitors in late October who assumed the bears were "asleep" and left food on their picnic table overnight. The bears were not asleep. A bear that finds food in winter learns a lesson it carries into the next season and the one after that. Food conditioning is cumulative. Every easy meal makes the next car window look more worth breaking.

#### Why a bear in April is more dangerous than a bear in August

Most of the park's bears are out of their dens between the middle of March and April, after four to five months at roughly a quarter of their normal metabolic rate. A denning bear's heart rate falls from 70 to 100 beats a minute to 8 to 10, it eats and drinks little or nothing, and it comes out having lost somewhere between 15 and 30 percent of its body weight. The trigger for waking is not hunger. Lengthening days and warming air reset the bear's circadian rhythm, and it wakes very hungry with a digestive system that is still restarting.

The landscape offers little to meet that demand. The first food at Yosemite's elevations is sedge shoots, new grass and ephemeral herbs, which are low in calories, so a spring bear forages for hours a day and is drawn toward cabins, campsites and parked cars. A spring bear is also less likely to be deterred by noise than a fall bear that is already fat. C. A. Harwell, then the park naturalist, wrote in the March 1931 Nature Notes that bears come out of their dens "usually by the middle of March" and "are careful how they break their long hibernation fast"; his account of that season is in the archive. The storage rules below apply all year. Spring is when a bear tests them hardest.

### What to do if you see a bear in Yosemite

Here is what actually happens when you encounter a bear, step by step, from someone who has been through it.

Stand up. If you're sitting at a picnic table or crouched by your tent, get vertical. Face the bear. Do not turn your back. Raise your arms above your head to make yourself look larger. Then yell. Not a polite "hey there." Yell aggressively, and keep yelling. "HEY BEAR. GO BEAR. GET OUT OF HERE." Clap your hands. Keep yelling. Do not stop after three seconds because you feel awkward. Most bears leave quickly. The ones that don't, yell louder. Bang sticks on trees. Clap rocks together.

A bear standing on its hind legs is not threatening you. It is investigating. Ears forward and nose raised means curiosity. The bear is trying to smell you and see you better. This is not aggression. Woofing, jaw-popping, and ears pinned back are fear-based displays, and what they indicate, more than anything, is that the bear is scared of you. It is telling you to back off, and you should, slowly.

The NPS says this, and I agree with it completely: "Do you have time to snap a quick picture? No." Put the phone away. I cannot count the number of times I've watched someone stand their ground yelling at a bear with one hand while holding up their phone with the other. The phone is not helping you. It is splitting your attention and keeping you closer to the bear than you need to be. There are better ways to see wildlife in this park than cornering a stressed animal.

Never run from a bear. Black bears can hit 35 miles per hour over short distances. You cannot. Running also triggers a pursuit instinct that standing your ground does not. Never climb a tree. Black bears are arboreal. They climb better than you do, faster than you do, and they started climbing trees before they could walk.

Yosemite bear safety comes down to your voice and your behavior. Report every bear encounter to the park: 209-372-0322. Even if nothing happened. Even if the bear left immediately. The Bear Team tracks every sighting, and the data drives management decisions about where to station rangers, which campgrounds need additional bear boxes, and which individual bears are becoming habituated and need hazing. Your sighting report is not bureaucratic overhead. It is data, and the Bear Team uses every piece of it.

### Yosemite food storage rules nobody reads carefully enough

The Yosemite food storage regulations carry a $5,000 fine, and the definition of "food" is broader than you think.

"Food" means: all food, all coolers (including empty ones), all trash, all toiletries, sunscreen, lip balm, insect repellent, deodorant, medications, and feminine hygiene products. If you put it in your mouth or on your skin, it goes in the bear box. If it has a scent, it goes in the bear box. That is not an exaggeration. It is the regulation, verbatim.

The storage rules on one page, drawn from the regulation as this article quotes it. The rules apply year-round, not only in summer.

The empty cooler provision is the one that trips everyone up. Bears recognize the shape. A cooler under a blanket in your trunk is still a cooler to a bear that has learned, through years of operant conditioning, that cooler shapes contain food. It does not matter that this particular cooler is empty. The bear doesn't know that, and the regulation doesn't care.

Car storage rules are strict. You cannot leave food visible in your vehicle even during the day. Overnight, everything with a scent must be in the bear box, no exceptions. A bag of trail mix in your glove compartment is a violation. A tube of toothpaste in your center console is a violation. If you're packing your car for Yosemite, plan for this.

Soft-sided vehicles get special rules, and they are not in your favor. You cannot store food in a pop-up camper, tent trailer, or any soft-sided vehicle. Bears can and do tear through canvas and vinyl. Hard-sided RVs and vehicles only, and everything must be closed: windows up, doors shut, roof vents sealed.

The violation fine runs up to $5,000, and it is enforced. Rangers write citations. They write them regularly. This is not a theoretical penalty.

For backcountry trips, bear canisters are required for all overnights. You can rent approved models at wilderness centers throughout the park. BearVault and Garcia are the two brands most commonly available and NPS-approved. Pack the canister at least 100 feet from your campsite, on flat ground, and do not try to secure it with rocks or rope. That just gives the bear something to grip. The smooth container on open ground is the design. Trust it. And pack your canister efficiently. Put dense, calorie-rich food in first. Crush packaging to save space. A well-packed BV500 holds about five days of food for one person if you are not bringing a week's worth of luxury items. If you are planning your first trip, factor canister space into your meal planning from the start.

### Yosemite bear incidents: the data from 1998 to 2026

This is a conservation success story, and I wish I could end it there. I cannot.

In 1998, Yosemite recorded 1,584 bear incidents. Bears were breaking into cars every night. Property damage topped $660,000 in a single year. The park was losing the battle decisively. Bears had learned that visitor cars and campgrounds were reliable food sources, and they had passed that knowledge to their cubs, creating generations of food-conditioned animals. It was a crisis.

The response was systematic and expensive. The park installed over 2,000 metal bear boxes at campsites and trailheads. In 2004, bear canisters became mandatory for all overnight wilderness trips. A massive education campaign reshaped how visitors understood food storage. Open garbage containers were replaced with bear-proof models throughout the park. The "Keep Bears Wild" messaging became pervasive, and rangers began writing citations with real teeth.

It worked. Slowly at first, then dramatically. Bear incidents dropped 95% and property damage dropped 99% from that 1998 peak. By 2019, the park recorded its lowest incident numbers in modern history. The bears that once tore car doors off their hinges were, within a generation, foraging naturally and avoiding developed areas. A UC Santa Cruz isotope study tracked the shift in bear diet and found that human food as a proportion of bear nutrition dropped from 35% during the 1975 to 1985 period back to 13% by 2007, roughly matching pre-tourism levels. The bears were eating bear food again.

But then there is the road.

In 2025, 28 bears were hit by cars in Yosemite. Six were killed. Beth Pratt's 11-year analysis of the data showed an 85.7% rise in vehicle-bear collisions correlating with a 44.9% increase in visitation after the park's reservation system was removed. More visitors meant more cars, more cars meant more miles driven on park roads, and more miles meant more dead bears. Through early July 2026 the park logged 34 incidents and $14,947 in property damage, up 26 percent on the same point in 2025, down 91 percent on 1998 and up 286 percent on 2019.

The uncomfortable truth is that Yosemite won the food storage fight. Decisively. The bears stopped breaking into cars because visitors finally learned to lock up their food. But the park is now losing the traffic fight. The animals that learned to stay out of coolers are getting killed crossing the road. The Red Bear Dead Bear program has been running since 2007, placing red markers at every vehicle collision site as a visceral reminder to slow down. Wildlife Protection Zones enforce speed limits of 25 to 35 miles per hour. It is still not enough. If you're visiting Yosemite for the first time, drive slowly. That is not a platitude. It is the single most impactful thing a visitor can do for bear conservation in this park right now.

### The takeaway

The bears are not the danger. You, the visitor, are the danger. Your food storage, your driving speed, your willingness to surround a mother with cubs for a photograph.

I have watched people form a semicircle around a sow and two cubs in Cook's Meadow while she stress-huffed and jaw-popped and tried to find an exit. I have watched people sprint toward a bear in Upper Pines Campground with their phones out. I have watched a man chase a bear into the tree line for a better angle. Behavior like this is the reason bears become habituated, then food-conditioned, then "problem bears," and then dead bears. That escalation is well-documented and entirely preventable.

The best thing you can do for Yosemite's bears is boring. Store your food properly. Drive slowly, especially at dawn and dusk when bears are most active on the roads. Give them space. Fifty yards, minimum. If a bear changes its behavior because of your presence, you are too close, and you are breaking the law.

The best bear encounter is the one where you see a cinnamon-colored bear in a meadow at dusk, watch it graze on grass for ten minutes from 50 yards away, and walk back to your campsite grinning. That's the wildlife encounter you came for. That's the one you will remember for the rest of your life. Not the one where you chased it for a photo and it bluff-charged you. Not the one where it tore into your car because you left a granola bar under the seat. The quiet one. The one where you let it be a bear.

## Yosemite Heat Safety: 90°F Valley Days, Trails to Avoid, Water to Carry

URL: https://thetalusfieldjournal.com/articles/yosemite-heat-safety-guide
Section: Seasonal Guides. Published: 2026-06-16. Last updated: 2026-06-16.
Summary: How hot does Yosemite get in summer? A naturalist's guide to which trails to avoid, where to swim, and how to stay safe in Yosemite Valley heat.

Many visitors picture Yosemite with mild weather all summer. I've been working as a naturalist in this park for close to two decades, and I can tell you that version exists for about six weeks a year, split between May and October. The rest of the summer, Yosemite Valley is hot. Not desert hot, but hot enough to catch people who didn't plan for it.

Yosemite Valley sits at roughly 4,000 feet in elevation, which sounds cool but isn't. The Valley is a granite box, roughly seven miles long and a mile wide, with walls that rise 3,000 to 4,000 feet on either side. In July and August, daytime highs reach 90 degrees Fahrenheit regularly and occasionally crack 100. The granite absorbs heat all morning, radiates it all afternoon, and doesn't let go until well after dark. There is no sea breeze or lake effect, and no relief until the sun drops behind the south rim somewhere around 7 PM. Heat is the thing that catches more visitors off guard than anything else, with the possible exception of the altitude. If you're planning your first trip, this is the piece most planning guides leave out.

Photo: Michael Hogarth / Wikimedia Commons (public domain)

### How hot Yosemite actually gets in summer

The monthly averages tell part of the story.

Month | Yosemite Valley (4,000 ft) | Tuolumne Meadows (8,600 ft)

June | ~82°F | ~62°F
July | ~90°F | ~72°F
August | ~90°F | ~70°F
September | ~83°F | ~65°F

Those numbers are measured in the shade, at a weather station, which is not where you'll be standing on the Mist Trail staircase at 1 PM. Yosemite summer temperatures are average highs, meaning half the days are hotter.

The averages are misleading in another way, too. Valley floor granite surfaces can hit 140 to 160 degrees Fahrenheit in direct sun. Dark granite, the kind that makes up large sections of the north wall, runs 30 degrees hotter than light granite. When you're hiking a south-facing trail in July, air temperature is only part of it. You're dealing with radiant heat bouncing off every surface around you. Granite walls reflect and radiate heat from three directions. The trail surface cooks from below. Nothing cuts it: no wind off a body of water, no altitude-driven cooling. One hundred degree days happen roughly once a year, usually in late July, but the days that hover at 95 and feel like 100 on exposed granite are the ones that actually fill up the clinic.

### Exposed trails that will cook you

If you're hiking Yosemite in summer, not all trails are equal in the heat, and the differences matter. Some trails that are perfectly reasonable in May become dangerous in July.

Four Mile Trail, the steep route from the Valley floor to Glacier Point, is the one the National Park Service has specifically called "very dangerous, exposed." It faces south. Long stretches have no shade whatsoever. It gains 3,200 feet in less than five miles. On a 90-degree day, the combination of sustained climbing, direct sun, and radiant heat off the granite produces heat casualties. I have personally helped evacuate people from this trail. Every time, they started too late.

Upper Yosemite Falls trail is the other big one. The first mile, up to Columbia Rock, has some shade and is manageable early in the day. Above Columbia Rock, the switchbacks become fully exposed. You're climbing granite slabs with the Valley wall reflecting heat directly onto you. There's no water source on the trail.

The Mist Trail above Vernal Fall footbridge is deceptive. Below the footbridge, you get the famous mist from the waterfall, which feels good on a hot day. Above it, you get a granite staircase in direct sun. The mist is gone. The shade is gone. You're climbing 600 stone steps with nothing between you and the sky. People don't expect the transition because the lower section felt so refreshing.

Half Dome's subdome and cables sit at 8,800 feet, which should be cooler, and the air temperature is. But the sun at that elevation is unrelenting, the granite reflects it from every angle, and there is nowhere to stop in shade on the subdome or the cables. You're completely committed once you start. Add the physical intensity of the cable climb and the fact that most people have already hiked 8 miles to get there, and you have a serious heat exposure problem even at elevation.

The Panorama Trail, an 8-mile descent from Glacier Point to the Valley, is the one people underestimate most. It sounds easy because it's "all downhill." It's 8 miles of exposed granite with limited shade, and the descent hammers your knees, which makes you drink more water, which you may not have brought enough of.

Heat also contributes to rockfall. A USGS study found that roughly 15 percent of unexplained rockfalls in Yosemite occur between noon and 6 PM from July through September. Thermal expansion of the granite. The rock swells in the heat and pieces break away.

The best strategy is simple and inflexible. The best time to hike Yosemite in summer is before 7 AM. Be done with exposed sections by 10 or 11 in the morning. It is early, and it is the window. Check the best hikes guide for trails that work well with an early start.

### The water math

The NPS guidance says to carry one quart of water per hour of hiking in the heat. That's the official number, and it's fine as a baseline. My real guidance, from someone who has worked here through every July since the mid-2000s, is to carry more than you think you need. A full day on an exposed trail in July means 4 to 6 liters per person. That's heavy. A liter of water weighs 2.2 pounds. Six liters is over 13 pounds of water alone. You carry it anyway.

There's a counterbalancing danger that doesn't get enough attention. Hyponatremia, low blood sodium, happens when you drink too much plain water without replacing electrolytes. Your body dilutes its own sodium levels. The symptoms look a lot like heat exhaustion: nausea, headache, confusion. Which means people sometimes respond by drinking more water, which makes it worse. Carry electrolyte tablets or salty snacks. Trail mix exists for a reason. Pretzels are good trail food in the heat.

You should know the difference between heat exhaustion and heat stroke because one is a bad afternoon and the other is a medical emergency. Heat exhaustion means heavy sweating, nausea, dizziness, pale and clammy skin. You feel terrible. You get into shade, you rest, you drink water with electrolytes, and you recover. Heat stroke means sweating stops. Skin goes red and dry. Confusion sets in, sometimes aggressiveness or slurred speech. This is a 911 call. This is a person whose body has lost the ability to cool itself. Cool them aggressively. Wet clothing, shade, fanning. Get medical help immediately. By some estimates, roughly a quarter of nontraumatic search and rescue missions in Yosemite are dehydration or heat related.

### What to wear on the trail

A quick note on clothing, because what you wear matters as much as what you carry. Light-colored, loose-fitting clothing reflects heat better than dark clothes. A wide-brim hat is not optional. UPF-rated sun hoodies have become standard gear for anyone who works outside in the Sierra, and there's a reason for that: they cover more skin than sunscreen and don't wear off. Speaking of sunscreen, reapply every two hours, and know that the UV at 4,000 feet is already stronger than at sea level, and at 8,000 feet it's meaningfully more intense. The granite reflects UV from below, the thin air filters less of it from above, and the combination will burn you faster than you expect. A bandana or cooling towel soaked in cold creek water and draped around your neck is the single cheapest piece of heat management gear you can carry.

### The escape uphill

The single best heat strategy in Yosemite is also the simplest: go higher. Temperature drops roughly 3.5 degrees Fahrenheit per thousand feet of elevation gain.

Tuolumne Meadows sits at 8,600 feet and runs 18 to 20 degrees cooler than the Valley. When it's 90 in Yosemite Valley, Tuolumne is 72. The hiking is better than anything in the Valley, the crowds are a fraction, and the temperature is mild. Glacier Point at 7,200 feet is meaningfully cooler than the Valley floor, and the views compete with anything you'll see from below. Crane Flat and White Wolf are intermediate options if you want to get out of the Valley heat without driving all the way to Tuolumne.

Tioga Road is the heat escape that matters most. The corridor from Crane Flat at 6,200 feet to Tioga Pass at 9,945 feet drops temperatures dramatically. You can leave the Valley at 95 degrees and be in a light jacket at Olmsted Point an hour later. It's open roughly late May through early November, depending on snow, and in July and August there is no reason not to use it if the heat is getting to you.

Tenaya Lake, at 8,150 feet along Tioga Road, deserves special mention. Cold water, a sandy beach on the east end, and a 20-degree temperature drop from the Valley. It's one of the best places in the park on a hot day. More on swimming spots below.

### Yosemite thunderstorms and lightning safety

Here's where the heat escape gets complicated. The high country that saves you from the heat also has the most dangerous weather in the park.

Sierra Nevada afternoon thunderstorms are one of the most predictable weather patterns in the American West. The mechanism is straightforward. Summer sun heats the granite, the granite heats the air, warm air rises, hits moisture at altitude, and builds into thunderheads. In July and August it happens most days. By 11 AM it's common to see cumulus clouds building over the peaks. By early afternoon, those clouds have gone vertical and dark. By 1 PM, lightning.

The rule is simple. Be off exposed ridges, peaks, and open granite by noon. I've watched lightning strike Cathedral Peak from Tuolumne Meadows on a day that started blue and cloudless. The buildup from "nice morning" to "violent electrical storm" can happen in under two hours.

Specific locations where you absolutely do not want to be when lightning starts: Half Dome cables, where you are standing on an exposed granite dome holding a metal cable. Cathedral Peak. Lembert Dome. Any high-country pass above treeline. The summit of Clouds Rest. If you are above treeline and you hear thunder, you are already within strike range.

Lightning safety is not complicated. Get below treeline. Get off water. Get low, not flat, but crouching with your feet together. Don't shelter under a lone tree; it's a lightning magnet. Don't huddle in a group. Spread out so a single strike can't hit everyone. The monsoon pattern typically runs from mid-July through September, with the most intense activity in late July and August. Check the seasonal guide for more on how weather patterns shift through the year.

### Where to swim in Yosemite

Swimming is the best thing about Yosemite in summer that most first-time visitors don't plan for. They come with hiking boots and trail maps. They should also bring a swimsuit and a towel. What follows is the heat-day summary; the full guide to swimming in the Merced covers the season, the flow, the places where swimming is prohibited outright, and what cold water actually does to a swimmer.

The realistic swimming season runs from about mid-July through mid-September. Before that, the Merced River is running too high, too fast, and too cold with Sierra snowmelt. This point is non-negotiable: do not swim in May or June. The river in spring is a powerful, cold, silty current that does not care how strong a swimmer you are. Most river fatalities in Yosemite occur during the high-water period.

By mid to late July, the river drops to swimmable levels and the water warms enough that getting in is a pleasure rather than a shock.

In the Valley, Sentinel Beach is the most accessible swimming spot. Sandy bank, a picnic area right there, views of Half Dome from the water. It's family-friendly and usually calm by late summer. Cathedral Beach, just downstream, is wider and deeper, with El Capitan framed in the view upstream. Watch the downstream current here, especially earlier in the season. The Housekeeping Camp area has a wider, slower section of river behind Curry Village. Raft rentals are available at Curry Village for the float from Stoneman Bridge to Sentinel Beach, a mellow three-mile drift that may be the best way to experience the Valley on a 90-degree day. Swinging Bridge offers shallow sandy bottoms that are good for wading and casual cooling off, especially with kids.

Outside the Valley, Tenaya Lake is the best subalpine swimming in the park. Sandy beach, clear water, mountain backdrop. The water temperature runs 55 to 60 degrees, which is bracing but tolerable once you commit. Wawona, at lower elevation with a smaller drainage, has the warmest swimming in the park.

The safety rules for swimming in Yosemite are short and absolute. Never swim above a waterfall. Ever. The current accelerates toward the lip in ways you cannot feel until it's too late, and people die this way. Don't swim in May or June. Cold water shock is real; water at 50 to 60 degrees triggers an immediate involuntary gasp reflex on immersion, and the shock response can impair muscle control for up to 90 seconds. Don't swim alone in deep cold water.

### Shady trails along the river

On a hot day, the best hike in Yosemite might be no hike at all. A flat, shaded walk along the river may beat any summit.

Sections of the Valley Loop Trail along the Merced River are shaded by black oaks, cottonwoods, and the Valley's dense riparian corridor. The temperature under that canopy can be 10 to 15 degrees cooler than the exposed meadows 200 yards away. The Mirror Lake and Tenaya Creek trail is one of the shadiest walks in the Valley, a flat meander through forest along a creek bed. In late summer, Mirror Lake itself is mostly a sandy flat, but the walk to get there is cool and quiet. The path from Swinging Bridge to Sentinel Beach along the south bank of the Merced is another good one, flat and shaded and never far from water you can wade into.

The Lower Yosemite Fall loop is short, partially shaded, and runs close to Yosemite Creek. In July the waterfall itself is usually reduced to a trickle or gone entirely, but the walk is still pleasant and the creek still has some flow.

The park is not going anywhere. You don't have to summit something every day. On a 95-degree afternoon, a walk along the river in the shade, a swim, a nap under a black oak while staring up at granite walls, is a good use of a day here. The wildlife guide has more on what you might spot along the river corridor in summer, mule deer in the meadows at dusk, dippers working the riffles, the occasional coyote. Animals use the shade trails in the heat too.

### Your car is also a problem

One more thing that people don't think about until they're living it. Your car, parked in a trailhead lot in full sun for six hours while you hike, will be nearly uninhabitable when you return. Car interiors can reach 130 degrees within an hour on a 90-degree day, and climb past 140 within a couple of hours. The steering wheel will burn your hands. The seatbelt buckle will brand your skin.

Don't leave pets in the car. Don't leave kids in the car. Don't leave medications in the car. Most medications degrade at those temperatures, including insulin, inhalers, and epinephrine. Trailhead parking lots in Yosemite are almost universally fully exposed. There are no covered parking structures. There are very few shaded spots, and they fill first.

Leave a towel draped over the steering wheel. Leave windows cracked if you feel safe doing so. Bring a second shirt to change into, because a dry one helps after a sweaty hike. And carry an extra liter of water in the car for the drive out. You will be thirstier than you expect.

### The takeaway

The heat in Yosemite is manageable with planning and dangerous without it. Start early. Carry more water than you think you need. Know which trails are exposed and plan your day around that exposure. Know the difference between heat exhaustion and heat stroke. Go uphill when the Valley is a furnace. Watch the sky when you do.

And consider that some of the best summer days in this park have nothing to do with trails at all. A riverside afternoon in the shade. A cold swim at Cathedral Beach with El Capitan turning gold above you. A drive up to Tenaya Lake where it's 70 degrees and the water is clear and the granite slabs are warm enough to lie on but not hot enough to burn. I have seen visitors who planned for the heat have those days, and I have seen visitors who didn't end up in an ambulance.

## Best Time to Visit Yosemite in 2026, by the Traffic Data

URL: https://thetalusfieldjournal.com/articles/when-to-visit-yosemite
Section: Planning. Published: 2026-06-11. Last updated: 2026-10-01.
Summary: No reservation system in 2026, and Yosemite is pacing toward its second-busiest year. NPS visitation data, a monthly crowd calendar, and the best days to go.

Yosemite needs no reservation in 2026, and it is on pace for the second-busiest year on record. The park counted 2,657,602 visits through July, 8 percent ahead of 2025. So the question is no longer whether you can get in. It is which month, which day and which hour. The short answer: midweek in October is the best window left this year, and on any other trip, be through the gate before 8 a.m. or arrive after 4 p.m.

In March, 225,817 people visited, 45 percent more than the March before and the busiest March since 2016. Memorial Day weekend showed what no throttle looks like: Valley parking filling as early as 8 a.m. and entrance waits that reports put past an hour. I made my argument about whether this was a good idea after that weekend. This piece answers the question that arrives in my inbox every week now: when should you actually come?

I went through the National Park Service's visitor use statistics: annual visits since 2016, the Park Service's 15-year monthly averages, and the 2026 counts as the park has published them. This edition was rebuilt on October 1, so the forecast looks at the months still ahead, then at 2027. Every figure is either a published number or arithmetic on published numbers, and anything that is my projection says so.

The short version

- No reservation is needed in 2026. The park manages traffic with staff, parking control and live information instead.
- July, August and June are the busiest months. January, February and December are the quietest.
- The best window left in 2026: midweek in October, then early-November weekdays.
- Any summer day: through the gate before 8 a.m., or after 4 p.m.
- Text YNPTRAFFIC to 333111 for live parking and traffic updates.

THE THROTTLE IS GONE

### Demand rose every year, with or without a gate

Yosemite has spent six years running an accidental experiment in demand management. Visitation has climbed every year since 2020, through every version of the rules. The reservation systems did not reduce the wish to be here. They moved it, spread it and metered it.

- 20165.03MNo reservations. The record year.
- 20174.34MNo reservations.
- 20184.01MNo reservations.
- 20194.42MNo reservations.
- 20202.27MCovid closure, then day-use limits.

- 20244.12MPeak Hours Plus, 5 a.m. to 4 p.m., April 13 to October 27.

Recreation visits per year, in millions. Source: NPS Visitor Use Statistics for 2016 to 2025; reservation dates from the park's announcements; 2026 projection by The Talus Field (method below).

2024 was the broadest system. Peak Hours Plus required a reservation from 5 a.m. to 4 p.m., on weekends from April 13 to June 30, every day from July 1 to August 16, and on weekends again from August 17 to October 27. Entry after 4 p.m. needed none.

2025 was the scaled-back version. A reservation was required from 6 a.m. to 2 p.m. over Memorial Day weekend (May 24 to 26), every day from June 15 to August 15, and over Labor Day weekend (August 30 to September 1). Each cost $2 and was good for three days.

2026 has none. The Park Service said it would no longer use a timed reservation system, and for the first time in three years the February firefall weekends ran without one. It is managing the year with real-time traffic monitoring, active parking management and visitor information tools instead.

2025 was the fourth-busiest year on record, behind 2016, 2019 and 2017. These are recreation visits, the series the Park Service publishes in its Visitor Use Statistics. The park's own statistics page prints a differently counted annual series (4,285,729 for 2024); nothing here mixes the two.

2026 SO FAR

### Eight percent ahead, with spring leading

Through July the park logged 2,657,602 visits against 2,460,675 in the same months of 2025. The growth was not even. Spring jumped, and the peak months rose more modestly.

March, the first full month after the no-reservation news, was up 45 percent, although the comparison flatters 2026 a little because storms held March 2025 down. February was up 12 percent and April up 2 percent. Headlines move visitation, and this year's headline was that Yosemite is open with no ticket required.

June came in at 634,508 visits, the second-busiest June on record behind only 2016. July was 654,356 by the August reports, up 6.1 percent on July 2025. A Park Service summary published September 1 quotes July as 665,877, up 8 percent, and the first seven months as about 2.59 million, up 9.5 percent. The counts do not agree to the visit, so read them as eight to ten percent ahead, not as a decimal.

WHAT THE RESERVATION YEARS DID

### Each loosening was followed by a busier summer

To see why 2026 summer set near-records, look at the two peak months under each rule. June and July rose in 2025 when the system was trimmed, and again in 2026 when it was removed.

#### June

- 2024588,251Peak Hours Plus
- 2025607,410Scaled back
- 2026634,508None

#### July

- 2024596,711Peak Hours Plus
- 2025616,551Scaled back
- 2026654,356None

Recreation visits in the two peak months. 2024 ran Peak Hours Plus, 2025 a scaled-back version, 2026 nothing. Source: NPS Visitor Use Statistics as quoted in park reports.

The Park Service's own 2025 count. Visitation through August 2025 totaled 2,919,722, up seven percent on the same months of 2024 (2,727,496), and every month outpaced 2024 except February, when winter storms limited access.

What stayed manageable. The park counts only two days of significant delays in 2026, both over Memorial Day weekend, against more than 120 days of gridlock in past years. It credits digital passes, fast lanes at the entrances, added Valley parking, extra shuttles and published entrance wait times.

What the visitors said. In a Washington State University survey for the park, taken August 7 to 16 with 1,203 responses, 91 percent had no entrance delay or waited less than 15 minutes, 56 percent spent less time looking for parking than they expected, and 11 percent said parking took somewhat or much too long.

A survey of ten August days is not a summer-long wait time. Memorial Day weekend is the counterexample, and holiday weekends are where a full road network binds.

THE PROJECTION

### How I built it, and what it says

This is the site's projection, not a Park Service number. It rests on one count and one assumption, and it holds up across a wide range of the assumption.

- Start with what is counted. January to July 2026: 2,657,602 visits.
- Add the rest of 2025. The 2025 total (4,278,413) minus January to July 2025 (2,460,675) is 1,817,738 visits for August to December.
- Scale it. Multiply that remainder by how much busier August to December 2026 runs than 2025. I show zero, four and eight percent; eight is the year-to-date pace.

I no longer publish a month-by-month visit forecast. The first version of this article estimated months the Park Service had not yet reported, and some of those estimates were wrong once the real numbers arrived. The Park Service posts August to December as the months close; this page will take those instead.

Where 2026 ends, by scenarioAugust to December | 2026 total | Rank

August to December match 2025 | 4,475,340 | 2nd
Four percent above 2025 | 4,548,050 | 2nd
Eight percent above 2025, this year's pace | 4,620,759 | 2nd

- Second place holds unless August to December comes in about 3 percent below 2025 or worse: 2019 (4,422,861) needs 1,765,259 more visits after July, against 1,817,738 in the same months of 2025.
- First place is out of reach. Beating 2016 (5,028,868) would take about 30 percent more than 2025 over those five months.

WHAT IS OPEN, WHEN

### The roads decide more than the crowds do

A quiet month is no use if the road you came for is closed. The seasonal roads follow snow, not the calendar, and this year's openings were early.

The Park Service's seasonal pattern: Tioga and Glacier Point roads close from sometime in November to late May or early June; the Mariposa Grove road and shuttle close on or about November 30 and reopen no earlier than April 15. Road status changes with the weather, so check the conditions page the morning you drive in.

As the Park Service's conditions page read on October 1, 2026, Glacier Point Road was closed for smoke and firefighting, and the Mist Trail was open Friday to Sunday and holidays, and Monday to Thursday only from 3:30 p.m. to 7 a.m., through October. Both change, so check it before you drive.

THE CLOCK BEATS THE CALENDAR

### The hour you reach the gate matters most

The difference between a miserable Yosemite day and a great one is mostly when you reach the gate. The Park Service has published its own definition of over capacity three times, in the hours it gated.

Every reservation system covered the same stretch of the day, from 5 or 6 in the morning to 2 or 4 in the afternoon. With no system in 2026, you enforce it on yourself. Valley parking fills early on peak days: reports put it as soon as 8 a.m. over Memorial Day weekend, and typically between 10 and 11 a.m. on summer Saturdays and holidays.

- Be through by 8
Before 7 on summer weekends. A Tuesday or Wednesday through the gate by 7:30 beats a Saturday.

- Or arrive after 4
Summer light lasts past 8. An evening visit with dinner outside the park beats a noon arrival.

- Skip 9 to 2
On a summer weekend, the entrance lines form and the Valley lots close behind you.

- Stay parked
Use the shuttles and bikes. A Valley spot on a July Saturday is not worth gambling for twice.

THE DAYS I WOULD PICK

### If I were planning from outside the area

Plan for enough days to give each part of the park its own day, then choose in this order.

- Best left in 2026Midweek in October
The 15-year average for October is 62 on the July scale, about 38 percent below July. Cooler days, quieter trails and fall color in the Valley by the back half of the month. Tioga Road usually stays open, but the first storm can close it: in 2025 the park closed it temporarily on October 13 and reopened it October 17. See also Yosemite in October 2026.

- Quieter stillEarly November, midweek
November averages 31 on the July scale: the Valley close to empty, at the price of short days. Skip Thanksgiving week, and expect the high roads to close.

- For 2027The days after Labor Day
September averages 82 on the July scale, and the Park Service gated Labor Day weekend in 2025, so plan around that weekend and take the days after it. The last week of September is also the Yosemite Facelift, the park's biggest volunteer cleanup (September 23 to 27 in 2026), and it fits into a normal visit.

- For 2027Spring, for the waterfalls
Waterfalls at full volume against a fraction of summer's crowds. But this year proved that spring is where new growth lands first: March was up 45 percent. Expect next March to look like this year's April.

- If summer is what you haveA Tuesday or Wednesday, in by 7:30
A well-run July weekday beats a badly run September Saturday. My no-reservations strategy piece covers the full playbook, and if it is your first visit, start here instead.

Days to plan around. Memorial Day weekend, the one weekend that backed up in 2026. Any summer Saturday arriving after 8:30 a.m. Labor Day weekend. The holiday week in late December if you are not staying in the park. The park says July 4 ran without significant delays this year, but a holiday Saturday is the day to leave the margin on.

WHAT COULD CHANGE

### What would bend the curve

Forecasts age badly in public, so here is what would change this one.

- Smoke
A bad smoke season can erase an August, and fire can close a road: Glacier Point Road was closed for it on October 1.

- Coverage
If early-season chaos keeps making national news, some casual visitors will stay home, and fall comes in under the line.

- Policy
A shutdown, a flood or a reversal of the no-reservation decision would bend the curve. None is announced.

- The management
By the park's own count the toolkit held: two delay days all year, against more than 120 in past years.

None of that changes the planning logic. Demand for this park has risen every year since 2020, the gate is open in 2026, and the only variables you control are the month, the day and the hour. Choose all three on purpose. The park at 6:45 on a September morning is still the park that made the record books, minus the line to get in.

### When to visit, answered

Where two sources differ, the page says so. The July 2026 count, the year-to-date total and the entrance percentages are the ones to recheck when the Park Service posts August.

Do I need a reservation to visit Yosemite in 2026?
No. The Park Service stopped using a timed reservation system for 2026, and its entrance reservations page, updated February 18, says so. You still pay the entrance fee, but no timed-entry ticket is required, and the February firefall weekends ran without reservations too.
How busy will Yosemite be in 2026?
Very. Through July the park logged 2,657,602 visits, 8 percent ahead of 2025, and June 2026 was the second-busiest June on record. If August through December match 2025, the year ends near 4.5 million visits; at this year's pace, near 4.6 million. Either would be the second-busiest year on record, behind 2016. That is the site's projection, not a Park Service number.
What is the best time to visit Yosemite in 2026?
Midweek in October is the best window left: the Park Service's 15-year average for October is about 38 percent below July, and Tioga Road is usually open for most of the month. Early-November weekdays are quieter still, with short days. Check the conditions page first: the Mist Trail is partly closed on weekdays through October.
What time of day should I enter Yosemite to avoid traffic?
Be through the gate before 8 a.m., before 7 on summer weekends, or arrive after 4 p.m. Valley parking has filled as early as 8 a.m. on peak days. In the Park Service's August survey, 91 percent of visitors had no entrance delay or waited less than 15 minutes. Text YNPTRAFFIC to 333111 for the park's live parking and traffic updates.
What are the worst days to visit Yosemite in 2026?
The Park Service counts only two days of significant delays in 2026, both over Memorial Day weekend, and says Juneteenth and July 4 ran without significant delays. Summer Saturdays arriving after 8:30 a.m., Labor Day weekend and the holiday week in late December are still the days to plan around.
What was Yosemite's busiest year ever?
2016, with 5,028,868 recreation visits. 2025 was the fourth-busiest at 4,278,413, behind 2016, 2019 and 2017, and 2026 is on pace to land second at roughly 4.5 to 4.6 million.

## Yosemite Trip Cost in 2026: Three Budgets, Real Numbers

URL: https://thetalusfieldjournal.com/articles/yosemite-trip-cost-budget
Section: Planning. Published: 2026-06-07. Last updated: 2026-09-30.
Summary: What a Yosemite trip costs in 2026: entrance fees, lodging, food, gas, and gear, with real budget, mid-range, and splurge totals.

People ask me what a Yosemite trip costs and I always give the same answer: it depends on how you do it. Here are the numbers.

I've worked in this park for years. I've watched people do Yosemite for $50 a day and I've watched people do it for $800 a day. Both groups had good trips. The difference is a handful of choices, and they are simpler than they look online.

Below is every cost category with 2026 numbers, then three sample trips added up.

### Entrance fees

The main one: $35 per vehicle for a seven-day pass. That's per car, not per person. A family of five pays the same $35 as a solo traveler.

If you're visiting more than one national park this year, or if you'll visit Yosemite more than twice, buy the America the Beautiful annual pass for $80. It covers every national park and federal recreation area in the country for a full year.

If you're entering on foot, bicycle, or horse, the fee is $20 per person. Motorcycles are $30 (valid for up to two motorcycles and four people).

New for 2026: since January 1, international visitors pay a $100 surcharge per person age 16 and older, on top of the standard entrance fee. A car of four foreign visitors pays the $35 vehicle fee plus $400. For a group like that, the $250 nonresident America the Beautiful annual pass can pay for itself in a single visit. The surcharge does not apply to U.S. residents.

One thing that simplifies planning: Yosemite is not requiring timed-entry reservations in 2026. In previous years, a reservation was needed to drive in during peak hours. That system is not in effect this year, so the entrance fee is all you pay to get in. Check the current status before your trip, since the policy can change year to year.

### Lodging: the biggest variable

This is where trips diverge. The range:

Camping (cheapest): $24–$36 per night for a campsite. Valley campgrounds (Upper Pines, Lower Pines, North Pines) are $36. The more remote Tioga Road campgrounds (Tamarack Flat, Yosemite Creek, Porcupine Flat) are $24. Camp 4, the walk-in Valley campground, is $10 per person per night. For a couple, that's $20.

In-park cabins and tent cabins: Curry Village tent cabins typically run $170–$200 per night. You're getting a canvas roof and a cot, but you're sleeping in Yosemite Valley. Hard-walled cabins with bathrooms are typically $220–$300.

In-park lodges: Yosemite Valley Lodge rooms typically run $300–$500 per night depending on room type and season (summer rates are highest). The Ahwahnee starts around $580 for a standard room and climbs past $1,400 for suites. (The Wawona Hotel has been closed since December 2024 for a condition assessment, and no reopening date has been announced.)

Gateway towns: Motels and hotels in Mariposa, Oakhurst, Groveland, and El Portal range from $120 to $300 per night depending on the town and the season. Vacation rentals (Airbnb, VRBO) can be a deal for groups. A cabin that sleeps six for $250 per night is under $42 per person. Rates move with the season and the day of the week, so for real numbers on your dates, a live availability search around the park beats any table of averages, including this one.

The lodging decision is covered in detail in my guide to the gateway towns, but for budgeting purposes: camping saves you hundreds of dollars, and gateway towns save you a hundred or more compared to in-park hotels.

### Food: bring your own or eat in the park

Park food is fine but expensive.

Casual dining in the park: A deli sandwich and a drink at Degnan's, or a hot plate at Base Camp Eatery in the Valley Lodge, typically runs $18–$25 per person. Pizza from the Pizza Deck at Curry Village is $15–$38 for a pie (medium to large), depending on the toppings. A decent sit-down dinner at the Mountain Room at Yosemite Valley Lodge is typically $35–$55 per person.

The Ahwahnee Dining Room: Breakfast is a self-serve buffet or an à la carte menu. As of April 2026, dinner is prix fixe only: $95 for five courses or $125 for seven, and the wine pairing on the five-course menu adds $40. Book dinner ahead: the concessioner takes reservations on OpenTable, and a room at the hotel does not guarantee a table. It is worth doing once if the budget allows.

Camp cooking: If you're camping or staying somewhere with a kitchen, bringing your own food is the single biggest money-saver on a Yosemite trip. A cooler stocked at a Mariposa or Oakhurst grocery store before you enter the park will cost $15–$25 per person per day for three meals plus snacks. I've seen families of four eat well for a full week on $400 of groceries.

The Village Store: There's a general store in Yosemite Village that sells groceries, but prices run well above a regular supermarket's. Use it for things you forgot, not as your primary shopping.

My advice: bring a cooler, stock it before you arrive, and plan to eat one meal per day at a park restaurant if you want the experience. Trail lunches of sandwiches, fruit, and trail mix are better than most of what the park sells.

### Gas and driving

Gas costs add up.

From San Francisco / Bay Area: About 195 miles each way. At late-September 2026 gas prices (about $6.19 a gallon for regular in California, by the U.S. Energy Information Administration's weekly count) and average fuel economy (28 mpg), that's roughly $40–$45 each way, or $80–$90 round trip. If you're making a day trip from the city, that's your floor just for fuel.

From Los Angeles: About 313 miles each way, most of it the drive up Highway 99 and Highway 41. Figure $65–$75 each way, $130–$150 round trip.

From Sacramento / Central Valley: About 176 miles, $35–$40 each way.

Once you're in the park: Gas is available at Wawona and at Crane Flat (both have 24-hour pay-at-the-pump with credit card). There's also a station in El Portal, just outside the Arch Rock entrance. All typically charge more per gallon than stations in gateway towns like Mariposa or Oakhurst. Fill up before you enter. The driving and parking logistics inside the park take planning, but you won't burn much gas on the Valley shuttle loop.

Don't forget parking: Parking in Yosemite is free but competitive. There's no paid parking anywhere in the park. The cost is time.

### Gear: what you actually need

You do not need $2,000 of gear to visit a national park.

Photo: Cory Goehring

Shoes: Sturdy, broken-in shoes with good tread. If you own hiking boots, great. If you don't, a pair of trail runners ($80–$150) will handle every trail in Yosemite except Half Dome. Running shoes and fashion sneakers are not safe on the steep, wet granite of the park's most popular hikes. This is the one gear purchase I'd say is non-negotiable.

Layers: Temperatures swing widely. A summer day can go from 40°F at dawn to 95°F by noon to 55°F after sunset. Bring a warm layer (fleece or puffy jacket) and a rain layer even in summer. You probably already own these.

Day pack: Something to carry water, snacks, sunscreen, and a layer. A school backpack works. If you want to buy one, $30–$60 gets a perfectly good pack.

Water bottles: Bring them. The park has water refill stations. Don't buy single-use plastic bottles in the park. It's wasteful and expensive.

What you don't need: Trekking poles (unless you're doing Half Dome or have knee issues), a GPS device (your phone works fine), bear spray (prohibited in Yosemite; the bears here are black bears, not grizzlies), specialized hiking pants, or a $200 headlamp.

Total gear cost for someone starting from scratch: $100–$200 if you're buying shoes and a pack. $0 if you already own reasonable outdoor clothing and a backpack.

### Guided programs and activities

Yosemite Conservancy runs guided programs in the park, including naturalist walks, stargazing programs, and custom adventures, that range from $15 to several hundred dollars depending on the program type and duration.

Free programs: Ranger talks and evening programs are completely free. Yosemite Conservancy naturalist walks and stargazing programs are affordable: sunset walks are $15 per person and stargazing programs are $25 per person. The stargazing programs are among the best things in the park.

Paid guided programs: Yosemite Conservancy custom adventures start at $500 for a half-day (up to four people) and $850 for a full day, with $50 per additional person. Multi-day and specialty programs cost more.

For budgeting, guided programs are optional but good. If you're a first-time visitor and can fit one into the budget, a guided program with a naturalist who knows the park will change what you see and understand about Yosemite.

### The three budget tiers

Here's what three different four-day, three-night trips look like for two people.

#### Shoestring: ~$400–$550 total ($200–$275 per person)

- Lodging: Campground, $36/night x 3 = $108
- Food: Cooler of groceries from home or a gateway-town grocery stop, ~$25/person/day x 3 days = $150
- Gas: Round trip from Bay Area, ~$85
- Entrance fee: $35
- Gear: $0 (using what you own)
- Dining out: One meal at a park restaurant, ~$50
- Total: ~$428

You eat well, see the main sights, and wake up in the park. Camping is a good way to do Yosemite.

#### Comfortable mid-range: ~$1,400–$1,800 total ($700–$900 per person)

- Lodging: Yosemite Valley Lodge or gateway-town hotel, $350/night x 3 = $1,050
- Food: Mix of camp-style lunches and park dining, ~$50/person/day x 3 = $300
- Gas: Round trip from Bay Area, ~$85
- Entrance fee: $35
- Gear: Trail shoes if needed, $80
- Guided program: One stargazing program, ~$50 for two
- Total: ~$1,600

This is the trip most people end up doing. Private room, some good meals, a mix of self-guided and guided activities. It is comfortable without being extravagant.

#### Splurge: ~$3,500–$5,000+ total ($1,750–$2,500 per person)

- Lodging: The Ahwahnee, $650/night x 3 = $1,950
- Food: Ahwahnee dining room dinners (prix fixe from $95/person) plus nice park lunches, ~$150/person/day x 3 = $900
- Gas: Round trip from Bay Area, ~$85
- Entrance fee: $35
- Guided program: Full-day custom adventure, ~$850 for two
- Extras: Souvenirs, specialty gear, etc. ~$200
- Total: ~$4,020

You sleep in a historic lodge and eat well. It is a special-occasion trip.

### Hidden costs people forget

Bear canisters: If you're backpacking, you need a bear canister. Rent one in the park for $5/week from any staffed wilderness permit station (plus a $95 refundable deposit). Car campers use the bear lockers at every campsite (free).

Tips: Guided programs and sit-down dining. Budget 18–20% on top of listed prices.

The gift shop purchase: Budget $20 for the mug or the patch or the sticker.

### The bottom line

Yosemite can be done cheaply. The park itself doesn't cost much. Thirty-five dollars to get in, free shuttles, free trails, free ranger programs. The expensive part is lodging, and even that is manageable if you camp or stay in a gateway town.

Don't let the cost keep you from going. The people having the best time here are not always the ones spending the most. If you're starting from scratch, my first-timer's guide to Yosemite ties it all together.

#### The one number this article cannot give you

Every figure above is a range, and lodging is the line item that moves the most: the same room is a different price in October than in July, and midweek is not weekend. Pricing your actual dates takes about as long as reading this paragraph.

Price Mariposa lodging on your dates →
