## Yosemite in September 2026: What Closes, What Gets Better

URL: https://thetalusfieldjournal.com/articles/yosemite-in-september-2026
Section: Seasonal Guides. Published: 2026-08-25. Last updated: 2026-08-25.
Summary: Yosemite in September 2026: dry waterfalls, closure dates for the pools, stores and shuttles, Mist Trail weekday closures, and the year's best Half Dome odds.

A man stopped me on the Valley loop in the first week of September last year, holding his phone up with a photograph of Yosemite Falls at full flood, and asked which trail got him to that. None of them, that month. The fall had been dry for six weeks. He had booked the trip in February off a photograph taken in May, which is the single most common way a Yosemite trip disappoints someone, and it is entirely avoidable.

On paper, September looks like the month the park runs out. The waterfalls are low. The concessions start closing in the first two weeks. The shuttles stop. And underneath all of that, the high country is in the finest condition it reaches all year, and the crowds thin out after Labor Day.

### The waterfalls are done, and that is not a reason to skip it

Yosemite Falls is dry. It runs on snowmelt from a shallow basin above the rim, and by September there is no snow left to melt. Mirror Lake is a meadow, which is what it is for most of the year and what surprises people who saw the spring photograph. Bridalveil, Vernal and Nevada still run, because their creeks drain bigger and higher ground, but they run thin.

In September the Valley is about granite: El Capitan in low afternoon light, the Cathedral Rocks across the meadow, Half Dome catching the last of it. If waterfalls are the reason for the trip, the trip belongs in May, and the waterfalls guide has the month-by-month version of that argument.

### The high country is the reason to come

Tioga Road is open, the whole 39 miles of it, and the high country in September is better than the high country in July: the mosquitoes are gone, the afternoon thunderstorms are less reliable, the meadows have turned, and the crowds are smaller. Tuolumne Meadows, Olmsted Point, Tenaya Lake and the Cathedral Lakes trail are all at their best.

Two caveats catch people out this year. The Tuolumne store and grill close on September 20, which removes the only food and the only reliable indoor shelter along the entire road, and the Tuolumne shuttle and the hikers bus both stop on September 13, after which the high country is drive-yourself. There has never been gas at Tuolumne. Fill up at Crane Flat on the way in and carry lunch. The Tuolumne day covers the drive properly, and Cathedral Lakes is the hike to spend a September day on.

### What closes, and when

The park contracts in the first three weeks of the month. The dates worth knowing: Jennie's Ice Cream and the Wawona stable finish on September 6; the Curry Village and Yosemite Valley Lodge pools on September 7; the Tuolumne store and grill on September 20. Of the High Sierra Camps, Glen Aulin and Sunrise close on September 6 and May Lake on September 9, with Vogelsang and Merced Lake shut for the whole season.

Two longer closures run through the month and are not seasonal: the Wawona Hotel and its dining room are closed for renovation, and White Wolf, its lodge, store and dining room, is closed for the season. If either was in the plan, it needs replacing rather than rescheduling. Raft rentals on the Merced are finished for the year.

The practical version: by the last week of September, the Valley still has food and beds and the high country has neither. Plan meals accordingly, and see where to eat for what stays open.

### The Mist Trail is closed four days a week

The most popular hike in the park is closed Monday through Thursday, 7 a.m. to 3:30 p.m., for repairs running through the end of October. The John Muir Trail detour is signed and adds distance and climbing. If Vernal and Nevada Falls are on the list, plan them for a Friday, Saturday or Sunday, or start very early and be through before seven.

Check again the week you travel: the Park Bulletin carries the current edition's version. The Mist Trail guide covers the hike itself and the detour.

### Half Dome, and the best permit odds of the year

The cables are still up in September and come down the day after the second Monday in October, which makes this the last full month of the season. It is also the best month to apply. Weekday odds in the daily lottery run meaningfully better than weekend odds, and late-season weekdays are the strongest draw of the year: fewer applicants, cooler air, and the same cables. The lottery page has the published numbers and the strategy.

If the permit does not come through, September is also the best month for the alternative. Clouds Rest is higher than Half Dome, needs no permit, and is reachable from Tioga Road while the road is open.

### Fire season, and the air

September sits in the worst stretch of California's fire season, and smoke is the variable that no amount of planning controls. It can turn a clear week hazy in a day and clear again just as fast. Check air quality the morning you drive in rather than the night before, and treat a smoky forecast as a reason to shift a hard hike rather than cancel a trip. Visiting during smoke season covers how to read it and what to do.

Fire restrictions are usually still in force this month: fires only in portable stoves, grills and established rings, never unattended, and out cold before you leave. The restrictions piece has the current rules and how to check them.

### Crowds, and the Labor Day line

The month splits cleanly. Before Labor Day the Valley behaves like August: busy by mid-morning, worse at weekends, and parking gone in the three hubs by nine. After Labor Day it thins noticeably, and by the last week of the month a weekday morning in the Valley is quiet.

If the dates are flexible at all, take the second half. The roads and cables are the same and the traffic is a fraction. That is the argument of the crowd forecast, and September is where it pays best.

### What is on in the evenings

The Conservation Heritage Center runs a free evening series through the month: poetry from Tahoe to Yosemite on the 11th, the legacy of the old Yosemite Village on the 12th, the park's mountain lions on the 18th and its bats on the 19th, all at 7:30 p.m. The Moonlight Tour runs its last trip of the season on September 22, ticketed through the concessioner. Tom Killion's woodblocks are up at the Ansel Adams Gallery through September 26, free to walk through.

Ranger programs continue through the month and thin as the seasonal staff leave. The programs piece explains how to find the current schedule, and the Bulletin carries this edition's clock.

### Two Septembers

There is the September people book by accident, chasing a waterfall photograph into a month with no waterfalls, arriving to find the pool closed and the shuttle finished and the Mist Trail shut on a Tuesday. And there is the September people come back for: Tioga Road wide open, the meadows gold, the Valley emptying out after Labor Day, and the best Half Dome odds of the year.

They are the same month. Start with the basics if this is your first visit, and plan the trip end to end if you want the full framework.

---

## Yosemite in June 2026: Two Junes, One Month

URL: https://thetalusfieldjournal.com/articles/yosemite-in-june
Section: Seasonal Guides. Published: 2026-06-02. Last updated: 2026-08-06.
Summary: A Yosemite naturalist breaks down June 2026 conditions: low snowpack, no reservations, early waterfall peak, Tioga Road open, and how to plan around all of it.

Every June, I watch the same thing happen. A family pulls into Yosemite Valley at 11 a.m. on a Saturday, spends forty minutes looking for parking, finds a spot at the overflow lot near the stables, walks to Lower Yosemite Fall, takes a photo, and leaves. They drove five hours for ninety minutes in a crowd. They didn't know the waterfalls were already fading, that the high country was open, or that two hours north of where they were standing, there were alpine lakes with nobody at them.

June is the month when the Valley is at its most crowded and, in a good year, at its most spectacular. Waterfalls hit their peak. The high country opens. The days are the longest of the year. With historically low snowpack and no reservation system, planning matters more than usual this June.

Here is how to plan for it.

### The waterfalls

The Sierra Nevada snowpack on April 1, 2026 was measured at roughly 18 percent of average, the second-lowest figure in recorded history. I covered what low snowpack means for the park this year in detail. Snowmelt feeds Yosemite's waterfalls, and this year there is little of it.

In a normal year, warm June days melt the snowpack and send torrents of water over the Valley's granite walls. Yosemite Falls, Bridalveil Fall, Vernal and Nevada Falls all run at or near their peak. This is not a normal year. With so little snow to melt, the waterfalls peaked early. By late May, flows that would normally build through June were already declining. Yosemite Falls typically peaks in late May and can run strong into mid-June in an average snowpack year. In 2026, expect it to weaken noticeably by mid-June and reduce to a trickle by early July. Bridalveil Fall, which has a smaller watershed, will thin out sooner.

If seeing waterfalls at full power is a priority, the first two weeks of June are your window. After that the falls are in decline. They will still be worth seeing, but the full-volume Yosemite Falls most visitors picture is a short window this year.

For waterfall-specific hiking, the Mist Trail is still the best way to experience Vernal and Nevada Falls up close. One complication: the National Park Service has announced weekday closures of the Mist Trail corridor beginning July 27 for a rehabilitation project. If you are visiting in late June or July, plan your Mist Trail hike for a weekend day or go before the closures begin.

### Tioga Road and the high country

Tioga Road opened on May 15, 2026, the earliest opening since 2015. In a typical year, it opens in late May or early June, and sometimes not until July. The low snowpack that is shortchanging the waterfalls gave us something in return: early access to the high country.

This matters more than usual in 2026. With no reservation system managing Valley crowds, the high country is the best way around them. Tuolumne Meadows, Cathedral Lakes, Tenaya Lake, the Dana Fork, Lembert Dome: these places are two hours from the Valley floor and far less crowded. I drove up on the opening weekend and counted eight cars at the Cathedral Lakes trailhead at 9 a.m. on a Saturday. That same morning, the Valley had been full since 7:30. If your trip overlaps with a Valley gridlock day, Tuolumne is the answer.

Cathedral Lakes is the signature Tuolumne day hike and one of the best in the park. The trail to Lower Cathedral Lake is about 3.5 miles one way with roughly 1,000 feet of gain, ending at a granite-rimmed alpine lake beneath Cathedral Peak. In early June it may still have snow patches on the upper trail. Bring traction devices if you are hiking before mid-month.

Tuolumne Meadows Lodge opens June 5. The Tuolumne Meadows Store and Grill opens on the same timeline. This is also prime wildflower season: the meadows should be blooming by mid-June, though the compressed snowmelt may push the peak earlier and shorter than usual.

Entering through Tioga Pass from the east side is also in play now. If you come over the pass from the Eastern Sierra, you can spend a full day in the high country without ever touching the Valley.

### Glacier Point Road

Glacier Point Road opened on May 9, another early opening. This gives you access to Glacier Point itself, Sentinel Dome and Taft Point, and the full Glacier Point Road experience.

It also opens the option I recommend to almost every June visitor: hike Four Mile Trail up and Panorama Trail down. This is the single best day hike in Yosemite, and in June you get waterfalls at every turn. Vernal and Nevada Falls are both visible from the Panorama Trail, and Illilouette Fall, which most visitors never see, is at its best in early June. Start by 7 a.m. to beat the heat on the Four Mile ascent.

### Crowds in June 2026

June 2026 is shaping up to be the most crowded month in the park in years. The reservation system is gone, and the numbers reflect it. More than 836,000 visits were recorded through late May, roughly 100,000 more than the same period last year. On Memorial Day weekend, Valley parking lots were full by mid-morning and entrance waits exceeded ninety minutes.

I wrote about why the park needs a reservation system. For planning your June trip, here is what you need to know:

Arrive before 7 a.m. On any Friday through Sunday, and especially on holidays, Valley parking lots will fill early. If you arrive at 10 a.m. on a Saturday, you will not find parking at any major trailhead. I watched it happen every weekend in May.

Park once and use the shuttle. The free Valley shuttle runs two routes, the Valleywide about every 22 to 32 minutes and the shorter East Valley about every 18 to 22, and between them they stop at every major trailhead, the Visitor Center, Curry Village, and the Ahwahnee.

Visit midweek. Tuesday through Thursday, the park is far less crowded. If you have flexibility, this is the biggest improvement you can make. If you are still deciding where to stay in or near Yosemite, booking midweek dates also opens up more lodging options.

Go outside the Valley. The Valley floor absorbs roughly 90 percent of Yosemite's visitors. Hetch Hetchy is fifteen minutes from the Big Oak Flat entrance and rarely crowded. Wawona and the Mariposa Grove are on the south end. The Merced Grove has almost no one in it. And with Tioga open, the entire high country is available. Plan at least one full day outside the Valley.

If you arrive in the afternoon, the day is not wasted. The golden hour in Yosemite Valley in June starts around 6:30 p.m. and lasts until sunset around 8:25. Some of the best light and thinnest crowds of the day happen between 6 and 8 p.m.

### Bears in June 2026

Bear-related property damage in Yosemite increased 316 percent year over year according to recent park reporting. Drought years make wild food scarcer. When natural berry and nut crops are thin, bears look for alternatives, including coolers left in cars.

Bear-proof food storage is not optional. Every campsite in the park has a bear box. Use it. Every piece of food, every scented item (toothpaste, sunscreen, lip balm), and every cooler goes in the box when you are not actively holding it. If you are day-hiking, do not leave food visible in your car. Not in a bag. Not under a blanket. Not in the trunk of a sedan, which a bear can pry open in under a minute.

A bear that learns to associate cars with food eventually gets killed. It happens every year in this park, and it starts with someone who ignored the storage rules.

### What to pack

June in Yosemite Valley means daytime highs typically between 80 and 90 degrees Fahrenheit. The high country runs 15 to 20 degrees cooler. Mornings in the Valley start around 50 to 55 degrees and warm fast.

Your day pack for a June hike needs at minimum two liters of water per person for any hike over four miles, sun protection (the granite reflects everything), and a layer for elevation. If you are spending a full day in the high country, bring a real jacket. Afternoon thunderstorms are possible in Tuolumne by late June, and they move in fast at 8,600 feet.

The Merced River will be swimmable in some sections by mid to late June. In a low snowpack year, it warms up earlier. Check current conditions before wading in. Early June flows can still be fast enough to be dangerous even in a drought year.

### Two Junes

Low snowpack pushed everything earlier: the waterfalls, the road openings, the wildflower bloom, the bear activity. The end of reservations made everything more crowded.

If you are visiting in the first two weeks, you will see waterfalls and wildflowers and the high country waking up and the Valley at its busiest. If you are visiting in the last two weeks, the waterfalls will be fading, the Mist Trail may be partially closed, and the heat will be climbing. Both are worth the trip, but they call for different plans.

Start with the basics if this is your first time. Plan your trip end to end if you want the full framework.

Plan accordingly.

## Cathedral Lakes hike: the high-country day worth the drive

URL: https://thetalusfieldjournal.com/articles/cathedral-lakes-day-hike
Section: Trails and Hikes. Published: 2026-06-02. Last updated: 2026-06-02.
Summary: Cathedral Lakes is the best day hike in Tuolumne Meadows. Trail distance, elevation, best months, and how to hike Lower and Upper Cathedral Lakes in Yosemite.

The first time I sat on the granite shelf above Lower Cathedral Lake, late July, midday, I watched a yellow-bellied marmot sun itself on a rock for forty minutes while a chickaree complained from a hemlock about thirty feet behind me. Cathedral Peak rose straight out of the lake on the opposite side. There were maybe nine other people in sight, spread across a hundred acres of granite shoreline. The water was 55 degrees and clear, and on a windless day the reflection of Cathedral is sharp enough that a phone photo is hard to read right side up.

Cathedral Lakes has been one of Yosemite's standard high-country day hikes since John Muir camped on the shoulder of Cathedral Peak in 1869 and described it in My First Summer in the Sierra as "one of Nature's cathedrals, hewn from the living rock." It is on every best hikes in Yosemite list. It still earns the listing.

What follows is how to do it, what to look at, and a few things most guides leave out.

### Cathedral Lakes trail distance, elevation, and trailhead

The Cathedral Lakes trail starts at the new Cathedral Lakes trailhead parking adjacent to the Tuolumne Meadows Visitor Center. The old trailhead at the side of Tioga Road was retired during the Tuolumne Meadows redevelopment, so the trail distances in older guidebooks read about three-quarters of a mile shorter than the current reality. For a broader look at the trailheads and routes in this area, and for the shorter walks that suit a day when this hike is too much, see Tuolumne Meadows in a day.

Current numbers, from the new trailhead:

- Total distance: roughly 9 to 10.5 miles round trip, depending on whether you visit Lower Cathedral Lake only, Upper Cathedral Lake only, or both.
- Elevation gain: about 1,000 to 1,400 feet of cumulative gain.
- Trailhead elevation: about 8,500 feet.
- Lower Cathedral Lake elevation: 9,288 feet.
- Upper Cathedral Lake elevation: 9,585 feet.

The trail begins flat through the meadow approach, then climbs steadily through lodgepole pine forest for about three miles, gaining most of its elevation in this stretch. It crests on a forested bench where a signed junction points right to the lakes and continues straight along the John Muir Trail toward Sunrise. The Lower Cathedral Lake spur descends about a half-mile through forest to the lake's outlet stream. Upper Cathedral Lake sits in a granite bowl a few hundred yards past the junction, directly below Cathedral Peak.

Plan five to seven hours for the round trip, including time at the lakes.

### Best time to hike Cathedral Lakes

Tioga Road has to be open, which means you're working with a window that runs roughly late May or early June through October or early November, depending on snow. In 2026, Tioga Road opened May 15, well ahead of the long-term average.

The Cathedral Lakes trail itself is not fully accessible the moment Tioga Road opens. The upper portions of the trail and the lake basins hold snow into late June or early July in normal years and into mid-July in heavy-snow years. If you're hiking before the second week of July, expect significant snow on parts of the trail and at the lakes. Bring a map. Be willing to turn around.

The best hiking conditions are typically mid-July through mid-September. Wildflowers in the meadows and forest understory peak in late July. The lake water reaches its warmest temperature (still cold) in early August. Fall light starts to change the character of the basin in mid-September.

This is one of the busier high-country day hikes. On summer weekends the trail is crowded at peak hours. The lakes themselves are large enough to absorb the crowd, and you can almost always find a granite shelf to yourself along the shore. But if you want solitude, weekday hikes or early starts (trailhead by 7 a.m.) are dramatically better. If you're basing yourself in the Valley or a gateway town, the drive to the trailhead takes roughly 90 minutes from Yosemite Village via Tioga Road.

### What to see on the Cathedral Lakes trail

The trail itself is more interesting than most guidebooks make it sound. Here's what to notice, in the order you'll encounter it.

The first half-mile through the meadow. The approach crosses the edge of Tuolumne Meadows. In July, this stretch is one of the better wildflower walks you'll get all day. Look for shooting star, paintbrush, columbine, lupine, and the yellow Sierra wallflower in the open patches. Sandhill cranes have been documented on the meadow floor in spring. Mule deer and the occasional black bear are regular.

The forest climb. Three miles through dense lodgepole pine, with mountain hemlock mixing in at higher elevations. This is the unglamorous middle of the hike, but it's where most of the bird life is. Western tanagers, Cassin's finches, mountain chickadees, and several warbler species all use this forest. The chickarees (Douglas's squirrels) will let you know when you're close to their cone caches. Stop walking for thirty seconds and listen.

The lodgepole bark beetles. Look at the trunks of the lodgepoles as you climb. Many have the characteristic exit holes and pitch tubes of mountain pine beetle activity. The Sierra has been losing significant lodgepole stands to beetle outbreaks driven by warmer winters and drought-stressed trees, and the Cathedral approach is part of that larger pattern. The standing dead trees along the trail are part of that transition.

The Cathedral Peak view. About two miles in, the trail breaks out of forest and gives you the first clear view of Cathedral Peak. Stop. Cathedral Peak is one of the most distinctively shaped peaks in the Sierra, a slender granite spire with two main summits, and the source of 150 years of church metaphors.

The trail junction. At about three miles, the spur trail to Lower Cathedral Lake branches right while the John Muir Trail continues toward Sunrise. The junction is signed. Take Lower Cathedral first if you're doing both lakes. The descent and re-ascent is real, and you don't want it on tired legs at the end of the day.

Lower Cathedral Lake. The outlet stream is on your right as you descend. The lake opens up suddenly, and the south shore, approached via a granite ramp, is the vantage point you've seen in photographs: Cathedral Peak rising directly across the water. The lake is deep enough to swim, cold enough to shock, and large enough that even with twenty other people scattered around the shoreline you can find a quiet shelf.

The granite slabs above the lake. Scramble up the slabs west of the outlet and you get a higher perspective with almost guaranteed solitude. This is where the marmots tend to sun themselves. The view extends across the basin and down toward Tenaya Canyon.

Upper Cathedral Lake. Smaller, with Cathedral Peak even closer overhead. The setting is more enclosed and the water colder. Many hikers visit only the Lower. Doing both gives you two readings of the same basin, and the Upper is the quieter one.

Cathedral Peak itself. The rock you're looking at is a particular granodiorite called Cathedral Peak Granodiorite, named for this peak. Geologists know it for having unusually large potassium feldspar crystals, commonly 2 to 3 inches long, embedded throughout the rock. Walk up to the slabs and look closely. The feldspar phenocrysts show up as off-white blocky crystals studding the gray-pink groundmass. The same rock makes up much of Tuolumne's high country, including most of the trail.

The peak is climbable. The standard route is a fifth-class climb of about 700 vertical feet from the base, often done as a long day from Tuolumne. Muir made the first recorded ascent in 1869 in work boots, alone. The Park Service does not encourage casual visitors to attempt it. If you have climbing experience and want to try, get current beta from the Yosemite climber community before going.

### The Muir connection

John Muir camped here in late summer 1869 during his first season as a sheep tender in the high country. His journal entries from those weeks became the basis of My First Summer in the Sierra, published forty-two years later. The book includes the description of Cathedral Peak as "one of Nature's cathedrals, hewn from the living rock," and his solitary first ascent. He climbed it in work boots, carrying nothing.

Muir returned to this basin repeatedly over the next few decades. He wrote about it in multiple books. The Cathedral region became a touchstone in his evolving argument for wildland protection, an argument that eventually reached a president and reshaped the boundaries of what became Yosemite National Park.

Sitting on the granite at Lower Cathedral Lake, you are sitting in roughly the same place Muir sat in 1869. The basin has not been logged. The lake has not been dammed. The peak has not been turned into a tourist attraction.

### What to bring on a Cathedral Lakes day hike

The day pack basics are covered elsewhere. The Cathedral-specific version: carry three liters of water minimum, because there's no reliable potable water between the trailhead and the basin. Bring layers. Late July at 9,500 feet can be 75 degrees and clear or 50 degrees with a thunderstorm building in the same afternoon, and the wind off the lake at midday can be sharp. A rain shell is not optional in July and August; afternoon thunderstorms are common and develop fast, so plan to be off exposed granite by early afternoon if storms are in the forecast. Sun protection matters at this altitude. UV at 9,500 feet is intense and the lake basins are exposed.

Bring a real lunch; plan to sit at the lake for an hour.

Day hikers don't need a bear canister, but secure your food when you stop. Black bears occasionally work the trails near the lakes, especially in the food-conditioning patterns that develop when too many hikers leave snacks unattended.

### Common mistakes

The main John Muir Trail continues from the Cathedral Lakes junction up over Cathedral Pass and on toward Sunrise. It is tempting to keep going. Don't, unless you've planned for it. Most day hikers should stop at the lakes and be content with that. (If you do want to keep going, see the through-hike section below.)

If you're camping, know the rules: campfires are prohibited at Lower Cathedral Lake, all camping must be at least 100 feet from water and trails, and you need to be at least four trail miles from Tuolumne Meadows. A wilderness permit is required for any overnight stay. If you're planning an overnight, see packing for a Yosemite backpack.

Don't swim before July. The water is too cold and snow patches around the lake make the shore slippery and unstable. The lake does not fully ice out in many years until late June. And don't rely on the trail being clear of snow before mid-July. I've seen the upper switchbacks buried into early July in heavy-snow years. Bring traction devices if you're hiking before mid-July, and be willing to turn around at the snowline.

### Cathedral Pass to Sunrise: the through-hike option

If you have the legs and the logistics, the through-hike from Tuolumne Meadows over Cathedral Pass to Sunrise High Sierra Camp or the trailhead at Tenaya Lake is one of the great Yosemite point-to-points. Roughly 13 miles with significant elevation change, crossing the high meadows above Cathedral Lakes that almost no day hikers see. You need a shuttle or a very understanding friend with a car at the far end. It is a long day. The high meadows above the lakes, with Cathedral Peak behind you and the Clark Range to the south, are the reason to do it.

### Why Cathedral Lakes is worth the drive to Tuolumne

Cathedral Lakes is the standard high-country day hike from Tuolumne for a reason. The trail is well built, and the peak is among the most photographed and written-about in the Sierra. If you're still planning your Yosemite trip, this hike belongs on the short list.

Plan an early start, bring a real lunch, sit on the granite for an hour after you arrive, and look closely at the rock under your hands. The crystals you're sitting on were cooling underground when this part of California was still under shallow seas. The peak above you was first described to a wider readership by a Scotsman with a notebook in 1869.

## Yosemite needs a reservation system

URL: https://thetalusfieldjournal.com/articles/yosemite-needs-a-reservation-system
Section: Planning. Published: 2026-05-26. Last updated: 2026-05-26.
Summary: Without a reservation system, Memorial Day 2026 left Yosemite Valley gridlocked and its meadows damaged. Why the park needs timed entry back.

I built this guide so people can enjoy their national park. I want them to see the Valley at sunrise, hear a hermit thrush at dusk, watch a bear graze a meadow edge in October. I want them to have an experience good enough that they go home and care about public lands for the rest of their lives. That is the whole point.

This Memorial Day weekend made it clear that without a reservation system, none of that is possible at Yosemite.

### The mission, in plain language

The National Park Service was created by the Organic Act of 1916. The mission statement is one sentence long, and it has governed every national park in the country for 110 years:

"...to conserve the scenery and the natural and historic objects and the wild life therein and to provide for the enjoyment of the same in such manner and by such means as will leave them unimpaired for the enjoyment of future generations."

There are two mandates in that sentence: conserve the resource, and provide for enjoyment. The second mandate comes with a condition: enjoyment must happen in a way that leaves the park unimpaired for the people who come after us.

Yosemite without a reservation system is currently failing on both counts.

### Failure one: people cannot enjoy their park

On Sunday of Memorial Day weekend 2026, visitors received a text alert at 7:39 a.m. telling them that parking lots in Yosemite Valley were already full. By mid-morning, the entrance stations had wait times exceeding ninety minutes. By evening, as one visitor told ABC7, "the entire park, it was impossible to park there. There's nowhere to park for anybody."

It was not an isolated incident. Since the reservation system was dropped for the 2026 season, Yosemite has recorded more than 836,000 visits through late May, roughly 100,000 more than the same period last year. March 2026 visitation jumped nearly 45 percent over the previous year. On peak days throughout the spring, Valley parking lots have been filling by 7 a.m.

When the lots fill, access to the eastern half of the Valley, including the Mist Trail, Happy Isles, Mirror Lake, and the Ahwahnee, becomes limited or effectively impossible for anyone arriving by car. The free shuttle system helps, but only if you can find a parking spot to begin with.

Think about what that means for the family that drove three hours from the Central Valley on their one day off. They arrive at 10 a.m. because they didn't know the lots fill by seven. They circle for an hour looking for parking. They give up and drive home, or they park illegally and get towed. Either way, they did not recreate in their national park. The Organic Act's promise of enjoyment was a dead letter for them.

The reservation system, which Yosemite ran in various forms from 2020 through 2025 (every year except 2023), was not perfect. It required advance planning. It frustrated some spontaneous visitors. But it did something essential: it spread the demand across the day so that the people who showed up could actually use the park. Under reservations, the Valley felt, for the first time in decades, like a place where you could park your car, walk to a trailhead, and breathe. That was the park working as designed.

### Failure two: the resource is being damaged

Memorial Day weekend 2026 was destructive.

Videos from the holiday weekend showed dozens of cars parked illegally on meadow edges and road shoulders throughout the Valley. Visitors, unable to find legal parking, drove off pavement and onto the ground. Three tow trucks were deployed simultaneously to clear illegally parked vehicles from shuttle routes. Beth Pratt, a conservationist and author who has worked on Yosemite wildlife issues for years, described the scene plainly: people were "pulling onto meadows, pulling off pavement, going off-road."

Yosemite's meadows are complex ecosystems, home to rare sedges, native grasses, and invertebrate communities that have evolved over millennia in the Sierra's specific hydrology. A car driven onto a wet meadow compresses the soil, destroys root systems, and creates channels that alter water flow. The damage from a single vehicle can take years to recover. Multiply that by dozens of cars across a holiday weekend, and the cost to the resource is visible.

This is the second failure. The Organic Act does not say "conserve the scenery unless the parking lot is full." It says conserve. And the condition on enjoyment, that it must leave the park "unimpaired for the enjoyment of future generations," means that when overcrowding causes direct, physical damage to the resource, the park is violating its own founding mandate. Cars on meadows are a conservation failure.

### The data we already had

None of this is surprising. We have data that tells us exactly what happens when reservation systems work, and exactly what parks lose when they are removed.

At Arches National Park, a Utah State University survey of more than 500 visitors during the 2022 timed-entry pilot found that 84 percent of respondents wanted the reservation system to continue. Fifty-seven percent said timed entry made their experience "somewhat or much better." Eighty-nine percent of visitors were able to get a ticket, 98 percent entered on their desired day, and 86 percent received their preferred time slot. By any measure, the system worked for visitors and for the park.

In Yosemite, a March 2026 survey by the employee union found that 85 percent of 135 verified staff responses did not approve of Superintendent Ray McPadden's decision to drop the reservation system. These are the people who work in the park every day. They saw the reservation system work across five seasons. They know what the alternative looks like.

The alternative is what we saw this weekend.

### Who made this decision

On February 18, 2026, Superintendent Ray McPadden announced that Yosemite would not require vehicle reservations for the 2026 season. He cited park data suggesting that "a season-wide reservation requirement is not the most effective approach for the coming season," pointing to weekday parking availability and manageable traffic flow on non-peak days.

That analysis is accurate and beside the point. Nobody was arguing that Tuesday mornings in April needed reservations. The problem has always been weekends from May through September, and especially holiday weekends. A season-wide evaluation that averages peak and off-peak days together will always dilute the severity of the peaks. It is an analytical choice that obscures the very problem it should be addressing.

The decision also did not happen in a vacuum. Interior Secretary Doug Burgum's Secretarial Order 3426, issued in April 2025, directed the National Park Service to keep parks "open and accessible" and required superintendent-level closures or service reductions to be reviewed by the NPS Director and the Assistant Secretary. The National Parks Conservation Association called the order "ill-conceived," warning that it "flies in the face of responsible management of national parks, risking both visitor safety and the very resources the Park Service was created and is mandated to protect." Four major parks dropped their reservation systems for 2026: Yosemite, Arches, Glacier, and Mount Rainier. Rocky Mountain National Park, notably, kept its timed entry in place.

Superintendent McPadden said the park would rely on "real-time traffic monitoring" and promotion of areas outside the Valley. Those are useful supplements, but they do not substitute for managing the number of vehicles that enter the park on a given day. Monitoring does nothing for a parking lot that filled three hours ago.

### Why this matters beyond Yosemite

I write this guide so that people can plan a visit that works. I tell them to arrive early. I tell them to pack their car right. I tell them where to go when the Valley is full. I do this because I believe that a good experience in a national park is the beginning of a lifetime of caring about public land.

But there is a limit to what planning can fix. When the infrastructure cannot support the number of people who show up, no amount of advice about arriving before sunrise will solve the problem. The family that got turned away, the couple that spent ninety minutes in an entrance line, the solo hiker who watched cars drive onto a meadow: those people did not have a good experience. Some of them will not come back. A person who drives away angry may stop caring about national parks.

The reservation system was imperfect. It needed refinement. Dynamic pricing, better shoulder-season incentives, improved cancellation policies, expanded public transit: all of these were available paths forward. Dropping the system entirely was the wrong call.

The data, the staff, and the visitors surveyed at parks that had them all support reservations. The Organic Act demands that enjoyment and conservation happen together. Right now, Yosemite is delivering neither.

I will be back out in the Valley tomorrow morning. If it is anything like this weekend, the parking lots will be full by seven, the meadow edges will have tire tracks in them, and a family from Fresno will be circling Yosemite Village wondering why they came. That is what the absence of a reservation system looks like from inside the park.

---

## Yosemite on Memorial Day 2026: skip the Valley, go high

URL: https://thetalusfieldjournal.com/articles/memorial-day-skip-the-valley-go-high-2026
Section: Seasonal Guides. Published: 2026-05-20. Last updated: 2026-09-16.
Summary: Yosemite Valley will be gridlock on Memorial Day weekend 2026. Tioga Road and Glacier Point Road are open early. Skip the Valley, go to the high country.

So you booked Yosemite for Memorial Day weekend 2026: the first reservation-free Memorial Day since 2023, the unofficial start of summer, and every Bay Area family with a long weekend and the same idea you had.

You can still have a good trip. The short answer is the one thing almost nobody arriving this weekend will do: skip Yosemite Valley and go up to the high country instead. Both Glacier Point Road and Tioga Road are open early this year, so the best places to be on Yosemite's Memorial Day weekend are 4,000 feet above the crowded Valley floor.

Here is the problem, and then the way out, which this year is better than usual.

### Yosemite Valley crowds on Memorial Day: a parking lot. Literally.

The National Park Service dropped the day-use reservation system for the 2026 season. No cap on cars, no gate to stop you. But the parking lots are the same size they were in 2019 and the Valley is still seven miles long. The constraint moved from the entrance gate to the parking lot.

We already got the preview. On Saturday, May 2, 2026, a normal early-May Saturday before the season had really started, the park's own alert reported every parking space in Yosemite Valley full by 10:59 a.m. Memorial Day weekend is far busier than that. Saturday morning is the worst of it. The Park Service knows this; its advice for the weekend has been to spend the busiest hours anywhere but the Valley floor: Tuolumne Meadows, Wawona, Hetch Hetchy.

The rangers and I agree on this one: go up.

### Why the Yosemite high country is the move this year

Most years, telling you to skip the Valley for the high country in late May would be a cruel joke, because the high country would still be under snow with the gates locked. Not this year.

It was a thin snow year (the park's April 1 snow survey at Tuolumne Meadows came in at 37 percent of average after a hot, dry March), the roads got plowed early, and both of the great high routes are already open ahead of their usual dates:

- Glacier Point Road opened May 9, 2026, a day earlier than it did in 2025.
- Tioga Road opened May 15, 2026, the earliest opening since 2015. (Tioga typically doesn't open until late May or even June.)

So while ten thousand people fight for a parking space 4,000 feet down in the Valley, you can be standing on a granite dome with Half Dome at eye level and almost nobody around you. On a holiday weekend, it is the better trip.

(One quick check before you commit: high-country roads can still close briefly in a late-season storm. Text "ynptraffic" to 333111 the morning you go, and don't trust whatever a stale web page tells you about road status.)

### Option 1: Glacier Point Road, the biggest view for the least effort

Turn off Highway 41 at Chinquapin and drive the road to its end. Glacier Point itself sits 3,200 feet directly above Curry Village. A paved, stroller-friendly path leads to an overlook with Half Dome at eye level, the whole Valley floor below you, and Vernal and Nevada Falls stair-stepping up the Merced canyon. It is the highest reward-per-step view in the entire park, and on an early-season weekend you may have the rail nearly to yourself.

If you want to stretch your legs, two of Yosemite's best short hikes share a trailhead a few miles before the end of the road:

- Sentinel Dome. About 2 miles round trip, roughly 400 feet of climbing, topping out at 8,122 feet on a bare granite summit with a true 360-degree panorama: Half Dome, El Capitan, the Cathedral Range, the Clark Range, the Sierra crest. Grandparents can do it. Six-year-olds can do it. Pick this one for the view and the photo.
- Taft Point. Also about 2.2 miles round trip, mostly easy, ending at a mostly unfenced clifftop and the Taft Point Fissures, deep granite cracks that drop away as much as 2,000 feet beneath your boots, with the viewpoint itself hanging over the Valley floor. It is also dangerous: every accident here comes from someone stepping too close for a photo. The view from six feet back is identical to the view from one foot back. Stand back.

We wrote a piece on choosing between them, and you can link the two into one quiet loop. The Four Mile Trail down to the Valley is a different day, 4.8 miles and 3,200 feet of descent with a plan of its own, not a detour to tack onto this one.

Two notes: there was no drinking water at Glacier Point when the road opened and the snack stand runs on the road's schedule, so bring a full water bottle and a sandwich. The Glacier Point tour bus, on the other hand, has run from Yosemite Valley Lodge since the road opened on May 9, twice a day, so you can ride up and walk down if you would rather not drive.

More: Glacier Point Road just opened for 2026

### Option 2: Tioga Road (open 2026), the high country two months ahead of the Valley

If Glacier Point is the easy headliner, Tioga Road is the adventure. Highway 120 climbs east through the park to Tioga Pass at 9,945 feet, the crossing that decides whether Las Vegas has a road into the park at all, and right now it's a ribbon of pavement through a high country still pulling itself out of winter. You'll see country that's a solid two months behind the green Valley you drove away from. A few stops to build a day around:

- Olmsted Point. The moment the high country opens up in front of you, and the only place you'll see the back of Half Dome, with Clouds Rest and Tenaya Canyon spread out below. Watch your footing; there can still be snow and ice near the point in late May.
- Tenaya Lake. An alpine lake right off the road. It will likely still be ice-rimmed this early. The east-end beach is a flat, easy stroll to the water, no real hike required.
- Tuolumne Meadows (8,600 feet). The vast subalpine heart of the high country at the foot of the Cathedral Range. Two short legs are reliable this early: Pothole Dome at the west end (a one-mile scramble up polished granite to a meadow panorama) and the flat walk to Soda Springs and Parsons Lodge (1.4 miles round trip, naturally carbonated springs the kids will love). Stay on the paths. The meadow is soaked and fragile this time of year.

Save the big alpine hikes for your next trip. Cathedral Lakes and the other classic Tuolumne destinations are usually still snowbound this early and don't come into condition until late June or July. Bookmark the Cathedral Lakes day hike for later.

The catch up here is self-sufficiency. The road is open, but Tuolumne Meadows itself is barely awake: the store, grill, and campground are weeks from opening (this year the grill's season began June 13 and the campground's July 1), there's no gas anywhere past Crane Flat, and no reliable drinking water along Tioga Road this early. Fill the tank, pack all your own food and water, and store it in a bear locker. Bring layers, including a packable insulated jacket. Sunny afternoons hit the low 60s, but nights drop to near freezing at this elevation, and an afternoon thunderstorm is possible.

More: what to expect on Tioga's opening weekend

### A few practical things

No day-use reservations are required to enter Yosemite in 2026. That's exactly why the Valley will be slammed, and exactly why a card-in-the-glovebox high-country plan beats the crowd. Your entrance pass is $35 per vehicle, good for seven days, and the park is cashless. Bring a card. One bonus: Memorial Day Monday, May 25, is a fee-free day, so if you can swing a Monday visit, it's both the cheapest and the lightest of the three days.

And if your plans go sideways anyway (lots full, weather turns, a road closes), don't fight the park. There is almost always an option the crowd hasn't thought of. (The Valley's marquee hike, the Mist Trail, goes under weekday closures for repair work later in the summer, Monday through Thursday from 7 a.m. to 3:30 p.m. from July 27 through October, but over Memorial Day weekend it is fully open and will be mobbed.)

### What I'd tell a friend

Skip the Valley on Saturday. Get up early, point the car uphill, and spend the morning on Glacier Point Road or Tioga Road while everyone else circles a full parking lot 4,000 feet below. You will not get the classic head-craning-up-at-the-falls Valley shot this trip. You'll get a high granite view with room to breathe, on the weekend when that is the right call.

Welcome to Yosemite. You made it harder than it had to be, but you can still get this right.

IS THERE FOOD IN YOSEMITE?

### Yes, and almost all of it is in the Valley

Yosemite Valley has the park's only real cluster of food: counters, decks and dining rooms in Yosemite Village, at Yosemite Valley Lodge and around Curry Village. Leave the Valley and the choices thin out fast. Wawona has a general store. Tuolumne Meadows, up on Tioga Road, has a seasonal store and grill and the dining tent at Tuolumne Meadows Lodge, and all of them close in September. Crane Flat and El Portal have small markets. Yosemite West has vacation rentals and nothing else: no restaurant, no store, no gas.

Staying outside the Valley?
Plan on a drive or a cooler.

Arriving after about 9 p.m.?
Assume everything is shut. This is a national park, not a town, and the kitchens keep park hours.

### One room, four meals, and a dress code at dinner

The room is 130 feet long with a 34-foot ceiling of timber trusses, granite piers between the windows and iron chandeliers, and it is open to anyone, not just hotel guests. A room at the hotel does not hold you a table, though, and dinner fills: book on OpenTable or at 209/372-1489, and do it when you book the trip.

GROCERIES AND SUPPLIES

### Where to buy the sandwich makings

The cooler lunch this page keeps recommending needs a store, and the park has more of them than restaurants. The Village Store in Yosemite Village is the one to plan around: the park's largest stock of groceries, including meat and produce, plus camping supplies, ice, firewood and an ATM. Everything else is smaller, and several close with their season. Prices are park prices, so the big shop happens in Mariposa, Oakhurst or Groveland on the way in. Hours change with the Yosemite Guide edition; the Park Bulletin carries them.

WAWONA, FISH CAMP AND THE SOUTH END

### A store in the park, dinner two miles past the gate

The Wawona General Store is a grocery and picnic-supply stop near the Mariposa Grove. The Wawona Hotel and its dining room are closed for a condition assessment. That is a closure, not a short break. Check the NPS hotel notice for news of a reopening.

Two miles south of the gate, Fish Camp covers what Wawona does not, and it is closer than most people staying at the south end realize. Embers at Tenaya Lodge is the sit-down dinner and the nearest real restaurant to the Mariposa Grove. Jackalopes, the bar in the same building, takes walk-ins when Embers is booked. The Pine Tree Market and the Fish Camp General Store cover groceries and a sandwich. Past that, you're driving to Oakhurst, fifteen more minutes down Highway 41.

TUOLUMNE MEADOWS AND THE HIGH COUNTRY

### Pack lunch. An open road is not an open kitchen

Tuolumne Meadows food service is seasonal, and its kitchens don't all close on the same day. The concessioner's 2026 schedule lists September 13 as the lodge dining room's last day and September 20 as the grill's. See the Tuolumne Meadows day guide for the rest of the trip.

YOSEMITE WEST RESTAURANTS

### There are none

Yosemite West is a private enclave just outside the park's southern boundary, reached through the park on Wawona Road, and it is almost all vacation rentals. The listings sell the location and skip the logistics, so guests are often caught short. A rental kitchen only helps if you bring the groceries. Shop before you arrive.

- No restaurant
- No store
- No gas station
- No shuttle

Nearest foodYosemite Valley
Roughly 40 minutes each way

OrWawona
About half an hour south

#### Four more places to bring lunch to

- Glacier Point
A gift shop and snack stand, and nothing more. It closes for the winter in late October, and the road it sits on closes with the snow. There is no designated picnic area at the point.

- Badger Pass
In ski season, the Skiers Grill and, Friday to Sunday and on holidays, the Snowflake Room. The season depends on snow and does not happen every year: the area did not open in the 2024 to 2025 winter.

- The Mariposa Grove
No food at the welcome plaza or in the grove. Drinking water is at the welcome plaza all year and at the arrival area in summer. The nearest food is the Wawona Store, or Fish Camp.

- Hetch Hetchy
No services of any kind. Evergreen Lodge, a mile outside the Hetch Hetchy entrance, is the nearest meal.

The first real coffee on the route, in either direction. The chamber's list adds Nicely's, Bodie Mike's BBQ, the Mono Cone and the Mono Market.

Highway 120 · the Big Oak Flat side

#### Groveland, and the two lodges near the gate

A historic main street with enough places to eat for a two-night stay, and two lodge kitchens close enough to the park to eat at after a day in it.

Yosemite Restaurant, Rush Creek Lodge
All three · $$$ · reservations on OpenTable

1.7 miles from the Big Oak Flat entrance, about five minutes. The restaurant and the tavern beside it serve the same menu, and the lodge's general store does lattes, breakfast and trail food.
Evergreen Lodge
All three · $$$ · reservations on OpenTable

Off Evergreen Road, seven miles from the Big Oak Flat entrance and one from the Hetch Hetchy entrance, which makes it the meal for a Hetch Hetchy day. The tavern serves the restaurant's menu under a covered patio.
Iron Door Saloon
Lunch, dinner · $$ · Main Street, Groveland

A building that went up before 1852 and became a saloon in 1896, with food, live music most weekends and karaoke on Thursdays. Groveland is a long half hour from the gate, so this is a dinner for people staying in town.

Groveland is missing from the county list below because it's in Tuolumne County, not because there's nothing there.

EVERYTHING THAT EXISTS, BY AREA

### The county's own list

The picks above are opinions. This is the August 2026 revision of the Mariposa eating-out list, a single sheet kept current in the county and handed out at visitor desks and lodge counters. It records what exists and roughly where. No hours, no prices, no judgment, and being on it is not a recommendation from anybody, including me. It does one thing a review list can't: it tells you a town of four hundred people has a cafe in it at all. Names are printed as the sheet prints them where a business's own spelling is unclear.

DIETARY NEEDS

### Vegan, gluten-free and allergies, kitchen by kitchen

The concessioner publishes no park-wide allergen guide, so the answer lives on each kitchen's own menu. Four of them say something useful.

- The Ahwahnee
A separate vegan menu and a children's menu, and the dining room takes requests.

- Pizza Deck
Vegan cheese and a gluten-free crust, the crust in medium only, each for a few dollars more.

- The Mountain Room
Allergen marks on the printed menu for the major allergens, and a vegan stew. Tell the server.

- Seven Tents
Dishes made without gluten are marked, with a warning that the kitchen is open and cross-contact is possible.

At the counters, Base Camp, Degnan's and the grills, ask before you order. For a serious allergy the Village Store is the fallback that lets you read every label.

PICNIC AREAS

### Where the granite slab has a table

The park's picnic areas are first come, first served, open dawn to dusk, and come with tables, vault toilets and trash and recycling, and most have grills. Two things catch people out. Only Lower Yosemite Fall and Church Bowl have drinking water and flush toilets, so carry water to the rest. And in Yosemite Valley a grill fire is legal only between 5 and 10 p.m., inside the grill, and only when the park's fire restrictions allow it (what the restrictions mean). Food stays within arm's reach the whole time; the rule is below.

#### Yosemite Valley

- Lower Yosemite FallDrinking water, flush toilets, no grills
- Church BowlDrinking water, flush toilets
- Cathedral BeachNot wheelchair accessible
- Sentinel Beach
- Swinging Bridge
- El Capitan

CAN YOU BRING YOUR OWN FOOD?

### Yes, and on most trips you should

Nothing limits bringing food into the park: no inspection at the gate, no rule against a cooler. The rule that does exist is about storage, and it is federal law, not advice. To a bear, food means anything with a scent. The bear guide covers what happens when people get this wrong, and the packing piece covers the cooler.

Watch the film: Black BearsYosemite Nature Notes · Episode 26Black BearsThe animal the storage rule is written for.Film: National Park Service. Nothing loads from YouTube until you press play.

- By day
Food stays within arm's reach.

- At night
Food goes into a bear locker.

- Never
In a car overnight, or in a truck bed.

- What counts as food
Anything with a scent, which includes trash, sunscreen and toothpaste.

The best lunch in Yosemite is a sandwich you made in a parking lot, eaten on a granite slab beside the Merced.

It costs four dollars and saves you an hour in line.

Cathedral Beach. Photo: Todd Petrie / Wikimedia Commons (CC BY 2.0)

QUESTIONS

### Eating in Yosemite, answered

#### Sources

- Dining in Yosemite, Yosemite Hospitality
- Tuolumne Meadows Lodge dining, Yosemite Hospitality
- Wawona Hotel, NPS
- The Ahwahnee Dining Room, Yosemite Hospitality
- Shopping, supplies and groceries, Yosemite Hospitality
- Yosemite Guide, September 23 to November 24, 2026, NPS
- Picnic areas, NPS Yosemite
- Mariposa Grove, NPS Yosemite
- Rush Creek Lodge dining and Evergreen Lodge dining
- Whoa Nellie Deli and Lee Vining Chamber of Commerce dining list
- The Park Bulletin, this edition's hours

Where can I get a quick meal in Yosemite Valley?
Curry Village Pizza Deck, Base Camp Eatery at Yosemite Valley Lodge, and Degnan's Kitchen in Yosemite Village are convenient options. Check current hours before relying on an early breakfast or late dinner.
Where can I book a sit-down dinner in Yosemite Valley?
The Mountain Room at Yosemite Valley Lodge and The Ahwahnee Dining Room are options. Both take reservations on OpenTable, and the Ahwahnee also by phone at 209/372-1489. A room at the hotel does not hold you a table, so book dinner separately.
Is there a dress code at the Ahwahnee Dining Room?
At dinner, yes. The hotel asks for long pants and a collared shirt, or a dress, skirt, or long pants with a blouse, and no hiking clothes, shorts, T-shirts, tank tops, flip-flops or baseball caps. Breakfast, lunch and Sunday brunch are casual.
Where can I buy groceries in Yosemite?
The Village Store in Yosemite Village has the park's largest selection, including meat, produce, ice and firewood. Curry Village has a grocery that stays open in winter, and there are smaller stores at Housekeeping Camp, Wawona, Crane Flat and, in summer, Tuolumne Meadows.
Are there restaurants in Yosemite West?
No. Yosemite West, a private enclave just outside the park's southern boundary, has no restaurant, store, gas station, or shuttle. Shop before arriving. Yosemite Valley is roughly forty minutes each way, or Wawona is about half an hour south.
Is there food at Tuolumne Meadows in fall?
Service is seasonal. The concessioner's 2026 schedule lists September 13 as the lodge dining room's last day and September 20 for the grill. Pack lunch for a Tioga Road day; an open road does not mean an open kitchen.
Is the Wawona Hotel dining room open?
The Wawona Hotel and its dining room are closed for a condition assessment. Check the NPS hotel notice for reopening updates. The Wawona General Store is a grocery and picnic-supply option.
Where should I eat near Yosemite?
Choose restaurants near your route or lodging. The guide recommends 1850, Smokin Oak BBQ, and Tacos Sonora in Mariposa; South Gate Brewing Company and The Elderberry House in Oakhurst; and Latte Da Cafe in Lee Vining. On Highway 120, Rush Creek Lodge and Evergreen Lodge have full restaurants a few miles from the Big Oak Flat entrance. Check current hours before making a special trip.
Do Yosemite picnic areas have water?
Mostly not. The Park Service says only Lower Yosemite Fall and Church Bowl have drinking water and flush toilets; the other picnic areas have tables, vault toilets and, at most, grills. Bring water, and keep food within arm's reach.
