## One day in Yosemite: an itinerary for one or two days

URL: https://thetalusfieldjournal.com/articles/yosemite-in-one-or-two-days
Section: Planning. Published: 2026-05-19. Last updated: 2026-09-21.
Summary: One day in Yosemite, done right: a 2026 itinerary for one or two days. The Valley waterfall sequence, what to skip, gas, parking, and a realistic hike.

One day in Yosemite is enough. Two days is enough plus the part where you actually slow down. The trip people most often regret is the four-day visit that shrinks to three because someone got the flu, then to two because Tioga Road was not open, then to one because the lot at Curry Village filled before they got there. The trip people most often remember is the one-day visit where they arrived at sunrise, did three things well, and drove home in the dark.

For years the constraint on a Yosemite day was a permit. You planned around whether you could get a reservation, and the planning often soured the trip before it started. In 2026 that constraint is gone. What replaces it is older and more honest: logistics, timing, and parking. A deliberate one-day Yosemite itinerary is not a compromise, and a two-day one is the same trip with room to breathe. It is the version of Yosemite that respects your time and rewards an early alarm. The rest of this guide is about what to do in Yosemite in a day: doing less, earlier, on purpose. If the scale of the place is what worries you, start with first-time Yosemite overwhelm and come back.

Photo: Madhu Shesharam / Unsplash

### The 2026 reservation and crowd context

There is no day-use reservation in Yosemite in 2026. There is no peak-hours reservation either. The timed-entry system that ran in various forms from 2020 through 2024, and the narrower peak-hours system that ran in 2025, are both gone. The Park Service announced the change on February 18, 2026, citing 2025 traffic data that suggested the systems no longer did enough to justify the hassle they caused. For the first time in years a Yosemite day trip needs no advance permit: decide on a Thursday night, drive in Friday morning, and go.

The catch is that demand did not disappear when the reservation did. It moved. It moved to the parking lots, which fill on their own schedule, and to the entrance-gate lines, which back up when everyone arrives at once. The reservation used to ration the road. Now nothing does, which means you ration yourself. The fix is the one rangers have given for decades, and the data still backs it: arrive before 8 a.m., and pick a weekday over a weekend if you have any choice at all. The September bulletin shows the pattern held all summer. Valley lots filled by late morning, and the park still tells visitors to arrive before 8 a.m. or after 4 p.m. The Valley parking guide has the three lots and what to do once they are gone. Text ynptraffic to 333111 for the park's live traffic alerts, and check the Park Bulletin for what is open and running the exact week you visit. For the rest of the no-reservation logistics, read Yosemite without reservations in 2026.

One more 2026 change, and this one is firm: international visitors now pay a $100 surcharge per person age 16 and older, on top of the standard entrance fee, in effect since January 1. A car of four foreign visitors pays the $35 vehicle fee plus $400, so for a group the $250 nonresident annual pass can pay for itself. It does not affect domestic visitors.

### Before you leave the gateway town

The single most useful thing you can do for a Yosemite day happens before you reach the gate. Fuel up outside the park. There is no gas in Yosemite Valley or Yosemite Village. In-park fuel exists only at Crane Flat on Highway 120 and at Wawona on Highway 41 (both pump 24 hours with a card), and both are priced like the captive options they are. The nearest reasonable fill is in the gateway towns: El Portal on Highway 140, Oakhurst on Highway 41 (generally the cheapest of the bunch), and Lee Vining on the east side (generally the most expensive). To choose a base, compare them in Yosemite gateway towns compared.

Buy your entrance in advance. The $35 seven-day vehicle pass on Recreation.gov moves you through the gate faster than paying on the spot, and if you visit parks more than once a year the $80 America the Beautiful annual pass pays for itself. Cell service inside the park is thin to nonexistent, so download offline maps the night before and grab a paper map at the gate; do not assume your phone will route you once you are past El Portal.

Then there are the bears, which are not a metaphor. Food, coolers, and anything scented stay out of sight with the windows closed, in daylight only, and never overnight in a parked car. A bear that learns your trunk is a bear that opens it, and the citations for an improperly stored car run up to $5,000. A bear-aware packing routine starts at home; see how to pack your car for Yosemite.

If parking is the part you dread, skip it. YARTS, the regional transit system, runs into the Valley on Highway 140 from Merced, Mariposa, and El Portal; on Highway 41 from Fresno; on Highway 120 from Sonora; and on Highway 395 from Mammoth and Lee Vining. Whether the fare covers your park entrance fee is unsettled: the Park Service and the YARTS fares page say opposite things, so budget for the gate. the shuttle and YARTS guide works through the fares and the cases where driving still wins.

### One day in Yosemite Valley: the four-stop sequence

One day in Yosemite turns entirely on when you arrive. Show up early enough that the day-use lots are still half empty: in the park by 8 a.m. on a weekday, by 7 a.m. on a Saturday. On busy weekends the lots fill from early to mid-morning, and once they are full your day becomes a hunt for a space instead of a visit. Get parked first. The free Valley shuttle works well once you are out of the car, running roughly 7 a.m. to 10 p.m. across about nineteen stops, but it is a tool for getting around after you have parked, not a substitute for having parked. It does not drive you in from the gate.

With that settled, here is the sequence. Four stops, in this order, because the order is the point.

- Tunnel View at first light. A roadside pullout on Wawona Road, and the most efficient view in the park: El Capitan on the left, Bridalveil Fall on the right, Half Dome at the back of the frame, all at once. Early light does the work for you and the lot is empty at dawn.
- Bridalveil Fall. About a half mile round trip on pavement, reopened in 2023 after a long rehabilitation. In May and June the spray reaches the trail; by August the fall thins to a ribbon and you are standing in a quiet granite amphitheater instead. Both are worth the walk.
- Lower Yosemite Fall loop. Roughly a mile, paved and flat. The 320-foot lower drop is the one you stand under; the 1,430-foot upper drop is the one you crane your neck at. With the middle cascades between them, the whole thing falls 2,425 feet, the tallest waterfall in North America, and the loop gives you the lower and upper without a climb. One seasonal note: the falls typically go thin by midsummer and dry by late summer, so from July on you are walking the loop for the amphitheater and the scale, not the water.
- Cook's Meadow loop. About a mile of boardwalk that hands you Half Dome, Yosemite Falls, Sentinel Rock, and Royal Arches without your having to try. This is Ansel Adams's meadow, and it photographs almost as well for you as it did for him.

Done at a reasonable pace, that sequence leaves you finished by mid-afternoon. Use what is left. Find a flat rock on the Merced River, sit down, and do nothing in particular for an hour. That hour is the part one-day visitors skip on their way to a fifth stop, and it is the part return visitors come back for.

Photo: Rodrigo Soares / Unsplash

### What to skip on a one-day visit

The hardest part of a one-day Valley itinerary is not what you do. It is what you refuse to do. Yosemite hands you a list of famous places, and most of them are an hour or more from the Valley floor in directions that point away from each other. Saying yes to two of them is how a one-day trip turns into a day spent in the car looking at the back of the car ahead of you. The cuts below are not the park being smaller than advertised. They are the park being honest about a clock.

Glacier Point Road. The overlook is one of the great views in North America, and on a one-day trip it is the wrong move. The round trip from the Valley runs roughly two to three hours of driving once you account for stops, which is a third of your usable daylight spent on a road. Save it. It is the centerpiece of a second day, not an add-on to the first.

Mariposa Grove. An hour-plus each way from the Valley, plus the shuttle from the Welcome Plaza, plus the time you will actually want to spend among trees that predate the Roman Empire. It is a wonderful half-day destination and a terrible thing to bolt onto a Valley day.

Tioga Road and Tuolumne Meadows. Half a day each way. The high country is a separate trip, not a side quest, and trying to fold it into a Valley day means you will see neither one properly. Our Tioga Road guide lays out how.

The full Mist Trail to the top of Vernal Fall, if you only have an afternoon. This is a real workout, not a casual stroll, and we cover the gentler version of it in the next section rather than cutting it outright.

That is the point that matters. On a one-day trip, skipping is the strategy, not a compromise on it. Anything that moves the car at midday is the enemy. Pick the Valley, stay in the Valley, and let the rest wait for a trip that has room for it.

### A realistic hike, if you want one

You do not have to hike to have done Yosemite right, and our non-hiker's guide makes that case without apology. But if you want a trail on a one-day trip, the question is not which hike is best. It is which hike fits the hours you have left and the legs you brought. Here are the honest tiers, easiest to hardest.

- Vernal Fall footbridge. About 1.6 miles round trip, roughly 400 feet of gain. This is the gentle option, and it is not a consolation prize. The footbridge delivers most of the visual payoff of the climb above it: Vernal Fall framed dead ahead, the Merced roaring underneath you.
- Top of Vernal Fall via the Mist Trail. About 3 miles round trip, roughly 1,000 feet of gain, and around 600 granite steps in the spray. This is a legitimate workout. Expect full sun on the climb out, a bottleneck of people on the stairs, and a soaking on the way up in high water. Read the dedicated Mist Trail guide before you go; it is the difference between a good morning and a miserable one.
- Top of Nevada Fall, for the ambitious. About 7 miles round trip, roughly 1,900 feet of gain. This is most of a day on its own, which makes it a stretch for a one-day Valley trip.
- Mirror Lake. About 2 miles round trip, paved and easy, with the option of the longer Tenaya Creek loop at roughly 4.5 to 5 miles. Best in spring, when there is actually water to reflect. By late summer the lake is a meadow.

A 2026 caveat that outranks the seasonal one: trail work closes sections of the Mist Trail on weekdays, Monday through Thursday from 7 a.m. to 3:30 p.m., into late October, with the John Muir Trail as the detour. If your one day is a Monday through Thursday, do the footbridge early, plan the climb for after 3:30 p.m., or save the corridor for a Friday-through-Sunday visit; the Mist Trail guide tracks the specifics.

A seasonal caveat that catches people every year: the steep Mist Trail steps close in winter and icy conditions, and hikers reroute via the longer, gentler John Muir Trail. Spray and slick rock peak in spring snowmelt, which is exactly when the trail is most beautiful and most treacherous. All of these leave from Happy Isles or the nearby shuttle stops. Start early, carry water, wear real shoes, and set a turnaround time before you leave the car. Then pick one and do it well. One trail done properly beats two trails done in a hurry.

### One day in Yosemite with kids

The four-stop sequence above is the kids' itinerary too, with two edits. Every stop on it is paved or boardwalk and under a mile: Bridalveil is a half mile, the Lower Yosemite Fall loop is a flat mile with a stroller-friendly paved path, and Cook's Meadow is a boardwalk that lets a five-year-old walk toward Half Dome without a hill. The first edit is the hike: swap the Mist Trail for the Vernal Fall footbridge (1.6 miles round trip, a real destination, and no granite staircase in the spray) or for Mirror Lake in spring. The second is the shape of the afternoon: park once, ride the free Valley shuttle instead of moving the car, and plan the midday around the river rather than a viewpoint, because a sandbar on the Merced in July is the best thing in the park for anyone under ten. Bring the bear rules into the car with you; children are the ones who leave the granola bar on the seat. Yosemite with kids covers bathrooms, shuttle stops, and the walks by age.

### One day in Yosemite from San Francisco

It can be done, and the arithmetic decides whether it is worth doing. The Bay Area to the Arch Rock or Big Oak Flat entrance is about four hours in clear traffic, plus 30 to 45 minutes of park road to the Valley floor. A 4 a.m. departure lands you at Tunnel View by nine and gives you until mid-afternoon before you have to turn around; a 7 a.m. departure lands you in the lots at the exact hour they fill and hands you a day of circling. The better version of the same trip is to drive up the evening before, sleep in Mariposa or Groveland, and start the four-stop sequence at dawn, which turns a fourteen-hour day into a real one. The Bay Area day trip does the daylight math by month and names the point at which the drive stops being worth it, and the entrances guide has the routes.

### Two days in Yosemite: if you have a second day

A second day changes the math more than twice the time would suggest. It lets you leave the Valley floor. Day One stays the Valley four-stop sequence above. Day Two earns altitude and leaves the floor entirely. There are three good ways to spend it.

#### Glacier Point

Glacier Point Road reopened May 9, 2026, after a multi-season rehabilitation, and it is the single best second day for most visitors. It is open as this is written in late September, and it closes for the winter with the first heavy snow, typically in November. For a late-season second day, check the Park Bulletin before you count on it. The overlook gives you Half Dome at eye level and the Valley 3,000 feet below in one frame, with no hike required to earn it. One note that matters: there is no drinking water at the overlook this season, so bring your own. On the way up, two short detours pay off well: Sentinel Dome (about 2.2 miles round trip) for a 360-degree summit, and Taft Point for a look straight down into the Valley. The full picture is in our Glacier Point Road guide.

Photo: Joshua Earle / Unsplash

#### Mariposa Grove

An hour south of the Valley, and the right second day if you came to California for the big trees. Private cars stop at the Welcome Plaza (about 300 spaces, which fills by late morning), and a free shuttle runs up to the grove from there. The lower-grove Grizzly Giant loop is about 2 miles and mostly flat. The Grizzly Giant itself is an estimated 2,000-plus years old, and standing under it does something a photograph cannot.

#### Tioga Road high country

Tioga Road opened May 15, 2026, the earliest opening since 2015, which makes this an unusually good season to point the second day east. Tuolumne Meadows, Tenaya Lake, and Olmsted Point are the marquee stops, and the whole thing is comfortably a half-day if you keep moving. Basing east at Lee Vining works well if your trip runs over Tioga Pass anyway.

Two days in September or October is the best version of this trip: every road is still open, the crowds are down from July, and the light is low and gold. The trade is water, since the falls are near dry by September, and a few 2026 specifics: the Mist Trail is closed for repairs Monday through Thursday through October, the Tuolumne Meadows store, grill, and High Sierra Camps close in the first two weeks of September, and the Glacier Point overlook has no drinking water this season. Yosemite in fall and Yosemite in September 2026 have the month-by-month detail.

Two things to keep in mind. Both Glacier Point Road and Tioga Road close in winter, so this entire menu is a late-spring-through-fall proposition. And if you are a strong hiker, there is a fourth option that beats all three for sheer payoff: the Four Mile up, Panorama down loop, which climbs from the Valley to Glacier Point and descends past Nevada and Vernal Falls. It is a full, hard day, and it is the one we would do. Our Four Mile and Panorama guide walks through it.

### Where to sleep

For a one-day trip, base in El Portal if you can get a room. It is 14 miles to the Valley and about 25 minutes to Tunnel View, which is the closest you can sleep without paying in-park prices. Mariposa adds roughly 20 minutes to that drive and gives you a real town in return: gas, groceries, dinner that is not a park concession. For most one-day visitors, Mariposa is the better balance of cost and convenience.

For a two-day trip, the right base depends on what Day Two is. If you are headed to Mariposa Grove, Oakhurst is closer to the south end of the park. If Day Two is Tuolumne, Lee Vining on the east side puts you at the top of Tioga Road instead of the bottom. Match the bed to the second day, not the first.

In-park lodging is the convenience play if you can land it. Yosemite Valley Lodge sits across from the falls, Curry Village (also called Half Dome Village) runs tent cabins at the lower end, and The Ahwahnee is the premium, historic option. All three book months out and cost more than the gateway towns. One scheduling note: the Wawona Hotel has been closed since December 2024 for a condition assessment, with no announced reopening, so do not plan around it.

### When to go to Yosemite: month by month

Yosemite is open all year, but it is four different parks across the seasons. The waterfalls, the crowds, the open roads, and the light all swing hard depending on when you arrive. Pick the month that matches what you actually came to see.

Spring (April through June). This is the reason most people should come. Snowmelt drives the waterfalls to their peak, and Yosemite Falls, Bridalveil, and Vernal all run loud and full. The Valley is cool and green, the meadows wake up, and the whole place feels alive in a way it does not for the rest of the year. The catch is the high country: Tioga Road and Glacier Point Road often stay closed into May while crews clear snow, so an early-spring trip is a Valley trip by default.

Summer (July and August). Hottest and most crowded, in that order. Valley parking lots fill in the early morning, and there are real delays at the entrance gates on weekends. The waterfalls are already dropping by late summer, so the spring spectacle is mostly gone. The relief valve is elevation: with Tioga Road open, the high country around Tuolumne Meadows runs cooler, emptier, and more open than the Valley floor.

Fall (September and October). Arguably the connoisseur's season. The crowds thin, the oaks and dogwoods turn in the Valley, and the light goes crisp and low. The trade is water: the waterfalls are reduced to a trickle or dry by now, so come for the color and the quiet rather than the cascades.

Winter (November through March). Tioga Road and Glacier Point Road close for the season, leaving the Valley, Wawona, and Hetch Hetchy as your range. What you get in return is quiet and snow on the granite. Mid-to-late February brings the Firefall, when the setting sun lights Horsetail Fall on El Capitan so it glows like molten orange. It is weather and water dependent, it does not happen every year, and no reservation is required in 2026. Treat any specific date you read as a forecast, not a guarantee.

### Where to eat

The honest answer is to bring your own food. A cooler in your trunk beats the Village Store on price, on time, and on everything else that matters, and it lets you eat at the overlook instead of waiting in a line behind it. Just remember the rule that governs everything edible in this park: food stays out of sight, windows closed, and nothing left in the car overnight.

If you do want a sit-down meal in the park, the options are short and known. Base Camp Eatery, the food court at Yosemite Valley Lodge, is the fast, reliable default for a hot plate, and it is usually the last kitchen in the Valley still taking orders in the evening. Degnan's in Yosemite Village handles a quick lunch without much ceremony. The Ahwahnee dining room is the splurge, a grand room with a dress code and prices to match, and worth doing once if the budget allows. For the full list of what is open and what it costs, read where to eat in Yosemite.

### What to bring

A day in Yosemite is altitude, weather, and granite glare, and most visitors do not pack for any of the three. The Valley floor sits around 4,000 feet and runs warm; Glacier Point sits at about 7,200 feet and can be ten degrees cooler and twenty miles an hour windier on the same afternoon. Dress for the day you will actually have, not the one in the parking lot.

- Water. There is no water at Glacier Point. Bring your own, and more than you think.
- Layers. A warm top for the overlooks even in summer; the temperature drops with elevation.
- Sun protection. Sunscreen and a hat. Granite reflects glare straight back at you.
- Sturdy shoes. The Mist Trail is granite steps, often wet. Sandals will betray you.
- A map. Paper or offline. Cell coverage in the Valley is unreliable and gone entirely on the high roads.
- A full tank of gas. Fill up before you enter.

For the full packing list, use the kit page, then read the essay on how to pack your car for Yosemite.

### Common questions

Is one day in Yosemite enough? Yes, for the Valley, if you are in the park by 8 a.m. and stay on the floor. Tunnel View, Bridalveil Fall, the Lower Yosemite Fall loop, and Cook's Meadow fit in one day with time to spare for a hike or an hour by the river. It is not enough for Glacier Point, the Mariposa Grove, or Tuolumne, which each need a second day.

Can you do Yosemite in 2 days? Yes, and two days is the trip we would hand most first-time visitors: the Valley on day one, and Glacier Point, the Mariposa Grove, or Tioga Road on day two. Two days does not cover all three of those; pick the one that matches what you came for.

How many days do you need in Yosemite? One full day, started early, covers the Valley highlights. A second day adds Glacier Point, Mariposa Grove, or Tioga Road above the Valley floor. Beyond two days you are into backpacking country and repeat-visit territory.

Do I need a reservation to enter Yosemite in 2026? No. Yosemite has no day-use or peak-hours reservation in 2026. You still need a valid entrance pass ($35 per vehicle for seven days).

When do the waterfalls run? Spring snowmelt is the engine, and the peak is roughly April through June. By late summer the falls are low to dry, and a few stop entirely.

Is Glacier Point Road open? Yes, as of late September 2026. It opened for the season on May 9 and closes for the winter with the first heavy snow, typically in November. There is no water at the overlook, so fill your bottles before you drive up.

Is Tioga Road open? Yes. It opened on May 15, 2026, the gateway to the high country and Tuolumne Meadows. It closes again with the first heavy snow in fall.

Where do I get gas? Not in Yosemite Valley; there are no pumps there. In-park gas is at Crane Flat and Wawona, and outside the park you can fill at El Portal, Oakhurst, or Lee Vining.

Is the Mist Trail open? Mostly. Trail work closes sections of it Monday through Thursday, 7 a.m. to 3:30 p.m., into late October 2026, with a detour via the John Muir Trail. Friday through Sunday it runs normally, and the Vernal Fall footbridge stays the reliable short option.

Can I leave food in my car? Out of sight, windows closed, in daylight only, and never overnight. The fines for improper food storage run up to $5,000. When in doubt, use the bear lockers at the trailheads.

How many days in Yosemite without hiking? One day covers the Valley from the car and the paved paths, and a second day adds Glacier Point, which has one of the great views in North America a few steps from the parking lot. The non-hiker's guide has the full list.

Is the Wawona Hotel open? No. It has been closed since December 2024 for a condition assessment, and there is no announced reopening date.

### The honest pitch

The thesis has not changed across all these words. One day in Yosemite, started early and spent deliberately, beats three days of arriving at noon and circling the lots for parking. If you can manage two days, make the second one above the Valley floor, on Glacier Point Road or up Tioga to the high country, and you will have seen the park most first-time visitors miss. That is the plan we would hand almost anyone coming for the first time.

Show up early. Do less than the lists tell you to. Sit by the Merced for an hour and watch the light move on the granite. You will remember that longer than you will remember the bucket list, and it costs you nothing but the willingness to stop.

#### Showing up early starts the night before

Every plan on this page depends on being at the trailhead before the day visitors, which means the drive in cannot be ninety minutes. El Portal is 25 to 30 minutes from the Valley and the closest bed outside the boundary. The full comparison of every option is one page over.

## Four Mile and Panorama Trails: Yosemite hike guide

URL: https://thetalusfieldjournal.com/articles/four-mile-up-panorama-down
Section: Trails and Hikes. Published: 2026-05-17. Last updated: 2026-09-27.
Summary: Hike Yosemite's Four Mile and Panorama Trails via Glacier Point: distance, total climbing, water sources, trail closures, and the shuttle return.

Hike up the Four Mile Trail to Glacier Point, then descend the Panorama Trail to Happy Isles for a strenuous day linking Valley views and waterfalls. Plan on roughly 13 to 14 miles between trailheads, about 4,000 feet of total climbing, and a full day on foot. The trailheads are different: arrange a shuttle ride or add the walk back to your car.

This is my favorite long Yosemite day hike for the variety: Glacier Point, Illilouette Creek, Nevada Fall, and the descent toward Vernal Fall. For a shorter waterfall hike, use the Mist Trail guide. For the viewpoint without the climb, see how to visit Glacier Point.

Check NPS trail conditions before starting. Road access, trail closures, drinking water, and shuttle service each need a separate check.

### The numbers

The hike runs roughly 13 to 14 miles between trailheads, depending on whether you take the Mist Trail or the John Muir Trail for the last stretch. The Four Mile Trail gains about 3,200 feet. The Panorama Trail isn't all downhill, though: there's an 800-foot climb out of the Illilouette Creek drainage that catches people off guard. Count on closer to 4,000 feet of total climbing for the day.

Allow a full day and start early. The NPS lists 3 to 4 hours for the Four Mile ascent and 6 to 8 for the Panorama descent. Strong hikers may finish faster, but plan for breaks, the longer JMT return if needed, and transport back to your car.

### Why up the Four Mile and down the Panorama

I recommend climbing Four Mile first, while your legs are fresh and the morning is cool.

There are three reasons.

First, the Four Mile Trail is a steady uphill grind: 3,200 feet of gain in 4.8 miles, over roughly 58 switchbacks. It's the hardest part of the day, so do it while your legs are fresh and the morning is cool.

Second, Glacier Point hits harder when you've climbed to it. You spend three hours in forest and granite while the views open up bit by bit: the Valley floor far below, then Half Dome rising over the rim at Union Point, then the whole panorama at the top. Drive up and you start with the best view of the day.

Third, the Panorama route gives you waterfall views on the way down. Save energy for its uphill section out of Illilouette Creek and for the final descent to Happy Isles.

### Getting to the Four Mile Trailhead

The Four Mile Trailhead is on Southside Drive near Sentinel Rock, with limited roadside parking. If it is full, park in a designated Valley lot and take the Valleywide shuttle to stop 11. The Valley parking guide covers the main lots.

Start around dawn and carry a headlamp. An early start gives you cooler climbing conditions and more daylight for the descent. If you start late, choose a shorter route rather than assuming you can make up time.

### The Four Mile Trail, what to expect

Stonemason John Conway built the original trail in 1872 for entrepreneur James McCauley, who charged a one-dollar toll. It was exactly four miles long. In the late 1920s the Park Service rebuilt it with gentler switchbacks, and the new route came out to 4.8 miles. The name stuck anyway.

The first mile is the steepest and the most exposed. You gain height fast on rocky switchbacks with little shade, and in summer this stretch bakes in the morning sun. Wear a hat and sunscreen. (If you haven't read my day pack packing list, read it before this hike. On a day like this, what's in your pack decides whether you have a great time or a miserable one.)

By mile two you're well above the Valley floor and the views start to open. El Capitan shows up across the Valley, and so does Yosemite Falls. The exposure increases as you climb toward the rim.

Union Point comes at about mile three. It's a named viewpoint with a small flat spot to sit and rest, and the view is exceptional: Yosemite Falls straight across the Valley, El Capitan to the west, Half Dome coming into view to the east. Plenty of people turn around here thinking they've "done the Four Mile Trail." They haven't, but the view explains why they stop.

The last mile and a half from Union Point to Glacier Point is gentler, winding through forest with the odd opening. The switchbacks ease off. Then you step out at the Glacier Point railing, with Half Dome, Nevada Fall, Vernal Fall and the whole High Sierra laid out in front of you.

Water on the Four Mile Trail: there is none. The trail is bone dry from bottom to top. No creeks, no springs, no seasonal sources. Everything you drink between the trailhead and Glacier Point comes out of your pack. Carry at least three liters per person. I carry three, and on hot days I usually wish I'd brought four.

### At Glacier Point

Glacier Point sits at 7,214 feet and has what may be the most complete view in the park: Half Dome at eye level, the Clark Range to the southeast, Nevada Fall and Vernal Fall below you, and the Valley floor 3,200 feet straight down.

There are restrooms. There's a snack bar and gift shop too, but whether they're open depends on the season and can vary early in the year. Important: do not count on water being available at Glacier Point early in the season. The NPS has noted that drinking water may not be available when the road first opens. Later in the season a water fountain near the amphitheater area is usually running. The safe move is still to carry enough to get you from the Four Mile Trailhead all the way to Illilouette Creek on the Panorama Trail, roughly 7 miles of dry trail.

If there is water, fill everything you've got. You'll need it on the way down.

Road access and trail access are different. A closed Glacier Point Road does not by itself close the Four Mile or Panorama trails. Snow, ice, fire, or repair work may close trails separately. Check the NPS trail and road reports; do not assume facilities are operating just because a trail is open.

Spend at least thirty minutes at Glacier Point. Eat something real. Refill if the fountain is running. Use the restroom. The Panorama Trail includes another 800-foot climb before the descent to the Valley.

### The Panorama Trail, the best descent in the park

From Glacier Point the Panorama Trail heads east along the rim, then drops toward Illilouette Creek. It earns its name: for the first two miles, Half Dome, Clouds Rest and the Clark Range fill the horizon the whole way. Half Dome, which looks like a wall from the Valley, turns out to be a narrow fin of granite with a sheer face and a domed back.

#### Illilouette Fall and Creek, Mile 2.5

About two and a half miles from Glacier Point you drop into the Illilouette Creek drainage and reach a bridge above Illilouette Fall. The fall drops 370 feet, and it's at its best in spring and early summer, when the creek is running full.

Illilouette Creek is a possible refill point. Check its flow before your hike; it is the first natural water since the Four Mile Trailhead, roughly 7 miles back. If you have a filter or purification tablets (and on this hike you should), fill up here. The creek runs reliably through July most years. By late August it can be low.

After the bridge, the trail climbs out of the drainage. This is the hike's surprise: 800 feet of gain over about a mile and a half, on legs that are already tired. It isn't as steep as the Four Mile Trail, but it comes late in the day. Save some energy for it.

#### The descent to Nevada Fall, Miles 4 to 6

Past the Illilouette climb, the trail crosses open granite with views down into the Merced River canyon. Nevada Fall comes into view ahead, 594 feet of thundering whitewater at peak flow. The trail then drops to a junction with the John Muir Trail near the top of the fall.

Here you have a choice to make.

#### Mist Trail vs. John Muir Trail, the final descent

From the JMT junction above Nevada Fall, there are two ways back to the Valley floor.

The Mist Trail is shorter (about 2.5 miles to Happy Isles), steeper and more dramatic. It runs down beside Nevada Fall and then Vernal Fall, and in places the spray soaks you through. The granite steps along Vernal Fall are the most photographed stretch of trail in Yosemite. It is also steep, the uneven stone steps are brutal on tired knees, and wet rock can be slippery. If your legs feel solid and you want the waterfalls up close, take the Mist Trail.

2026 Mist Trail repairs: From July 27 through October, subject to change, the staircase between the JMT junction above Vernal Fall footbridge and the top of Vernal Fall closes Monday through Thursday, 7 a.m. to 3:30 p.m. Use the signed JMT detour during work hours. Check the Mist Trail access details before choosing your descent.

The John Muir Trail is longer (about 4 miles to Happy Isles), gentler and easier on the knees. It switchbacks down through forest with the occasional distant look at Nevada Fall. It's less dramatic, but a lot more comfortable at the end of a long day. After 13 miles and 4,000 feet of total climbing, your knees may decide for you.

Either way you end at Happy Isles, the Nature Center at the east end of Yosemite Valley. There's water and there are restrooms. The Valley shuttle stops at Happy Isles (shuttle stop 16), and you can ride it back to wherever you parked.

### The logistics checklist

Start time: 5:30 to 6:30 a.m. at the Four Mile Trailhead. Earlier is better.

Total distance: Roughly 13 to 14 miles between trailheads; the JMT option is longer, and walking back to your car adds distance.

Total elevation gain: About 4,000 feet: 3,200 on Four Mile plus about 800 after Illilouette Creek. There is also a long descent.

Time: Plan a full day. NPS segment estimates total 9 to 12 hours, before a shuttle wait or a walk back to the start.

Water plan: This is the logistic that matters most on this hike. Carry at least three liters from the trailhead. The Four Mile Trail is completely dry. Glacier Point may have water (check conditions). Check creek flow before relying on Illilouette Creek for a refill, and bring a filter or treatment. There's water again at Happy Isles at the bottom.

Water sources in order:

- Four Mile Trailhead. Fill up before you start.
- Glacier Point. Maybe. Check seasonal availability.
- Illilouette Creek (mile ~7 from start). Filter required.
- Merced River near Nevada Fall. Filter required.
- Happy Isles. Water fountain and restrooms at the finish.

Food: Pack a real lunch and plenty of snacks, 1,500 to 2,000 calories for the day. Eat at Glacier Point, then eat again on the Panorama Trail. Low blood sugar on the Illilouette climb is how bad decisions get made.

Gear: Read the day pack packing list. For this hike in particular, don't leave without: 3+ liters of water, a water filter or purification tablets, a hat, sunscreen, a headlamp (in case you're slower than you planned), layers (Glacier Point at 7,200 feet can be 20 degrees cooler than the Valley floor), and trekking poles if you use them (your knees will thank you on the way down).

Getting back to your car: From Happy Isles, take the Valleywide shuttle at stop 16 to Four Mile Trail at stop 11. The East Valley shuttle does not serve Four Mile. Confirm operating hours with the NPS shuttle information and allow for waits. If you finish after service ends, you will need another way back or additional walking.

When to do this hike: Late May through October, depending on snow, trail closures, and weather. Peak waterfall season (late May through June) is the best time, when Illilouette Fall and Nevada Fall are at full power. By August the falls have shrunk, but the trails are dry and conditions are more predictable. Skip this hike when thunderstorms are active. The Four Mile Trail is heavily exposed, and you'll be at 7,200 feet at Glacier Point.

A shorter alternative: When the seasonal Glacier Point Tour operates, book a ride up and hike the Panorama Trail down. This skips the Four Mile ascent but still includes the Illilouette climb. Confirm the tour before booking your day; there is no free Valley-to-Glacier Point shuttle and no guaranteed pickup at Glacier Point.

### Why this is my favorite

I've hiked most of the trails in this park, and I've led programs on dozens of them. This route is the one I keep coming back to.

The Four Mile Trail climbs the glacier-carved wall of the Valley, and by the time you reach the rim you have a sense of the park's scale that no roadside pullout gives.

Glacier Point has the view: the whole park spread out below you, Half Dome at eye level, the Sierra running to the horizon.

The Panorama Trail adds waterfalls, creek crossings, granite traverses and forest in a single afternoon.

No other hike in the park does all three.

Start early. Carry enough water. Bring a filter. And slow down at Union Point, at Glacier Point, at the Illilouette bridge and at the top of Nevada Fall.

Plan the return to your car as carefully as the hike.

Route references: NPS Four Mile Trail and NPS Panorama Trail distances and conditions.

## Yosemite with kids: a naturalist's honest last-minute guide

URL: https://thetalusfieldjournal.com/articles/yosemite-with-kids-no-reservations-2026
Section: Planning. Published: 2026-05-14. Last updated: 2026-08-06.
Summary: A senior naturalist's guide to Yosemite with kids in 2026, no reservations needed. Kid-friendly hikes, timing, YARTS, and what families get wrong.

If you're reading this in the car: Arrive before 9 AM. Park at Yosemite Village. Get the Junior Ranger booklet at the visitor center. Hike Lower Yosemite Fall. Don't swim before mid-July. Bear boxes are not optional. You're going to have a great day.

You're going to Yosemite with your kids. Maybe you decided last week. Maybe you decided this morning. You Googled "Yosemite with kids" and got seventeen articles that assume you booked a campsite in February and planned your itinerary on a spreadsheet. You didn't. Your trunk has a cooler with last night's leftovers, somebody's soccer cleats, and a bag of goldfish crackers that may or may not be open.

Yosemite dropped the timed-entry reservation system for 2026. No reservation needed to drive into the park. That's new, and it means the spontaneous family trip is back on the table for the first time in years.

I've worked as a naturalist in Yosemite for close to two decades. I've watched thousands of families come through, the ones who have the trip of their lives and the ones who spend six hours in a parking lot and leave frustrated. The difference is rarely fitness or money. It is mostly what time they showed up, what they did first, and whether they let their kids set the pace.

This is the guide for the family that didn't plan six months ahead. Everything here works for a one-day trip, and I'll tell you what to do if you're lucky enough to have a second.

### The night before

If you're staying outside the park, and if you're reading this article, you probably are, because campgrounds and lodges inside Yosemite book up months in advance, here's what to do tonight.

Book a room in Mariposa. It's the best gateway town for families. About 45 minutes from the Valley, with more lodging options than any other gateway, a real grocery store, gas stations, and restaurants that aren't terrible. Our gateway towns guide has the full comparison, but if you're booking tonight: Mariposa. Call around. Last-minute rooms exist, especially midweek.

If you're camping, the campgrounds inside the park are almost certainly full. But there are first-come-first-served options in the Sierra National Forest just outside the park boundary, and the Mariposa Fairgrounds campground runs about $35 a night with no reservation needed. It's not glamorous, but it's a place to sleep, and your kids won't care.

Pack the car tonight, not tomorrow morning. The car packing guide has the full list, but grab these five things you'll forget: sunscreen (the UV at elevation is brutal), a refillable water bottle for every person (including the toddler), a headlamp (if you stay for sunset, which you should, you'll walk back in the dark), layers (the Valley can be 95 degrees at noon and 55 degrees at sunset), and a credit or debit card for the entrance fee if you don't have an America the Beautiful pass (the gate is cashless).

Download offline maps. Cell service in Yosemite is unreliable at best and nonexistent in most of the Valley. Download Google Maps offline or grab the NPS app before you lose signal. You will need navigation.

### Get there before the Valley wakes up

Arrive before 9 AM.

Yosemite doesn't have a reservation system anymore, but parking in the Valley hasn't changed. The main lots fill up between 9 and 11 AM on weekends, between 10 and noon on weekdays. Once they're full, you're circling.

From Mariposa, it's about 45 minutes to the Valley via Highway 140 through El Portal. Leave by 7:15 and you'll be parked by 8. From Oakhurst, add 15 minutes. From Groveland, it's more like 75 minutes. Leave by 6:45.

Where to park. Head straight for the day-use parking at Yosemite Village. It's centrally located, close to the visitor center (which you need), and the shuttle stops here. If the Village lot is full, the lot near Yosemite Valley Lodge usually has turnover by mid-morning as early risers leave. Don't waste time circling Curry Village. It's far from everything you want to do first.

The YARTS bus move. YARTS (the regional bus system) runs from Mariposa, El Portal, and other gateway towns directly into Yosemite Valley. Children under five ride free, and one child aged six to twelve rides free with each full-fare adult, so check the count against your group before assuming the whole back seat travels free. You skip the parking and get dropped off in the Village. Check the YARTS schedule the night before. Buses run several times a day in summer. Few families use it.

### Your first two hours

You're parked (or you stepped off the bus). The kids are awake. Use the first hours while their energy is high.

First stop: Yosemite Valley Visitor Center. Walk in, go to the desk, and ask for a Junior Ranger booklet. This is free, and it is the most useful thing the park hands out to parents.

The booklet has activities keyed to different spots in the park, things to find, questions to answer, sketches to make. It gives your entire day a structure without you having to create one. Your kids have missions now. At every stop, they're looking for something specific. When they finish enough activities, they bring the booklet back to a ranger, take the Junior Ranger oath, and get a badge. They will care about that badge more than any souvenir in the gift shop.

While you're at the visitor center, check the ranger program schedule posted at the door. Free ranger-led programs, nature walks, campfire talks, evening programs, run all summer. Some are specifically designed for kids. They are a good answer to the 4 PM slump.

Bathrooms and food. The Village Store has bathrooms, snacks, sandwiches, and overpriced everything. Use the bathrooms now. Buy nothing yet. Your cooler is better than anything in the store. Save the Village Store for the emergency afternoon Popsicle run (you'll need it).

### The hikes that actually work with kids

Here is which trails work for which kids, because most Yosemite family guides recommend the Mist Trail as a "must-do family hike," and I think that's irresponsible. The Mist Trail is a legitimate workout with 600 granite steps, cliff exposure, and crowds that can make it dangerous. It's an outstanding hike for fit teens and adults. It's a miserable experience for a six-year-old. If your kids are 12 and up and in good shape, read the Mist Trail guide separately.

Lower Yosemite Fall Loop, the obvious first hike. One mile, fully paved, mostly flat. Stroller-friendly the entire way. The trail loops from the shuttle stop to the base of Lower Yosemite Fall, which is a 320-foot waterfall that's roaring in spring and trickling by August. In peak flow (May and June), the mist at the base soaks everyone. In late summer, the dry fall bed is a massive granite amphitheater your kids can explore. Allow 45 minutes to an hour. (All ages. Strollers: yes. Best in May to June for water, July to August for rock scrambling in the dry bed.)

Cook's Meadow Loop, the one with the views. Two miles, paved, flat as a parking lot. This is the walk through the heart of the Valley with postcard views of Half Dome, Yosemite Falls, and Sentinel Rock. It connects to Sentinel Bridge, where the famous Half Dome reflection photo is taken. The meadow is gorgeous, the trail is wide, and there's almost no crowd because everyone else went to the waterfalls. (All ages. Strollers: yes. Best in morning or evening light.)

Mirror Lake, the adventure walk. Two miles to the lake on a packed-dirt road that's stroller-possible with real wheels (not an umbrella stroller). The lake itself is seasonal, full in spring, a sandy meadow by late summer. But the walk along Tenaya Creek is beautiful regardless, and at the "lake" site there are boulders to climb, creek edges to explore, and fewer people than elsewhere in the Valley. (Ages 3+. Under-2s fine in a carrier. Over-8s will want to scramble on the rocks.)

Bridalveil Fall, the quick hit. Half a mile round trip from the parking lot. Paved but steep in spots, stroller-difficult on the uphill. The waterfall is one of the most photogenic in the Valley. In spring, the mist at the base is a full-body shower. Short enough that even a reluctant walker can do it. (All ages, but carry small children on the steep section. Best in May to June.)

If you have the whole day and older kids. Two hikes off the beaten path are worth the drive. McGurk Meadow (1.6 miles round trip, flat, off Glacier Point Road) is a wildflower meadow with a historic sheepherder's cabin that kids find fascinating. Lukens Lake (2.4 miles round trip, minimal elevation, off Tioga Road) is a shallow alpine lake warm enough to wade in by August, surrounded by wildflower meadows. Both are quiet and see a fraction of the Valley crowds. You'll need Glacier Point Road or Tioga Road to be open. Check conditions before driving up.

### Water, rocks, and the stuff kids actually remember

In nearly two decades of watching families here, I've found that kids don't remember the vista. They remember the creek. They remember the bear box. They remember the ranger badge and the moment they touched snow in June and the lizard doing push-ups on a warm rock that nobody rushed them past.

Plan for that. Budget unstructured time near water and rocks. The best Yosemite day with kids has two hours of "hiking" and four hours of sitting by a creek while your children throw pebbles into the current.

Swimming and creek play. The Merced River runs through the Valley with sandy beaches, granite slabs, and calm pools, but the water is snowmelt, and the current is dangerous before mid-July. The swimming guide is the long version of this paragraph, and worth reading before a river day with small children. The Merced looks calm and it is not calm in spring. People drown in this river. Do not let kids wade above their knees before mid-July, and never let them near the water above any waterfall. By late July, the current mellows and there are legitimately great swimming and wading spots. Housekeeping Camp has the best river access for families: sandy beach, granite slabs, calm water in midsummer. The Cascade Picnic Area is quieter, with picnic tables, a pit toilet, and its own stretch of wadeable river.

Picnic spots. Skip the Village Store bench. The Cascade Picnic Area is shaded, has tables, has a bathroom, and sits on the river. El Capitan Meadow has no tables but has the best views in the Valley. Bring a blanket and eat lunch with 3,000 feet of granite in front of you. Sentinel Bridge has a spot on the south bank of the Merced with river access and shade.

### The stuff that will ruin your day

I've seen all of these happen to families, most of them more than once.

Arriving after 10 AM. You will circle for parking. Your kids will melt down in the back seat. You'll burn an hour of your best daylight on frustration. The fix: leave earlier. Or take YARTS.

Not bringing enough water. The Valley floor can hit 95°F in July. Kids dehydrate faster than adults and complain about it louder. One liter per person is the minimum for a half-day. Two is better. Bring a water bottle for every person, including the toddler. The only water refill on most Valley trails is the drinking fountain at the Vernal Fall footbridge, a mile from the trailhead.

Skipping sunscreen and hats. The elevation means more UV. A burned toddler at 2 PM means a screaming toddler at 6 PM. Apply before you leave the car. Reapply at lunch. Hats on everyone.

Ignoring bear rules. Black bears live in the Valley. They're not aggressive, but they will break into your car for a granola bar. Everything with a scent: food, coolers, sunscreen, lip balm, car seats that smell like crackers, goes in a bear box at your campsite or in your trunk (not the back seat, not the truck bed) when you're in the park. Bear boxes are metal lockers at every campsite and picnic area. Rangers check cars and issue real fines, up to $5,000. Your kids will think the bear box is the coolest thing at the campsite. Let them operate it. But take it seriously.

Overscheduling. You do not need to see everything. You need to see three things well. The family that hikes one trail, eats lunch by the river, gets the Junior Ranger badge, and watches sunset from a meadow has a better trip than the family that drives to eight viewpoints and sees none of them. Let your kids set the pace and stop when they want to stop.

### If you have a second day

Three options, depending on what's open and what your kids can handle.

Glacier Point by car. Glacier Point Road opened May 9 this year. The drive takes about an hour from the Valley. The viewpoint at the end is fenced and safe for kids, and the view, Half Dome at eye level, the Valley 3,200 feet below, the entire Clark Range spread out to the south, is arguably the best in the park. No hiking required. Drive up, get out, look, eat lunch at the picnic area, drive back. On the way, stop at the Sentinel Dome trailhead for an easy 2.2-mile round trip to a bald granite dome with 360-degree views. Kids love the scramble to the top.

Mariposa Grove. The giant sequoias. A free shuttle runs from a parking area to the grove (the road to the grove is closed to private vehicles). The lower grove loop is about 2 miles on a paved trail, stroller-accessible and flat enough for all ages. The Grizzly Giant is 2,700 years old and 96 feet around. The shuttle ride is part of the fun for small children.

Tioga Road and Tuolumne Meadows. If Tioga Road is open (it typically opens late May to early June, and is open this year as of May 15), the drive from the Valley up to Tuolumne Meadows is one of the great road trips in the American West. The meadow at 8,600 feet is cool, wide, and crisscrossed with easy walking paths. Soda Springs, a natural carbonated spring bubbling out of the ground, is a short walk from the road and kids like tasting the fizzy water. No reservation needed to drive Tioga Road.

Your kids don't need to see everything. They need to see one waterfall, throw rocks in one creek, and earn one Junior Ranger badge.

## Tioga Road opening 2026: a plan for opening weekend

URL: https://thetalusfieldjournal.com/articles/tioga-road-opening-weekend
Section: Seasonal Guides. Published: 2026-05-13. Last updated: 2026-09-09.
Summary: Tioga Road opens May 15, 2026. What's open in Tuolumne Meadows, road conditions, short hikes for mid-May, and a day east to Lee Vining and Mono Lake.

Tioga Road (Highway 120) in Yosemite National Park opened Friday, May 15, 2026, at 8 a.m. That was well ahead of the long-term average opening of May 28. Glacier Point Road had already opened on May 9. No day-use reservations are required to enter Yosemite this year, just a standard entrance pass.

Tioga Pass status (September 9, 2026): open, and it has been since May 15. The Park Service's standing line is that the road stays open until sometime in November; the last five seasons closed between October 21 and November 15. For live updates, call 209/372-0200 (press 1, then 1) or check nps.gov/yose/planyourvisit/conditions.htm. If you just need the standing version, the window, what is actually open in week one, and what to bring, the Tioga opening page is the short version, kept current each season.

### What's open on Tioga Road opening weekend

There is a difference between "the road is open" and "Tuolumne Meadows is open for the season," and opening weekend lives entirely in the first one. On Friday the pavement is plowed, but the store, the grill, the lodge, the campground services and the wilderness center staff come online over the following weeks.

What you get on opening weekend is the road itself: pavement between twelve-foot snow walls, half-frozen lakes, and snowmelt creeks running hard. It is a good drive and a bad one to be unprepared for.

Snow conditions in mid-May still include big drifts at Olmsted Point, ice along Tenaya Lake's shaded shore, and lingering snowpack on most trails above 8,500 feet.

Here is what was open on opening weekend, with the dates the rest of Tuolumne came online this year.

#### What's open

- Tioga Road and Tioga Pass entrance station
- Olmsted Point and the major pullouts
- Tenaya Lake parking (the lake itself may still hold ice along the shaded shores)
- Tuolumne Meadows pullouts
- Crane Flat gas station (24/7, pay at pump, credit and debit only)
- Vault toilets along the road

#### What's not open yet

- Tuolumne Meadows Campground: closed on opening weekend. The campground reopened in August 2025 after a three-year rehabilitation, and its 2026 season runs July 1 through September 27, reservable on Recreation.gov
- Tuolumne Meadows Grill: closed on opening weekend. Yosemite Hospitality lists a June 13 opening, and the current Yosemite Guide has it running 8 a.m. to 6 p.m. until September 20
- Tuolumne Meadows Lodge and dining room: June 5 through September 13
- Tuolumne Meadows Store and Post Office: closed until later in the summer. Both are running now, the store 8 a.m. to 8 p.m. until September 20, the post office weekdays 9 a.m. to 5 p.m. and Saturdays 9 a.m. to 1 p.m.
- Tuolumne Meadows Visitor Center and Wilderness Center: limited or no staffing until late May. In season the visitor center runs 9 a.m. to 5 p.m. and the wilderness center 8 a.m. to 5 p.m.
- White Wolf Lodge, with its store and dining room: closed for all of 2026 due to sewer line damage. The campground did open, July 2 through September 14, with no drinking water
- Gas at Tuolumne Meadows: not in operation (offline for several years now)
- Potable water: not available anywhere along the road on opening weekend

Pack like you are heading into the backcountry, even if you are just driving up for the day.

### Tioga Road conditions and what to bring before you go

Gas up before you start climbing. Crane Flat is the only fuel inside the park on the western side, and it is pay-at-pump only. On the east side, your next gas is in Lee Vining, about 45 minutes past Tuolumne. Bring all your water (two liters per person minimum if you are walking anywhere), bring all your food (sandwiches, snacks, a thermos of coffee), and plan for vault toilets. There is nothing to buy along Tioga Road on opening weekend, and there is no potable water. Cell service is essentially zero from Crane Flat to Lee Vining, so download offline maps before you leave the Valley.

Carry chains, layers, and a full tank. Tioga Pass tops out at 9,945 feet. Morning temperatures will be in the 20s and 30s, even when the Valley is mild. Black ice at dawn and dusk is real, especially near Olmsted Point and the climb to the pass.

Arrive early. Before 8 a.m. is the target if you want to beat the congestion and the full parking lots, especially on opening weekend. Sunrise at Olmsted is a strong photograph, and you will share it with almost no one. The rest of the turnouts between Crane Flat and the pass, with the history under each, are in Tioga Road, stop by stop.

### The best Tioga Road stops and short hikes for opening weekend

Here is how I build the day every year the road opens.

#### Stop one: Olmsted Point

You can see Half Dome from a lot of angles in Yosemite, but only from Olmsted Point do you see its back side, the broad northern face, with Clouds Rest rising to its left and Tenaya Canyon dropping away below. The short nature trail south of the parking lot is usually walkable on opening weekend; the slickrock catches the sun and dries fast, even with snow patches in the shaded hollows. The boulders scattered across the polished granite are glacial erratics. Each one was carried here by an ice sheet and left when the ice melted out from under it.

Wear shoes with grip. Bring sunglasses. Snow glare at altitude is intense.

#### Stop two: Tenaya Lake

Ten minutes further east, Tenaya Lake will likely still be ice-rimmed on opening weekend, with open water in the middle reflecting Tenaya Peak. Park at the east beach pullout. The walk down to the sand is short and easy, and it is one of the few places where you can be at the edge of an alpine lake in mid-May without committing to a real hike.

The full Tenaya Lake Loop Trail crosses the inlet on a boardwalk that Yosemite Conservancy donors helped fund and then traces the south shore through forest. That south shore holds snow and mud longer than anywhere else in the area. If you want to attempt the full loop around the lake, bring waterproof boots, expect slush, and stay on the trail. The revegetation work along the loop is fragile, and meadow soils take years to recover from a single boot print in the wrong place.

For most people, an hour along the east beach is enough.

#### Stop three: a short wander in Tuolumne Meadows

A few more miles east, the road drops into Tuolumne Meadows. The meadow itself will be a patchwork of last year's brown grass, the first hints of green, sheets of meltwater, and lingering drifts. Do not walk across the meadow. Pull off at one of the half-dozen designated pullouts and look from the edge.

If you want to stretch your legs, two short options are reliable on opening weekend:

- Pothole Dome at the west end of the meadow. A one-mile round-trip scramble up polished granite with a panoramic view of Tuolumne, Lembert Dome, and the Sierra crest. The approach across the meadow edge will be wet, sometimes flooded, so stick to the established path. The granite itself dries fast.
- Soda Springs and Parsons Lodge from the Lembert Dome parking area, 1.4 miles round-trip on a flat dirt road. The historic lodge building is closed until summer staffing arrives, but the exterior, the naturally carbonated springs bubbling up through iron-orange sediment, and the Tuolumne River running hard with snowmelt are all yours. Kids love the springs.

Skip Lukens Lake, May Lake, Cathedral Lakes, and Lembert Dome's summit. Those trails are snowbound at this point in May, and a few of them will not be reasonable until late June.

### Driving Tioga Pass east to Lee Vining and Mono Lake

This is the part that makes opening weekend a full trip rather than a day in the park, and the pass is the reason the Highway 395 route from Los Angeles exists at all for the summer months. Once you cross Tioga Pass at 9,945 feet, the road drops more than 3,000 feet in twelve miles down to the Mono Basin, and granite gives way to volcanic landscape. The Sierra wall stands behind you, the Great Basin opens ahead, and Mono Lake spreads out below with its white tufa towers and a summer population of up to two million migratory birds.

Three pullouts are worth a stop on the way down. Tioga Lake just below the pass, where Mount Dana sits in the reflection. Ellery Lake a mile farther. And the Mono Lake Vista Point before the canyon drops, where the Mono Basin opens up for the first time.

#### Where to eat in Lee Vining

Lee Vining has few dining options, and the most famous one has slipped.

Whoa Nellie Deli at the Tioga Gas Mart is the famous one. The fish tacos built its reputation in the late 1990s, and they are still on the menu. The original chef, Matt Toomey, left in 2012 to open his own place in Mammoth, and over the years the deli has slipped a little. Portions are still generous, the view of Mono Lake from the picnic tables is still wonderful, and the summer live music, Thursday evenings and Sunday afternoons in 2026, is still a great scene. But prices have crept up, the food is more uneven than it used to be, and the "world famous" billing oversells it now. Go for the experience and the view. Order the tacos and the fries. Manage your expectations.

Latte Da Coffee Café at the El Mono Motel, just down Highway 395 in town, is what I find myself recommending more often these days. It is small, and the coffee is organic. There is a garden out back with a few tables, and it is quieter than the Mobil station. Pastries, espresso, an unhurried breakfast. The El Mono Motel itself is one of those quirky eleven-room places that the eastern Sierra still has a few of, every room decorated differently, and the café is folded right into it. If you are doing a full day on the road, Latte Da in the morning and a Whoa Nellie picnic in the afternoon covers both.

Other reliable options in town: Nicely's for a classic diner breakfast, Bodie Mike's for barbecue, the Mono Market for picnic supplies.

#### Make a day of Mono Lake

If you have a few hours left in the afternoon, drive south of Lee Vining on Highway 395 to South Tufa at the Mono Lake Tufa State Natural Reserve (south on 395, then east on Highway 120, about ten miles all told). Three dollars per person at the Forest Service fee station, and your America the Beautiful pass covers it. A boardwalk and a one-mile loop carry you through a forest of calcium carbonate towers that grew underwater at freshwater springs, then emerged when the lake dropped after Los Angeles began diverting the basin's streams in 1941. The Mono Lake Committee Information Center and Bookstore in downtown Lee Vining (open 9 a.m. to 5 p.m. daily) is the place to learn how the lake was saved. Their HD film, "The Mono Lake Story," is the primer.

In mid-May the lake is filling with nesting California gulls (the eared grebes and phalaropes that make Mono Lake famous arrive later, in summer and fall). By August the shoreline is carpeted in dark, shifting bands of brine flies. The birds come to eat them.

### What to pack for Tioga Road in May

For the high country on opening weekend, the difference between a good day and a frustrating one is footwear.

- Waterproof hiking boots. Not optional. Every trail will have wet, muddy, or partially snow-covered sections.
- Microspikes (Kahtoola or equivalent) in the pack for any shaded snow patch.
- Trekking poles for slush, mud, and slick granite.
- Layers: a puffy jacket and a shell, even if the forecast looks mild. Temperatures swing 30 to 40 degrees between dawn and afternoon.
- Sunglasses and sunscreen. Snow glare and 9,000-foot UV are a combination.
- Plenty of water and food. There is no source for either on Tioga Road yet.
- A bear-aware approach to food even on a day hike. Black bears are out of dens, hungry, and active in the meadows at first and last light. Use the lockers at trailheads.

For my full lists, see the day pack and car trip kit.

### A note on visiting responsibly in the early season

In early season the meadow soils are saturated, the vegetation is just emerging, and the trails are soft. A single off-trail boot print in the wrong place in May can leave a scar that will still be visible in August.

Stay on trails. Stay on boardwalks. Use the pullouts. Pack out everything you bring in. Give wildlife room (50 yards from black bears is the park standard). Bear spray is not permitted in Yosemite, in the car or on the trail. Store all scented items in lockers or canisters, even snacks in your car at a trailhead.

The high country is protected because of decisions made in 1864, 1890, 1916 and 1984. Leave it as you found it.

### Tioga Road 2026: frequently asked questions

#### When does Tioga Road open in 2026?

It opened Friday, May 15, 2026, well ahead of Tioga's long-term average opening date of May 28.

#### Is Tioga Pass open right now?

As of September 9, 2026, yes. It typically closes for the season in November, with the first lasting snow. Call 209/372-0200 (press 1, then 1) for live updates, or check nps.gov/yose/planyourvisit/conditions.htm.

#### Is Highway 120 through Yosemite open?

Yes. Highway 120 (Tioga Road) through Yosemite opened Friday, May 15, 2026, and stays open until the first lasting snow, typically in November. Highway 120 west of the park (Big Oak Flat to Crane Flat) is open year-round, and it is one of the two routes the park points to when Highway 140 closes.

#### What is the elevation of Tioga Pass?

Tioga Pass sits at 9,945 feet (3,031 meters), the highest state highway pass in California. Tioga Road climbs from 6,200 feet at Crane Flat to the pass over roughly 47 miles.

#### Do I need a reservation to enter Yosemite in 2026?

No. The day-use reservation system is not in effect this year. A standard entrance pass is required.

#### Is the Tuolumne Meadows store open on opening weekend?

No. This year the lodge opened June 5, the grill in mid-June, and the store and post office later in the summer. The store and grill close September 20, the lodge September 13.

#### Can I camp at Tuolumne Meadows on opening weekend?

No. The campground's 2026 season runs July 1 through September 27, reservable on Recreation.gov. It reopened in August 2025 after a three-year rehabilitation.

#### How long does it take to drive Tioga Road?

Tioga Road runs 39 miles from Crane Flat to Tuolumne Meadows and about 47 to the Tioga Pass entrance station. Allow roughly 90 minutes one-way without stops, or a full day with Olmsted Point, Tenaya Lake, and Tuolumne Meadows. With Lee Vining and Mono Lake added on, plan a long day.

For more on the early season up high, see Glacier Point Road is open. For 2026 strategy, see Yosemite without reservations in 2026. Once Tioga is open, the high country also becomes the best stargazing in the park.
