## How to pack your car for a Yosemite trip

URL: https://thetalusfieldjournal.com/articles/pack-your-car-for-yosemite
Section: Planning. Published: 2026-04-26. Last updated: 2026-04-26.
Summary: Nobody writes about packing the car. But the car is the base camp for most Yosemite trips, and what's in it decides crisis from inconvenience.

Nobody writes about packing the car. Everybody writes about packing the backpack, the day pack, the cooler. But the car is the base camp for most Yosemite trips, car campers, lodge guests, and day-trippers alike, and what you have in it determines whether a flat tire at Crane Flat is a twenty-minute inconvenience or a three-hour ordeal, whether a surprise thunderstorm sends you home early or sends you to the backup plan, and whether the best spontaneous detour of your trip actually happens or gets killed by "we don't have what we need."

I've spent close to twenty years watching people arrive at this park. The ones who have great trips and the ones who have frustrating ones are almost never separated by fitness or budget. They're separated by what was in the car when they pulled through the entrance station. (If it's your first trip, the first-timer's guide is the broader-strategy companion to this one.) Here's what should be in yours, and why each item earns its space.

### The cooler changes everything

This is not optional and it is not a nice-to-have. A good cooler, packed correctly, fundamentally changes the math on your entire Yosemite trip.

Yosemite is not a place where you can easily grab food. The Valley has the Village Store, a food court and a dining room at the Lodge, a deli in Yosemite Village, and a pizza deck and a taqueria at Half Dome Village. That's it. Prices are national-park high, selection is limited, and in peak season the lines are long. Tuolumne has a small grill and a tiny store. Glacier Point has nothing. Wawona has a small store. Once you leave the Valley floor, your options narrow fast and don't come back.

A cooler stocked before you arrive means you eat when you're hungry, not when you can find an open restaurant. It means cold water waiting at the trailhead when you finish a hike at two in the afternoon. It means you can stay out at Glacier Point for sunset and eat dinner in the parking lot watching the alpenglow instead of racing back to the Valley for the last seating at the Lodge. That kind of flexibility is what turns a good trip into the trip you'll talk about for years.

Pack the cooler in layers. Ice on the bottom, things you'll eat last on the bottom, things you'll eat first on top. Freeze water bottles and use them as ice blocks. They double as cold drinking water as they melt. Pre-make sandwiches and wraps for the first two days. Cut fruit and vegetables at home and store them in containers. If you're car camping, bring eggs, cheese, and tortillas for camp breakfasts.

The discipline that matters most: keep the cooler in the shade, in the trunk, lid closed. A cooler that stays shut and stays out of direct sun will hold ice for three to four days in Yosemite's summer. One that gets opened every thirty minutes and sits in the back seat in July lasts about eight hours. Every time you open it, you're letting the cold out and the clock starts over.

### A real water setup

This is one I see people get wrong constantly. They bring two plastic water bottles for a family of four and assume they'll refill at a fountain somewhere. Then they're at Olmsted Point at 8,500 feet with four thirsty people and no water source in sight.

Bring a rigid water jug, four to seven gallons depending on your group size and trip length. The square-shaped jugs with a bottom spigot are best because they don't tip in the trunk and you can dispense water without lifting and tilting a heavy container. That matters more than you think after three days of use. Fill it at home before you leave.

You'll use this water for everything. Drinking. Refilling day-hike bottles at the trailhead. Rinsing hands after lunch. Rinsing off dusty legs after a trail. Filling the dog's bowl (dogs are allowed in campgrounds and on paved paths, not on most trails). Brushing teeth at the campsite.

Tap water is available in the Valley, filling stations at the visitor center and at campgrounds. But the jug in the trunk is the thing that keeps you from driving twenty minutes back to the Valley every time someone's thirsty. It lives in the car, it's always available, and on a hot July day you'll go through more of it than you expect.

### The sealed trash container

This is something I picked up years ago, and I'm surprised more people don't do it. Instead of a loose garbage bag that fills your car with the smell of yesterday's lunch by day two, use a hard-sided food-storage container with a sealing lid as your trash bin. Line it with a small kitchen bag. When it's closed, no smell gets out.

This matters in Yosemite more than most places because of the bears. A loose trash bag in the back seat is a scent beacon. A sealed container manages the odor, and it's portable enough to carry around your campsite and easy to clean at the end of the trip.

Bring two large garbage bags as well. One for overflow trash when you find a bear-proof dumpster to empty into, and one for wet or dirty gear that you don't want touching the inside of your car. But the daily-use trash goes in the sealed bin.

### Layers in the car, not just on your back

The temperature swing in a single Yosemite day can be 40 degrees or more. You might start a morning in the Valley at 55, hike in 85-degree heat at midday, drive to Tuolumne at 70, and stand at a viewpoint at sunset in 48. If your warm layer is at the bottom of your day pack, fine. But if you left it at the campsite because "it's July," you're going to be cold, and the campsite might be an hour's drive away.

Keep a fleece, a rain jacket, and a warm hat in the car at all times, for every person in the vehicle. I don't care if the forecast says 95 and sunny. The forecast is for the Valley floor. The park goes from 2,000 feet at El Portal to 13,000 feet at the crest, and the weather at those two elevations has almost nothing to do with each other.

Long pants, too. Even if you hike in shorts, having pants in the car means you can switch for an evening program, a mosquito-heavy meadow walk at dusk, or a late-afternoon breeze at Taft Point that turns cold fast. I keep a full change of clothes in a dry bag in the trunk. I need it on more trips than I expect.

### A ground mat at the tailgate

This is a small thing that solves a constant annoyance. A simple outdoor mat, nothing fancy, just a two-by-three-foot piece of durable fabric, placed on the ground at your tailgate or car door.

When you come back from a hike, you can stand on it while you change shoes without getting your socks in the dirt. On cold mornings, you can hop onto it while you layer up outside the car. At the campsite, it's where you sit to take off boots without tracking dust into your tent. It rolls up small, weighs nothing, and earns its space every single day.

I didn't start using one until a few years ago. Now I can't imagine not having it.

### A tarp for shade and rain

Yosemite campgrounds have trees, but not every campsite has the shade you want exactly where you want it. And afternoon thunderstorms in July and August can appear with about thirty minutes of warning.

A simple tarp, nothing elaborate, just an eight-by-ten or ten-by-twelve with grommets and some cord, creates a livable outdoor space that works in both conditions. Rig it between two trees, or between the car and a tree, and you've got a shaded kitchen, a dry place to sit when it's raining, and a spot where you can relax during the heat of the day without retreating into a broiling tent.

If you want something purpose-built, there are vehicle-anchoring tarps that attach to your roof rack or rear hatch. They go up fast and create a covered patio off the back of the car. But even a basic hardware-store tarp and fifty feet of paracord will do the job.

The key insight: a tarp makes your campsite a place you want to be during the hours between hikes. Without one, a lot of people end up sitting in their car with the engine running for the air conditioning. With one, you're sitting outside in the shade, reading a book, watching Steller's jays steal crumbs.

### Navigation when your phone dies

Your phone will lose signal outside the Valley. Consistently. Reliably. If your whole navigation strategy is Google Maps, you will at some point be staring at a blank screen at a fork in the road wondering if Tioga Road goes left or right.

Carry a paper park map. You get one free at the entrance station. Put it in the glove box. It shows every road, major trailhead, campground, and service area in the park.

Download offline maps before you enter. Google Maps lets you cache a region. CalTopo and Gaia GPS give you topo detail. AllTrails lets you download specific trail maps. Do all of this over wifi the night before, not at the entrance station where the signal is already gone.

If you're driving to Yosemite from the east on Tioga Road, know that there is no gas between Lee Vining and Crane Flat. That's 60 miles of mountain highway with serious elevation changes. Fill up before you enter the park from any direction.

### The roadside kit

Yosemite's roads include steep grades, tight switchbacks, extreme heat, and occasionally extreme cold. A basic roadside kit is not paranoia. It's common sense for a park where cell service is unreliable and the nearest tow truck might be in Mariposa.

A portable jump starter. These are better than jumper cables because they don't require a second car, and dead batteries in Yosemite parking lots are absurdly common. Headlights left on, cold mornings at elevation, old batteries pushed past their limit. A good portable unit is the size of a paperback book and starts a car engine multiple times on a single charge.

A spare tire and the tools to change it, and the knowledge of how to use them. Roadside assistance might take hours to reach you in Yosemite, if it can reach you at all. Practice a tire change at home before the trip.

A basic tool kit: pliers, a screwdriver, duct tape, zip ties, a few spring clamps. The clamps are surprisingly versatile in camp, securing a tarp grommet, clamping a tablecloth to a picnic table in the wind, holding a wet towel to the roof rack to dry. They cost a dollar each and weigh nothing.

A real flashlight. Not your phone flashlight. A flashlight that works when your phone is dead, which it will be, because you've been using it for photos and navigation all day.

### The things people forget

Binoculars. Yosemite is a place where things happen far away. A peregrine falcon hunting off the face of El Capitan, a black bear crossing a meadow at 300 yards, climbers on the Regular Northwest Face at a distance that makes them look like ants. A pair of binoculars turns those moments from squinting into actually seeing. An 8x42 pair lives in my car year-round and gets used almost every trip. If you only bring one "extra" thing, make it binoculars.

A windshield sunshade. A car sitting in a Yosemite parking lot in July in direct sun reaches oven temperatures inside. A reflective sunshade keeps the steering wheel touchable and the car interior tolerable when you get back from a six-hour hike. This is a three-dollar item that makes a thirty-dollar difference in comfort. I don't know why anyone doesn't carry one.

Camp chairs. Even if you're staying in a lodge. A pair of lightweight camp chairs in the trunk means you can set up anywhere: at a picnic area, at a pullout on Glacier Point Road, in a meadow at sunset. Some of the best hours I've ever spent in this park happened sitting in a camp chair doing absolutely nothing, watching the light change on the granite.

Cash. Twenty dollars in small bills. Most Valley food locations take cards, but some campground transactions, the occasional roadside produce stand between home and the park, and the rare vending machine still run on cash.

A phone charging setup that actually works. A car charger and a cable long enough to reach the back seat. Or better, a portable battery bank that you charge while driving and use at the campsite. Your phone is your camera, your map, your flashlight, your alarm clock, and your weather report. A dead phone at mile three of a hike is a problem. Charge it every time you're in the car.

### Bear rules apply to your car

This gets its own section because it matters that much, and because most people get it wrong.

If you're in Yosemite and there is food in your car (any food, including sealed coolers, wrapped granola bars, canned drinks, gum, sunscreen, chapstick, and that banana you forgot in the door pocket) the food must be stored properly when you're not in the vehicle.

In campgrounds, all food and scented items go in the bear box (metal food locker) at your campsite when you're asleep or away from the car. The car itself is not bear-proof. Bears in Yosemite have learned to recognize coolers through car windows, and they will break into vehicles to get food. This is not rare. It happens every week in peak season. They peel door frames back like opening a can.

When you're at a trailhead or parking area during the day, the rule is simpler: food stays in the trunk, out of sight, windows closed. If you have a hatchback or SUV with no separate trunk, cover the cooler and any food bags so they're not visible. A sealed trash container helps here too. The bear can't smell what it can't detect.

A bear breaking into your car means a $500 to $5,000 repair bill, a trashed interior, lost food, and a bear that's now more likely to do it again. Every car break-in teaches that bear that cars contain food. Eventually, a bear that's broken into enough cars gets euthanized. Your laziness about the bear box has a body count. Use it.

### How to load the car

When you pack the car, think about access order. The things you need first should be the things you can reach without unpacking everything else.

Back seat or top of trunk: Day packs, water bottles, sunscreen, the layer bag. You'll grab these every morning.

Accessible but shaded: The cooler. Trunk is ideal. If it's a truck bed, cover it.

Back seat, in a grab bag: Rain gear, extra layers, the first-aid kit. Things you might need fast.

Middle of the trunk: The water jug (heavy, low, stable), the sealed trash bin, camp chairs.

Bottom of the trunk: Tent, sleeping bags, stove, camp kitchen gear. You set this up once and leave it at the site.

Buried deep: The roadside kit, the spare tire, the jump starter. Out of the way until the moment you need them.

Valuables: Take them with you or lock them in the glove box. Yosemite has vehicle break-ins from humans too, especially at trailhead parking areas. Don't leave laptops, wallets, or visible bags in the car. Ever.

### The real point

Your car is the thing that gets you to and from the trailhead, the campsite, the viewpoint, the restaurant. But it's also the safety net, the pantry, the closet, and the reason you can say "the plan changed, let's drive to Tuolumne instead" and actually do it without worrying about whether you have what you need.

Most people spend hours researching which trail to hike and about fifteen minutes throwing things in the car. Flip that ratio a little. Thirty minutes of thoughtful packing before you leave home pays off every single day you're in the park. It's the difference between a trip that's reactive, always driving back for the thing you forgot, and a trip that's free. Free to chase the light, stay for sunset, take the detour, say yes to the thing you didn't plan for.

Pack the car like you're packing for the trip you don't know you're going to take yet. That's the one that's usually the best.

## Mariposa vs Oakhurst vs Groveland: Best Town to Stay Near Yosemite

URL: https://thetalusfieldjournal.com/articles/yosemite-gateway-towns-compared
Section: Planning. Published: 2026-04-26. Last updated: 2026-10-01.
Summary: Mariposa, Oakhurst, Groveland, El Portal and Lee Vining compared: the closest town to each entrance, drive times, winter access, kids, and which to book.

For a Yosemite Valley trip, start with El Portal for a shorter drive or Mariposa for more restaurants and services. Choose Oakhurst for Wawona and the Mariposa Grove, Groveland for the Highway 120 approach, and Lee Vining for the high country when Tioga Road is open.

I've stayed in all five towns. The comparison below separates the drive to an entrance from the drive to Yosemite Valley, which is where most first-time visitors spend their days. Treat the drive times as planning estimates and allow extra time for traffic, entrance queues, and stops.

Mariposa or Oakhurst? For Yosemite Valley, Mariposa, closer by 30 minutes or more. For the South Entrance and the Mariposa Grove, Oakhurst. The five towns side by side:

Town | Drive to the Valley | Nearest entrance | Highway | Elevation | Best for

El Portal | 25 to 35 min | Arch Rock, a few miles | 140, year-round | about 1,900 ft | Sunrise starts, the shortest drive
Mariposa | 45 to 60 min | Arch Rock, via El Portal | 140, year-round | about 2,000 ft | Most first-timers, families, winter
Groveland | 65 to 80 min | Big Oak Flat, 30 to 40 min | 120, chains common in winter | about 3,100 ft | Character, Hetch Hetchy, Bay Area route
Oakhurst | 75 to 90 min | South, 20 to 25 min | 41, year-round | about 2,300 ft | Wawona and the Mariposa Grove
Lee Vining | 90+ min, summer only | Tioga Pass, about 12 miles | 120 East over Tioga Pass | about 6,800 ft | The high country and Mono Lake

### The geography you actually need to know

Think of the park as having four front doors. There are four entrance stations on the through roads, roughly one at each point of the compass, and each gateway town belongs to one of them. There's a fifth, the Hetch Hetchy entrance, but it's a dead end into a single valley and doesn't connect to anything.

- Arch Rock Entrance, Highway 140 from the west: the most direct route to Yosemite Valley. El Portal is at the gate, Mariposa further down the road.
- Big Oak Flat Entrance, Highway 120 from the northwest: Groveland.
- South Entrance, Highway 41 from the south: the route to Wawona and the Mariposa Grove. Oakhurst.
- Tioga Pass Entrance, Highway 120 East from the east, open only in summer: Lee Vining.

1Arch Rock Entrance, Highway 140: El Portal, Mariposa2South Entrance, Highway 41: Oakhurst3Big Oak Flat Entrance, Highway 120 west: Groveland4Tioga Pass Entrance, US 395 and Highway 120 east, closed in winter: Lee ViningMariposa, Groveland and Oakhurst lie farther down their highways, off the edge of the map. Tap a pin or a town to jump to its section. Map: National Park Service (public domain).

The four routes aren't equal. Highway 140 is the lowest, most reliable, year-round road into the Valley. Highway 41 climbs and drops more and comes in by way of Wawona. Highway 120 from Groveland runs higher still, and Tioga Pass is shut for roughly half the year. The table above puts numbers on each.

The elevation column is the best single predictor of whether you'll be putting chains on in February. El Portal and Mariposa sit low enough that winter storms usually arrive as rain. Groveland is a thousand feet higher and gets chain controls the Highway 140 towns do not. Lee Vining's road into the park is shut half the year.

One catch applies to every drive time on this page. Yosemite Valley is about seven miles long, and a time quoted "to the Valley" means its west end, near Bridalveil Fall. Curry Village and the east-end trailheads are another fifteen or twenty minutes past that, plus parking. Plan for the end of the Valley you're actually headed to. The legs the table does not cover (Oakhurst to the South Entrance, Groveland to Big Oak Flat, Lee Vining to Tuolumne Meadows) are collected on the drive times page.

### The closest town to Yosemite, by entrance

"Closest town to Yosemite" has four answers, because the park has four through-road entrances and the closest town to one is two hours from another. What matters is what's closest to where you're going:

- Closest town to Yosemite Valley: El Portal, about 14 miles and 25 to 35 minutes on Highway 140, through the Arch Rock entrance. Mariposa is next at about 45 miles. Foresta, inside the boundary, has a handful of rental cabins and nothing else.
- Closest town to the South Entrance: Fish Camp, two miles from the gate, with Tenaya Lodge and a few inns; Oakhurst, about 14 miles and 20 to 25 minutes, is the closest full town. The Mariposa Grove is just inside this gate and Wawona six miles beyond it.
- Closest town to the Big Oak Flat Entrance (the west, from the Bay Area): Buck Meadows and the Highway 120 lodges, a few minutes from the gate; Groveland, about 24 miles and 30 to 40 minutes, is the closest town with a main street.
- Closest town to Tioga Pass (the east): Lee Vining, about a dozen miles down Highway 120 East, summer only. When the pass is closed there is no town near this entrance because there is no entrance.
- Closest city with an airport: Fresno, about 65 miles from the South Entrance and 94 from the Valley by the Park Service's count, with summer YARTS service up Highway 41. Merced, on Highway 140, is the year-round YARTS hub for the Valley.

If you'd rather have the answer before the detail, it's one of these five:

- El Portal if the drive is the thing to shorten: first light in the Valley, or a winter trip on the lowest, most reliable road.
- Mariposa if you want a real town at the end of the day, more than one price point, and a year-round road. The default answer for a first trip.
- Groveland if you are coming from the Bay Area, want a smaller and cheaper town with more character than Oakhurst, or Hetch Hetchy is on the list.
- Oakhurst if the Mariposa Grove and Wawona are the point, you are driving up from Los Angeles or Fresno, or you want predictable chain lodging and a full-size supermarket.
- Lee Vining if Tioga Road is open and the high country is the trip. It isn't a Valley base, and treating it like one is the most common mistake on this list.

Which town fits your trip?

Answer all three and the pick appears here. It follows the article's reasoning and gets there faster.

Now the towns themselves.

### El Portal

Valley driveabout 14 miles, 25 to 35 minutesEntranceArch Rock, a few miles up the roadRoadHighway 140, open year-roundElevationabout 1,900 feet, the lowest of the fiveThe towna small park-adjacent settlement: riverside lodges, a market, a 24-hour gas station

Photo: Cory Goehring

El Portal is the closest gateway to the Valley by a wide margin, and it exists because of the park: a handful of lodges (the Yosemite View Lodge, the Cedar Lodge) along the Merced River, the gas station, a small market, and not much else. Rooms are priced like in-park lodging, because the location is that good.

Why people pick it:

- The shortest possible drive to anywhere in the Valley. Roll out of bed at 5:30 a.m. and be at Tunnel View by 6:15.
- The approach up the Merced River canyon is a reason to come this way, and in spring the high water and wildflowers are their own attraction.
- Highway 140 is the lowest-elevation entry to the park and the most reliable in winter.

Why they regret it:

- Dining and shopping are minimal. You'll end up driving to Mariposa for variety.
- Tiny inventory: it books up early and stays expensive all summer.
- The riverside lodges come with river noise. Some people love it. Some don't sleep.

Services: the gas station and market matter more than they look, because there is no gas station anywhere in Yosemite Valley; the in-park pumps are at Crane Flat and Wawona, both well off the Valley floor. Groceries here are convenience-store groceries, so buy the week's food in Mariposa on the way in.

Pick El Portal if being inside the park as much as possible is the top priority: sunrise photography, beating the peak-season crowds, a short Valley trip, or any winter trip where road reliability matters. Skip it if you want a choice of dinner, you're booking late in summer, or you're travelling with people who'll be back at the room by mid-afternoon. There's very little to do in El Portal that isn't the park.

Current rates and availability: El Portal lodging →

### Mariposa

Valley driveabout 45 miles, 45 minutes to an hourEntranceArch Rock, via El PortalRoadHighway 140, open year-roundElevationabout 2,000 feetThe townhistoric gold-rush county seat, the most full-service of the five
Mariposa is the most complete of the western gateways. It has a real downtown with restaurants, bars, coffee, a couple of bookstores, and the Mariposa Museum and History Center (worth a visit). It has the 1854 Mariposa County Courthouse, the oldest continuously operating courthouse west of the Rockies. Its lodging runs from chain hotels on the highway to historic bed-and-breakfasts in town. It's also where a lot of people who work in the park end up when they age out of in-park staff housing.

Why people pick it:

- Real food, real coffee, multiple grocery stores, a real town.
- The widest range of price points of any gateway, budget motel to upscale country inn.
- Year-round access on the same Merced canyon route as El Portal, just longer.

Why they regret it:

- At least 90 minutes of round-trip driving a day. That means earlier alarms for sunrise and tighter evenings getting back.
- In summer traffic the drive can stretch well past the hour.

Services: the deepest of the five. Full-size supermarkets, a pharmacy, hardware, banks, and the last reliable place to fix a problem before you are an hour from anywhere. It is also the only gateway with year-round bus service into the park. YARTS runs the Highway 140 corridor from Merced and Mariposa all year; the routes from the other towns run only in summer. If you'd rather not drive the canyon in the dark or in snow, this is the only town on the list where the bus is an answer in January.

Halfway to El Portal, the hamlet of Midpines splits the difference with a few camps and lodges and no town attached: the Yosemite Bug Rustic Mountain Resort, which spans dorm bunks to private cabins and runs the June Bug Cafe, and AutoCamp Yosemite, a property of Airstream trailers, canvas tents, and cabins on Highway 140. Both trade Mariposa's dinner options for a shorter morning drive.

Pick Mariposa if you are most first-time visitors: families, anyone who values a real town in the evening, anyone on a budget, and anyone visiting in shoulder season or winter when El Portal and in-park rooms are gone.

Current rates and availability: Mariposa lodging →

### Oakhurst

Valley driveabout 50 miles, 75 to 90 minutesSouth Entranceabout 14 miles, 20 to 25 minutes; the Mariposa Grove is immediately inside the gate, Wawona six miles onRoadHighway 41, open year-roundElevationabout 2,300 feetThe towna regional commercial hub: chain hotels, chain dining, big-box services

Photo: Dietmar Rabich / Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 4.0)

Oakhurst is the biggest gateway by population and amenities, with more chain lodging and chain dining than the other four combined. It is a regular Central California town that happens to be near a national park.

Why people pick it:

- Fast access to Wawona and the Mariposa Grove of giant sequoias.
- Predictable chain rooms at predictable prices, bookable late.
- The widest range of standard amenities of any gateway: chain supermarkets, national pharmacies, urgent care. The easiest of the five for filling a prescription or replacing forgotten gear.

Why they regret it:

- The longest Valley drive of any gateway. At 75 to 90 minutes each way, a Valley day means three hours in the car, and people shrug it off until about the third morning.
- Less character than Mariposa or Groveland, if the gateway-town atmosphere is part of your trip.
- Highway 41 climbs over a ridge and descends into Wawona before reaching the Valley: longer and more winding than 140.

The closer option on this corridor: Fish Camp, twelve miles up the road at the park line, puts you four minutes from the South Entrance. It is Tenaya Lodge at Yosemite, a full resort on 75 acres two miles from the gate, plus a few small inns, all at resort prices, trading Oakhurst's services for the setting.

Pick Oakhurst if the itinerary centers on the Mariposa Grove and Wawona, if you want chain predictability, or if you are driving up from Los Angeles or Fresno, since it sits on the natural path. Skip it if this is really a Yosemite Valley trip. Three hours a day in the car is what it costs you.

Current rates and availability: Oakhurst lodging →

One current note for this side of the park: the Wawona Hotel, the historic in-park option just inside the South Entrance, has been closed since December 2024. The Park Service has said it stays closed for this visitor season while it completes a condition assessment of the hotel complex, after a roof project turned up structural concerns. No reopening date has been announced. That removes the in-park alternative on the Highway 41 corridor and puts more pressure on Oakhurst and Fish Camp rooms in summer. Book earlier than you think you'll need to.

### Groveland

Valley driveabout 48 miles, 65 to 80 minutesEntranceBig Oak Flat, about 24 miles, 30 to 40 winding minutesRoadHighway 120, chain controls common in winterElevationabout 3,100 feet, the highest of the western gatewaysThe towna small historic gold-rush main street with strong personality
Groveland is the most overlooked gateway: a historic main street with the Groveland Hotel, the Iron Door Saloon (one of the oldest continuously operating saloons in California), and the same kind of character as Mariposa, on a smaller scale.

Why people pick it:

- A town that's worth an evening on its own. The Iron Door is a reason to go.
- Less crowded and often cheaper than Mariposa or El Portal, with easier last-minute rooms in shoulder seasons.
- The best position for Hetch Hetchy, the Tuolumne side of the park, and Tuolumne Meadows when Tioga Road is open.

Why they regret it:

- The drive to the Valley starts a thousand feet higher than the 140 towns, and chain controls are common in winter.
- The route crosses the burn scar of the 2013 Rim Fire. The forest is recovering, but it still looks different from the Highway 140 approach.
- Fewer total lodging options than Mariposa, and a town that closes early.

Services: a market rather than a supermarket, gas, and that's about it. Groveland is the last town of any size on Highway 120 before the entrance; the nearest in-park pumps are at Crane Flat. Fill the tank and the cooler here, or in Oakdale or Sonora on the way in from the Bay Area, before you start climbing.

The closer options on this corridor: the largest lodges on this side are not in Groveland itself but strung along Highway 120 east of it, and that matters on a Valley morning. Rush Creek Lodge sits on twenty wooded acres roughly half a mile from the Big Oak Flat entrance. Its sister property, the historic Evergreen Lodge, is about seven miles on, down Evergreen Road toward Hetch Hetchy, which makes it the closest bed to that corner of the park. Firefall Ranch, cottages and villas on a former stagecoach stop between Groveland and the gate, is the newest of the three. All three are priced well above a Groveland motel and book like it.

If Hetch Hetchy is your reason: the road in is open daylight hours only, so don't plan on sunset there, and vehicles over 25 feet aren't allowed on it. From November through March it can close entirely or require chains, which is when a low-elevation reservoir hike sounds best. Check before you commit a day to it.

Pick Groveland for gateway-town character, for Hetch Hetchy and the northern park, or as the natural base on the route from the Bay Area. Skip it for a deep-winter trip without snow-driving experience or chains in the trunk, or if you'll need real services at nine at night.

Current rates and availability: Groveland lodging →

### Lee Vining

Valley driveabout 75 miles over Tioga Pass, 90 minutes minimum, summer onlyTuolumne Meadowsabout 20 miles, 30 minutesMono Lake5 minutes to the visitor center, 15 to South TufaRoadHighway 120 East over Tioga Pass, seasonal; US 395 year-roundElevationabout 6,800 feet, and the pass above town just under 10,000The towna tiny eastern Sierra outpost between Mono Lake and the pass

Photo: Michael Hogarth / Wikimedia Commons (public domain)

Lee Vining is the only east-side gateway, and it makes for a different kind of trip. Tuolumne Meadows is 30 minutes away when Tioga Road is open, while the Valley is over an hour and a half each way. The road is typically open from late May or June through October or early November. The Park Service opened it on May 15 in 2026, the earliest in sixteen years, and the road conditions page lists current access. Lodging is a few small motels (the Yosemite Gateway Motel, the El Mono Motel, an inn or two). Dining is thin but includes the Whoa Nellie Deli at the Mobil station, some of the best food in the eastern Sierra.

Why people pick it:

- Direct access to Tuolumne Meadows and the high country in season, with far fewer crowds.
- Mono Lake next door, and an entirely different landscape: sagebrush, alkali, the Mono Basin, unlike anything west of the park.
- A natural stop on a longer eastern Sierra trip (Mammoth Lakes, Bishop, Death Valley).

Why they regret it:

- When Tioga Pass is closed there is no crossing at all: the drive around the south end of the Sierra turns 90 minutes into most of a day. The Park Service publishes the detour, and it is the first thing to read if your dates are anywhere near the shoulders.
- Limited rooms and food, so you book early and pay a summer premium.
- The Valley run crosses a near-10,000-foot pass, punishing in bad weather.

Services: thin and seasonal. The Tioga Gas Mart, which is also the Whoa Nellie Deli, runs roughly late April to late October, so the town's best-known meal is not available on a winter Mono Lake trip. Groceries are a small market; the nearest full supermarket is in Mammoth Lakes, about 30 miles south. Fuel on 395 is reliable but expensive, so fill up in Bishop or Bridgeport if you pass through either.

Pick Lee Vining if the high country is the trip (Tuolumne, Cathedral Lakes, Mount Dana, the Tioga Road itself), or if you are combining Yosemite with Mono Lake and the eastern Sierra. Skip it if your list says Yosemite Falls, Half Dome, or Tunnel View. Those are Valley sights, three hours round trip from here over a pass that isn't open when you're likely to want it.

Current rates and availability: Lee Vining lodging →

### The decision matrix in plain English

The short version:

You want sunrise in the Valley every day. El Portal.

You want a balanced trip with comfort and value. Mariposa.

Your itinerary is mostly Wawona and the Mariposa Grove. Oakhurst.

You want gateway-town character without the Mariposa price. Groveland.

You're focused on the high country, or combining with Mono Lake. Lee Vining.

You're visiting in winter. El Portal or Mariposa offer the lowest-elevation approach. Check road conditions and chain requirements on every route.

You have one day and you want the Valley. El Portal, and swallow the price. The drive you save is a real chunk of the only day you've got.

You would rather not drive at all. Mariposa or Merced, and take YARTS. It is the only corridor with year-round service.

You're travelling with a large RV or a trailer. Mariposa or Oakhurst, on the wider approaches. Rule out Hetch Hetchy Road, which bans anything over 25 feet.

You're flying into San Francisco. Groveland or Mariposa is on the way.

You're flying into Fresno. Oakhurst or Mariposa is on the way.

You're flying into Reno or driving from Las Vegas. Consider Lee Vining only if Tioga Road is open for your dates. Otherwise plan a route to a western entrance.

### What each town looks like in winter

Winter changes the road choices. Check conditions before booking and again before driving:

- El Portal and Mariposa. Highway 140 stays open, it is the lowest-elevation approach, and storms there more often fall as rain than snow. Year-round YARTS service runs this corridor, so it is the one base where not driving is a real option.
- Groveland. Highway 120 stays open to the park, but you are starting a thousand feet higher and chain controls are routine. Hetch Hetchy Road may be closed or chain-controlled from November through March. Workable, with chains and a plan.
- Oakhurst. Highway 41 stays open. The town is fine in winter; the constraint is the two hours of driving on a Valley day. If your winter trip is Badger Pass or the sequoias in snow, this side works well.
- Lee Vining. Tioga Road is closed and there is no way into the park from here. The town largely shuts down, the Whoa Nellie Deli with it. Come for a frozen Mono Lake if you like, but don't come for Yosemite.

### Practical notes

Before booking, check the drive to your planned sights, grocery access, and current road conditions.

Distance affects more than driving time. The farther your gateway, the earlier you leave to beat the crowds: a 60-minute drive at 5:30 a.m. is easier than a 90-minute drive at 4:30. The Park Service is not requiring a season-wide vehicle reservation for 2026. It manages peak days with traffic monitoring and active parking control in the Valley instead. That is good news if you like to be spontaneous and bad news if you roll in at ten. Every mile between your room and the entrance station is a mile you make up before the lots fill.

Gas. There is no gas station in Yosemite Valley. The in-park pumps are at Crane Flat, year-round with pay-at-the-pump around the clock, and at Wawona, where the store keeps daytime hours but the pumps also take a card overnight. Outside the park, the El Portal station is the last stop on Highway 140. Rolling into the Valley on a quarter tank is a bad plan in any season and a worse one in winter, when you'll sit idling in stopped traffic.

Groceries. Mariposa and Oakhurst have full-size supermarkets. Groveland has a market. El Portal and Lee Vining have convenience-scale markets and nothing more. Whichever town you pick, do the real shop in Mariposa or Oakhurst on the way in, because in-park food is limited, expensive, and keeps shorter hours than you expect. How to pack your car for a Yosemite trip covers the rest.

Cell service. Patchy in all five gateways and unreliable to nonexistent through most of the park, including long stretches of the approach roads. Download the offline map for the whole region before you leave the gateway town, screenshot your reservation details, and agree on a meeting point with anyone you might get separated from. Don't count on live navigation past the entrance station. Cell service in Yosemite has what each carrier actually gets, town by town and inside the park.

Car-free access follows the bus corridors. YARTS runs the Highway 140 corridor from Merced and Mariposa all year. The routes from Sonora and Groveland on 120, from Oakhurst on 41, and from Mammoth Lakes and Lee Vining on 395 are summer-only. A car-free trip narrows the gateway choice to one corridor for most of the year.

Reservations book out fast. In summer and on holiday weekends, gateway lodging fills six to twelve months in advance. Plan early, or be ready to flex on the town.

Check current status the week you travel. Roads, chain controls, and closures change faster than any lodging comparison can keep up with. The Park Bulletin puts the park's current roads, hours, closures, and trail conditions on one page.

### Where to stay near Yosemite with kids

Mariposa, for most families, and Oakhurst if the sequoias are the point of the trip. A family needs a full supermarket, a pharmacy, more than one dinner option, and a room that can be booked late, and Mariposa and Oakhurst are the only two gateways that have all four. Mariposa wins on the Valley drive, which matters more with children who have a limit on car time, and on the year-round road. El Portal's short drive is a real advantage for early starts with small kids, if you can get a room and do not mind driving to Mariposa for dinner. Groveland's main street is charming for adults and thin on the things that rescue a family evening. Yosemite with kids has the in-park half: which walks, which shuttle stops, and where the bathrooms are.

### Yosemite and Sequoia in one trip

Base south. Oakhurst is the pivot between the two parks. The South Entrance is 20 to 25 minutes north on Highway 41. Sequoia is roughly two to two and a half hours south: Fresno, then Highway 180 to the Kings Canyon entrance and the Generals Highway into the park. Doing both from Mariposa or Groveland adds an hour to every leg. The usual shape is two nights in Oakhurst for Yosemite (one Valley day, one Mariposa Grove and Wawona day), then a drive to Three Rivers or the Kings Canyon side for the second park. Don't try Sequoia as a day trip from any Yosemite gateway. The round trip is five hours of driving before you've seen a single tree.

### Common questions

What is the closest town to Yosemite? El Portal, about 14 miles and 25 to 35 minutes from Yosemite Valley on Highway 140. For the South Entrance and the Mariposa Grove it is Fish Camp, then Oakhurst; for the Big Oak Flat Entrance it is Groveland; for Tioga Pass, in summer, Lee Vining.

What is the best town to stay in near Yosemite? For most first-time visitors, Mariposa: a real town, several price points, full supermarkets, and the year-round Highway 140 road at 45 to 60 minutes from the Valley. El Portal if the drive is the thing to shorten, Oakhurst for the sequoias, Groveland for character and the Bay Area route, Lee Vining for the high country.

Is Oakhurst or Mariposa closer to Yosemite Valley? Mariposa, by 30 minutes or more: 45 to 60 minutes on Highway 140 against 75 to 90 on Highway 41. Oakhurst is closer to the South Entrance and the Mariposa Grove, 20 to 25 minutes.

Where should I stay near the Yosemite south entrance? Fish Camp, two miles from the gate, if you want to be closest; Oakhurst, 14 miles, if you want a full town. The Wawona Hotel, the in-park option on this side, has been closed since December 2024.

Where should I stay near Yosemite with kids? Mariposa for a Valley trip, Oakhurst for a sequoia trip. Both have full supermarkets, pharmacies, several restaurants, and rooms that can be booked later than El Portal or the in-park lodges.

Which gateway town is cheapest? Groveland and Mariposa typically have the widest range and the most budget rooms. El Portal is priced like in-park lodging. Oakhurst has predictable chain prices. Lee Vining has little inventory and prices accordingly.

Which towns have full grocery stores? Mariposa and Oakhurst. Groveland has a market. El Portal and Lee Vining have convenience-scale markets only.

Which town works in winter? El Portal or Mariposa, on Highway 140, the lowest and most reliable road. Groveland works with chains. Lee Vining has no road into the park at all when Tioga Pass is closed.

### The takeaway

The right gateway town depends on your trip. Mariposa is the safest first-timer's choice. El Portal is the strongest if you can get a room. Groveland is the underrated pick for character without the crowd. Oakhurst is for the southern-entrance trip. Lee Vining is the east-side experience that most western visitors never see.

Choose your base around the places you plan to visit. Stay west for Yosemite Valley, south for the giant sequoias, or east for the high country when Tioga Road is open.

If you're still working out how to approach the park, start with the first-timer's guide, read what changed for 2026 before you book, and see how to spend one or two days once your base is set.

## Yosemite during smoke season: how to actually plan around it

URL: https://thetalusfieldjournal.com/articles/yosemite-during-smoke-season
Section: Seasonal Guides. Published: 2026-04-26. Last updated: 2026-04-26.
Summary: Smoke season in California now runs July through October. The question isn't whether your Yosemite trip overlaps. It's whether you have a plan.

The first time I watched Yosemite Valley fill with wildfire smoke from a fire I couldn't see, the smoke arrived as a smell before it arrived as a sight. By midday, El Capitan was barely visible behind a layer of smoke that started about 200 feet up. By late afternoon, the entire upper Valley had vanished. The visitors who'd planned to drive to Glacier Point that day were standing at Tunnel View looking at haze. The visitors who flexed and drove up Tioga Road to Tuolumne were sitting at 8,600 feet in clean air, with the smoke below them.

Smoke is now routine. Smoke season in California now runs from roughly July through October most years, and parts of June in dry years. Yosemite is in the middle of one of the most fire-prone regions in the West. Plan for your trip to overlap with it. Smoke and closures are separate problems, and when the fire itself comes near your dates, what closes and what to do with the bookings is its own question.

Planning around smoke is doable, though few guides explain how. The official sources (the NPS air quality page, AirNow, the fire situation reports) are accurate but generic. They tell you to check the AQI. They don't tell you what to do with the number.

### The geography of smoke in Yosemite

Smoke does not fill the park evenly. The shape of the Sierra Nevada and Yosemite Valley itself determines where the smoke lands and how long it stays.

Yosemite Valley is a 4,000-foot-deep granite trough oriented roughly east-west. When smoke is pushed in by westerly or southwesterly winds (the most common direction in summer), it pours into the Valley and settles. Cold air drainage at night pulls smoke down from the surrounding ridges into the Valley floor. The result is that the Valley is often the worst air in the park during a smoke event, sometimes by a wide margin.

By contrast, the high country (Glacier Point, Tuolumne Meadows, anywhere above about 7,500 feet) is sometimes above the inversion layer that holds the smoke down. On a day when the Valley reads "Unhealthy" on the air quality index, Tuolumne can read "Moderate" or even "Good." This isn't always true, but it's true often enough that high-country flexibility is the single most important smoke strategy you have.

Hetch Hetchy and Wawona, both at lower elevations than Tuolumne, get smoke when the Valley does, but the patterns are different. Wawona is sometimes spared by wind direction. Hetch Hetchy can be either better or worse depending on where the fire is.

The same day can be hazardous in the Valley and decent at Tuolumne. The right move is often to drive 90 minutes uphill rather than to cancel.

### The real-time toolkit

Three resources, in order of usefulness.

AirNow (airnow.gov) and the AirNow Fire and Smoke Map (fire.airnow.gov) are the official EPA sources. They give you an Air Quality Index (AQI) reading for monitors in and near the park, updated multiple times a day. The Yosemite Valley monitor is at the Visitor Center. There are additional monitors in Wawona and Tuolumne when staffed and operating.

The AQI scale you actually need to know:

- 0 to 50: Good. Almost no health concerns for anyone. Normal park visit.
- 51 to 100: Moderate. Generally fine for most visitors. People with severe asthma or other respiratory conditions should be cautious.
- 101 to 150: Unhealthy for sensitive groups. Children, older adults, and anyone with respiratory issues should reduce outdoor exertion. Healthy adults can usually still hike but at a slower pace.
- 151 to 200: Unhealthy. Reduce outdoor activity. Don't do strenuous hikes. Sensitive groups should stay indoors.
- 201 to 300: Very Unhealthy. Don't hike. Spend time indoors when possible.
- 301+: Hazardous. Don't be outside. This is when you cancel or relocate.

The NPS Yosemite air quality page (nps.gov/yose/learn/nature/aqmonitoring.htm) gives you park-specific updates and is worth checking the morning of any planned hike during smoke season.

The NPS current conditions page (nps.gov/yose/planyourvisit/conditions.htm) flags smoke events along with road and trail closures. Read it within 24 hours of any trip during fire season.

Check these the night before you drive in and again before any major hike. Smoke conditions can change in two hours.

### Decision tree: flex, push through, or cancel

When smoke is in the forecast for your trip, run through the following:

If the AQI is forecast to be 50 or under, ignore the smoke risk and proceed normally.

If the AQI is forecast to be 51 to 100, you can have a normal trip with normal expectations. The vistas may be slightly hazy. Long-distance photography won't be as sharp. Your hike isn't going to be ruined.

If the AQI is forecast to be 101 to 150, you've got a yellow-light day. Use it for shorter, lower-effort activities. Walk the meadow loops, drive to Tunnel View, sit at Sentinel Bridge. Don't pick this day for a Half Dome ascent. If you have flexibility, consider driving up to Tuolumne, which is often better.

If the AQI is forecast to be 151 to 200, flex hard. Stay at lower elevations only if you absolutely must. Drive to the high country. If the high country is also smoky, switch to indoor activities (the museum, the Ansel Adams Gallery, sit-down meals at the Lodge or the Ahwahnee). Sensitive groups should stay indoors entirely.

If the AQI is forecast above 200, seriously consider canceling or rescheduling. Most lodging and tour providers will work with you if you call far enough in advance.

The hardest case is the day-of surprise. You wake up in the park, check AirNow, and the reading has jumped overnight from "Moderate" to "Unhealthy." The right move depends on what's possible. If you can drive up to higher elevation, do it. If you have an indoor alternative, take it. If you're committed to a hike, shorten it dramatically and turn around at the first sign of respiratory irritation.

### Tactics that actually work

Mornings are usually better than afternoons. Smoke patterns often peak in the late afternoon as wind picks up. Early starts (in the park by 6 a.m.) frequently catch a cleaner window before the day's smoke arrives.

Wind direction matters more than fire distance. A fire 80 miles away with a direct wind can put smoke in the Valley faster than a fire 20 miles away with the wind blowing the other direction. Watch the National Weather Service forecast for wind direction as well as the fire perimeter.

Some short walks are still worthwhile in moderate smoke. The Lower Yosemite Falls path, Cook's Meadow, Bridalveil Fall, and the Mariposa Grove inner loop are all short enough that even on a yellow-light day, you can get something out of them without significant exertion.

Cancel the long hikes first. A long, exposed, high-effort hike (Half Dome, Cloud's Rest, Upper Yosemite Falls) is the wrong call on a smoky day. Save those for cleaner air.

N95 masks help. They reduce the dose of fine particulate you're inhaling, especially during exertion. Pack a few. They're cheap and they take up no space.

### Special considerations

Children. Kids breathe faster and have smaller airways. They are more affected by smoke than adults. On a 100-150 AQI day, a healthy adult is usually fine for a moderate hike. A six-year-old probably isn't. Be more conservative for younger visitors.

Older adults and people with cardiovascular or respiratory conditions. Smoke affects you faster and harder. Use a tighter threshold. Treat 100 as your line, not 150.

Athletes and high-effort hikers. You're inhaling more smoke per minute than someone walking a meadow. Know your physiology and be willing to throttle back.

Asthma. Carry your rescue inhaler. Don't push through chest tightness or coughing. Asthmatic adults have ended up in the ER from smoke-induced attacks during routine hikes.

### A note on photography

Smoke can produce useful photographic conditions: a deep red sun at sunrise and sunset, layered atmospheric depth on the canyon walls, soft morning light that's normally only available in winter haze. Photographers who work with the conditions sometimes get images they couldn't get on a clear day.

The catch is that this only works at certain smoke densities and with the right light. A Valley view at AQI 250 is a wall of gray. The interesting conditions tend to come at AQI 75 to 130, with sun angles low and the smoke catching the light.

### The takeaway

Smoke is part of California summer now, and the visitors who plan around it have better trips.

Check AirNow before you book if you're booking close to a fire event. Check it the night before you drive. Check it the morning of every major hike. Have a high-elevation flex plan ready. Know your AQI thresholds. Carry N95s. Be willing to swap a Mist Trail day for a Tuolumne day if the readings call for it.

The Sierra will remain fire-prone, so a backup plan is part of any summer or fall trip.

And remember: in 2026 the entrance reservation system is gone, which means the smoke decision and the crowd decision now compound on the same day. See the 2026 crowd strategy for the other half of it.

Plan for both.

#### Sources

- Smoke Management and Air Quality, NPS Yosemite
- Current Air Quality and Smoke Monitoring, NPS Yosemite
- AirNow Fire and Smoke Map
- Current Conditions, NPS Yosemite

## Do you need a reservation for Yosemite in 2026? No. The plan

URL: https://thetalusfieldjournal.com/articles/yosemite-without-reservations-2026
Section: Planning. Published: 2026-04-26. Last updated: 2026-09-21.
Summary: No reservation is needed to enter Yosemite in 2026, on any date. What still needs booking, what 2027 might bring, and the plan for a park with no throttle.

On February 18, 2026, the Park Service announced that Yosemite would not require entrance reservations in 2026. Most people read that as news that the park had gotten easier to visit. It hasn't. It has gotten harder, and most visitors find out in a four-mile line outside the Arch Rock entrance station on a Saturday morning in July.

The reservation system was a throttle. It capped the number of vehicles that could enter the park during peak hours. Without it, that cap is gone. Park staff have said publicly, and the Yosemite Conservancy has flagged in its planning advisories, that the result should be the heaviest crowds since the last summers without a cap. The 2024 and 2025 seasons, with reservations, set a baseline. 2026 is going to push past it.

That is a reason to plan, not to stay home. (If it's your first trip, the first-timer's guide is the broader-strategy companion. If you are already in the park holding nothing, skip ahead to what you can still get today.)

One thing did change at the gate, and it is not about crowds. As of January 1, 2026, international visitors pay a $100 surcharge per person age 16 and older, on top of the standard entrance fee. A $250 nonresident annual pass waives it. Domestic visitors are unaffected.

### Do you need a reservation for Yosemite right now?

To enter the park, no. Not today, not this weekend, not on any date in 2026. The timed-entry systems that ran in some form from 2020 through 2024, and the peak-hours version that ran in 2025, are all gone. A car can drive up to any entrance station on any day of the year with nothing but an entrance pass. That answer holds for every month people ask about: September, October, the February Firefall, Memorial Day weekend, the Fourth of July. What still needs booking is everything you would sleep in or climb, and that list has not changed:

What you want | Reservation in 2026? | Where and when

Driving into the park, any day | No | An entrance pass only: $35 per car for seven days, sold at the gate or in advance on Recreation.gov
Firefall, mid-to-late February | No | No entrance reservation was required for February 2026; 2027 is unannounced
Camping | Yes | Recreation.gov, released on the 15th of each month at 7 a.m. Pacific for dates five months out; a few first-come sites outside the Valley
In-park lodging | Yes | travelyosemite.com, 366 days ahead
Half Dome, cable season | Yes, a permit | Preseason lottery in March, daily lottery two days ahead
Overnight wilderness trips | Yes, a permit | Recreation.gov, 24 weeks ahead, plus a walk-up share
Mariposa Grove | No | Park at the Welcome Plaza and ride the free shuttle; the lot fills by late morning

The permits are their own subject: the wilderness permit guide for overnight trips, the Half Dome guide for the cables, and the camping guide for the 15th-of-the-month release. Every dated window sits on one page at Yosemite dates and deadlines, with calendar files.

### What about 2027?

Nothing has been announced, and nothing is likely to be until winter. The pattern is worth knowing. The 2026 decision came on February 18, after the park analyzed the 2025 season. The park framed it as a finding, that most weekdays had enough parking without a park-wide cap, not as a permanent policy. In place of reservations it uses live traffic monitoring, active parking management in the Valley, and staff at the busy intersections, and it can bring a reservation back if the 2026 numbers say so. If you are planning a 2027 summer trip, book lodging as if a reservation might return (the beds are the scarce thing either way) and check the Park Bulletin in February, which is when the last two announcements came. When the park says anything, this page will change the same day.

Here is the strategy for this year: specific timing, alternatives, and contingencies for when your first plan doesn't work.

### Why this matters more than the news made it sound

In 2023, the year before the reservation system ran at full force, peak days brought multi-hour waits at the entrance stations and full parking lots across the Valley by mid-morning. The reservation system, when it operated in 2024 and 2025, smoothed those peaks. With it gone in 2026, the question is not whether the peaks will return. It's whether they'll pass 2023 levels. They could: more people know about Yosemite now, and demand is higher.

The summer has now run, and the spring predictions held. As of the September park bulletin, Valley day-use parking still fills by late morning on ordinary days, earlier on weekends, and the park's standing advice is the same as this article's: arrive before 8 a.m. or after 4 p.m. The fall shoulder helps, but a Saturday in October is not a quiet day. The Park Bulletin carries the current closures, hours, and trail status in one place; check it the week you travel.

The places that will feel the crowd hardest:

- Yosemite Valley parking. Specifically the day-use lots near Lower Yosemite Falls, the Visitor Center, and the trailheads at Happy Isles and Mirror Lake. Expect these to fill by 8 a.m. on summer weekends, possibly earlier.
- Tunnel View parking. Has always been the first to fill. In 2026, expect it to be full by 7:30 a.m. on weekends in May, June, and July.
- The Glacier Point Road parking lot. Fills early. Expect waits.
- Tioga Road's high-use turnouts (Olmsted Point, Tenaya Lake, Tuolumne Meadows day-use). Fewer people drive Tioga, but the ones who do all stop at the same five places.
- Mariposa Grove shuttle line. The shuttle from the Welcome Plaza to the grove can run a 30-to-60-minute wait at peak.

The places that will feel it less:

- The middle hours of the night. The park stays open. A 4 a.m. arrival is a different park than a 9 a.m. arrival.
- Midweek days outside summer. A Tuesday in late May is going to be quieter than a Saturday in July, by a lot.
- The southern and western corners. Wawona, Mariposa Grove off-peak, and Hetch Hetchy draw far smaller crowds.
- Any place more than a mile off the road. Crowds in Yosemite are crowds at the parking lot. They thin fast with every step away from it.

### The toolkit: three levers you actually have

You can't book your way to a quiet Yosemite in 2026. You have three levers instead.

#### Lever 1: timing

The crowd at any point in Yosemite Valley follows a daily curve that's been the same for fifty years. It builds from about 8 a.m., peaks between 11 a.m. and 3 p.m., and tails off after 5 p.m. By 8 p.m., the Valley is nearly empty.

What this means for you:

- Aim to be inside the park by 6:30 a.m. on any peak day. Earlier if you can. The drive in is faster, the entrance stations are quiet, and you'll be parked at your first stop while everyone else is still in line.
- Text ynptraffic to 333111 before you commit to the drive. The park's live traffic alerts tell you which lots are already gone, which beats finding out from the driver's seat.
- Plan your major stops for before 9 a.m. or after 5 p.m. Tunnel View, Lower Yosemite Falls, Cook's Meadow, and Glacier Point all change character entirely outside the 9-to-5 window.
- Take a deliberate "bad hours" plan. Between 11 a.m. and 3 p.m., do something that doesn't depend on parking or solitude. Eat lunch at a sit-down restaurant. Visit the museum. Walk the river. The crowds thin again later.
- If you can shift your trip to midweek, do it. A Tuesday-Wednesday-Thursday Yosemite trip in 2026 is a different trip from Friday-Saturday-Sunday. The crowd difference is not 10%. It's closer to 50% on the worst days.

#### Lever 2: location

Most of the crowd is in three or four places.

The Valley draws the largest share of visitation. Within the Valley, Lower Yosemite Falls and the Mist Trail trailheads draw the most. Stay away from those two places at peak hours and you've avoided most of the crowd.

The under-visited zones:

- Wawona and Mariposa Grove (the southern entrance area). Mariposa Grove gets busy at the front of the loop, but the Outer Loop trail clears the crowd quickly. Wawona itself, with its meadow and pioneer cemetery, is rarely full.
- Hetch Hetchy. The northwestern entrance leads to a different valley with a reservoir, a dam walk, and trails that see a fraction of Valley traffic. The drive in is long, and few visitors make it.
- Tioga Road outside the headline stops. Pothole Dome, Lembert Dome, the east end of Tenaya Lake, the trail to Glen Aulin. All accessible from Tioga Road but rarely backed up. One 2026 caveat: road work has traffic controls on Tioga Road this season, about ten minutes through Tuolumne Meadows and fifteen from Olmsted Point to Tioga Pass, Monday through Thursday from 8 a.m. to 3:30 p.m., so build that into your timing if Tioga is your crowd-escape route.
- Anywhere a half mile off a major trail. The standard hike to Vernal Fall is often a conga line. The trail past the top of Vernal Fall, continuing to Nevada Fall via the John Muir Trail, drops the crowd by 80%.

Add wildfire smoke to the mix and the under-visited zones become even more valuable: the high country often sits above the inversion layer, the lid of warm air that holds smoke in the Valley. Smoke season planning has the full version.

#### Lever 3: attitude

This is the lever most people don't use, and it matters when the first two fail.

Expect the plan to change. Some days, you will arrive at Tunnel View at 6:30 a.m. and have it to yourself. Some days, you will arrive at Tunnel View at 6:30 a.m. and find a tour bus already there. Some days, the road will be backed up before you even reach the entrance, and your "be in the park by 6:30" plan dies on the way in.

When that happens, swap rather than push. If Tunnel View is full, drive to Valley View instead, which gives you a different angle on the same Valley and is rarely crowded. If Glacier Point parking is full, drive to Sentinel Dome trailhead instead, which gives you a similar view from above at the end of a one-mile hike, and almost always has parking.

The visitors who have a great 2026 trip will be the ones who plan for three options at every major decision point and pick whichever is easiest when they arrive. The visitors who have a bad trip will be the ones who insist on the original plan even when the park is telling them to flex.

### Strategy by trip type

A few patterns by trip length:

#### A single weekend day

This is the hardest mode. You have one day, the park is at peak, and you need everything to line up. For the full single-day sequence, see one or two days in Yosemite. The strategy:

- Sleep in or near the park the night before. El Portal or Mariposa is the strongest base for an early-Saturday start, and El Portal is the better of the two if you can get it. Driving in from the Bay Area on the morning of a peak Saturday is a recipe for arriving at 11 a.m. with no parking. Check what El Portal has on your dates →
- Be inside the gate by 6 a.m. Do Tunnel View, the Cook's Meadow loop, and Lower Yosemite Falls before 9 a.m.
- Eat an early lunch (10:30 to 11 a.m.) at Degnan's or pack from outside.
- Use the midday hours for something that needs no new parking space. The Valley museum, a slow walk on the south-side path along the Merced, the Ansel Adams Gallery.
- Re-emerge for the late afternoon and evening light. Sentinel Bridge at 6 p.m., Tunnel View at sunset.

#### A long weekend (three to four days)

You have flexibility. Use it.

- Arrive a day before your friends or family expect to do anything. Spend the arrival evening at Sentinel Bridge or the meadow.
- Pick one peak day and one off-peak day for your top sights. If you have to do Glacier Point on a Saturday, do it at sunrise. Save the lesser sights for the day you expect the biggest crowds.
- Spend at least one day deliberately outside the Valley. Drive to Tuolumne. Visit Mariposa Grove via the Wawona side rather than the standard shuttle. Hike the southern trails near Wawona.
- Reserve the last morning for whatever surprised you on the trip. The best memories often come from places you never planned to stop.

#### A full week or more

A week gives you the most room to work around the crowds.

- Build a routine where you do the high-traffic Valley sights only at the edges of the day. Sunrise and the hour before dark. Use the middle of every day for trails or zones less affected by crowds.
- Take at least one full day off from "doing things." Float the Merced. Sit in El Capitan Meadow with a book. Watch climbers. The visitors who come for a week and try to do something every minute miss what makes a long Yosemite trip different from a short one.
- Plan one trip up to Tuolumne Meadows or Wawona that's longer than a half-day. Both deserve more time than they usually get.

### When the first plan dies

Swaps for when the first plan isn't working.

Original plan | Substitute when crowded

Tunnel View | Valley View (Gates of the Valley)
Glacier Point | Sentinel Dome or Taft Point
Mist Trail to Vernal Fall | The Panorama Trail from Glacier Point downward
Mirror Lake | The river path from Curry Village to Sentinel Bridge
Lower Yosemite Falls | Bridalveil Fall (less crowded after lunch)
Mariposa Grove | Tuolumne Grove or Merced Grove
Tuolumne Meadows | Lower Lyell Canyon or the meadows around White Wolf

Several of these substitutions (Sentinel Dome, Taft Point, Valley View) are arguably better than the famous stops they replace. Treat them as first choices.

Two rows of that table come with 2026 footnotes. Trail work closes sections of the Mist Trail on weekdays, Monday through Thursday from 7 a.m. to 3:30 p.m., into late October, with a detour via the John Muir Trail. On those days the swap is not optional: hike the Vernal and Nevada corridor Friday through Sunday, or start after the crews knock off (the Mist Trail guide has the details). And White Wolf's lodge, store, and dining room are closed for the 2026 season. The meadows are still worth the stop, but bring everything you need.

### Entrance wait times: check the gate before you drive

The park now publishes live wait estimates for its three western entrances: Arch Rock, Big Oak Flat, and South. The site's conditions board shows them beside the Valley parking-lot counts, updated as the feeds are. On a summer weekend the Arch Rock line is long by mid-morning and nonexistent at 6:30 a.m., and the difference between the two is the whole point of this article. Text ynptraffic to 333111 for the park's own alerts, and check the webcams to see Tunnel View right now. If the gate you planned on is backed up, the swap table above works for entrances too. Big Oak Flat rarely queues the way Arch Rock does. From Mariposa, the standing detour runs Highway 49 north to Coulterville and across to Highway 120: a longer, twistier drive to a gate that is not backed up.

### The takeaway

Yosemite in 2026 rewards visitors who plan for crowds and punishes those who do not.

Be in the park by 6:30 a.m. on any peak day. Have a swap ready for every major sight. Spend at least one full day deliberately outside the Valley. And accept, before you arrive, that the plan will change.

### Common questions

Do I need a reservation to enter Yosemite in 2026? No. There is no day-use, timed-entry, or peak-hours reservation in 2026, on any date. You need a standard entrance pass, $35 per vehicle for seven days.

Do I need a reservation for Yosemite in September or October? No. The fall shoulder is one of the best windows of the year and there is no entrance reservation for it. Camping and in-park lodging still need booking.

Do I need a reservation for the Firefall in February? Not for 2026, when no entrance reservation was required. February 2027 has not been announced. Watch for it in the winter.

Will Yosemite require reservations in 2027? Unknown. The park has said nothing about 2027, and the 2026 decision was based on 2025 data, so a change for 2027 would most likely be announced in the winter, as the last two were.

When does Yosemite Valley fill up? Day-use parking fills by late morning on ordinary days and by 8 a.m. or earlier on summer weekends. The park's standing advice is to arrive before 8 a.m. or after 4 p.m.

What time should I enter Yosemite to beat the crowds? Be inside the park by 6:30 a.m. on any peak day. The drive in is faster, the entrance stations are quiet, and you are parked at your first stop while everyone else is still in line.

How long is the wait at the Yosemite entrance? From nothing at dawn to a long line by mid-morning on a summer weekend, worst at Arch Rock. The park publishes live estimates for the three western gates; they are on the conditions board.

What changed in Yosemite in 2026? Two things. The entrance reservation system was dropped, so the throttle that limited vehicles in 2024 and 2025 is gone. And since January 1, 2026, visitors who are not U.S. residents pay a $100 surcharge per person age 16 and older, or $250 for a nonresident annual pass. Domestic visitors are unaffected.

How do I find parking in Yosemite Valley? Arrive before 8 a.m. for the central lots. Yosemite Village day-use parking is the most useful base; the lot near Yosemite Valley Lodge usually has turnover by mid-morning. Do not circle Curry Village.

Is the Mist Trail open in 2026? Mostly. Repairs close sections of it Monday through Thursday, 7 a.m. to 3:30 p.m., through October 2026, with a detour via the John Muir Trail. Hike the Vernal and Nevada corridor Friday through Sunday, or after the crews finish for the day.

#### The 6:30 a.m. plan is a lodging decision

Everything above depends on being inside the gate before the crowd, and that is decided the night before, by how far from the entrance you are sleeping. El Portal is the closest base on the Highway 140 side, Mariposa is the fallback with more inventory, and in-park beds book through travelyosemite.com a year out. The gap between those two facts is what a search on your own dates is for.

## First time in Yosemite: the guide to read before you book

URL: https://thetalusfieldjournal.com/articles/first-time-yosemite-overwhelm
Section: Planning. Published: 2026-04-25. Last updated: 2026-10-04.
Summary: First time in Yosemite? How many days you need, the best month, where to stay, what to see in what order, and the 2026 fees. From a park naturalist.
